informal_statement:
Definitions:
- Restrict Cols. $M | S$ --- B&M's column restriction (\texttt{Matrix.submatrix}).
- A basis matrix of a submodule $W \le (A \to F)$: its rows are a basis of $W$. Package a basis as the rows of a matrix, so questions about the space
become questions about the matrix.  This is what lets theorem 12.2 phrase acyclicity
as linear independence of \emph{columns}, and theorem 12.4 count spanning trees by a
determinant.

"Rows form a basis" is unfolded into its two halves ---
\texttt{LinearIndependent F M} and \texttt{span (range M) = W} --- rather than using \texttt{Basis}, which
would require a chosen index equivalence.  The row index $n$ is a free \texttt{Fintype},
so the same predicate serves matrices indexed by $T$, by $T^{c}$, or by ${v // v \ne y}$.
- B&M's oriented incidence matrix $M$ (p. 222). Record, for each vertex and each arc, whether the arc leaves the
vertex ($+1$), enters it ($-1$), or misses it ($0$).  The signs make this the
\emph{oriented} incidence matrix, distinct from the $0/1$ matrix of \S{}1.3, and they encode
the conservation condition exactly: $M *_{v} f = 0$ says inflow balances outflow at
every vertex.

\textbf{!} Missing from Mathlib: \texttt{SimpleGraph.incMatrix} is the
\emph{unoriented} $0/1$ matrix, and the oriented version is one of Mathlib's own open
TODOs.  B&M's "if $a$ is a link" clause (i.e. loops map to $0$) is \textbf{automatic} in
this encoding: a loop has \texttt{tail a = head a = v}, so the two indicators cancel to
$1 - 1 = 0$.  Stated over a general \texttt{[Ring R]} so the same definition serves the
$F$-valued \S{}12.1 and the $\mathbb{Z}$-valued \S{}12.2.
- An arc-level cycle in the digraph, as a nonempty closed arc-sequence. A cycle of the \emph{underlying} graph, traversed in one of its two
directions; some arcs point along the direction of travel and some against it,
which is what the sign in $f_C$ records.

\textbf{\textbf{!} Defective: this structure is degenerate.}  It carries only a nonempty list of
arcs, with \textbf{no} closed-walk condition and \textbf{no} distinctness condition --- the
docstring's "the closed/interior-distinct invariants are elided" understates the
cost.  As a result \emph{any} nonempty list of arcs is an \texttt{ArcCycle}, and the derived
predicate collapses:

    IsArcAcyclic tail head S  $\leftrightarrow$  S = $\emptyset$

(for nonempty $S$, pick $a \in S$ and take the one-element list $[a]$).  Downstream,
theorem 12.2(i) then reads \emph{"the columns of $B | S$ are independent iff $S = \emptyset$"} ---
false --- and lemma 12.2.1 becomes trivially true for the wrong reason.  This is not
\texttt{sorry}, which makes it more dangerous: the definition \emph{looks} honest.

\emph{The repair} needs three fields beyond \texttt{arcs} and \texttt{nonempty}:
\item \textbf{closed walk} --- a vertex sequence \texttt{verts : List V} with \texttt{verts.length = arcs.length}
  such that consecutive arcs meet head-to-tail, cyclically: for each $i$,
  \texttt{\{tail arcs[i], head arcs[i]\} = \{verts[i], verts[i+1 mod n]\}} (the set form allows
  an arc to be traversed against its direction, which is exactly what $C^{+}$ records);
\item \textbf{interior distinctness} --- \texttt{verts.Nodup};
\item optionally \textbf{no repeated arc} --- \texttt{arcs.Nodup}.

\textbf{!} \texttt{SimpleGraph.Walk.IsCycle} genuinely cannot serve, as the note says: the chapter's
digraphs admit loops (\texttt{tail a = head a}) and parallel arcs, which a \texttt{SimpleGraph}
cannot express.  But that argues for building the structure properly, not for
omitting its invariants.
- $S \subseteq A$ is acyclic: it contains no arc-cycle. No cycle of the digraph lies entirely inside $S$.  Theorem 12.2 makes
this combinatorial property equivalent to a linear-algebraic one --- the bridge that
turns counting spanning trees into counting nonsingular submatrices.

\textbf{\textbf{!} Defective by inheritance.}  Because \texttt{ArcCycle} has no closure or distinctness
conditions, this predicate collapses to $S = \emptyset$; see \texttt{ArcCycle}'s docstring for the
one-line argument and the repair.  The definition here is *correct given a correct
\texttt{ArcCycle}* --- nothing needs changing at this declaration.
- The bond space $\mathcal{B}$: potential differences, i.e. Assign a voltage to every vertex and read off the drop across every
wire.  Theorem 12.1 identifies $\mathcal{B}$ as the row space of $M$ and $\mathcal{C}$ as its
orthogonal complement --- the duality organising the whole chapter.

$\delta p$ is $M^{T} \emph{_{v} p$, so $\mathcal{B}$ is the }range* of that map.  \textbf{!} Note
the asymmetry with \texttt{cycleSpace}: $\mathcal{C}$ is a \textbf{kernel} and $\mathcal{B}$ a \textbf{range}, which is
why theorem 12.2(ii) is a genuinely separate argument rather than a formal dual of
(i).

Statement: basisMatrix_bondSpace_cols_linearIndependent_iff. *Let $B$ be a basis matrix of $\mathcal{B}$.  Then for any $S \subseteq A$,
the columns of $B | S$ are linearly independent if and only if $S$ is acyclic.*

The theorem converting a combinatorial question into a linear-algebraic
one --- and it holds over \textbf{any} field, which is why exercise 12.1.5 is subsumed by
stating \S{}12.1 over \texttt{[Field F]}.

\textbf{\textbf{!} Currently false.}  With \texttt{ArcCycle} degenerate, \texttt{IsArcAcyclic S $\leftrightarrow$ S = $\emptyset$}, so the
right-hand side says $S = \emptyset$ while the left is true for any independent column set.
Repair \texttt{ArcCycle} first.  Step 4 additionally needs \texttt{cycleCirculation}, also
\texttt{sorry}-bodied.
formal_statement:
import Mathlib

open scoped Matrix
open scoped Classical

namespace CycleSpace
variable {V A : Type*} [Fintype V] [Fintype A] [DecidableEq V] [DecidableEq A]
variable {F : Type*} [Field F]
variable (tail head : A → V)
variable {n : Type*} [Fintype n]
abbrev restrictCols (M : Matrix n A F) (S : Finset A) : Matrix n {a // a ∈ S} F :=
  M.submatrix id Subtype.val
end CycleSpace

namespace CycleSpace
variable {V A : Type*} [Fintype V] [Fintype A] [DecidableEq V] [DecidableEq A]
variable {F : Type*} [Field F]
variable (tail head : A → V)
variable {n : Type*} [Fintype n]
def IsBasisMatrix (M : Matrix n A F) (W : Submodule F (A → F)) : Prop :=
  LinearIndependent F M ∧ Submodule.span F (Set.range M) = W
end CycleSpace

namespace CycleSpace
variable {V A : Type*} [Fintype V] [Fintype A] [DecidableEq V] [DecidableEq A]
variable {F : Type*} [Field F]
variable (tail head : A → V)
variable {n : Type*} [Fintype n]
def orientedIncMatrix (R : Type*) [Ring R] : Matrix V A R :=
  Matrix.of fun v a => (if tail a = v then 1 else 0) - (if head a = v then 1 else 0)
end CycleSpace

namespace CycleSpace
variable {V A : Type*} [Fintype V] [Fintype A] [DecidableEq V] [DecidableEq A]
variable {F : Type*} [Field F]
variable (tail head : A → V)
variable {n : Type*} [Fintype n]
structure ArcCycle (tail head : A → V) where
  arcs : List A
  nonempty : arcs ≠ []
end CycleSpace

namespace CycleSpace
variable {V A : Type*} [Fintype V] [Fintype A] [DecidableEq V] [DecidableEq A]
variable {F : Type*} [Field F]
variable (tail head : A → V)
variable {n : Type*} [Fintype n]
def IsArcAcyclic (tail head : A → V) (S : Finset A) : Prop :=
  ¬ ∃ c : ArcCycle tail head, ∀ a ∈ c.arcs, a ∈ S
end CycleSpace

namespace CycleSpace
variable {V A : Type*} [Fintype V] [Fintype A] [DecidableEq V] [DecidableEq A]
variable {F : Type*} [Field F]
variable (tail head : A → V)
variable {n : Type*} [Fintype n]
def bondSpace : Submodule F (A → F) :=
  LinearMap.range (orientedIncMatrix tail head F)ᵀ.mulVecLin
end CycleSpace

namespace CycleSpace
variable {V A : Type*} [Fintype V] [Fintype A] [DecidableEq V] [DecidableEq A]
variable {F : Type*} [Field F]
variable (tail head : A → V)
variable {n : Type*} [Fintype n]
theorem basisMatrix_bondSpace_cols_linearIndependent_iff
    (S : Finset A) {B : Matrix n A F} (hB : IsBasisMatrix B (bondSpace tail head)) :
    LinearIndependent F (fun a : {a // a ∈ S} => (restrictCols B S)ᵀ a) ↔
      IsArcAcyclic tail head S := sorry
end CycleSpace

on arcs leaving $S$ and $-1$ on those entering it --- the edge cut is undirected, its
potential difference is not.

over arbitrary \texttt{S : Set V}.
- B&M's oriented incidence matrix $M$ (p. 222). Record, for each vertex and each arc, whether the arc leaves the
vertex ($+1$), enters it ($-1$), or misses it ($0$).  The signs make this the

12.2.2 says the support of a nonzero potential difference contains a bond, exactly
as lemma 12.2.1 says the support of a nonzero circulation contains a cycle.

\textbf{!} Missing from Mathlib --- and beware two false friends.
\texttt{Dart.lean} uses "bond" for an unrelated half-edge notion, and the repo's

import Mathlib

open scoped Matrix
open scoped Classical

namespace CycleSpace
variable {V A : Type*} [Fintype V] [Fintype A] [DecidableEq V] [DecidableEq A]
variable {F : Type*} [Field F]
variable (tail head : A → V)
variable {n : Type*} [Fintype n]
abbrev restrictCols (M : Matrix n A F) (S : Finset A) : Matrix n {a // a ∈ S} F :=
  M.submatrix id Subtype.val
end CycleSpace

namespace CycleSpace
variable {V A : Type*} [Fintype V] [Fintype A] [DecidableEq V] [DecidableEq A]
variable {F : Type*} [Field F]
variable (tail head : A → V)
variable {n : Type*} [Fintype n]
def IsBasisMatrix (M : Matrix n A F) (W : Submodule F (A → F)) : Prop :=
  LinearIndependent F M ∧ Submodule.span F (Set.range M) = W
end CycleSpace

namespace CycleSpace
variable {V A : Type*} [Fintype V] [Fintype A] [DecidableEq V] [DecidableEq A]
variable {F : Type*} [Field F]
variable (tail head : A → V)
variable {n : Type*} [Fintype n]
def edgeCutSet (S : Set V) : Set A :=
  {a | (tail a ∈ S ∧ head a ∉ S) ∨ (tail a ∉ S ∧ head a ∈ S)}
end CycleSpace

namespace CycleSpace
variable {V A : Type*} [Fintype V] [Fintype A] [DecidableEq V] [DecidableEq A]
variable {F : Type*} [Field F]
variable (tail head : A → V)
variable {n : Type*} [Fintype n]
def orientedIncMatrix (R : Type*) [Ring R] : Matrix V A R :=
  Matrix.of fun v a => (if tail a = v then 1 else 0) - (if head a = v then 1 else 0)
end CycleSpace

namespace CycleSpace
variable {V A : Type*} [Fintype V] [Fintype A] [DecidableEq V] [DecidableEq A]
variable {F : Type*} [Field F]
variable (tail head : A → V)
variable {n : Type*} [Fintype n]
def IsBond (tail head : A → V) (B : Set A) : Prop :=
  (∃ S : Set V, B = edgeCutSet tail head S) ∧ B.Nonempty ∧
    ∀ B' ⊆ B, B'.Nonempty → (∃ S : Set V, B' = edgeCutSet tail head S) → B' = B
end CycleSpace

namespace CycleSpace
variable {V A : Type*} [Fintype V] [Fintype A] [DecidableEq V] [DecidableEq A]
variable {F : Type*} [Field F]
variable (tail head : A → V)
variable {n : Type*} [Fintype n]
def cycleSpace : Submodule F (A → F) :=
  LinearMap.ker (orientedIncMatrix tail head F).mulVecLin
end CycleSpace

namespace CycleSpace
variable {V A : Type*} [Fintype V] [Fintype A] [DecidableEq V] [DecidableEq A]
variable {F : Type*} [Field F]
variable (tail head : A → V)
variable {n : Type*} [Fintype n]
theorem basisMatrix_cycleSpace_cols_linearIndependent_iff
    (S : Finset A) {C : Matrix n A F} (hC : IsBasisMatrix C (cycleSpace tail head)) :
    LinearIndependent F (fun a : {a // a ∈ S} => (restrictCols C S)ᵀ a) ↔
      ¬ ∃ B, IsBond tail head B ∧ B ⊆ (S : Set A) := sorry
end CycleSpace

open scoped Matrix
open scoped Classical

namespace CycleSpace
variable {V A : Type*} [Fintype V] [Fintype A] [DecidableEq V] [DecidableEq A]
variable {F : Type*} [Field F]
variable (tail head : A → V)
variable {n : Type*} [Fintype n]
def dotForm (K ι : Type*) [Field K] [Fintype ι] :
    LinearMap.BilinForm K (ι → K) :=
  LinearMap.mk₂ K (fun x y => ∑ i, x i * y i)
    (fun _ _ _ => by simp [add_mul, Finset.sum_add_distrib])
    (fun _ _ _ => by simp [Finset.mul_sum, mul_assoc])
    (fun _ _ _ => by simp [mul_add, Finset.sum_add_distrib])
    (fun _ _ _ => by simp [Finset.mul_sum, mul_left_comm])
end CycleSpace

which is what the sign in $f_C$ records.

\textbf{\textbf{!} Defective: this structure is degenerate.}  It carries only a nonempty list of
arcs, with \textbf{no} closed-walk condition and \textbf{no} distinctness condition --- the
docstring's "the closed/interior-distinct invariants are elided" understates the
cost.  As a result \emph{any} nonempty list of arcs is an \texttt{ArcCycle}, and the derived
predicate collapses:

    IsArcAcyclic tail head S  $\leftrightarrow$  S = $\emptyset$

\texttt{sorry}, which makes it more dangerous: the definition \emph{looks} honest.

\item \textbf{closed walk} --- a vertex sequence \texttt{verts : List V} with \texttt{verts.length = arcs.length}
  such that consecutive arcs meet head-to-tail, cyclically: for each $i$,
  \texttt{\{tail arcs[i], head arcs[i]\} = \{verts[i], verts[i+1 mod n]\}} (the set form allows
  an arc to be traversed against its direction, which is exactly what $C^{+}$ records);
\item \textbf{interior distinctness} --- \texttt{verts.Nodup};
\item optionally \textbf{no repeated arc} --- \texttt{arcs.Nodup}.

omitting its invariants.

a loop.

open scoped Matrix
open scoped Classical

namespace CycleSpace

variable {F : Type*} [Field F]
variable (tail head : A → V)
variable {n : Type*} [Fintype n]
structure ArcCycle (tail head : A → V) where
  arcs : List A
  nonempty : arcs ≠ []
end CycleSpace

namespace CycleSpace
variable {V A : Type*} [Fintype V] [Fintype A] [DecidableEq V] [DecidableEq A]

variable {F : Type*} [Field F]
variable (tail head : A → V)
variable {n : Type*} [Fintype n]
theorem exists_arcCycle_subset_support_of_isCirculation {f : A → F}
    (hf : f ∈ cycleSpace tail head) (hne : f ≠ 0) :
    ∃ c : ArcCycle tail head, ∀ a ∈ c.arcs, a ∈ Function.support f := sorry
end CycleSpace

import Mathlib

open scoped Matrix
open scoped Classical

namespace CycleSpace
variable {V A : Type*} [Fintype V] [Fintype A] [DecidableEq V] [DecidableEq A]
variable {F : Type*} [Field F]
variable (tail head : A → V)
variable {n : Type*} [Fintype n]
def edgeCutSet (S : Set V) : Set A :=
  {a | (tail a ∈ S ∧ head a ∉ S) ∨ (tail a ∉ S ∧ head a ∈ S)}
end CycleSpace

namespace CycleSpace
variable {V A : Type*} [Fintype V] [Fintype A] [DecidableEq V] [DecidableEq A]
variable {F : Type*} [Field F]
variable (tail head : A → V)
variable {n : Type*} [Fintype n]
def orientedIncMatrix (R : Type*) [Ring R] : Matrix V A R :=
  Matrix.of fun v a => (if tail a = v then 1 else 0) - (if head a = v then 1 else 0)
end CycleSpace

namespace CycleSpace
variable {V A : Type*} [Fintype V] [Fintype A] [DecidableEq V] [DecidableEq A]
variable {F : Type*} [Field F]
variable (tail head : A → V)
variable {n : Type*} [Fintype n]
def IsBond (tail head : A → V) (B : Set A) : Prop :=
  (∃ S : Set V, B = edgeCutSet tail head S) ∧ B.Nonempty ∧
    ∀ B' ⊆ B, B'.Nonempty → (∃ S : Set V, B' = edgeCutSet tail head S) → B' = B
end CycleSpace

namespace CycleSpace
variable {V A : Type*} [Fintype V] [Fintype A] [DecidableEq V] [DecidableEq A]
variable {F : Type*} [Field F]
variable (tail head : A → V)
variable {n : Type*} [Fintype n]
def bondSpace : Submodule F (A → F) :=
  LinearMap.range (orientedIncMatrix tail head F)ᵀ.mulVecLin
end CycleSpace

namespace CycleSpace
variable {V A : Type*} [Fintype V] [Fintype A] [DecidableEq V] [DecidableEq A]
variable {F : Type*} [Field F]
variable (tail head : A → V)
variable {n : Type*} [Fintype n]
theorem exists_isBond_subset_support_of_mem_bondSpace {g : A → F}
    (hg : g ∈ bondSpace tail head) (hne : g ≠ 0) :
    ∃ B, IsBond tail head B ∧ B ⊆ Function.support g := sorry
end CycleSpace

import Mathlib

open scoped Matrix
open scoped Classical

namespace CycleSpace
variable {V A : Type*} [Fintype V] [Fintype A] [DecidableEq V] [DecidableEq A]
variable {F : Type*} [Field F]
variable (tail head : A → V)
variable {n : Type*} [Fintype n]
def IsSpanningTree (tail head : A → V) (T : Finset A) : Prop := sorry
end CycleSpace

namespace CycleSpace
variable {V A : Type*} [Fintype V] [Fintype A] [DecidableEq V] [DecidableEq A]
variable {F : Type*} [Field F]
variable (tail head : A → V)
variable {n : Type*} [Fintype n]
def orientedIncMatrix (R : Type*) [Ring R] : Matrix V A R :=
  Matrix.of fun v a => (if tail a = v then 1 else 0) - (if head a = v then 1 else 0)
end CycleSpace

namespace CycleSpace
variable {V A : Type*} [Fintype V] [Fintype A] [DecidableEq V] [DecidableEq A]
variable {F : Type*} [Field F]
variable (tail head : A → V)
variable {n : Type*} [Fintype n]
def bondSpace : Submodule F (A → F) :=
  LinearMap.range (orientedIncMatrix tail head F)ᵀ.mulVecLin
end CycleSpace

namespace CycleSpace
variable {V A : Type*} [Fintype V] [Fintype A] [DecidableEq V] [DecidableEq A]
variable {F : Type*} [Field F]
variable (tail head : A → V)
variable {n : Type*} [Fintype n]
def cycleSpace : Submodule F (A → F) :=
  LinearMap.ker (orientedIncMatrix tail head F).mulVecLin
end CycleSpace

namespace CycleSpace
variable {V A : Type*} [Fintype V] [Fintype A] [DecidableEq V] [DecidableEq A]
variable {F : Type*} [Field F]
variable (tail head : A → V)
variable {n : Type*} [Fintype n]
noncomputable def tau (tail head : A → V) : ℕ :=
  ((Finset.univ : Finset (Finset A)).filter (IsSpanningTree tail head)).card
end CycleSpace

namespace CycleSpace
variable {V A : Type*} [Fintype V] [Fintype A] [DecidableEq V] [DecidableEq A]
variable {F : Type*} [Field F]
variable (tail head : A → V)
variable {n : Type*} [Fintype n]
theorem finrank_inf_pos_iff_dvd_tau {p : ℕ} [Fact p.Prime] [CharP F p] :
    0 < Module.finrank F
        ((bondSpace tail head (F := F)) ⊓ (cycleSpace tail head (F := F)) :
          Submodule F (A → F)) ↔

end CycleSpace

definitions.title: A spanning tree of the digraph
definitions.informal:
A maximal acyclic set of arcs touching every vertex.  By theorem 12.2,
spanning trees are exactly the $(\nu-1)$-element subsets $S$ for which $B | S$ is
nonsingular --- which is what makes \S{}12.2's determinant formula count them.

\textbf{\textbf{!} Defective: \texttt{sorry} body --- the most damaging one in the file.}  \texttt{tau} counts the
\texttt{Finset}s satisfying this predicate, so \textbf{$\tau(G)$ is an opaque natural number}, and
every \S{}12.2 statement about it is vacuous: theorem 12.4, (12.8), corollary 12.4, the
matrix-tree theorem, and exercises 12.2.1(b), 12.2.2(b), 12.2.4(a), (b).

\emph{The repair}, once \texttt{ArcCycle} is fixed:

    IsSpanningTree tail head T := IsArcAcyclic tail head T $\land$ T.card + 1 = Fintype.card V
                                  $\land$ (the underlying subgraph on T is connected)

or equivalently "acyclic and spanning", using the connectivity notion suggested for
\texttt{IsConnectedDigraph}.  Acyclic plus $|T| = \nu - 1$ already forces connectivity for a
graph on $\nu$ vertices, so the middle clause plus acyclicity suffices --- but only once
\texttt{IsArcAcyclic} is genuine.

definitions.informal:

vertex ($+1$), enters it ($-1$), or misses it ($0$).  The signs make this the

every vertex.

\emph{unoriented} $0/1$ matrix, and the oriented version is one of Mathlib's own open

$F$-valued \S{}12.1 and the $\mathbb{Z}$-valued \S{}12.2.

open scoped Classical

namespace CycleSpace

  LinearIndependent F M ∧ Submodule.span F (Set.range M) = W

vertex ($+1$), enters it ($-1$), or misses it ($0$).  The signs make this the

\item \textbf{closed walk} --- a vertex sequence \texttt{verts : List V} with \texttt{verts.length = arcs.length}

cannot express.  But that argues for building the structure properly, not for
omitting its invariants.

vertices exactly once.  These are the elementary circulations from which all others

vertices; here it holds \textbf{everywhere}, so there is no net source or sink.

import Mathlib

open scoped Matrix
open scoped Classical

namespace CycleSpace
variable {V A : Type*} [Fintype V] [Fintype A] [DecidableEq V] [DecidableEq A]
variable {F : Type*} [Field F]
variable (tail head : A → V)
variable {n : Type*} [Fintype n]
def IsBasisMatrix (M : Matrix n A F) (W : Submodule F (A → F)) : Prop :=
  LinearIndependent F M ∧ Submodule.span F (Set.range M) = W
end CycleSpace

namespace CycleSpace
variable {V A : Type*} [Fintype V] [Fintype A] [DecidableEq V] [DecidableEq A]
variable {F : Type*} [Field F]
variable (tail head : A → V)
variable {n : Type*} [Fintype n]
def IsMaximalForest (tail head : A → V) (T : Finset A) : Prop := sorry
end CycleSpace

namespace CycleSpace
variable {V A : Type*} [Fintype V] [Fintype A] [DecidableEq V] [DecidableEq A]
variable {F : Type*} [Field F]
variable (tail head : A → V)
variable {n : Type*} [Fintype n]
def orientedIncMatrix (R : Type*) [Ring R] : Matrix V A R :=
  Matrix.of fun v a => (if tail a = v then 1 else 0) - (if head a = v then 1 else 0)
end CycleSpace

namespace CycleSpace
variable {V A : Type*} [Fintype V] [Fintype A] [DecidableEq V] [DecidableEq A]
variable {F : Type*} [Field F]
variable (tail head : A → V)
variable {n : Type*} [Fintype n]
structure ArcCycle (tail head : A → V) where
  arcs : List A
  nonempty : arcs ≠ []
end CycleSpace

namespace CycleSpace
variable {V A : Type*} [Fintype V] [Fintype A] [DecidableEq V] [DecidableEq A]
variable {F : Type*} [Field F]
variable (tail head : A → V)
variable {n : Type*} [Fintype n]
def cycleCirculation (tail head : A → V) (c : ArcCycle tail head) : A → F := sorry
end CycleSpace

namespace CycleSpace
variable {V A : Type*} [Fintype V] [Fintype A] [DecidableEq V] [DecidableEq A]
variable {F : Type*} [Field F]
variable (tail head : A → V)
variable {n : Type*} [Fintype n]
def cycleSpace : Submodule F (A → F) :=
  LinearMap.ker (orientedIncMatrix tail head F).mulVecLin
end CycleSpace

namespace CycleSpace
variable {V A : Type*} [Fintype V] [Fintype A] [DecidableEq V] [DecidableEq A]
variable {F : Type*} [Field F]
variable (tail head : A → V)
variable {n : Type*} [Fintype n]
def fundamentalCycle (tail head : A → V) (T : Finset A) (hT : IsMaximalForest tail head T)
    {a : A} (ha : a ∉ T) : ArcCycle tail head := sorry
end CycleSpace

namespace CycleSpace
variable {V A : Type*} [Fintype V] [Fintype A] [DecidableEq V] [DecidableEq A]
variable {F : Type*} [Field F]
variable (tail head : A → V)
variable {n : Type*} [Fintype n]
theorem isBasisMatrix_cycleSpace_of_maximalForest
    (T : Finset A) (hT : IsMaximalForest tail head T) :
    IsBasisMatrix
      (fun a : {a // a ∉ T} => cycleCirculation tail head (fundamentalCycle tail head T hT a.2))
      (cycleSpace tail head (F := F)) := sorry
end CycleSpace

informal_statement:
Definitions:
- $B$ is the tree-$T$ basis matrix of the bond space (rows indexed by $T$). Its defining feature is that $B | T$ is an identity matrix --- the
fundamental bond of $a$ contains $a$ itself with coefficient $1$ and no other tree
arc.  That is what pins down \texttt{det(B | T) = 1} in the proof of theorem 12.3, and
what makes exercise 12.1.2(b)'s change-of-basis identity readable.

\textbf{\textbf{!} Defective: \texttt{sorry} body.}  This predicate is a hypothesis of theorems 12.3,
12.4, corollary 12.4 and exercises 12.2.1(b), 12.2.3(a), 12.2.4(a) --- all of which
therefore constrain nothing.

\emph{The repair:} $B$ is the tree-$T$ basis matrix when its rows are the fundamental-bond
potential differences, i.e.

    B = fun a : {a // a $\in$ T} => bondPotentialDiff tail head (fundamentalBondVertexSet tail head T a.1)

--- exactly the matrix appearing in \texttt{isBasisMatrix\_bondSpace\_of\_maximalForest}.  \textbf{!}
Alternatively, characterise it axiomatically as *"a basis matrix of $\mathcal{B}$ whose
restriction $B | T$ is the identity"*, which is weaker to state, enough for theorem
12.3, and does not depend on \texttt{fundamentalBondVertexSet} --- probably the better
choice, since it is the property every proof actually uses.
- A spanning tree of the digraph. A maximal acyclic set of arcs touching every vertex.  By theorem 12.2,
spanning trees are exactly the $(\nu-1)$-element subsets $S$ for which $B | S$ is
nonsingular --- which is what makes \S{}12.2's determinant formula count them.

\textbf{\textbf{!} Defective: \texttt{sorry} body --- the most damaging one in the file.}  \texttt{tau} counts the
\texttt{Finset}s satisfying this predicate, so \textbf{$\tau(G)$ is an opaque natural number}, and
every \S{}12.2 statement about it is vacuous: theorem 12.4, (12.8), corollary 12.4, the
matrix-tree theorem, and exercises 12.2.1(b), 12.2.2(b), 12.2.4(a), (b).

\emph{The repair}, once \texttt{ArcCycle} is fixed:

    IsSpanningTree tail head T := IsArcAcyclic tail head T $\land$ T.card + 1 = Fintype.card V
                                  $\land$ (the underlying subgraph on T is connected)

or equivalently "acyclic and spanning", using the connectivity notion suggested for
\texttt{IsConnectedDigraph}.  Acyclic plus $|T| = \nu - 1$ already forces connectivity for a
graph on $\nu$ vertices, so the middle clause plus acyclicity suffices --- but only once
\texttt{IsArcAcyclic} is genuine.
- B&M's unimodular (Thm 12.3, p. 226): every \emph{full} square submatrix (order $\nu- 1$, selected by an\dots. "Full" means as large as the matrix allows --- for a $(\nu-1) \times \varepsilon$ basis
matrix of the bond space, the square submatrices of order $\nu - 1$.  Theorem 12.3
says such a basis matrix is unimodular, and that is exactly what makes theorem
12.4's determinant count the spanning trees: each nonsingular full submatrix
contributes $(\pm 1)^{2} = 1$.

\textbf{!} \textbf{Not} \texttt{Matrix.IsTotallyUnimodular}, which quantifies over
\emph{all} square submatrices --- that is B&M's strictly stronger \emph{totally} unimodular of
exercise 12.2.3, stated separately below.  "Full square submatrix" is rendered as
\texttt{M.submatrix id g} for an injective $g : n \to m$: all rows, and \texttt{card n} columns
chosen injectively.  Placed in the \texttt{Matrix} namespace so it reads
\texttt{B.IsUnimodular}.

Statement: isUnimodular_basisMatrix_bondSpace. (proof due to Tutte, 1965b).  *The basis matrix $B$ is
unimodular.*

Exactly what theorem 12.4 needs: every full submatrix contributes $0$
or a determinant of absolute value $1$, so squaring and summing counts the spanning
trees.  The proof is due to Tutte (1965b).

\textbf{\textbf{!} Currently vacuous} --- \texttt{IsSpanningTree} and \texttt{IsBasisMatrixOfTree} both have
\texttt{sorry} bodies.  Note step 4 is where the \emph{axiomatic} reading of
\texttt{IsBasisMatrixOfTree} (\emph{"basis matrix with $B | T$ the identity"}) would pay off
directly.

import Mathlib

open scoped Matrix
open scoped Classical

namespace CycleSpace
variable {V A : Type*} [Fintype V] [Fintype A] [DecidableEq V] [DecidableEq A]
variable {F : Type*} [Field F]
variable (tail head : A → V)
variable {n : Type*} [Fintype n]
def IsBasisMatrixOfTree (tail head : A → V) (T : Finset A) {R : Type*} [CommRing R]
    (B : Matrix {a // a ∈ T} A R) : Prop := sorry
end CycleSpace

namespace CycleSpace
variable {V A : Type*} [Fintype V] [Fintype A] [DecidableEq V] [DecidableEq A]
variable {F : Type*} [Field F]
variable (tail head : A → V)
variable {n : Type*} [Fintype n]
def IsSpanningTree (tail head : A → V) (T : Finset A) : Prop := sorry
end CycleSpace

namespace Matrix
def IsUnimodular {n m : Type*} [Fintype n] [DecidableEq n] [Fintype m] [DecidableEq m]
    (M : Matrix n m ℤ) : Prop :=
  ∀ g : n → m, Function.Injective g → (M.submatrix id g).det ∈ ({0, 1, -1} : Set ℤ)
end Matrix

namespace CycleSpace
variable {V A : Type*} [Fintype V] [Fintype A] [DecidableEq V] [DecidableEq A]
variable {F : Type*} [Field F]
variable (tail head : A → V)
variable {n : Type*} [Fintype n]
theorem isUnimodular_basisMatrix_bondSpace
    (T : Finset A) (hT : IsSpanningTree tail head T)
    {B : Matrix {a // a ∈ T} A ℤ} (hB : IsBasisMatrixOfTree tail head T B) :
    B.IsUnimodular := sorry
end CycleSpace

open scoped Classical

namespace Matrix

namespace CycleSpace
variable {V A : Type*} [Fintype V] [Fintype A] [DecidableEq V] [DecidableEq A]

variable (tail head : A → V)

      (fun v : {v // v ≠ y} => (v : V)) id).IsUnimodular := sorry
end CycleSpace

informal_statement:
Definitions:
- $G$ is the underlying (simple) graph of the digraph \texttt{(tail, head)}. $u$ and $v$ are adjacent in $G$ exactly when some arc runs between them
in one direction or the other.  The chapter's counting results --- \texttt{dim $\mathcal{B}$ = $\nu$ - $\omega$},
\texttt{dim $\mathcal{C}$ = $\varepsilon$ - $\nu$ + $\omega$}, $\tau(G)$ --- are all statements about this underlying graph, the
orientation being an auxiliary device that cancels out.

\textbf{!} A \texttt{SimpleGraph} underlying graph loses information the arc
carrier has: loops (\texttt{tail a = head a}) and parallel arcs both vanish.  That is
harmless for the \emph{counting} results, which are about $G$, but means $G$ does not
determine \texttt{(tail, head)} --- hence this is a relation, not a function.
- B&M's oriented incidence matrix $M$ (p. 222). Record, for each vertex and each arc, whether the arc leaves the
vertex ($+1$), enters it ($-1$), or misses it ($0$).  The signs make this the

the conservation condition exactly: $M *_{v} f = 0$ says inflow balances outflow at
every vertex.

\emph{unoriented} $0/1$ matrix, and the oriented version is one of Mathlib's own open
TODOs.  B&M's "if $a$ is a link" clause (i.e. loops map to $0$) is \textbf{automatic} in

$1 - 1 = 0$.  Stated over a general \texttt{[Ring R]} so the same definition serves the
$F$-valued \S{}12.1 and the $\mathbb{Z}$-valued \S{}12.2.
- \texttt{(tail, head)} is an orientation of the simple graph $G$. $G$ is recovered by forgetting directions.  The point of \S{}12.2 is that
$\tau(G)$ is an invariant of $G$ alone, yet is most easily computed through the
\emph{oriented} incidence matrix of an arbitrarily chosen orientation --- the signs cancel
in the determinant, which is exactly what exercise 12.2.2(a) makes precise.

\textbf{!} Definitionally equal to \texttt{IsUnderlyingGraph}, so "orientation
of $G$" here means only "has $G$ as underlying graph" --- it does \textbf{not} forbid $D$
from having both $(u,v)$ and $(v,u)$, which chapter 10's \texttt{IsOrientationOf} does.

import Mathlib

open scoped Matrix
open scoped Classical

namespace CycleSpace
variable {V A : Type*} [Fintype V] [Fintype A] [DecidableEq V] [DecidableEq A]
variable {F : Type*} [Field F]
variable (tail head : A → V)
variable {n : Type*} [Fintype n]
def IsUnderlyingGraph (G : SimpleGraph V) : Prop :=
  ∀ u v : V, G.Adj u v ↔ (∃ a : A, (tail a = u ∧ head a = v) ∨ (tail a = v ∧ head a = u))
end CycleSpace

variable {V A : Type*} [Fintype V] [Fintype A] [DecidableEq V] [DecidableEq A]
variable {F : Type*} [Field F]

namespace CycleSpace
variable {V A : Type*} [Fintype V] [Fintype A] [DecidableEq V] [DecidableEq A]
variable {F : Type*} [Field F]
variable (tail head : A → V)
variable {n : Type*} [Fintype n]
def IsOrientationOf (G : SimpleGraph V) : Prop := IsUnderlyingGraph tail head G
end CycleSpace

namespace CycleSpace
variable {V A : Type*} [Fintype V] [Fintype A] [DecidableEq V] [DecidableEq A]
variable {F : Type*} [Field F]
variable (tail head : A → V)
variable {n : Type*} [Fintype n]
theorem lapMatrix_eq_orientedIncMatrix_mul_transpose
    (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj] (hor : IsOrientationOf tail head G) :
    G.lapMatrix ℤ = orientedIncMatrix tail head ℤ * (orientedIncMatrix tail head ℤ)ᵀ := sorry
end CycleSpace

import Mathlib

open scoped Matrix
open scoped Classical

namespace CycleSpace
variable {V A : Type*} [Fintype V] [Fintype A] [DecidableEq V] [DecidableEq A]
variable {F : Type*} [Field F]
variable (tail head : A → V)
variable {n : Type*} [Fintype n]
def IsSpanningTree (tail head : A → V) (T : Finset A) : Prop := sorry
end CycleSpace

namespace CycleSpace
variable {V A : Type*} [Fintype V] [Fintype A] [DecidableEq V] [DecidableEq A]
variable {F : Type*} [Field F]
variable (tail head : A → V)
variable {n : Type*} [Fintype n]
def orientedIncMatrix (R : Type*) [Ring R] : Matrix V A R :=
  Matrix.of fun v a => (if tail a = v then 1 else 0) - (if head a = v then 1 else 0)
end CycleSpace

namespace CycleSpace
variable {V A : Type*} [Fintype V] [Fintype A] [DecidableEq V] [DecidableEq A]
variable {F : Type*} [Field F]
variable (tail head : A → V)
variable {n : Type*} [Fintype n]

  ((Finset.univ : Finset (Finset A)).filter (IsSpanningTree tail head)).card
end CycleSpace

namespace CycleSpace
variable {V A : Type*} [Fintype V] [Fintype A] [DecidableEq V] [DecidableEq A]
variable {F : Type*} [Field F]
variable (tail head : A → V)
variable {n : Type*} [Fintype n]
theorem matrix_tree_theorem (hconn : IsConnectedDigraph tail head) (y : V) :
    (tau tail head : ℤ) =

end CycleSpace

definitions.informal:
Record, for each vertex and each arc, whether the arc leaves the

every vertex.

general form is the one usually cited, because it is what licenses deleting \emph{any} row

row and column index types are the \emph{different} subtypes ${v // v \ne i}$ and

the two is therefore threaded through explicitly --- the same device
\texttt{tau\_eq\_det\_fromBlocks\_K} uses further down this file for the same reason.  Because $e$
is not canonical it fixes the column order only up to a permutation, so the conclusion
is stated up to sign, absorbing $(-1)^(i+j)$ and \texttt{sign e} together.  Taking $i = j$ and
\texttt{e = Equiv.refl} recovers the principal case above.

def IsUnderlyingGraph (G : SimpleGraph V) : Prop :=

    (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj] (hor : IsOrientationOf tail head G) (i j : V)

title: tau_eq_lapMatrix_cofactor
statement_informal:
tau_eq_lapMatrix_cofactor. , full form.  *All cofactors of the conductance matrix $C$
are equal to $\tau(G)$.*

\texttt{tau\_eq\_det\_lapMatrix\_deleteRowCol} above states only the
principal $(y,y)$-minor.  The triage (\texttt{log/graphtheory-EXERCISE\_TRIAGE.md} \S{}A.11)
recorded this as a fidelity gap and recommended stating the exercise as written.  The
general form is the one usually cited, because it is what licenses deleting \emph{any} row
and \emph{any} column --- the principal case alone does not.

\textbf{!} Deleting row $i$ and column $j$ for $i \ne j$ leaves a matrix whose
row and column index types are the \emph{different} subtypes ${v // v \ne i}$ and
${v // v \ne j}$, so \texttt{Matrix.det} does not apply to it.  A reindexing equiv $e$ between
the two is therefore threaded through explicitly --- the same device
\texttt{tau\_eq\_det\_fromBlocks\_K} uses further down this file for the same reason.  Because $e$
is not canonical it fixes the column order only up to a permutation, so the conclusion
is stated up to sign, absorbing $(-1)^(i+j)$ and \texttt{sign e} together.  Taking $i = j$ and
\texttt{e = Equiv.refl} recovers the principal case above.

\textbf{!} Currently vacuous via \texttt{tau} and \texttt{IsConnectedDigraph}, exactly as the principal case
is.

definitions.title: A spanning tree of the digraph
definitions.informal:
A maximal acyclic set of arcs touching every vertex.  By theorem 12.2,
spanning trees are exactly the $(\nu-1)$-element subsets $S$ for which $B | S$ is
nonsingular --- which is what makes \S{}12.2's determinant formula count them.

\textbf{\textbf{!} Defective: \texttt{sorry} body --- the most damaging one in the file.}  \texttt{tau} counts the
\texttt{Finset}s satisfying this predicate, so \textbf{$\tau(G)$ is an opaque natural number}, and
every \S{}12.2 statement about it is vacuous: theorem 12.4, (12.8), corollary 12.4, the
matrix-tree theorem, and exercises 12.2.1(b), 12.2.2(b), 12.2.4(a), (b).

\emph{The repair}, once \texttt{ArcCycle} is fixed:

    IsSpanningTree tail head T := IsArcAcyclic tail head T $\land$ T.card + 1 = Fintype.card V
                                  $\land$ (the underlying subgraph on T is connected)

or equivalently "acyclic and spanning", using the connectivity notion suggested for
\texttt{IsConnectedDigraph}.  Acyclic plus $|T| = \nu - 1$ already forces connectivity for a
graph on $\nu$ vertices, so the middle clause plus acyclicity suffices --- but only once
\texttt{IsArcAcyclic} is genuine.

definitions.title: $G$ is the underlying (simple) graph of the digraph \texttt{(tail, head)}
definitions.informal:
$u$ and $v$ are adjacent in $G$ exactly when some arc runs between them
in one direction or the other.  The chapter's counting results --- \texttt{dim $\mathcal{B}$ = $\nu$ - $\omega$},
\texttt{dim $\mathcal{C}$ = $\varepsilon$ - $\nu$ + $\omega$}, $\tau(G)$ --- are all statements about this underlying graph, the
orientation being an auxiliary device that cancels out.

\textbf{!} A \texttt{SimpleGraph} underlying graph loses information the arc
carrier has: loops (\texttt{tail a = head a}) and parallel arcs both vanish.  That is
harmless for the \emph{counting} results, which are about $G$, but means $G$ does not
determine \texttt{(tail, head)} --- hence this is a relation, not a function.

definitions.title: \texttt{(tail, head)} is an orientation of the simple graph $G$
definitions.informal:
$G$ is recovered by forgetting directions.  The point of \S{}12.2 is that
$\tau(G)$ is an invariant of $G$ alone, yet is most easily computed through the
\emph{oriented} incidence matrix of an arbitrarily chosen orientation --- the signs cancel
in the determinant, which is exactly what exercise 12.2.2(a) makes precise.

\textbf{!} Definitionally equal to \texttt{IsUnderlyingGraph}, so "orientation
of $G$" here means only "has $G$ as underlying graph" --- it does \textbf{not} forbid $D$
from having both $(u,v)$ and $(v,u)$, which chapter 10's \texttt{IsOrientationOf} does.
For this chapter that is deliberate and harmless: the results are about $M$ and
\texttt{MM$^{T}$}, which tolerate digons and loops.

definitions.title: $\tau(G)$: the number of spanning trees
definitions.informal:
The object \S{}12.2 exists to compute.  Theorem 2.8 gave a recursion and
theorem 2.9 a closed formula for complete graphs; chapter 12 finally delivers the
general determinant formula --- the \textbf{matrix-tree theorem}, implicit in Kirchhoff
(1847).

\textbf{\textbf{!} Defective by inheritance.}  \texttt{IsSpanningTree} has a \texttt{sorry} body, so \texttt{tau} counts
an opaque predicate and is itself opaque.  \textbf{This is the single most consequential
defect in the file} --- every \S{}12.2 result is a statement about \texttt{tau}.  Nothing here
needs changing; repairing \texttt{IsSpanningTree} repairs this.

Definitions:
- Local minimal \texttt{vertexConnectivity $\kappa$(G)} (repo has the real one). Corollary 11.7 relates it to internally-disjoint paths: $G$ with
$\nu \ge k + 1$ is $k$-connected exactly when any two distinct vertices are joined by
$k$ internally-disjoint paths.  This is the form of Menger's theorem \S{}3.2 announced
without proof.

A minimal local copy, as for \texttt{edgeConnectivity}.  The $\nu - 1$
branch is the book's convention for graphs with no vertex cut (complete graphs).
\textbf{!} Both \texttt{sInf} conventions bite at the boundaries --- see the outline.

Statement: dirac_k_vertices_on_cycle. High connectivity forces any prescribed set of $k$ vertices onto a
single cycle.  For $k = 2$ this is corollary 3.2.1 --- in a 2-connected graph any two
vertices lie on a common cycle.  One of the classic applications of Menger's
theorem, illustrating B&M's remark that *many results on graphs turn out to be easy
consequences* of max-flow min-cut.

Depends on exercise 11.4.3, hence on two \texttt{sorry}-bodied
definitions; but note the \emph{statement} here mentions none of them --- it is about
\texttt{Walk}/\texttt{IsCycle} only, so it is well-formed and would be meaningful once its
dependency is repaired.  Among the \S{}11.4 items, this is the one whose statement is
already honest.
formal_statement:
import Mathlib

open scoped Classical

namespace Networks
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V]
noncomputable def vertexConnectivity (G : SimpleGraph V) : ℕ :=
  if ∃ S : Finset V, (↑S : Set V) ⊂ Set.univ ∧ ¬ (G.induce ((↑S : Set V)ᶜ)).Connected then
    sInf {n : ℕ | ∃ S : Finset V,
      ((↑S : Set V) ⊂ Set.univ ∧ ¬ (G.induce ((↑S : Set V)ᶜ)).Connected) ∧ S.card = n}
  else
    Fintype.card V - 1
end Networks

namespace Networks
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V]
theorem dirac_k_vertices_on_cycle (G : SimpleGraph V) (k : ℕ) (hk : 2 ≤ k)
    (hconn : k ≤ vertexConnectivity G) (T : Finset V) (hT : T.card = k) :
    ∃ (w : V) (c : G.Walk w w), c.IsCycle ∧ ∀ v ∈ T, v ∈ c.support := sorry
end Networks

informal_statement:
Definitions:
- A network $N = (D, X, Y, c)$. A transportation network: goods are produced at the sources, consumed
at the sinks, and shipped along the arcs, each with a maximum throughput.

\textbf{!} Missing from Mathlib (0 hits for flow/network/capacity).
Capacity is carried as a \emph{function} \texttt{cap : V $\to$ V $\to$ $\mathbb{N}$}, with \texttt{cap u v = 0} encoding
"no arc $u \to v$"; this makes $f^{+}$/$f^{-}$ plain \texttt{Finset.sum}s.  \textbf{!} It cannot represent
\textbf{parallel arcs}, which is a real restriction --- lemma 11.4 is about a network in
which every arc has unit capacity, and B&M's digraphs may have several arcs between
the same pair.

The structure carries \textbf{both} $X$, $Y$ (the source/sink \emph{sets} of \S{}11.1) and the
distinguished $x$, $y$ used from \S{}11.2 onward.  That is because the book reduces
the first to the second: *adjoin two new vertices $x$ and $y$; join $x$ to each
vertex in $X$ by an arc of capacity $\infty$; join each vertex in $Y$ to $y$ by an arc
of capacity $\infty$; designate $x$ as the source and $y$ as the sink of $N'$* --- after
which *throughout the next three sections, we shall confine our attention to
networks that have a single source $x$ and a single sink $y$*.  That reduction is
exercise 11.1.4, which is deferred here (it needs an $\mathbb{N}\infty$-capacity parallel
carrier), so the two are simply both recorded in the structure.

\textbf{\textbf{!} Structural defect: $x$, $y$ are unrelated to $X$, $Y$.}  Nothing in the
structure requires \texttt{N.x $\in$ N.X}, let alone \texttt{N.X = \{N.x\}}.  But \texttt{val} is defined over
the \emph{set} $X$ while every \S{}11.2--\S{}11.3 result is about cuts separating the single
$x$ from the single $y$.  The two therefore measure different things, and \textbf{lemma
11.1, theorem 11.1 in both forms, corollary 11.1 and theorem 11.3 are all false as
stated}.

\emph{Counterexample} (one network refutes all of them).  $V = {x_{1}, x_{2}, y_{1}}$,
$X = {x_{1}, x_{2}}$, $Y = {y_{1}}$, \texttt{N.x = x$_{1}$}, \texttt{N.y = y$_{1}$}; capacities $c(x_{1},y_{1}) = c(x_{2},y_{1}) = 1$
and $0$ elsewhere.  Then $I = \emptyset$, so any $f$ within capacity is a flow; take
$f(x_{1},y_{1}) = f(x_{2},y_{1}) = 1$.
\item \texttt{val f = f$^{+}$(X) - f$^{-}$(X) = 2}.
\item $S = {x_{1}}$ is a cut ($x_{1} \in S$, $y_{1} \notin S$), with $f^{+}(S) - f^{-}(S) = 1$ and
  \texttt{cap S = 1}.
\item So lemma 11.1 asserts $2 = 1$; theorem 11.1 asserts $2 \le 1$.
\item Max flow value is $2$, minimum cut capacity is $1$, so theorem 11.3 asserts
  $2 = 1$.
\item Corollary 11.1 fails too: $f'(x_{1},y_{1}) = 1$, $f'(x_{2},y_{1}) = 0$ has
  \texttt{val f' = 1 = cap\{x$_{1}$\}}, yet $f'$ is not a maximum flow.

\emph{The repair} is to add the fields \texttt{hx : N.X = \{N.x\}} and \texttt{hy : N.Y = \{N.y\}} to the
structure (the book's standing convention for \S{}\S{}11.2--11.4), or equivalently to add
them as hypotheses on the affected theorems.  The \S{}11.1 results --- exercises 11.1.2
and 11.1.3 --- are unaffected and should keep the general $X$, $Y$.
- Intermediate vertices $I = V \ (X \cup Y)$. The transit points of the network, which neither produce nor consume.
The conservation condition (11.2) applies exactly here --- what flows in must flow
out --- and that is what makes \texttt{val f} well defined (exercise 11.1.3).

\texttt{Finset.univ \textbackslash\{\} (X $\cup$ Y)}, so $I$ is a \texttt{Finset} and membership is
decidable --- needed by \texttt{IsFlow}'s second clause.
- A cut $(S, \bar{S})$ with $x \in S$, $y \notin S$. A way of severing the network so the source is on one side and the
sink on the other.  Every unit of flow must cross every cut, which is why cuts
bound flows from above (theorem 11.1) --- and, more surprisingly, why the best cut
exactly matches the best flow (theorem 11.3).

\textbf{!} Missing from Mathlib.  Identified with the \emph{vertex set} $S$
rather than the arc set $(S, \bar{S})$, since $S$ determines the arcs and is far easier
to quantify over.  \texttt{capOf} then computes the arc set's capacity.  Note $y \notin S$ is
the book's $y \in \bar{S}$.
- \texttt{cap (S, $\bar{S}$) = $\sum$\_\{u$\in$S\} $\sum$\_\{v$\notin$S\} c u v}. The total throughput of the severed arcs --- how much traffic could at
most cross that divide.  Since all the flow must pass through, it bounds \texttt{val f}
above.

\textbf{!} Missing from Mathlib.  Structurally identical to \texttt{fOut} with
\texttt{cap} in place of $f$, which is exactly why theorem 11.1's proof is a two-line
comparison.
- $f^{-}(S) = f(\bar{S}, S) = \sum_{u\notin S} \sum_{v\in S} f u v$. The total flow entering $S$.  Conservation forces the resultant flow
out of every intermediate vertex to vanish, which is what makes the resultant flow
out of $X$ equal the resultant flow into $Y$ (exercise 11.1.3) and hence \texttt{val f}
well defined.

The mirror of \texttt{fOut} with the two sums swapped.
- $f^{+}(S) = f(S, \bar{S}) = \sum_{u\in S} \sum_{v\notin S} f u v$. The total flow leaving $S$ --- sum over every arc with tail inside $S$
and head outside.  \textbf{!} This is \emph{not} the sum of the $f^{+}(v)$ over $v \in S$: arcs
internal to $S$ are counted there but not here.  Exercise 11.1.2 makes the exact
relationship precise, and it is the difference $f^{+} - f^{-}$ that behaves well.

\textbf{!} Missing from Mathlib.  A double \texttt{Finset.sum} over $S$ and
$S^{c}$, which the capacity-as-a-function carrier makes possible; $f u v = 0$ for a
non-arc contributes nothing.
- A flow: (11.1) capacity constraint + (11.2) conservation at intermediate vertices. Nothing over-loaded, nothing accumulating.  The zero flow's existence
is what makes \texttt{exists\_maxFlow} non-vacuous.

The lower bound $0 \le f(a)$ of (11.1) is free: $f$ is $\mathbb{N}$-valued.
Conservation is stated as \texttt{fIn f \{v\} = fOut f \{v\}} on singletons, which unfolds to
the book's $f^{-}(v) = f^{+}(v)$ --- note \texttt{fIn}/\texttt{fOut} on a singleton are genuinely the
per-vertex quantities, since there are no arcs internal to a singleton.
- \texttt{val f = f$^{+}$(X) $-$ f$^{-}$(X)}. The net rate at which the commodity travels from producers to
consumers.  Conservation at the intermediate vertices is what makes the two ways of
measuring it agree.

\textbf{!} \textbf{$\mathbb{Z}$-valued, and this is load-bearing.}  In $\mathbb{N}$ the
truncated subtraction would make exercise 11.1.2 --- the identity the whole chapter
rests on --- false, since individual terms $f^{+}(v) - f^{-}(v)$ are genuinely negative at
vertices absorbing more than they emit.  Every $f^{+} - f^{-}$ in this file is therefore
cast to $\mathbb{Z}$ before subtracting.

Statement: exists_cut_of_no_incrementing_path. *If $N$ contains no
$f$-incrementing path, then there is a cut $K$ with \texttt{val f = cap K}.*

The constructive core of theorem 11.2's converse: the cut built from
the $f$-unsaturated reachability set has capacity exactly \texttt{val f}.

\textbf{*} This has to be \textbf{extracted separately} because theorem 11.2's
\emph{statement} asserts only maximality and discards the cut, while theorem 11.3 needs
the cut itself.  Fill this one first and derive theorem 11.2's converse from it,
rather than the other way round --- otherwise the reachability construction has to be
written twice.
formal_statement:
import Mathlib

open scoped Classical

namespace Networks
structure Network (V : Type*) where
  /-- Capacity of arc `u → v` (`0` ⟺ no arc). -/
  cap : V → V → ℕ
  /-- Source set. -/
  X : Finset V
  /-- Sink set. -/
  Y : Finset V
  /-- Distinguished single source (§11.2+). -/
  x : V
  /-- Distinguished single sink (§11.2+). -/
  y : V
  hdisj : Disjoint X Y
  hX : X.Nonempty
  hY : Y.Nonempty
end Networks

namespace Networks
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V]
def Network.I (N : Network V) : Finset V := Finset.univ \ (N.X ∪ N.Y)
end Networks

namespace Networks
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V]
def Network.IsCut (N : Network V) (S : Finset V) : Prop := N.x ∈ S ∧ N.y ∉ S
end Networks

namespace Networks
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V]
def Network.capOf (N : Network V) (S : Finset V) : ℕ := ∑ u ∈ S, ∑ v ∈ Sᶜ, N.cap u v
end Networks

namespace Networks
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V]
def Network.fIn (_N : Network V) (f : V → V → ℕ) (S : Finset V) : ℕ :=
  ∑ u ∈ Sᶜ, ∑ v ∈ S, f u v
end Networks

namespace Networks
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V]
def Network.fOut (_N : Network V) (f : V → V → ℕ) (S : Finset V) : ℕ :=
  ∑ u ∈ S, ∑ v ∈ Sᶜ, f u v
end Networks

namespace Networks
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V]
def Network.IsFlow (N : Network V) (f : V → V → ℕ) : Prop :=
  (∀ u v, f u v ≤ N.cap u v) ∧
  (∀ v ∈ N.I, N.fIn f {v} = N.fOut f {v})
end Networks

namespace Networks
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V]
def Network.val (N : Network V) (f : V → V → ℕ) : ℤ :=
  (N.fOut f N.X : ℤ) - (N.fIn f N.X : ℤ)
end Networks

namespace Networks
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V]
theorem exists_cut_of_no_incrementing_path (N : Network V) {f : V → V → ℕ} (hf : N.IsFlow f)
    (h : ¬ Nonempty (N.IncPath f N.y)) :
    ∃ S : Finset V, N.IsCut S ∧ N.val f = (N.capOf S : ℤ) := sorry
end Networks
title: exists_cut_of_no_incrementing_path

\textbf{*} This has to be \textbf{extracted separately} because theorem 11.2's

the cut itself.  Fill this one first and derive theorem 11.2's converse from it,
rather than the other way round --- otherwise the reachability construction has to be

formal_statement:
import Mathlib

open scoped Classical

namespace Networks
structure Network (V : Type*) where
  /-- Capacity of arc `u → v` (`0` ⟺ no arc). -/
  cap : V → V → ℕ
  /-- Source set. -/
  X : Finset V
  /-- Sink set. -/
  Y : Finset V
  /-- Distinguished single source (§11.2+). -/
  x : V
  /-- Distinguished single sink (§11.2+). -/
  y : V
  hdisj : Disjoint X Y
  hX : X.Nonempty
  hY : Y.Nonempty
end Networks

namespace Networks
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V]
def Network.I (N : Network V) : Finset V := Finset.univ \ (N.X ∪ N.Y)
end Networks

namespace Networks
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V]
def Network.fIn (_N : Network V) (f : V → V → ℕ) (S : Finset V) : ℕ :=
  ∑ u ∈ Sᶜ, ∑ v ∈ S, f u v
end Networks

namespace Networks
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V]
def Network.fOut (_N : Network V) (f : V → V → ℕ) (S : Finset V) : ℕ :=
  ∑ u ∈ S, ∑ v ∈ Sᶜ, f u v
end Networks

namespace Networks
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V]
def Network.IsFlow (N : Network V) (f : V → V → ℕ) : Prop :=
  (∀ u v, f u v ≤ N.cap u v) ∧
  (∀ v ∈ N.I, N.fIn f {v} = N.fOut f {v})
end Networks

namespace Networks
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V]
def Network.val (N : Network V) (f : V → V → ℕ) : ℤ :=
  (N.fOut f N.X : ℤ) - (N.fIn f N.X : ℤ)
end Networks

namespace Networks
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V]
def Network.IsMaxFlow (N : Network V) (f : V → V → ℕ) : Prop :=
  N.IsFlow f ∧ ∀ f', N.IsFlow f' → N.val f' ≤ N.val f
end Networks

namespace Networks
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V]
theorem exists_maxFlow (N : Network V) : ∃ f : V → V → ℕ, N.IsMaxFlow f := sorry
end Networks

import Mathlib

open scoped Classical

namespace Networks
structure Network (V : Type*) where
  /-- Capacity of arc `u → v` (`0` ⟺ no arc). -/
  cap : V → V → ℕ
  /-- Source set. -/
  X : Finset V
  /-- Sink set. -/
  Y : Finset V
  /-- Distinguished single source (§11.2+). -/
  x : V
  /-- Distinguished single sink (§11.2+). -/
  y : V
  hdisj : Disjoint X Y
  hX : X.Nonempty
  hY : Y.Nonempty
end Networks

namespace Networks
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V]
def Network.IsCut (N : Network V) (S : Finset V) : Prop := N.x ∈ S ∧ N.y ∉ S
end Networks

namespace Networks
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V]
def Network.capOf (N : Network V) (S : Finset V) : ℕ := ∑ u ∈ S, ∑ v ∈ Sᶜ, N.cap u v
end Networks

namespace Networks
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V]
def Network.IsMinCut (N : Network V) (S : Finset V) : Prop :=
  N.IsCut S ∧ ∀ S', N.IsCut S' → N.capOf S ≤ N.capOf S'
end Networks

namespace Networks
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V]
theorem exists_minCut (N : Network V) : ∃ S : Finset V, N.IsMinCut S := sorry
end Networks

definitions.informal:
A way of severing the network so the source is on one side and the
sink on the other.  Every unit of flow must cross every cut, which is why cuts
bound flows from above (theorem 11.1) --- and, more surprisingly, why the best cut
exactly matches the best flow (theorem 11.3).

rather than the arc set $(S, \bar{S})$, since $S$ determines the arcs and is far easier
to quantify over.  \texttt{capOf} then computes the arc set's capacity.  Note $y \notin S$ is
the book's $y \in \bar{S}$.

definitions.informal:

most cross that divide.  Since all the flow must pass through, it bounds \texttt{val f}
above.

\texttt{cap} in place of $f$, which is exactly why theorem 11.1's proof is a two-line
comparison.

says its capacity is exactly the maximum throughput.  B&M record the easy half
first: \emph{If $f}$ is a maximum flow and $\tilde{K}$ is a minimum cut, we have, as a special
case of theorem 11.1, that \texttt{val f\emph{ $\le$ cap $\tilde{K}$}} (11.8).

As with \texttt{IsMaxFlow}, stated positively.

formal_statement:
import Mathlib

open scoped Classical

namespace Networks
structure Network (V : Type*) where
  /-- Capacity of arc `u → v` (`0` ⟺ no arc). -/
  cap : V → V → ℕ
  /-- Source set. -/
  X : Finset V
  /-- Sink set. -/
  Y : Finset V
  /-- Distinguished single source (§11.2+). -/
  x : V
  /-- Distinguished single sink (§11.2+). -/
  y : V
  hdisj : Disjoint X Y
  hX : X.Nonempty
  hY : Y.Nonempty
end Networks

namespace Networks
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V]
def Network.I (N : Network V) : Finset V := Finset.univ \ (N.X ∪ N.Y)
end Networks

namespace Networks
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V]
def Network.fIn (_N : Network V) (f : V → V → ℕ) (S : Finset V) : ℕ :=
  ∑ u ∈ Sᶜ, ∑ v ∈ S, f u v
end Networks

namespace Networks
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V]
def Network.fOut (_N : Network V) (f : V → V → ℕ) (S : Finset V) : ℕ :=
  ∑ u ∈ S, ∑ v ∈ Sᶜ, f u v
end Networks

namespace Networks
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V]
def Network.IsFlow (N : Network V) (f : V → V → ℕ) : Prop :=
  (∀ u v, f u v ≤ N.cap u v) ∧
  (∀ v ∈ N.I, N.fIn f {v} = N.fOut f {v})
end Networks

namespace Networks
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V]
theorem fOut_X_sub_fIn_X_eq_fIn_Y_sub_fOut_Y (N : Network V) {f : V → V → ℕ} (hf : N.IsFlow f) :
    (N.fOut f N.X : ℤ) - (N.fIn f N.X : ℤ) = (N.fIn f N.Y : ℤ) - (N.fOut f N.Y : ℤ) := sorry
end Networks

informal_statement:
Definitions:
- $(p,q)$ is realisable by a simple bipartite graph: there is a $(0,1)$-matrix $B$ with row sums $p$ and\dots. Can two prescribed lists of degrees occur as the two sides of a
bipartite graph?  The book's $p = (3,2,2,2,1)$, $q = (3,3,2,1,1)$ is realisable
(figure 11.12), whereas $p = q = (5,4,4,2,1)$ is not (exercise 11.5.2) even though
the sums agree.

\textbf{!} Missing from Mathlib (0 hits for Gale--Ryser).  Carried as a
$(0,1)$-\textbf{matrix} \texttt{B : Fin m $\to$ Fin n $\to$ Bool} rather than a bipartite \texttt{SimpleGraph},
following the book's own closing remark: *With each simple bipartite graph $G$ \dots
we can associate an $m \times n$ matrix $B$ in which $b_ij = 1$ or $0$, depending on
whether $x_{i}y_{j}$ is an edge of $G$ or not.  Conversely, every $m \times n$ $(0,1)$-matrix
corresponds in this way to a simple bipartite graph.*  The two are equivalent and
the matrix avoids constructing a graph on \texttt{Fin m $\oplus$ Fin n} with a bipartition proof.
Due to Ryser (1957).

Statement: galeRyser_realisable. Equal sums (11.16) are necessary --- both count the edges --- but not
sufficient, as $p = q = (5,4,4,2,1)$ shows.  Condition (11.18) adds that the $k$
largest demands can actually be met: each $x_{i}$ can supply at most \texttt{min\{p$_{i}$, k\}} of
them, having only $p_{i}$ edges and only $k$ targets.

\emph{Matrix form.}  Let $B*$ have its first $p_{i}$ entries of row $i$ equal to $1$, and let
$p*$ be its column sums --- the \textbf{conjugate} of $p$ (that of $(5,4,4,2,1)$ is
$(5,4,3,3,1)$).  Row $i$ contributes \texttt{min\{p$_{i}$, k\}} to $\sum_{j\le k} p*_{j}$, so (11.18) says
exactly $\sum_{j\le k} p*_{j} \ge \sum_{j\le k} q_{j}$ --- the conjugate of $p$ dominates $q$.  Due to
Ryser (1957).

The chapter's hardest item.  $k$ is a \texttt{Fin n} and the book's
$1 \le k \le n$ becomes \texttt{k.val + 1} in the \texttt{min}, so check the off-by-one against the
book when filling.  The $(0,1)$-matrix carrier is used rather than a bipartite-graph
predicate; see \texttt{RealisableBipartite}.
formal_statement:
import Mathlib

open scoped Classical

namespace Networks
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V]
def RealisableBipartite {m n : ℕ} (p : Fin m → ℕ) (q : Fin n → ℕ) : Prop :=
  ∃ B : Fin m → Fin n → Bool,
    (∀ i, (Finset.univ.filter (fun j => B i j = true)).card = p i) ∧
    (∀ j, (Finset.univ.filter (fun i => B i j = true)).card = q j)
end Networks

namespace Networks
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V]
theorem galeRyser_realisable {m n : ℕ} (p : Fin m → ℕ) (q : Fin n → ℕ)
    (hsum : ∑ i, p i = ∑ j, q j)                          -- (11.16)
    (hmono : ∀ j j' : Fin n, j ≤ j' → q j' ≤ q j) :        -- (11.17)
    RealisableBipartite p q ↔
      ∀ k : Fin n, ∑ j ∈ Finset.univ.filter (· ≤ k), q j
                     ≤ ∑ i, min (p i) (k.val + 1) := sorry
end Networks

import Mathlib

open scoped Classical

namespace Networks
structure Network (V : Type*) where
  /-- Capacity of arc `u → v` (`0` ⟺ no arc). -/
  cap : V → V → ℕ
  /-- Source set. -/
  X : Finset V
  /-- Sink set. -/
  Y : Finset V
  /-- Distinguished single source (§11.2+). -/
  x : V
  /-- Distinguished single sink (§11.2+). -/
  y : V
  hdisj : Disjoint X Y
  hX : X.Nonempty
  hY : Y.Nonempty
end Networks

namespace Networks
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V]
def Network.I (N : Network V) : Finset V := Finset.univ \ (N.X ∪ N.Y)
end Networks

namespace Networks
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V]
def Network.capOf (N : Network V) (S : Finset V) : ℕ := ∑ u ∈ S, ∑ v ∈ Sᶜ, N.cap u v
end Networks

namespace Networks
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V]
def Network.fIn (_N : Network V) (f : V → V → ℕ) (S : Finset V) : ℕ :=
  ∑ u ∈ Sᶜ, ∑ v ∈ S, f u v
end Networks

namespace Networks
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V]
def Network.fOut (_N : Network V) (f : V → V → ℕ) (S : Finset V) : ℕ :=
  ∑ u ∈ S, ∑ v ∈ Sᶜ, f u v
end Networks

namespace Networks
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V]
def Network.IsFlow (N : Network V) (f : V → V → ℕ) : Prop :=
  (∀ u v, f u v ≤ N.cap u v) ∧
  (∀ v ∈ N.I, N.fIn f {v} = N.fOut f {v})
end Networks

namespace Networks
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V]
def Network.IsFeasible (N : Network V) (σ dem : V → ℕ) (f : V → V → ℕ) : Prop :=
  N.IsFlow f ∧
  (∀ xi ∈ N.X, (N.fOut f {xi} : ℤ) - (N.fIn f {xi} : ℤ) ≤ (σ xi : ℤ)) ∧
  (∀ yj ∈ N.Y, (dem yj : ℤ) ≤ (N.fIn f {yj} : ℤ) - (N.fOut f {yj} : ℤ))
end Networks

namespace Networks
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V]
theorem gale_feasible_flow (N : Network V) (σ dem : V → ℕ) :
    (∃ f, N.IsFeasible σ dem f) ↔
      ∀ S : Finset V,
        ((∑ v ∈ (N.Y ∩ Sᶜ), dem v : ℤ)) - ((∑ v ∈ (N.X ∩ Sᶜ), σ v : ℤ))
          ≤ (N.capOf S : ℤ) := sorry
end Networks

  hY : Y.Nonempty

namespace Networks
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V]
def Network.I (N : Network V) : Finset V := Finset.univ \ (N.X ∪ N.Y)
end Networks

namespace Networks
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V]
def Network.IsCut (N : Network V) (S : Finset V) : Prop := N.x ∈ S ∧ N.y ∉ S
end Networks

namespace Networks
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V]
def Network.capOf (N : Network V) (S : Finset V) : ℕ := ∑ u ∈ S, ∑ v ∈ Sᶜ, N.cap u v
end Networks

namespace Networks
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V]
def Network.fIn (_N : Network V) (f : V → V → ℕ) (S : Finset V) : ℕ :=
  ∑ u ∈ Sᶜ, ∑ v ∈ S, f u v
end Networks

namespace Networks
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V]
def Network.fOut (_N : Network V) (f : V → V → ℕ) (S : Finset V) : ℕ :=
  ∑ u ∈ S, ∑ v ∈ Sᶜ, f u v
end Networks

namespace Networks
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V]
def Network.IsFlow (N : Network V) (f : V → V → ℕ) : Prop :=
  (∀ u v, f u v ≤ N.cap u v) ∧
  (∀ v ∈ N.I, N.fIn f {v} = N.fOut f {v})
end Networks

namespace Networks
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V]
def Network.IsMinCut (N : Network V) (S : Finset V) : Prop :=
  N.IsCut S ∧ ∀ S', N.IsCut S' → N.capOf S ≤ N.capOf S'
end Networks

namespace Networks
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V]
def Network.val (N : Network V) (f : V → V → ℕ) : ℤ :=
  (N.fOut f N.X : ℤ) - (N.fIn f N.X : ℤ)
end Networks

namespace Networks
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V]
def Network.IsMaxFlow (N : Network V) (f : V → V → ℕ) : Prop :=
  N.IsFlow f ∧ ∀ f', N.IsFlow f' → N.val f' ≤ N.val f
end Networks

theorem isMaxFlow_and_isMinCut_of_val_eq_cap (N : Network V) {f : V → V → ℕ} (hf : N.IsFlow f)
    {S : Finset V} (hS : N.IsCut S) (h : N.val f = (N.capOf S : ℤ)) :
    N.IsMaxFlow f ∧ N.IsMinCut S := sorry
end Networks
title: isMaxFlow_and_isMinCut_of_val_eq_cap
statement_informal:
isMaxFlow_and_isMinCut_of_val_eq_cap. The standard "weak duality certifies optimality" argument, the exact
analogue of lemma 5.3 for matchings and coverings.  It is what makes the labelling
method self-verifying: when the algorithm stops it produces a matching flow and cut,
and their equality proves both optimal.

definitions.title: A network $N = (D, X, Y, c)$
definitions.informal:
A transportation network: goods are produced at the sources, consumed
at the sinks, and shipped along the arcs, each with a maximum throughput.

\textbf{!} Missing from Mathlib (0 hits for flow/network/capacity).
Capacity is carried as a \emph{function} \texttt{cap : V $\to$ V $\to$ $\mathbb{N}$}, with \texttt{cap u v = 0} encoding
"no arc $u \to v$"; this makes $f^{+}$/$f^{-}$ plain \texttt{Finset.sum}s.  \textbf{!} It cannot represent
\textbf{parallel arcs}, which is a real restriction --- lemma 11.4 is about a network in
which every arc has unit capacity, and B&M's digraphs may have several arcs between
the same pair.

The structure carries \textbf{both} $X$, $Y$ (the source/sink \emph{sets} of \S{}11.1) and the
distinguished $x$, $y$ used from \S{}11.2 onward.  That is because the book reduces
the first to the second: *adjoin two new vertices $x$ and $y$; join $x$ to each
vertex in $X$ by an arc of capacity $\infty$; join each vertex in $Y$ to $y$ by an arc
of capacity $\infty$; designate $x$ as the source and $y$ as the sink of $N'$* --- after
which *throughout the next three sections, we shall confine our attention to
networks that have a single source $x$ and a single sink $y$*.  That reduction is
exercise 11.1.4, which is deferred here (it needs an $\mathbb{N}\infty$-capacity parallel
carrier), so the two are simply both recorded in the structure.

\textbf{\textbf{!} Structural defect: $x$, $y$ are unrelated to $X$, $Y$.}  Nothing in the
structure requires \texttt{N.x $\in$ N.X}, let alone \texttt{N.X = \{N.x\}}.  But \texttt{val} is defined over
the \emph{set} $X$ while every \S{}11.2--\S{}11.3 result is about cuts separating the single
$x$ from the single $y$.  The two therefore measure different things, and \textbf{lemma
11.1, theorem 11.1 in both forms, corollary 11.1 and theorem 11.3 are all false as
stated}.

\emph{Counterexample} (one network refutes all of them).  $V = {x_{1}, x_{2}, y_{1}}$,
$X = {x_{1}, x_{2}}$, $Y = {y_{1}}$, \texttt{N.x = x$_{1}$}, \texttt{N.y = y$_{1}$}; capacities $c(x_{1},y_{1}) = c(x_{2},y_{1}) = 1$
and $0$ elsewhere.  Then $I = \emptyset$, so any $f$ within capacity is a flow; take
$f(x_{1},y_{1}) = f(x_{2},y_{1}) = 1$.
\item \texttt{val f = f$^{+}$(X) - f$^{-}$(X) = 2}.
\item $S = {x_{1}}$ is a cut ($x_{1} \in S$, $y_{1} \notin S$), with $f^{+}(S) - f^{-}(S) = 1$ and
  \texttt{cap S = 1}.
\item So lemma 11.1 asserts $2 = 1$; theorem 11.1 asserts $2 \le 1$.
\item Max flow value is $2$, minimum cut capacity is $1$, so theorem 11.3 asserts
  $2 = 1$.
\item Corollary 11.1 fails too: $f'(x_{1},y_{1}) = 1$, $f'(x_{2},y_{1}) = 0$ has
  \texttt{val f' = 1 = cap\{x$_{1}$\}}, yet $f'$ is not a maximum flow.

\emph{The repair} is to add the fields \texttt{hx : N.X = \{N.x\}} and \texttt{hy : N.Y = \{N.y\}} to the
structure (the book's standing convention for \S{}\S{}11.2--11.4), or equivalently to add
them as hypotheses on the affected theorems.  The \S{}11.1 results --- exercises 11.1.2
and 11.1.3 --- are unaffected and should keep the general $X$, $Y$.

definitions.title: Intermediate vertices $I = V \ (X \cup Y)$
definitions.informal:
The transit points of the network, which neither produce nor consume.
The conservation condition (11.2) applies exactly here --- what flows in must flow
out --- and that is what makes \texttt{val f} well defined (exercise 11.1.3).

\texttt{Finset.univ \textbackslash\{\} (X $\cup$ Y)}, so $I$ is a \texttt{Finset} and membership is
decidable --- needed by \texttt{IsFlow}'s second clause.

definitions.title: A cut $(S, \bar{S})$ with $x \in S$, $y \notin S$
definitions.informal:
A way of severing the network so the source is on one side and the
sink on the other.  Every unit of flow must cross every cut, which is why cuts
bound flows from above (theorem 11.1) --- and, more surprisingly, why the best cut
exactly matches the best flow (theorem 11.3).

\textbf{!} Missing from Mathlib.  Identified with the \emph{vertex set} $S$
rather than the arc set $(S, \bar{S})$, since $S$ determines the arcs and is far easier
to quantify over.  \texttt{capOf} then computes the arc set's capacity.  Note $y \notin S$ is
the book's $y \in \bar{S}$.

definitions.title: \texttt{cap (S, $\bar{S}$) = $\sum$\_\{u$\in$S\} $\sum$\_\{v$\notin$S\} c u v}
definitions.informal:
The total throughput of the severed arcs --- how much traffic could at
most cross that divide.  Since all the flow must pass through, it bounds \texttt{val f}
above.

\textbf{!} Missing from Mathlib.  Structurally identical to \texttt{fOut} with
\texttt{cap} in place of $f$, which is exactly why theorem 11.1's proof is a two-line
comparison.

definitions.title: $f^{-}(S) = f(\bar{S}, S) = \sum_{u\notin S} \sum_{v\in S} f u v$
definitions.informal:
The total flow entering $S$.  Conservation forces the resultant flow
out of every intermediate vertex to vanish, which is what makes the resultant flow
out of $X$ equal the resultant flow into $Y$ (exercise 11.1.3) and hence \texttt{val f}
well defined.

The mirror of \texttt{fOut} with the two sums swapped.

definitions.title: $f^{+}(S) = f(S, \bar{S}) = \sum_{u\in S} \sum_{v\notin S} f u v$
definitions.informal:
The total flow leaving $S$ --- sum over every arc with tail inside $S$
and head outside.  \textbf{!} This is \emph{not} the sum of the $f^{+}(v)$ over $v \in S$: arcs
internal to $S$ are counted there but not here.  Exercise 11.1.2 makes the exact
relationship precise, and it is the difference $f^{+} - f^{-}$ that behaves well.

\textbf{!} Missing from Mathlib.  A double \texttt{Finset.sum} over $S$ and
$S^{c}$, which the capacity-as-a-function carrier makes possible; $f u v = 0$ for a
non-arc contributes nothing.

definitions.title: A flow: (11.1) capacity constraint + (11.2) conservation at intermediate vertices
definitions.informal:
Nothing over-loaded, nothing accumulating.  The zero flow's existence
is what makes \texttt{exists\_maxFlow} non-vacuous.

The lower bound $0 \le f(a)$ of (11.1) is free: $f$ is $\mathbb{N}$-valued.
Conservation is stated as \texttt{fIn f \{v\} = fOut f \{v\}} on singletons, which unfolds to
the book's $f^{-}(v) = f^{+}(v)$ --- note \texttt{fIn}/\texttt{fOut} on a singleton are genuinely the
per-vertex quantities, since there are no arcs internal to a singleton.

definitions.title: A minimum cut
definitions.informal:
The cheapest way to sever the network --- the bottleneck.  Theorem 11.3
says its capacity is exactly the maximum throughput.  B&M record the easy half
first: \emph{If $f}$ is a maximum flow and $\tilde{K}$ is a minimum cut, we have, as a special
case of theorem 11.1, that \texttt{val f\emph{ $\le$ cap $\tilde{K}$}} (11.8).

As with \texttt{IsMaxFlow}, stated positively.

definitions.title: \texttt{val f = f$^{+}$(X) $-$ f$^{-}$(X)}
definitions.informal:
The net rate at which the commodity travels from producers to
consumers.  Conservation at the intermediate vertices is what makes the two ways of
measuring it agree.

\textbf{!} \textbf{$\mathbb{Z}$-valued, and this is load-bearing.}  In $\mathbb{N}$ the
truncated subtraction would make exercise 11.1.2 --- the identity the whole chapter
rests on --- false, since individual terms $f^{+}(v) - f^{-}(v)$ are genuinely negative at
vertices absorbing more than they emit.  Every $f^{+} - f^{-}$ in this file is therefore
cast to $\mathbb{Z}$ before subtracting.

definitions.title: A maximum flow
definitions.informal:
Ship as much as the network allows.  Theorem 11.2 characterises these
as exactly the flows admitting no incrementing path --- the flow-theoretic analogue
of Berge's theorem 5.1 for matchings.

"No flow of larger value" is stated positively as
\texttt{$\forall$ f', IsFlow f' $\to$ val f' $\le$ val f}, which is the form every consumer wants.

formal_statement:
import Mathlib

open scoped Classical

namespace Networks
structure Network (V : Type*) where
  /-- Capacity of arc `u → v` (`0` ⟺ no arc). -/
  cap : V → V → ℕ
  /-- Source set. -/
  X : Finset V
  /-- Sink set. -/
  Y : Finset V
  /-- Distinguished single source (§11.2+). -/
  x : V
  /-- Distinguished single sink (§11.2+). -/
  y : V
  hdisj : Disjoint X Y
  hX : X.Nonempty
  hY : Y.Nonempty
end Networks

namespace Networks
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V]
def Network.IsCut (N : Network V) (S : Finset V) : Prop := N.x ∈ S ∧ N.y ∉ S
end Networks

namespace Networks
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V]
def Network.capOf (N : Network V) (S : Finset V) : ℕ := ∑ u ∈ S, ∑ v ∈ Sᶜ, N.cap u v
end Networks

namespace Networks
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V]
def Network.IsMinCut (N : Network V) (S : Finset V) : Prop :=
  N.IsCut S ∧ ∀ S', N.IsCut S' → N.capOf S ≤ N.capOf S'
end Networks

namespace Networks
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V]
theorem isMinCut_union_inter (N : Network V) {S T : Finset V}
    (hS : N.IsMinCut S) (hT : N.IsMinCut T) :
    N.IsMinCut (S ∪ T) ∧ N.IsMinCut (S ∩ T) := sorry
end Networks
title: isMinCut_union_inter
statement_informal:
isMinCut_union_inter. The minimum cuts form a lattice.  A consequence is that there is a
unique \emph{smallest} minimum cut and a unique \emph{largest} one, which is useful
algorithmically.

Unaffected by the $X$/$x$ defect --- the argument is entirely about
\texttt{capOf} and \texttt{IsCut}, never about \texttt{val}.  Step 2 is a good candidate to prove first
and independently.

informal_statement:
Definitions:
- $G$ is $(m,n)$-orientable: it admits an orientation in which every indegree is $m$ or $n$. Make every edge one-way so each vertex ends up receiving exactly $m$
arrows, or exactly $n$.  Since $G$ is $(m+n)$-regular, indegree $m$ forces outdegree
$n$ and conversely, so an orientation splits the vertices into two classes.
Exercise 11.5.5(a) characterises orientability by a cut condition, and (b) shows the
classes can always be rebalanced one step towards each other.

\textbf{!} Missing from Mathlib (0 hits for "orientable").  The
orientation is spelled out inline as a \texttt{Digraph D} with three clauses --- $D \subseteq G$, $D$
never two-way, $D$ covers every edge --- rather than reusing chapter 10's
\texttt{IsOrientationOf}, which this file does not import.  The fourth clause is the
indegree condition.  Note the $(m+n)$-regularity is \emph{not} part of this definition;
it appears as a hypothesis on the theorems that use it.
- $|(S, \bar{S})|$: the number of edges of $G$ crossing the cut $(S, \bar{S})$ (Ex 11.5.5). The size of the undirected edge cut at $S$ --- how many edges would have
to be severed to separate $S$ from the rest.  In exercise 11.5.5(a) it is the
capacity available to carry the imbalance the prescribed indegrees force across
$S$'s boundary.

A double sum of indicators rather than a \texttt{Finset.card}, matching
the shape of \texttt{fOut}/\texttt{capOf} so the three compare directly.  Since \texttt{G.Adj} is
symmetric and the sum runs over $S \times S^{c}$, each crossing edge is counted \textbf{once}.

Statement: isOrientable_iff_exists_partition. An $(m+n)$-regular graph is to be oriented so every indegree is $m$ or
$n$.  The partition names in advance which vertices get which, and the inequality is
a feasibility condition in Gale's sense.

\textbf{!} Step 2 needs an \textbf{eulerian orientation}, which comes from
chapters 4 and 10 (every graph with all degrees even has an Euler tour; orient along
it) --- a genuine import, absent from this file.  Note $(m+n)$-regular forces every
degree even only when $m + n$ is even, so the eulerian step may itself need the
odd-degree patch of chapter 10's exercise 10.1.10.  The absolute value is written as
a \textbf{two-sided bound} to avoid \texttt{abs} and keep the arithmetic in $\mathbb{Z}$.
formal_statement:
import Mathlib

open scoped Classical

namespace Networks
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V]
def IsOrientable (G : SimpleGraph V) (m n : ℕ) : Prop :=
  ∃ D : Digraph V,
    (∀ u v, D.Adj u v → G.Adj u v) ∧
    (∀ u v, D.Adj u v → ¬ D.Adj v u) ∧
    (∀ u v, G.Adj u v → (D.Adj u v ∨ D.Adj v u)) ∧
    (∀ v, (Finset.univ.filter (fun u => D.Adj u v)).card = m ∨
          (Finset.univ.filter (fun u => D.Adj u v)).card = n)
end Networks

namespace Networks
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V]
noncomputable def edgeBoundaryCard (G : SimpleGraph V) (S : Finset V) : ℕ :=
  ∑ u ∈ S, ∑ v ∈ Sᶜ, (if G.Adj u v then 1 else 0)
end Networks

namespace Networks
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V]
theorem isOrientable_iff_exists_partition (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj] (m n : ℕ)
    (hreg : G.IsRegularOfDegree (m + n)) :
    IsOrientable G m n ↔
      ∃ V₁ V₂ : Finset V, V₁ ∪ V₂ = Finset.univ ∧ Disjoint V₁ V₂ ∧
        -- `|(m-n)(|V₁∩S| - |V₂∩S|)| ≤ |[S,S̄]|`, written as a two-sided bound to avoid `abs`.
        ∀ S : Finset V,
          ((m : ℤ) - n) * (((V₁ ∩ S).card : ℤ) - ((V₂ ∩ S).card : ℤ)) ≤ (edgeBoundaryCard G S : ℤ) ∧
          -(edgeBoundaryCard G S : ℤ)
            ≤ ((m : ℤ) - n) * (((V₁ ∩ S).card : ℤ) - ((V₂ ∩ S).card : ℤ)) := sorry
end Networks
title: isOrientable_iff_exists_partition
statement_informal:
isOrientable_iff_exists_partition. An $(m+n)$-regular graph is to be oriented so every indegree is $m$ or
$n$.  The partition names in advance which vertices get which, and the inequality is
a feasibility condition in Gale's sense.

\textbf{!} Step 2 needs an \textbf{eulerian orientation}, which comes from
chapters 4 and 10 (every graph with all degrees even has an Euler tour; orient along
it) --- a genuine import, absent from this file.  Note $(m+n)$-regular forces every
degree even only when $m + n$ is even, so the eulerian step may itself need the
odd-degree patch of chapter 10's exercise 10.1.10.  The absolute value is written as
a \textbf{two-sided bound} to avoid \texttt{abs} and keep the arithmetic in $\mathbb{Z}$.

definitions.title: $G$ is $(m,n)$-orientable: it admits an orientation in which every indegree is $m$ or $n$
definitions.informal:
Make every edge one-way so each vertex ends up receiving exactly $m$
arrows, or exactly $n$.  Since $G$ is $(m+n)$-regular, indegree $m$ forces outdegree
$n$ and conversely, so an orientation splits the vertices into two classes.
Exercise 11.5.5(a) characterises orientability by a cut condition, and (b) shows the
classes can always be rebalanced one step towards each other.

\textbf{!} Missing from Mathlib (0 hits for "orientable").  The
orientation is spelled out inline as a \texttt{Digraph D} with three clauses --- $D \subseteq G$, $D$
never two-way, $D$ covers every edge --- rather than reusing chapter 10's
\texttt{IsOrientationOf}, which this file does not import.  The fourth clause is the
indegree condition.  Note the $(m+n)$-regularity is \emph{not} part of this definition;
it appears as a hypothesis on the theorems that use it.

definitions.title: $|(S, \bar{S})|$: the number of edges of $G$ crossing the cut $(S, \bar{S})$ (Ex 11.5.5)
definitions.informal:
The size of the undirected edge cut at $S$ --- how many edges would have
to be severed to separate $S$ from the rest.  In exercise 11.5.5(a) it is the
capacity available to carry the imbalance the prescribed indegrees force across
$S$'s boundary.

A double sum of indicators rather than a \texttt{Finset.card}, matching
the shape of \texttt{fOut}/\texttt{capOf} so the three compare directly.  Since \texttt{G.Adj} is
symmetric and the sum runs over $S \times S^{c}$, each crossing edge is counted \textbf{once}.

Definitions:
- Local minimal \texttt{vertexConnectivity $\kappa$(G)} (repo has the real one). Corollary 11.7 relates it to internally-disjoint paths: $G$ with
$\nu \ge k + 1$ is $k$-connected exactly when any two distinct vertices are joined by
$k$ internally-disjoint paths.  This is the form of Menger's theorem \S{}3.2 announced
without proof.

A minimal local copy, as for \texttt{edgeConnectivity}.  The $\nu - 1$
branch is the book's convention for graphs with no vertex cut (complete graphs).
\textbf{!} Both \texttt{sInf} conventions bite at the boundaries --- see the outline.

Statement: k_connected_iff_internally_disjoint_paths. $k$-connectivity says no $k - 1$ vertices disconnect the graph; theorem
11.7 converts the local separation number for a nonadjacent pair into a path count,
and minimising over pairs converts global into local.

\textbf{!} B&M call this \emph{immediate}; it is not --- step 2 is genuine work,
and the $k = 2$ case alone is a full proof in the repo (\texttt{TwoConnected.lean:537}).
Uses the local \texttt{vertexConnectivity}, whose $\nu - 1$ fallback for complete graphs
interacts with step 2 (a complete graph has \emph{only} adjacent pairs), so check that
boundary.  \texttt{h : k + 1 $\le$ card V} is the book's $\nu \ge k + 1$.
formal_statement:
import Mathlib

open scoped Classical

namespace Networks
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V]
noncomputable def vertexConnectivity (G : SimpleGraph V) : ℕ :=
  if ∃ S : Finset V, (↑S : Set V) ⊂ Set.univ ∧ ¬ (G.induce ((↑S : Set V)ᶜ)).Connected then
    sInf {n : ℕ | ∃ S : Finset V,
      ((↑S : Set V) ⊂ Set.univ ∧ ¬ (G.induce ((↑S : Set V)ᶜ)).Connected) ∧ S.card = n}
  else
    Fintype.card V - 1
end Networks

namespace Networks
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V]
theorem k_connected_iff_internally_disjoint_paths (G : SimpleGraph V) (k : ℕ)
    (h : k + 1 ≤ Fintype.card V) :
    k ≤ vertexConnectivity G ↔
      ∀ u v : V, u ≠ v → k ≤ maxInternallyDisjointPaths G u v := sorry
end Networks
