Definitions:
- Local minimal \texttt{edgeConnectivity $\kappa$'(G)} (repo has the real one). Corollary 11.5 relates it to edge-disjoint paths: $G$ is
$k$-edge-connected exactly when any two distinct vertices are joined by $k$
edge-disjoint paths --- the global connectivity number turned into a local path
count.

A minimal local copy; the real one lives in
\texttt{TCSlib.GraphTheory.Connectivity}, deliberately not imported so this file stands
alone.  \textbf{!} \texttt{sInf $\emptyset$ = 0}, so a graph with no edge cut (a one-vertex graph) gets
$\kappa' = 0$ --- a boundary case that will bite corollary 11.5 exactly as it bit
chapter 10's \texttt{associatedDigraph\_isKArcConnected\_iff}.
- Max number of edge-disjoint $(x,y)$-paths in a graph. The left-hand side of Menger's edge theorem 11.5, the undirected

\textbf{\textbf{!} \texttt{sorry} body --- definable today.}  \emph{Repair:}
\texttt{sSup \{k | $\exists$ ps : Fin k $\to$ G.Walk x y, ($\forall$ i, (ps i).IsPath) $\land$ $\forall$ i j, i $\ne$ j $\to$ List.Disjoint (ps i).edges (ps j).edges\}}.

Statement: k_edge_connected_iff_edge_disjoint_paths. $k$-edge-connectedness says no $k - 1$ edges disconnect the graph; by
theorem 11.5 the minimum number of edges separating a \emph{specific} pair equals the
maximum number of edge-disjoint paths between them.  Minimising over pairs converts
the global statement into the local one.  This is the edge form of Menger's theorem
quoted without proof in \S{}3.2, generalising exercise 3.2.1 ($k = 2$) to all $k$.

Uses the local \texttt{edgeConnectivity} copy.  \textbf{!} Watch the \texttt{sInf $\emptyset$ = 0}
boundary flagged there: on a one-vertex graph no edge cut exists, so
\texttt{edgeConnectivity = 0}, while the right-hand side is vacuously true for every $k$
(there is no pair $u \ne v$).  So the $\leftrightarrow$ fails at $k \ge 1$, \texttt{card V $\le$ 1} --- a
\texttt{[Nontrivial V]} hypothesis is the fix, exactly as in chapter 10's
\texttt{associatedDigraph\_isKArcConnected\_iff}.

variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V]
noncomputable def edgeConnectivity (G : SimpleGraph V) : ℕ :=
  sInf {n : ℕ | ∃ F : Finset (Sym2 V),
    ((F : Set (Sym2 V)) ⊆ G.edgeSet ∧ ¬ (G.deleteEdges (F : Set (Sym2 V))).Connected) ∧ F.card = n}

    k ≤ edgeConnectivity G ↔
      ∀ u v : V, u ≠ v → k ≤ maxEdgeDisjointPaths G u v := sorry
end Networks

informal_statement:
Definitions:
- A network $N = (D, X, Y, c)$. A transportation network: goods are produced at the sources, consumed
at the sinks, and shipped along the arcs, each with a maximum throughput.

\textbf{!} Missing from Mathlib (0 hits for flow/network/capacity).
Capacity is carried as a \emph{function} \texttt{cap : V $\to$ V $\to$ $\mathbb{N}$}, with \texttt{cap u v = 0} encoding
"no arc $u \to v$"; this makes $f^{+}$/$f^{-}$ plain \texttt{Finset.sum}s.  \textbf{!} It cannot represent
\textbf{parallel arcs}, which is a real restriction --- lemma 11.4 is about a network in
which every arc has unit capacity, and B&M's digraphs may have several arcs between
the same pair.

The structure carries \textbf{both} $X$, $Y$ (the source/sink \emph{sets} of \S{}11.1) and the
distinguished $x$, $y$ used from \S{}11.2 onward.  That is because the book reduces
the first to the second: *adjoin two new vertices $x$ and $y$; join $x$ to each
vertex in $X$ by an arc of capacity $\infty$; join each vertex in $Y$ to $y$ by an arc
of capacity $\infty$; designate $x$ as the source and $y$ as the sink of $N'$* --- after
which *throughout the next three sections, we shall confine our attention to
networks that have a single source $x$ and a single sink $y$*.  That reduction is
exercise 11.1.4, which is deferred here (it needs an $\mathbb{N}\infty$-capacity parallel
carrier), so the two are simply both recorded in the structure.

\textbf{\textbf{!} Structural defect: $x$, $y$ are unrelated to $X$, $Y$.}  Nothing in the
structure requires \texttt{N.x $\in$ N.X}, let alone \texttt{N.X = \{N.x\}}.  But \texttt{val} is defined over
the \emph{set} $X$ while every \S{}11.2--\S{}11.3 result is about cuts separating the single
$x$ from the single $y$.  The two therefore measure different things, and \textbf{lemma
11.1, theorem 11.1 in both forms, corollary 11.1 and theorem 11.3 are all false as
stated}.

\emph{Counterexample} (one network refutes all of them).  $V = {x_{1}, x_{2}, y_{1}}$,
$X = {x_{1}, x_{2}}$, $Y = {y_{1}}$, \texttt{N.x = x$_{1}$}, \texttt{N.y = y$_{1}$}; capacities $c(x_{1},y_{1}) = c(x_{2},y_{1}) = 1$
and $0$ elsewhere.  Then $I = \emptyset$, so any $f$ within capacity is a flow; take
$f(x_{1},y_{1}) = f(x_{2},y_{1}) = 1$.
\item \texttt{val f = f$^{+}$(X) - f$^{-}$(X) = 2}.
\item $S = {x_{1}}$ is a cut ($x_{1} \in S$, $y_{1} \notin S$), with $f^{+}(S) - f^{-}(S) = 1$ and
  \texttt{cap S = 1}.
\item So lemma 11.1 asserts $2 = 1$; theorem 11.1 asserts $2 \le 1$.
\item Max flow value is $2$, minimum cut capacity is $1$, so theorem 11.3 asserts
  $2 = 1$.
\item Corollary 11.1 fails too: $f'(x_{1},y_{1}) = 1$, $f'(x_{2},y_{1}) = 0$ has
  \texttt{val f' = 1 = cap\{x$_{1}$\}}, yet $f'$ is not a maximum flow.

\emph{The repair} is to add the fields \texttt{hx : N.X = \{N.x\}} and \texttt{hy : N.Y = \{N.y\}} to the
structure (the book's standing convention for \S{}\S{}11.2--11.4), or equivalently to add
them as hypotheses on the affected theorems.  The \S{}11.1 results --- exercises 11.1.2
and 11.1.3 --- are unaffected and should keep the general $X$, $Y$.
- Intermediate vertices $I = V \ (X \cup Y)$. The transit points of the network, which neither produce nor consume.
The conservation condition (11.2) applies exactly here --- what flows in must flow
out --- and that is what makes \texttt{val f} well defined (exercise 11.1.3).

\texttt{Finset.univ \textbackslash\{\} (X $\cup$ Y)}, so $I$ is a \texttt{Finset} and membership is
decidable --- needed by \texttt{IsFlow}'s second clause.
- A cut $(S, \bar{S})$ with $x \in S$, $y \notin S$. A way of severing the network so the source is on one side and the
sink on the other.  Every unit of flow must cross every cut, which is why cuts
bound flows from above (theorem 11.1) --- and, more surprisingly, why the best cut
exactly matches the best flow (theorem 11.3).

\textbf{!} Missing from Mathlib.  Identified with the \emph{vertex set} $S$
rather than the arc set $(S, \bar{S})$, since $S$ determines the arcs and is far easier
to quantify over.  \texttt{capOf} then computes the arc set's capacity.  Note $y \notin S$ is
the book's $y \in \bar{S}$.
- \texttt{cap (S, $\bar{S}$) = $\sum$\_\{u$\in$S\} $\sum$\_\{v$\notin$S\} c u v}. The total throughput of the severed arcs --- how much traffic could at
most cross that divide.  Since all the flow must pass through, it bounds \texttt{val f}
above.

\textbf{!} Missing from Mathlib.  Structurally identical to \texttt{fOut} with
\texttt{cap} in place of $f$, which is exactly why theorem 11.1's proof is a two-line
comparison.
- $f^{-}(S) = f(\bar{S}, S) = \sum_{u\notin S} \sum_{v\in S} f u v$. The total flow entering $S$.  Conservation forces the resultant flow
out of every intermediate vertex to vanish, which is what makes the resultant flow
out of $X$ equal the resultant flow into $Y$ (exercise 11.1.3) and hence \texttt{val f}
well defined.

The mirror of \texttt{fOut} with the two sums swapped.
- $f^{+}(S) = f(S, \bar{S}) = \sum_{u\in S} \sum_{v\notin S} f u v$. The total flow leaving $S$ --- sum over every arc with tail inside $S$
and head outside.  \textbf{!} This is \emph{not} the sum of the $f^{+}(v)$ over $v \in S$: arcs
internal to $S$ are counted there but not here.  Exercise 11.1.2 makes the exact
relationship precise, and it is the difference $f^{+} - f^{-}$ that behaves well.

\textbf{!} Missing from Mathlib.  A double \texttt{Finset.sum} over $S$ and
$S^{c}$, which the capacity-as-a-function carrier makes possible; $f u v = 0$ for a
non-arc contributes nothing.
- A flow: (11.1) capacity constraint + (11.2) conservation at intermediate vertices. Nothing over-loaded, nothing accumulating.  The zero flow's existence
is what makes \texttt{exists\_maxFlow} non-vacuous.

The lower bound $0 \le f(a)$ of (11.1) is free: $f$ is $\mathbb{N}$-valued.
Conservation is stated as \texttt{fIn f \{v\} = fOut f \{v\}} on singletons, which unfolds to
the book's $f^{-}(v) = f^{+}(v)$ --- note \texttt{fIn}/\texttt{fOut} on a singleton are genuinely the
per-vertex quantities, since there are no arcs internal to a singleton.
- A minimum cut. The cheapest way to sever the network --- the bottleneck.  Theorem 11.3
says its capacity is exactly the maximum throughput.  B&M record the easy half
first: \emph{If $f}$ is a maximum flow and $\tilde{K}$ is a minimum cut, we have, as a special
case of theorem 11.1, that \texttt{val f\emph{ $\le$ cap $\tilde{K}$}} (11.8).

As with \texttt{IsMaxFlow}, stated positively.
- \texttt{val f = f$^{+}$(X) $-$ f$^{-}$(X)}. The net rate at which the commodity travels from producers to
consumers.  Conservation at the intermediate vertices is what makes the two ways of
measuring it agree.

\textbf{!} \textbf{$\mathbb{Z}$-valued, and this is load-bearing.}  In $\mathbb{N}$ the
truncated subtraction would make exercise 11.1.2 --- the identity the whole chapter
rests on --- false, since individual terms $f^{+}(v) - f^{-}(v)$ are genuinely negative at
vertices absorbing more than they emit.  Every $f^{+} - f^{-}$ in this file is therefore
cast to $\mathbb{Z}$ before subtracting.
- A maximum flow. Ship as much as the network allows.  Theorem 11.2 characterises these
as exactly the flows admitting no incrementing path --- the flow-theoretic analogue
of Berge's theorem 5.1 for matchings.

"No flow of larger value" is stated positively as
\texttt{$\forall$ f', IsFlow f' $\to$ val f' $\le$ val f}, which is the form every consumer wants.

Statement: maxFlow_and_minCut_zero_of_no_path. If the sink cannot be reached at all, nothing can be shipped and
nothing needs to be cut.

\textbf{!} Step 4 uses theorem 11.1, so it inherits the $X$/$x$ defect
recorded in the \texttt{Network} docstring; with the repair \texttt{N.X = \{N.x\}} it goes through.
The hypothesis is phrased with \texttt{ReflTransGen} over positive-capacity arcs rather
than as "no directed $(x,y)$-path", which is the same thing and needs no path
API.
formal_statement:
import Mathlib

open scoped Classical

namespace Networks
structure Network (V : Type*) where
  /-- Capacity of arc `u → v` (`0` ⟺ no arc). -/
  cap : V → V → ℕ
  /-- Source set. -/

namespace Networks

namespace Networks

title: maxFlow_and_minCut_zero_of_no_path
statement_informal:
maxFlow_and_minCut_zero_of_no_path. If the sink cannot be reached at all, nothing can be shipped and
nothing needs to be cut.

\textbf{!} Step 4 uses theorem 11.1, so it inherits the $X$/$x$ defect
recorded in the \texttt{Network} docstring; with the repair \texttt{N.X = \{N.x\}} it goes through.
The hypothesis is phrased with \texttt{ReflTransGen} over positive-capacity arcs rather
than as "no directed $(x,y)$-path", which is the same thing and needs no path
API.

definitions.title: A network $N = (D, X, Y, c)$
definitions.informal:
A transportation network: goods are produced at the sources, consumed
at the sinks, and shipped along the arcs, each with a maximum throughput.

\textbf{!} Missing from Mathlib (0 hits for flow/network/capacity).
Capacity is carried as a \emph{function} \texttt{cap : V $\to$ V $\to$ $\mathbb{N}$}, with \texttt{cap u v = 0} encoding
"no arc $u \to v$"; this makes $f^{+}$/$f^{-}$ plain \texttt{Finset.sum}s.  \textbf{!} It cannot represent
\textbf{parallel arcs}, which is a real restriction --- lemma 11.4 is about a network in
which every arc has unit capacity, and B&M's digraphs may have several arcs between
the same pair.

The structure carries \textbf{both} $X$, $Y$ (the source/sink \emph{sets} of \S{}11.1) and the
distinguished $x$, $y$ used from \S{}11.2 onward.  That is because the book reduces
the first to the second: *adjoin two new vertices $x$ and $y$; join $x$ to each
vertex in $X$ by an arc of capacity $\infty$; join each vertex in $Y$ to $y$ by an arc
of capacity $\infty$; designate $x$ as the source and $y$ as the sink of $N'$* --- after
which *throughout the next three sections, we shall confine our attention to
networks that have a single source $x$ and a single sink $y$*.  That reduction is
exercise 11.1.4, which is deferred here (it needs an $\mathbb{N}\infty$-capacity parallel
carrier), so the two are simply both recorded in the structure.

\textbf{\textbf{!} Structural defect: $x$, $y$ are unrelated to $X$, $Y$.}  Nothing in the
structure requires \texttt{N.x $\in$ N.X}, let alone \texttt{N.X = \{N.x\}}.  But \texttt{val} is defined over
the \emph{set} $X$ while every \S{}11.2--\S{}11.3 result is about cuts separating the single
$x$ from the single $y$.  The two therefore measure different things, and \textbf{lemma
11.1, theorem 11.1 in both forms, corollary 11.1 and theorem 11.3 are all false as
stated}.

\emph{Counterexample} (one network refutes all of them).  $V = {x_{1}, x_{2}, y_{1}}$,
$X = {x_{1}, x_{2}}$, $Y = {y_{1}}$, \texttt{N.x = x$_{1}$}, \texttt{N.y = y$_{1}$}; capacities $c(x_{1},y_{1}) = c(x_{2},y_{1}) = 1$
and $0$ elsewhere.  Then $I = \emptyset$, so any $f$ within capacity is a flow; take
$f(x_{1},y_{1}) = f(x_{2},y_{1}) = 1$.
\item \texttt{val f = f$^{+}$(X) - f$^{-}$(X) = 2}.
\item $S = {x_{1}}$ is a cut ($x_{1} \in S$, $y_{1} \notin S$), with $f^{+}(S) - f^{-}(S) = 1$ and
  \texttt{cap S = 1}.
\item So lemma 11.1 asserts $2 = 1$; theorem 11.1 asserts $2 \le 1$.
\item Max flow value is $2$, minimum cut capacity is $1$, so theorem 11.3 asserts
  $2 = 1$.
\item Corollary 11.1 fails too: $f'(x_{1},y_{1}) = 1$, $f'(x_{2},y_{1}) = 0$ has
  \texttt{val f' = 1 = cap\{x$_{1}$\}}, yet $f'$ is not a maximum flow.

\emph{The repair} is to add the fields \texttt{hx : N.X = \{N.x\}} and \texttt{hy : N.Y = \{N.y\}} to the
structure (the book's standing convention for \S{}\S{}11.2--11.4), or equivalently to add
them as hypotheses on the affected theorems.  The \S{}11.1 results --- exercises 11.1.2
and 11.1.3 --- are unaffected and should keep the general $X$, $Y$.

definitions.title: Intermediate vertices $I = V \ (X \cup Y)$
definitions.informal:
The transit points of the network, which neither produce nor consume.
The conservation condition (11.2) applies exactly here --- what flows in must flow
out --- and that is what makes \texttt{val f} well defined (exercise 11.1.3).

\texttt{Finset.univ \textbackslash\{\} (X $\cup$ Y)}, so $I$ is a \texttt{Finset} and membership is
decidable --- needed by \texttt{IsFlow}'s second clause.

definitions.title: A cut $(S, \bar{S})$ with $x \in S$, $y \notin S$
definitions.informal:
A way of severing the network so the source is on one side and the
sink on the other.  Every unit of flow must cross every cut, which is why cuts
bound flows from above (theorem 11.1) --- and, more surprisingly, why the best cut
exactly matches the best flow (theorem 11.3).

\textbf{!} Missing from Mathlib.  Identified with the \emph{vertex set} $S$
rather than the arc set $(S, \bar{S})$, since $S$ determines the arcs and is far easier
to quantify over.  \texttt{capOf} then computes the arc set's capacity.  Note $y \notin S$ is
the book's $y \in \bar{S}$.

definitions.title: \texttt{cap (S, $\bar{S}$) = $\sum$\_\{u$\in$S\} $\sum$\_\{v$\notin$S\} c u v}
definitions.informal:
The total throughput of the severed arcs --- how much traffic could at
most cross that divide.  Since all the flow must pass through, it bounds \texttt{val f}
above.

\textbf{!} Missing from Mathlib.  Structurally identical to \texttt{fOut} with
\texttt{cap} in place of $f$, which is exactly why theorem 11.1's proof is a two-line
comparison.

definitions.title: $f^{-}(S) = f(\bar{S}, S) = \sum_{u\notin S} \sum_{v\in S} f u v$
definitions.informal:
The total flow entering $S$.  Conservation forces the resultant flow
out of every intermediate vertex to vanish, which is what makes the resultant flow
out of $X$ equal the resultant flow into $Y$ (exercise 11.1.3) and hence \texttt{val f}
well defined.

The mirror of \texttt{fOut} with the two sums swapped.

definitions.title: $f^{+}(S) = f(S, \bar{S}) = \sum_{u\in S} \sum_{v\notin S} f u v$
definitions.informal:
The total flow leaving $S$ --- sum over every arc with tail inside $S$
and head outside.  \textbf{!} This is \emph{not} the sum of the $f^{+}(v)$ over $v \in S$: arcs
internal to $S$ are counted there but not here.  Exercise 11.1.2 makes the exact
relationship precise, and it is the difference $f^{+} - f^{-}$ that behaves well.

\textbf{!} Missing from Mathlib.  A double \texttt{Finset.sum} over $S$ and
$S^{c}$, which the capacity-as-a-function carrier makes possible; $f u v = 0$ for a
non-arc contributes nothing.

definitions.title: A flow: (11.1) capacity constraint + (11.2) conservation at intermediate vertices
definitions.informal:
Nothing over-loaded, nothing accumulating.  The zero flow's existence
is what makes \texttt{exists\_maxFlow} non-vacuous.

The lower bound $0 \le f(a)$ of (11.1) is free: $f$ is $\mathbb{N}$-valued.
Conservation is stated as \texttt{fIn f \{v\} = fOut f \{v\}} on singletons, which unfolds to
the book's $f^{-}(v) = f^{+}(v)$ --- note \texttt{fIn}/\texttt{fOut} on a singleton are genuinely the
per-vertex quantities, since there are no arcs internal to a singleton.

definitions.title: A minimum cut
definitions.informal:
The cheapest way to sever the network --- the bottleneck.  Theorem 11.3
says its capacity is exactly the maximum throughput.  B&M record the easy half
first: \emph{If $f}$ is a maximum flow and $\tilde{K}$ is a minimum cut, we have, as a special
case of theorem 11.1, that \texttt{val f\emph{ $\le$ cap $\tilde{K}$}} (11.8).

As with \texttt{IsMaxFlow}, stated positively.

definitions.title: \texttt{val f = f$^{+}$(X) $-$ f$^{-}$(X)}
definitions.informal:
The net rate at which the commodity travels from producers to
consumers.  Conservation at the intermediate vertices is what makes the two ways of
measuring it agree.

\textbf{!} \textbf{$\mathbb{Z}$-valued, and this is load-bearing.}  In $\mathbb{N}$ the
truncated subtraction would make exercise 11.1.2 --- the identity the whole chapter
rests on --- false, since individual terms $f^{+}(v) - f^{-}(v)$ are genuinely negative at
vertices absorbing more than they emit.  Every $f^{+} - f^{-}$ in this file is therefore
cast to $\mathbb{Z}$ before subtracting.

definitions.title: A maximum flow
definitions.informal:
Ship as much as the network allows.  Theorem 11.2 characterises these
as exactly the flows admitting no incrementing path --- the flow-theoretic analogue
of Berge's theorem 5.1 for matchings.

"No flow of larger value" is stated positively as
\texttt{$\forall$ f', IsFlow f' $\to$ val f' $\le$ val f}, which is the form every consumer wants.

formal_statement:
import Mathlib

open scoped Classical

namespace Networks
structure Network (V : Type*) where
  /-- Capacity of arc `u → v` (`0` ⟺ no arc). -/
  cap : V → V → ℕ
  /-- Source set. -/
  X : Finset V
  /-- Sink set. -/
  Y : Finset V
  /-- Distinguished single source (§11.2+). -/
  x : V
  /-- Distinguished single sink (§11.2+). -/
  y : V
  hdisj : Disjoint X Y
  hX : X.Nonempty
  hY : Y.Nonempty
end Networks

namespace Networks
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V]
def Network.I (N : Network V) : Finset V := Finset.univ \ (N.X ∪ N.Y)
end Networks

namespace Networks
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V]
def Network.fIn (_N : Network V) (f : V → V → ℕ) (S : Finset V) : ℕ :=
  ∑ u ∈ Sᶜ, ∑ v ∈ S, f u v
end Networks

namespace Networks
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V]
def Network.fOut (_N : Network V) (f : V → V → ℕ) (S : Finset V) : ℕ :=
  ∑ u ∈ S, ∑ v ∈ Sᶜ, f u v
end Networks

namespace Networks
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V]
def Network.IsFlow (N : Network V) (f : V → V → ℕ) : Prop :=
  (∀ u v, f u v ≤ N.cap u v) ∧
  (∀ v ∈ N.I, N.fIn f {v} = N.fOut f {v})
end Networks

namespace Networks
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V]
def Network.val (N : Network V) (f : V → V → ℕ) : ℤ :=
  (N.fOut f N.X : ℤ) - (N.fIn f N.X : ℤ)
end Networks

namespace Networks
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V]
def Network.IsMaxFlow (N : Network V) (f : V → V → ℕ) : Prop :=
  N.IsFlow f ∧ ∀ f', N.IsFlow f' → N.val f' ≤ N.val f
end Networks

namespace Networks
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V]
theorem maxFlow_iff_no_incrementing_path (N : Network V) {f : V → V → ℕ} (hf : N.IsFlow f) :
    N.IsMaxFlow f ↔ ¬ Nonempty (N.IncPath f N.y) := sorry
end Networks
title: maxFlow_iff_no_incrementing_path
statement_informal:
maxFlow_iff_no_incrementing_path. B&M stress the analogy: *the r\^ole played by incrementing paths in flow
theory is analogous to that of augmenting paths in matching theory* --- compare
Berge's theorem 5.1.

Note steps 2--4 are exactly where \texttt{IncPath} being a \emph{walk} rather
than a path is convenient: $S$ is a reachability closure, and closure under \texttt{fwd}
and \texttt{back} is immediate for walks.  \textbf{!} Step 5 uses theorem 11.1 and corollary 11.1,
so it inherits the $X$/$x$ defect.

formal_statement:
import Mathlib

open scoped Classical

namespace Networks
structure Network (V : Type*) where
  /-- Capacity of arc `u → v` (`0` ⟺ no arc). -/
  cap : V → V → ℕ
  /-- Source set. -/
  X : Finset V
  /-- Sink set. -/
  Y : Finset V
  /-- Distinguished single source (§11.2+). -/
  x : V
  /-- Distinguished single sink (§11.2+). -/
  y : V
  hdisj : Disjoint X Y
  hX : X.Nonempty
  hY : Y.Nonempty
end Networks

namespace Networks
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V]
def Network.I (N : Network V) : Finset V := Finset.univ \ (N.X ∪ N.Y)
end Networks

namespace Networks
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V]
def Network.IsCut (N : Network V) (S : Finset V) : Prop := N.x ∈ S ∧ N.y ∉ S
end Networks

namespace Networks
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V]
def Network.capOf (N : Network V) (S : Finset V) : ℕ := ∑ u ∈ S, ∑ v ∈ Sᶜ, N.cap u v
end Networks

namespace Networks
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V]
def Network.fIn (_N : Network V) (f : V → V → ℕ) (S : Finset V) : ℕ :=
  ∑ u ∈ Sᶜ, ∑ v ∈ S, f u v
end Networks

namespace Networks
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V]
def Network.fOut (_N : Network V) (f : V → V → ℕ) (S : Finset V) : ℕ :=
  ∑ u ∈ S, ∑ v ∈ Sᶜ, f u v
end Networks

namespace Networks
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V]
def Network.IsFlow (N : Network V) (f : V → V → ℕ) : Prop :=
  (∀ u v, f u v ≤ N.cap u v) ∧
  (∀ v ∈ N.I, N.fIn f {v} = N.fOut f {v})
end Networks

namespace Networks
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V]
def Network.IsMinCut (N : Network V) (S : Finset V) : Prop :=
  N.IsCut S ∧ ∀ S', N.IsCut S' → N.capOf S ≤ N.capOf S'
end Networks

namespace Networks
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V]
def Network.val (N : Network V) (f : V → V → ℕ) : ℤ :=
  (N.fOut f N.X : ℤ) - (N.fIn f N.X : ℤ)
end Networks

namespace Networks
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V]
def Network.IsMaxFlow (N : Network V) (f : V → V → ℕ) : Prop :=
  N.IsFlow f ∧ ∀ f', N.IsFlow f' → N.val f' ≤ N.val f
end Networks

namespace Networks
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V]
theorem maxFlow_min_cut (N : Network V) :
    ∃ (f : V → V → ℕ) (S : Finset V),
      N.IsMaxFlow f ∧ N.IsMinCut S ∧ N.val f = (N.capOf S : ℤ) := sorry
end Networks

Definitions:
- Max number of arc-disjoint directed $(x,y)$-paths in a digraph. The left-hand side of Menger's arc theorem 11.4: how many routes from
$x$ to $y$ can run simultaneously without any two sharing an arc.

\textbf{\textbf{!} \texttt{sorry} body.}  \emph{Repair:} \texttt{sSup} over $k$ admitting $k$ pairwise arc-disjoint
directed $(x,y)$-paths.  Needs a directed-path notion (\texttt{Digraph.IsDirectedPath} in
the ch-10 file) \textbf{and} an arc-list, which is \texttt{arcsOf} there --- itself
\texttt{sorry}-bodied.  Of the twelve, this is the one with the deepest dependency.

Statement: menger_arc_digraph. The number of independent routes you can run equals the number of links
an adversary must cut to stop you.  This is the first of the four Menger theorems
the chapter derives --- arc/edge and vertex versions, for digraphs and graphs --- two of
which were quoted without proof back in \S{}3.2.

\textbf{!} Steps 2 and 3 are not free: the network-level counts
(\texttt{Network.maxArcDisjointPaths}) and the digraph-level ones
(\texttt{maxArcDisjointDirectedPaths}) are \emph{separate} stubbed definitions, so once both are
repaired a lemma identifying them across the construction of step 1 will be needed.
Defining the network-level pair \emph{in terms of} the digraph-level pair applied to the
underlying digraph would make steps 2--3 definitional and is the better design.

an adversary must cut to stop you.  This is the first of the four Menger theorems
the chapter derives --- arc/edge and vertex versions, for digraphs and graphs --- two of
which were quoted without proof back in \S{}3.2.

(\texttt{Network.maxArcDisjointPaths}) and the digraph-level ones
(\texttt{maxArcDisjointDirectedPaths}) are \emph{separate} stubbed definitions, so once both are

\texttt{sorry}-bodied.  Of the twelve, this is the one with the deepest dependency.

informal_statement:
Definitions:
- $(p,q)$ is realisable by a simple bipartite graph: there is a $(0,1)$-matrix $B$ with row sums $p$ and\dots. Can two prescribed lists of degrees occur as the two sides of a
bipartite graph?  The book's $p = (3,2,2,2,1)$, $q = (3,3,2,1,1)$ is realisable
(figure 11.12), whereas $p = q = (5,4,4,2,1)$ is not (exercise 11.5.2) even though
the sums agree.

\textbf{!} Missing from Mathlib (0 hits for Gale--Ryser).  Carried as a
$(0,1)$-\textbf{matrix} \texttt{B : Fin m $\to$ Fin n $\to$ Bool} rather than a bipartite \texttt{SimpleGraph},
following the book's own closing remark: *With each simple bipartite graph $G$ \dots
we can associate an $m \times n$ matrix $B$ in which $b_ij = 1$ or $0$, depending on
whether $x_{i}y_{j}$ is an edge of $G$ or not.  Conversely, every $m \times n$ $(0,1)$-matrix
corresponds in this way to a simple bipartite graph.*  The two are equivalent and
the matrix avoids constructing a graph on \texttt{Fin m $\oplus$ Fin n} with a bipartition proof.
Due to Ryser (1957).

Statement: realisable_iff_reduced. The bipartite analogue of the Havel--Hakimi reduction for degree
sequences (exercise 1.5.7): the vertex $x_{1}$ may as well spend its $p_{1}$ edges on the
$p_{1}$ highest-demand vertices of $Y$.  Part (b) --- dropped here as procedural --- turns
this into a construction algorithm.

\textbf{!} Two departures, both flagged in the source comment.  (i) $q'$
uses \textbf{truncated} natural subtraction ($q j - 1$ is $0$ when $q j = 0$), which is
harmless only because a realisable $q$ has $q j \ge 1$ wherever row $0$ puts an edge ---
worth checking rather than assuming.  (ii) B&M's $q'$ is \textbf{re-sorted} into
nonincreasing order, which this statement elides; without re-sorting, $q'$ need not
satisfy (11.17), so this reduction cannot be chained with theorem 11.9 as the book
intends.  If the intent is to iterate the reduction, the re-sorting must be
restored.
formal_statement:
import Mathlib

open scoped Classical

namespace Networks
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V]
def RealisableBipartite {m n : ℕ} (p : Fin m → ℕ) (q : Fin n → ℕ) : Prop :=
  ∃ B : Fin m → Fin n → Bool,
    (∀ i, (Finset.univ.filter (fun j => B i j = true)).card = p i) ∧
    (∀ j, (Finset.univ.filter (fun i => B i j = true)).card = q j)
end Networks

namespace Networks
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V]
theorem realisable_iff_reduced {m n : ℕ} (p : Fin (m + 1) → ℕ) (q : Fin n → ℕ) :
    RealisableBipartite p q ↔
      RealisableBipartite (fun i : Fin m => p i.succ)
        (fun j : Fin n => q j - (if (j : ℕ) < p 0 then 1 else 0)) := sorry
end Networks

informal_statement:
Definitions:
- A network $N = (D, X, Y, c)$. A transportation network: goods are produced at the sources, consumed
at the sinks, and shipped along the arcs, each with a maximum throughput.

\textbf{!} Missing from Mathlib (0 hits for flow/network/capacity).
Capacity is carried as a \emph{function} \texttt{cap : V $\to$ V $\to$ $\mathbb{N}$}, with \texttt{cap u v = 0} encoding
"no arc $u \to v$"; this makes $f^{+}$/$f^{-}$ plain \texttt{Finset.sum}s.  \textbf{!} It cannot represent
\textbf{parallel arcs}, which is a real restriction --- lemma 11.4 is about a network in
which every arc has unit capacity, and B&M's digraphs may have several arcs between
the same pair.

The structure carries \textbf{both} $X$, $Y$ (the source/sink \emph{sets} of \S{}11.1) and the
distinguished $x$, $y$ used from \S{}11.2 onward.  That is because the book reduces
the first to the second: *adjoin two new vertices $x$ and $y$; join $x$ to each
vertex in $X$ by an arc of capacity $\infty$; join each vertex in $Y$ to $y$ by an arc
of capacity $\infty$; designate $x$ as the source and $y$ as the sink of $N'$* --- after
which *throughout the next three sections, we shall confine our attention to
networks that have a single source $x$ and a single sink $y$*.  That reduction is
exercise 11.1.4, which is deferred here (it needs an $\mathbb{N}\infty$-capacity parallel
carrier), so the two are simply both recorded in the structure.

\textbf{\textbf{!} Structural defect: $x$, $y$ are unrelated to $X$, $Y$.}  Nothing in the
structure requires \texttt{N.x $\in$ N.X}, let alone \texttt{N.X = \{N.x\}}.  But \texttt{val} is defined over
the \emph{set} $X$ while every \S{}11.2--\S{}11.3 result is about cuts separating the single
$x$ from the single $y$.  The two therefore measure different things, and \textbf{lemma
11.1, theorem 11.1 in both forms, corollary 11.1 and theorem 11.3 are all false as
stated}.

\emph{Counterexample} (one network refutes all of them).  $V = {x_{1}, x_{2}, y_{1}}$,
$X = {x_{1}, x_{2}}$, $Y = {y_{1}}$, \texttt{N.x = x$_{1}$}, \texttt{N.y = y$_{1}$}; capacities $c(x_{1},y_{1}) = c(x_{2},y_{1}) = 1$
and $0$ elsewhere.  Then $I = \emptyset$, so any $f$ within capacity is a flow; take
$f(x_{1},y_{1}) = f(x_{2},y_{1}) = 1$.
\item \texttt{val f = f$^{+}$(X) - f$^{-}$(X) = 2}.
\item $S = {x_{1}}$ is a cut ($x_{1} \in S$, $y_{1} \notin S$), with $f^{+}(S) - f^{-}(S) = 1$ and
  \texttt{cap S = 1}.
\item So lemma 11.1 asserts $2 = 1$; theorem 11.1 asserts $2 \le 1$.
\item Max flow value is $2$, minimum cut capacity is $1$, so theorem 11.3 asserts
  $2 = 1$.
\item Corollary 11.1 fails too: $f'(x_{1},y_{1}) = 1$, $f'(x_{2},y_{1}) = 0$ has
  \texttt{val f' = 1 = cap\{x$_{1}$\}}, yet $f'$ is not a maximum flow.

\emph{The repair} is to add the fields \texttt{hx : N.X = \{N.x\}} and \texttt{hy : N.Y = \{N.y\}} to the
structure (the book's standing convention for \S{}\S{}11.2--11.4), or equivalently to add
them as hypotheses on the affected theorems.  The \S{}11.1 results --- exercises 11.1.2
and 11.1.3 --- are unaffected and should keep the general $X$, $Y$.
- $f^{-}(S) = f(\bar{S}, S) = \sum_{u\notin S} \sum_{v\in S} f u v$. The total flow entering $S$.  Conservation forces the resultant flow
out of every intermediate vertex to vanish, which is what makes the resultant flow
out of $X$ equal the resultant flow into $Y$ (exercise 11.1.3) and hence \texttt{val f}
well defined.

The mirror of \texttt{fOut} with the two sums swapped.
- $f^{+}(S) = f(S, \bar{S}) = \sum_{u\in S} \sum_{v\notin S} f u v$. The total flow leaving $S$ --- sum over every arc with tail inside $S$
and head outside.  \textbf{!} This is \emph{not} the sum of the $f^{+}(v)$ over $v \in S$: arcs
internal to $S$ are counted there but not here.  Exercise 11.1.2 makes the exact
relationship precise, and it is the difference $f^{+} - f^{-}$ that behaves well.

\textbf{!} Missing from Mathlib.  A double \texttt{Finset.sum} over $S$ and
$S^{c}$, which the capacity-as-a-function carrier makes possible; $f u v = 0$ for a
non-arc contributes nothing.

Statement: sum_resultant_eq_fOut_sub_fIn. Summing the \emph{net} outflow over the vertices of $S$ gives the net
outflow of $S$ as a whole.  The book flags the trap: *in general,
$\sum_{v \in S} f^{+}(v) \ne f^{+}(S)$ and $\sum_{v \in S} f^{-}(v) \ne f^{-}(S)$* --- only the difference
behaves, and only because the internal arcs cancel.

\textbf{*} \textbf{Build this first} --- lemma 11.1 and theorem 11.1 both rest on
it, and it is where the $\mathbb{Z}$-valuedness of \texttt{val} earns its keep: in $\mathbb{N}$ step 3's
cancellation is false, since $f^{+}{v} - f^{-}{v}$ truncates at each vertex individually.
Note it needs \textbf{no} \texttt{IsFlow} hypothesis: it is pure bookkeeping about an arbitrary
$f$.
formal_statement:
import Mathlib

open scoped Classical

namespace Networks
structure Network (V : Type*) where
  /-- Capacity of arc `u → v` (`0` ⟺ no arc). -/
  cap : V → V → ℕ
  /-- Source set. -/
  X : Finset V
  /-- Sink set. -/
  Y : Finset V
  /-- Distinguished single source (§11.2+). -/
  x : V
  /-- Distinguished single sink (§11.2+). -/
  y : V
  hdisj : Disjoint X Y
  hX : X.Nonempty
  hY : Y.Nonempty
end Networks

namespace Networks
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V]
def Network.fIn (_N : Network V) (f : V → V → ℕ) (S : Finset V) : ℕ :=
  ∑ u ∈ Sᶜ, ∑ v ∈ S, f u v
end Networks

namespace Networks
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V]
def Network.fOut (_N : Network V) (f : V → V → ℕ) (S : Finset V) : ℕ :=
  ∑ u ∈ S, ∑ v ∈ Sᶜ, f u v
end Networks

namespace Networks
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V]
theorem sum_resultant_eq_fOut_sub_fIn (N : Network V) (f : V → V → ℕ) (S : Finset V) :
    ∑ v ∈ S, ((N.fOut f {v} : ℤ) - (N.fIn f {v} : ℤ))
      = (N.fOut f S : ℤ) - (N.fIn f S : ℤ) := sorry
end Networks

behaves, and only because the internal arcs cancel.

formal_statement:
import Mathlib

open scoped Classical

namespace Networks
structure Network (V : Type*) where
  /-- Capacity of arc `u → v` (`0` ⟺ no arc). -/
  cap : V → V → ℕ
  /-- Source set. -/
  X : Finset V
  /-- Sink set. -/
  Y : Finset V
  /-- Distinguished single source (§11.2+). -/
  x : V
  /-- Distinguished single sink (§11.2+). -/
  y : V
  hdisj : Disjoint X Y
  hX : X.Nonempty
  hY : Y.Nonempty
end Networks

namespace Networks
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V]
def Network.I (N : Network V) : Finset V := Finset.univ \ (N.X ∪ N.Y)
end Networks

namespace Networks
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V]
def Network.fIn (_N : Network V) (f : V → V → ℕ) (S : Finset V) : ℕ :=
  ∑ u ∈ Sᶜ, ∑ v ∈ S, f u v
end Networks

namespace Networks
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V]
def Network.fOut (_N : Network V) (f : V → V → ℕ) (S : Finset V) : ℕ :=
  ∑ u ∈ S, ∑ v ∈ Sᶜ, f u v
end Networks

namespace Networks
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V]
noncomputable def Network.maxArcDisjointPaths (_N : Network V) : ℕ := sorry
end Networks

namespace Networks
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V]
def Network.IsFlow (N : Network V) (f : V → V → ℕ) : Prop :=
  (∀ u v, f u v ≤ N.cap u v) ∧
  (∀ v ∈ N.I, N.fIn f {v} = N.fOut f {v})
end Networks

namespace Networks
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V]
def Network.val (N : Network V) (f : V → V → ℕ) : ℤ :=
  (N.fOut f N.X : ℤ) - (N.fIn f N.X : ℤ)
end Networks

namespace Networks
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V]
def Network.IsMaxFlow (N : Network V) (f : V → V → ℕ) : Prop :=
  N.IsFlow f ∧ ∀ f', N.IsFlow f' → N.val f' ≤ N.val f
end Networks

namespace Networks
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V]
theorem unitCapacity_maxFlow_eq_arcDisjoint (N : Network V) (hunit : ∀ u v, N.cap u v ≤ 1)
    {f : V → V → ℕ} (hf : N.IsMaxFlow f) :
    N.val f = (N.maxArcDisjointPaths : ℤ) := sorry
end Networks

import Mathlib

open scoped Classical

namespace Networks
structure Network (V : Type*) where
  /-- Capacity of arc `u → v` (`0` ⟺ no arc). -/
  cap : V → V → ℕ
  /-- Source set. -/
  X : Finset V
  /-- Sink set. -/
  Y : Finset V
  /-- Distinguished single source (§11.2+). -/
  x : V
  /-- Distinguished single sink (§11.2+). -/
  y : V
  hdisj : Disjoint X Y
  hX : X.Nonempty
  hY : Y.Nonempty
end Networks

namespace Networks
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V]
def Network.IsCut (N : Network V) (S : Finset V) : Prop := N.x ∈ S ∧ N.y ∉ S
end Networks

namespace Networks
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V]
def Network.capOf (N : Network V) (S : Finset V) : ℕ := ∑ u ∈ S, ∑ v ∈ Sᶜ, N.cap u v
end Networks

namespace Networks
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V]
def Network.IsMinCut (N : Network V) (S : Finset V) : Prop :=
  N.IsCut S ∧ ∀ S', N.IsCut S' → N.capOf S ≤ N.capOf S'
end Networks

namespace Networks
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V]
theorem unitCapacity_minCut_eq_minDestroying (N : Network V) (hunit : ∀ u v, N.cap u v ≤ 1)
    {S : Finset V} (hS : N.IsMinCut S) :
    N.capOf S = N.minArcsDestroyingPaths := sorry
end Networks

formal_statement:
import Mathlib

open scoped Classical

namespace Networks
structure Network (V : Type*) where
  /-- Capacity of arc `u → v` (`0` ⟺ no arc). -/
  cap : V → V → ℕ
  /-- Source set. -/
  X : Finset V
  /-- Sink set. -/
  Y : Finset V
  /-- Distinguished single source (§11.2+). -/
  x : V
  /-- Distinguished single sink (§11.2+). -/
  y : V
  hdisj : Disjoint X Y
  hX : X.Nonempty
  hY : Y.Nonempty
end Networks

namespace Networks
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V]
def Network.I (N : Network V) : Finset V := Finset.univ \ (N.X ∪ N.Y)
end Networks

namespace Networks
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V]
def Network.IsCut (N : Network V) (S : Finset V) : Prop := N.x ∈ S ∧ N.y ∉ S
end Networks

namespace Networks
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V]
def Network.capOf (N : Network V) (S : Finset V) : ℕ := ∑ u ∈ S, ∑ v ∈ Sᶜ, N.cap u v
end Networks

namespace Networks
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V]
def Network.fIn (_N : Network V) (f : V → V → ℕ) (S : Finset V) : ℕ :=
  ∑ u ∈ Sᶜ, ∑ v ∈ S, f u v
end Networks

namespace Networks
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V]
def Network.fOut (_N : Network V) (f : V → V → ℕ) (S : Finset V) : ℕ :=
  ∑ u ∈ S, ∑ v ∈ Sᶜ, f u v
end Networks

namespace Networks
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V]
def Network.IsFlow (N : Network V) (f : V → V → ℕ) : Prop :=
  (∀ u v, f u v ≤ N.cap u v) ∧
  (∀ v ∈ N.I, N.fIn f {v} = N.fOut f {v})
end Networks

namespace Networks
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V]
def Network.val (N : Network V) (f : V → V → ℕ) : ℤ :=
  (N.fOut f N.X : ℤ) - (N.fIn f N.X : ℤ)
end Networks

namespace Networks
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V]
theorem val_eq_capOf_iff (N : Network V) {f : V → V → ℕ} (hf : N.IsFlow f)
    {S : Finset V} (hS : N.IsCut S) :
    N.val f = (N.capOf S : ℤ) ↔
      (∀ u ∈ S, ∀ v ∈ Sᶜ, f u v = N.cap u v) ∧ (∀ u ∈ Sᶜ, ∀ v ∈ S, f u v = 0) := sorry
end Networks

import Mathlib

open scoped Classical

namespace Networks
structure Network (V : Type*) where
  /-- Capacity of arc `u → v` (`0` ⟺ no arc). -/
  cap : V → V → ℕ
  /-- Source set. -/
  X : Finset V
  /-- Sink set. -/
  Y : Finset V
  /-- Distinguished single source (§11.2+). -/
  x : V
  /-- Distinguished single sink (§11.2+). -/
  y : V
  hdisj : Disjoint X Y
  hX : X.Nonempty
  hY : Y.Nonempty
end Networks

namespace Networks
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V]
def Network.I (N : Network V) : Finset V := Finset.univ \ (N.X ∪ N.Y)
end Networks

namespace Networks
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V]
def Network.IsCut (N : Network V) (S : Finset V) : Prop := N.x ∈ S ∧ N.y ∉ S
end Networks

namespace Networks
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V]
def Network.fIn (_N : Network V) (f : V → V → ℕ) (S : Finset V) : ℕ :=
  ∑ u ∈ Sᶜ, ∑ v ∈ S, f u v
end Networks

namespace Networks
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V]
def Network.fOut (_N : Network V) (f : V → V → ℕ) (S : Finset V) : ℕ :=
  ∑ u ∈ S, ∑ v ∈ Sᶜ, f u v
end Networks

namespace Networks
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V]
def Network.IsFlow (N : Network V) (f : V → V → ℕ) : Prop :=
  (∀ u v, f u v ≤ N.cap u v) ∧
  (∀ v ∈ N.I, N.fIn f {v} = N.fOut f {v})
end Networks

namespace Networks
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V]
def Network.val (N : Network V) (f : V → V → ℕ) : ℤ :=
  (N.fOut f N.X : ℤ) - (N.fIn f N.X : ℤ)
end Networks

namespace Networks
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V]
theorem val_eq_fOut_sub_fIn (N : Network V) {f : V → V → ℕ} (hf : N.IsFlow f)
    {S : Finset V} (hS : N.IsCut S) :
    N.val f = (N.fOut f S : ℤ) - (N.fIn f S : ℤ) := sorry
end Networks

definitions.informal:
A transportation network: goods are produced at the sources, consumed
at the sinks, and shipped along the arcs, each with a maximum throughput.

\textbf{!} Missing from Mathlib (0 hits for flow/network/capacity).
Capacity is carried as a \emph{function} \texttt{cap : V $\to$ V $\to$ $\mathbb{N}$}, with \texttt{cap u v = 0} encoding
"no arc $u \to v$"; this makes $f^{+}$/$f^{-}$ plain \texttt{Finset.sum}s.  \textbf{!} It cannot represent

which every arc has unit capacity, and B&M's digraphs may have several arcs between
the same pair.

The structure carries \textbf{both} $X$, $Y$ (the source/sink \emph{sets} of \S{}11.1) and the
distinguished $x$, $y$ used from \S{}11.2 onward.  That is because the book reduces
the first to the second: *adjoin two new vertices $x$ and $y$; join $x$ to each
vertex in $X$ by an arc of capacity $\infty$; join each vertex in $Y$ to $y$ by an arc
of capacity $\infty$; designate $x$ as the source and $y$ as the sink of $N'$* --- after
which *throughout the next three sections, we shall confine our attention to
networks that have a single source $x$ and a single sink $y$*.  That reduction is
exercise 11.1.4, which is deferred here (it needs an $\mathbb{N}\infty$-capacity parallel
carrier), so the two are simply both recorded in the structure.

\textbf{\textbf{!} Structural defect: $x$, $y$ are unrelated to $X$, $Y$.}  Nothing in the
structure requires \texttt{N.x $\in$ N.X}, let alone \texttt{N.X = \{N.x\}}.  But \texttt{val} is defined over

networks that have a single source $x$ and a single sink $y$*.  That reduction is
exercise 11.1.4, which is deferred here (it needs an $\mathbb{N}\infty$-capacity parallel
carrier), so the two are simply both recorded in the structure.

\textbf{\textbf{!} Structural defect: $x$, $y$ are unrelated to $X$, $Y$.}  Nothing in the
structure requires \texttt{N.x $\in$ N.X}, let alone \texttt{N.X = \{N.x\}}.  But \texttt{val} is defined over
the \emph{set} $X$ while every \S{}11.2--\S{}11.3 result is about cuts separating the single
$x$ from the single $y$.  The two therefore measure different things, and \textbf{lemma
11.1, theorem 11.1 in both forms, corollary 11.1 and theorem 11.3 are all false as
stated}.

\emph{Counterexample} (one network refutes all of them).  $V = {x_{1}, x_{2}, y_{1}}$,
$X = {x_{1}, x_{2}}$, $Y = {y_{1}}$, \texttt{N.x = x$_{1}$}, \texttt{N.y = y$_{1}$}; capacities $c(x_{1},y_{1}) = c(x_{2},y_{1}) = 1$
and $0$ elsewhere.  Then $I = \emptyset$, so any $f$ within capacity is a flow; take
$f(x_{1},y_{1}) = f(x_{2},y_{1}) = 1$.
\item \texttt{val f = f$^{+}$(X) - f$^{-}$(X) = 2}.
\item $S = {x_{1}}$ is a cut ($x_{1} \in S$, $y_{1} \notin S$), with $f^{+}(S) - f^{-}(S) = 1$ and
  \texttt{cap S = 1}.
\item So lemma 11.1 asserts $2 = 1$; theorem 11.1 asserts $2 \le 1$.
\item Max flow value is $2$, minimum cut capacity is $1$, so theorem 11.3 asserts
  $2 = 1$.
\item Corollary 11.1 fails too: $f'(x_{1},y_{1}) = 1$, $f'(x_{2},y_{1}) = 0$ has
  \texttt{val f' = 1 = cap\{x$_{1}$\}}, yet $f'$ is not a maximum flow.

\emph{The repair} is to add the fields \texttt{hx : N.X = \{N.x\}} and \texttt{hy : N.Y = \{N.y\}} to the
structure (the book's standing convention for \S{}\S{}11.2--11.4), or equivalently to add
them as hypotheses on the affected theorems.  The \S{}11.1 results --- exercises 11.1.2
and 11.1.3 --- are unaffected and should keep the general $X$, $Y$.

definitions.title: Intermediate vertices $I = V \ (X \cup Y)$
definitions.informal:
The transit points of the network, which neither produce nor consume.
The conservation condition (11.2) applies exactly here --- what flows in must flow
out --- and that is what makes \texttt{val f} well defined (exercise 11.1.3).

\texttt{Finset.univ \textbackslash\{\} (X $\cup$ Y)}, so $I$ is a \texttt{Finset} and membership is
decidable --- needed by \texttt{IsFlow}'s second clause.

definitions.title: A cut $(S, \bar{S})$ with $x \in S$, $y \notin S$
definitions.informal:
A way of severing the network so the source is on one side and the
sink on the other.  Every unit of flow must cross every cut, which is why cuts
bound flows from above (theorem 11.1) --- and, more surprisingly, why the best cut
exactly matches the best flow (theorem 11.3).

\textbf{!} Missing from Mathlib.  Identified with the \emph{vertex set} $S$
rather than the arc set $(S, \bar{S})$, since $S$ determines the arcs and is far easier
to quantify over.  \texttt{capOf} then computes the arc set's capacity.  Note $y \notin S$ is
the book's $y \in \bar{S}$.

definitions.title: \texttt{cap (S, $\bar{S}$) = $\sum$\_\{u$\in$S\} $\sum$\_\{v$\notin$S\} c u v}
definitions.informal:
The total throughput of the severed arcs --- how much traffic could at
most cross that divide.  Since all the flow must pass through, it bounds \texttt{val f}
above.

\textbf{!} Missing from Mathlib.  Structurally identical to \texttt{fOut} with
\texttt{cap} in place of $f$, which is exactly why theorem 11.1's proof is a two-line
comparison.

definitions.title: $f^{-}(S) = f(\bar{S}, S) = \sum_{u\notin S} \sum_{v\in S} f u v$
definitions.informal:
The total flow entering $S$.  Conservation forces the resultant flow
out of every intermediate vertex to vanish, which is what makes the resultant flow
out of $X$ equal the resultant flow into $Y$ (exercise 11.1.3) and hence \texttt{val f}
well defined.

The mirror of \texttt{fOut} with the two sums swapped.

definitions.title: $f^{+}(S) = f(S, \bar{S}) = \sum_{u\in S} \sum_{v\notin S} f u v$
definitions.informal:
The total flow leaving $S$ --- sum over every arc with tail inside $S$
and head outside.  \textbf{!} This is \emph{not} the sum of the $f^{+}(v)$ over $v \in S$: arcs
internal to $S$ are counted there but not here.  Exercise 11.1.2 makes the exact
relationship precise, and it is the difference $f^{+} - f^{-}$ that behaves well.

\textbf{!} Missing from Mathlib.  A double \texttt{Finset.sum} over $S$ and
$S^{c}$, which the capacity-as-a-function carrier makes possible; $f u v = 0$ for a
non-arc contributes nothing.

definitions.title: A flow: (11.1) capacity constraint + (11.2) conservation at intermediate vertices
definitions.informal:
Nothing over-loaded, nothing accumulating.  The zero flow's existence
is what makes \texttt{exists\_maxFlow} non-vacuous.

The lower bound $0 \le f(a)$ of (11.1) is free: $f$ is $\mathbb{N}$-valued.
Conservation is stated as \texttt{fIn f \{v\} = fOut f \{v\}} on singletons, which unfolds to
the book's $f^{-}(v) = f^{+}(v)$ --- note \texttt{fIn}/\texttt{fOut} on a singleton are genuinely the
per-vertex quantities, since there are no arcs internal to a singleton.

definitions.title: \texttt{val f = f$^{+}$(X) $-$ f$^{-}$(X)}
definitions.informal:
The net rate at which the commodity travels from producers to
consumers.  Conservation at the intermediate vertices is what makes the two ways of
measuring it agree.

\textbf{!} \textbf{$\mathbb{Z}$-valued, and this is load-bearing.}  In $\mathbb{N}$ the
truncated subtraction would make exercise 11.1.2 --- the identity the whole chapter
rests on --- false, since individual terms $f^{+}(v) - f^{-}(v)$ are genuinely negative at
vertices absorbing more than they emit.  Every $f^{+} - f^{-}$ in this file is therefore
cast to $\mathbb{Z}$ before subtracting.

informal_statement:
Definitions:
- $G$ is critical: $\chi(H) < \chi(G)$ for every proper subgraph $H \subset G$. A critical graph is "minimally" $k$-chromatic: remove any vertex or
any edge and the chromatic number drops.  Critical graphs are useful precisely
because they carry the whole difficulty of a colouring problem --- every
$k$-chromatic graph contains a $k$-critical subgraph, so statements about
$k$-chromatic graphs reduce to the critical case, which is how corollary 8.1.1,
Brooks' theorem 8.4 and theorem 8.5 all begin.

The quantifier ranges over \texttt{G.Subgraph}, not over the order
on \texttt{SimpleGraph V}.  This is load-bearing (Scaffolding judgement 1): the
\texttt{SimpleGraph V} order can only \emph{remove edges}, never vertices, whereas the book's
"proper subgraph" includes $G - v$.  Under the weaker order $\bot$ on two vertices
would be vacuously 1-critical --- it has no proper edge-subgraph --- contradicting
exercise 8.1.7, which says the only 1-critical graph is $K_{1}$.

Statement: connected. If a graph were disconnected, its chromatic number would be the
maximum of those of its components --- colour each component independently.  So one
component already achieves $\chi(G)$, and that component is a proper subgraph with
the same chromatic number, contradicting criticality.  Corollary 8.2 strengthens
this considerably: every critical graph is not merely connected but a \emph{block},
having no cut vertex at all.

Step 3 is the whole content and is reusable: the same
"components colour independently" lemma is exercise 8.4.6 in its counting form
($\pi_k$ multiplies over components).  Worth proving once in a shared form.
formal_statement:
import Mathlib

open scoped Classical

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
def IsCritical {V : Type*} (G : SimpleGraph V) : Prop :=
  ∀ H : G.Subgraph, H < ⊤ → H.coe.chromaticNumber < G.chromaticNumber
end SimpleGraph

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
theorem IsCritical.connected
    {V : Type*} [Finite V] [Nonempty V] {G : SimpleGraph V} (h : G.IsCritical) :
    G.Connected := sorry
end SimpleGraph

would be vacuously 1-critical --- it has no proper edge-subgraph --- contradicting
exercise 8.1.7, which says the only 1-critical graph is $K_{1}$.

definitions.title: $G$ is uniquely $k$-colourable: any two $k$-colourings induce the same partition
definitions.informal:
Colours are arbitrary labels, so what a colouring really determines
is the partition into colour classes.  $G$ is uniquely $k$-colourable when that
partition is forced --- two $k$-colourings can then differ only by renaming the
colours.  Complete graphs are the obvious examples, which is why exercise 8.1.8
(no vertex cut of a $k$-critical graph induces a uniquely $(k-1)$-colourable
subgraph) generalises theorem 8.2 (no vertex cut is a clique).

\texttt{Coloring.colorClasses} is the induced partition, so the book's
"induce the same partition" is a literal equality of \texttt{colorClasses}.  Note this is
vacuously true when $G$ has no $k$-colouring at all; every use site supplies
colourability separately.

definitions.title: $G$ is $k$-critical: $k$-chromatic and critical
definitions.informal:
$k$-critical graphs are the irreducible witnesses to needing $k$
colours.  Exercise 8.1.7 classifies the small cases completely --- the only
1-critical graph is $K_{1}$, the only 2-critical graph is $K_{2}$, and the 3-critical
graphs are exactly the odd cycles --- and Brooks' theorem 8.4 consumes precisely
that classification to get its standing hypothesis $k \ge 4$.

\texttt{G.chromaticNumber = k} compares an $\mathbb{N}\infty$ with a coerced $\mathbb{N}$,
so $k$-chromaticity here also carries the information that $\chi(G) \ne \top$.

informal_statement:
Definitions:
- \texttt{IsRamseyBound n k l}: every graph on $n$ vertices has a $k$-clique or an $l$-indep set.\dots. \texttt{IsRamseyBound n k l} says $n$ is already large enough for that conclusion:
\texttt{$\forall$ G : SimpleGraph (Fin n), ($\exists$ s, G.IsNClique k s) $\lor$ ($\exists$ t, G.IsNIndepSet l t)}.

Fixing the carrier as \texttt{Fin n} rather than quantifying over all $n$-element types
is what makes \texttt{ramseyNumber} an \texttt{sInf} over $\mathbb{N}$ below.

Total disorder is impossible: any sufficiently large graph contains one kind of
order or the other.
- The Ramsey number $r(k, l)$. The exact threshold at which order becomes unavoidable.

\textbf{!} \textbf{\texttt{sInf $\emptyset$ = 0} is a live trap} until \texttt{exists\_isRamseyBound} is proved: without
it every \texttt{ramseyNumber k l} could silently be $0$, and every theorem below would
be about the wrong number.  That existence result is therefore not optional
scaffolding --- it gates the meaning of the definition itself.

Statement: abbott_lower_bound. Iterate part (b) from $r(3,3) = 6$, so $r(3,3) - 1 = 5$.  Taking $k = l = 2^{n-1}$
each step multiplies by $5$.  The witness is the $n$-fold composition of $C_{5}$
with itself.

The best \textbf{constructive} bound, versus Corollary 7.6's probabilistic one.  With
$k = 2^{n}$, \texttt{5$^{n}$ = k\^{}\{log$_{2}$5\} $\approx$ k\^{}\{2.32\}} is merely polynomial in $k$, while $2^{k/2}$
is exponential --- the gap the book remarks on.
formal_statement:
import Mathlib

open scoped Finset

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
def IsRamseyBound (n k l : ℕ) : Prop :=
  ∀ G : SimpleGraph (Fin n), (∃ s, G.IsNClique k s) ∨ (∃ t, G.IsNIndepSet l t)
end SimpleGraph

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
noncomputable def ramseyNumber (k l : ℕ) : ℕ :=
  sInf {n | SimpleGraph.IsRamseyBound n k l}
end SimpleGraph

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
theorem abbott_lower_bound (n : ℕ) :
    5 ^ n + 1 ≤ SimpleGraph.ramseyNumber (2 ^ n + 1) (2 ^ n + 1) := sorry
end SimpleGraph

informal_statement:
Definitions:
- A maximum matching: a matching no larger than which exists. Mathlib supplies "matching" (\texttt{Subgraph.IsMatching}), "saturates"
(\texttt{v $\in$ M.verts}) and "perfect" (\texttt{Subgraph.IsPerfectMatching}), but has \textbf{no
matching-number notion}, so maximality has to be said by hand:

    M.IsMatching $\land$ $\forall$ M', M'.IsMatching $\to$ M'.edgeSet.ncard $\le$ M.edgeSet.ncard

This is a \emph{global} maximum, not a maximal matching (one admitting no extension).
The two genuinely differ, and Berge's Theorem 5.1 is exactly the tool that
certifies the global property from a local check.
- $M$-alternating walk: consecutive edges alternate in/out of $M$. Walk along the graph using a matching edge, then a non-matching edge, then a
matching edge, and so on.  Rendered as a chain condition on consecutive edges:

    List.IsChain (fun e f => e $\in$ M.edgeSet $\leftrightarrow$ f $\notin$ M.edgeSet) p.edges

\textbf{!} Mathlib's \texttt{SimpleGraph.IsAlternating} (\texttt{Matching.lean}) is a \emph{graph-level}
relation between two graphs and is \textbf{not} this notion; do not reach for it.

Note the definition is on a \texttt{Walk}, not a \texttt{Path} --- the book's "path" is imposed
separately in \texttt{IsAugmenting} below via \texttt{p.IsPath}.

Alternating paths are the mechanism by which a matching improves: swapping which
edges along such a path belong to $M$ keeps $M$ a matching.
- $M$-augmenting path: alternating, both ends $M$-unsaturated. An alternating path both of whose endpoints are still unmatched.  Such a path has
odd length and begins and ends with non-matching edges, so it holds one more
non-$M$ edge than $M$ edge.  Flipping the roles along it --- discarding its
$M$-edges, adopting its non-$M$-edges --- yields a matching one edge \emph{larger},
which is why it is called augmenting.

\textbf{!} The conjunct $u \ne v$ is \textbf{load-bearing} and has no counterpart in the book's
wording.  Without it \texttt{Walk.nil} at an $M$-unsaturated vertex would satisfy every
other clause vacuously, so \emph{every} non-perfect matching would admit an
"augmenting path" and Berge's theorem would be false in the ($\Leftarrow$) direction.  The
book gets this for free because a path in its sense has at least one edge.

Statement: Thm 5.1 (Berge): a matching is maximum iff there is no augmenting path. Both directions are stated contrapositively relative to the book's phrasing: the
Lean $\leftrightarrow$ has "no augmenting path" on the right, so the book's first paragraph
proves ($\Rightarrow$) by contraposition and its second proves ($\Leftarrow$) by contraposition.

Augmenting paths are simultaneously the certificate of non-maximality and the
means of improvement --- which is what makes the Hungarian method of \S{}5.4 work.
formal_statement:
import Mathlib

open scoped Pointwise

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
def Subgraph.IsMaximumMatching {V : Type*} {G : SimpleGraph V} (M : G.Subgraph) : Prop :=
  M.IsMatching ∧ ∀ M' : G.Subgraph, M'.IsMatching → M'.edgeSet.ncard ≤ M.edgeSet.ncard
end SimpleGraph

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
def Walk.IsAlternatingWalk {V : Type*} [DecidableEq V] {G : SimpleGraph V}
    (M : G.Subgraph) {u v : V} (p : G.Walk u v) : Prop :=
  List.IsChain (fun e f => e ∈ M.edgeSet ↔ f ∉ M.edgeSet) p.edges
end SimpleGraph

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
def Walk.IsAugmenting {V : Type*} [DecidableEq V] {G : SimpleGraph V}
    (M : G.Subgraph) {u v : V} (p : G.Walk u v) : Prop :=
  u ≠ v ∧ p.IsPath ∧ p.IsAlternatingWalk M ∧ u ∉ M.verts ∧ v ∉ M.verts
end SimpleGraph

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
theorem berge_maximum_matching
    {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] {G : SimpleGraph V}
    {M : G.Subgraph} (hM : M.IsMatching) :
    M.IsMaximumMatching ↔ ¬ ∃ (u v : V) (p : G.Walk u v), p.IsAugmenting M := sorry
end SimpleGraph

Statement: Ex 5.3.4*: the Berge--Tutte defect formula (stated additively to avoid $\mathbb{N}$ subtraction). Tutte says a perfect matching exists exactly when $o(G - S) - |S| \le 0$ for all
$S$.  Berge's formula quantifies failure: the maximum, the \textbf{deficiency} $d$, is
exactly how many vertices a maximum matching leaves unsaturated; the remaining
$\nu - d$ pair up.

$d = 0$ recovers Theorem 5.4.  The general-graph analogue of the K\"onig--Ore defect
formula (5.2.6(a)).

Formalised additively as $2|M| + d = \nu$ to avoid $\mathbb{N}$ subtraction on the outside.

\textbf{!} Same caveat as \texttt{konig\_ore\_defect}: the \emph{inner} \texttt{oddComponents.ncard - S.ncard}
is still natural subtraction and truncates at $0$.  Here that is actually
\emph{correct}, since $S = \emptyset$ always contributes $o(G) - 0 \ge 0$ and the book's max is
over a set containing a non-negative value --- but it should be re-verified rather
than assumed.
formal_statement:
import Mathlib

open scoped Pointwise

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
def Subgraph.IsMaximumMatching {V : Type*} {G : SimpleGraph V} (M : G.Subgraph) : Prop :=
  M.IsMatching ∧ ∀ M' : G.Subgraph, M'.IsMatching → M'.edgeSet.ncard ≤ M.edgeSet.ncard
end SimpleGraph

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
theorem berge_tutte_defect
    {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] {G : SimpleGraph V}
    {M : G.Subgraph} (hM : M.IsMaximumMatching) :
    2 * M.edgeSet.ncard + (⨆ S : Set V, (((⊤ : G.Subgraph).deleteVerts S).coe.oddComponents.ncard
      - S.ncard)) = Fintype.card V := sorry
end SimpleGraph

informal_statement:
Ex 5.2.2(a): bipartite perfect-matching criterion. Hall's Theorem 5.2 gives a matching saturating $X$ from the condition on subsets
of $X$ alone.  Demanding it for \emph{all} subsets of $V$ is symmetric in $X$ and $Y$,
so it yields matchings saturating each side; together these force $|X| = |Y|$ and
a perfect matching.

\textbf{!} \texttt{hcov : X $\cup$ Y = Set.univ} is \textbf{required} and has no counterpart in the book's
wording, which takes "bipartition" to cover all vertices by definition.
Mathlib's \texttt{IsBipartiteWith} does not, so without \texttt{hcov} the bipartition could
miss vertices that no matching could ever saturate.
formal_statement:
import Mathlib

open scoped Pointwise

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
theorem bipartite_perfectMatching_iff
    {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
    {X Y : Set V} (hbip : G.IsBipartiteWith X Y) (hcov : X ∪ Y = Set.univ) :
    (∃ M : G.Subgraph, M.IsPerfectMatching) ↔
      ∀ S : Set V, S.ncard ≤ (⋃ v ∈ S, G.neighborSet v).ncard := sorry
end SimpleGraph
title: Ex 5.2.2(a): bipartite perfect-matching criterion

informal_statement:
Definitions:
- $v$ is a cut vertex: $G$ is connected but deleting $v$ disconnects it. A \texttt{SimpleGraph} is loopless by construction, so the second (component-counting)
characterisation is the usable one and is what is taken as the definition here.
Specialising it to a \emph{connected} $G$ --- where $\omega(G) = 1$ --- turns
$\omega(G - v) > \omega(G)$ into "$G - v$ is disconnected", giving
\texttt{G.Connected $\land$ $\lnot$ (G.induce \{v\}$^{c}$).Connected}.

Folding \texttt{G.Connected} into the definition is what makes \texttt{IsBlock} below read as
the book's "connected graph that has no cut vertices".
- A block: connected with no cut vertex. Only the first sentence is formalised: \texttt{G.Connected $\land$ $\forall$ v, $\lnot$ G.IsCutVertex v},
i.e. "$G$ \emph{is} a block".  The relative notion "a block \emph{of} $G$" (a maximal such
subgraph) and the decomposition "every graph is the union of its blocks" are not
defined in this file --- nothing in chapter 3 as formalised here needs them.

The second sentence is a theorem, proved below as
\texttt{block\_three\_vertices\_two\_connected}.

Statement: block_edges_on_common_cycle. The standard device of turning an edge into a vertex, upgrading "any two
\emph{vertices} lie on a common cycle" to "any two \emph{edges} do".
formal_statement:
import Mathlib

open scoped Classical

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
def IsCutVertex (G : SimpleGraph V) (v : V) : Prop :=
  G.Connected ∧ ¬ (G.induce ({v}ᶜ : Set V)).Connected
end SimpleGraph

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
def IsBlock (G : SimpleGraph V) : Prop :=
  G.Connected ∧ ∀ v : V, ¬ G.IsCutVertex v
end SimpleGraph

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
theorem block_edges_on_common_cycle
    (hblock : G.IsBlock) (h : 3 ≤ Fintype.card V)
    (e₁ e₂ : Sym2 V) (he₁ : e₁ ∈ G.edgeSet) (he₂ : e₂ ∈ G.edgeSet) (hne : e₁ ≠ e₂) :
    ∃ (w : V) (c : G.Walk w w), c.IsCycle ∧ e₁ ∈ c.edges ∧ e₂ ∈ c.edges := sorry
end SimpleGraph
title: block_edges_on_common_cycle

import Mathlib

open scoped Classical

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
def IsCutVertex (G : SimpleGraph V) (v : V) : Prop :=
  G.Connected ∧ ¬ (G.induce ({v}ᶜ : Set V)).Connected
end SimpleGraph

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
def IsVertexCut (G : SimpleGraph V) (S : Finset V) : Prop :=
  (↑S : Set V) ⊂ Set.univ ∧ ¬ (G.induce ((↑S : Set V)ᶜ)).Connected
end SimpleGraph

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
def IsBlock (G : SimpleGraph V) : Prop :=
  G.Connected ∧ ∀ v : V, ¬ G.IsCutVertex v
end SimpleGraph

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
noncomputable def vertexConnectivity (G : SimpleGraph V) : ℕ :=
  if ∃ S : Finset V, G.IsVertexCut S then
    sInf {n : ℕ | ∃ S : Finset V, G.IsVertexCut S ∧ S.card = n}
  else
    Fintype.card V - 1
end SimpleGraph

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
theorem block_three_vertices_two_connected
    (hb : G.IsBlock) (h : 3 ≤ Fintype.card V) :
    2 ≤ G.vertexConnectivity := sorry
end SimpleGraph

informal_statement:
Lem 4.4.1: for nonadjacent $u,v$ with $d(u)+d(v) \ge \nu$, $G$ is hamiltonian iff $G+uv$ is. The book's proof is two sentences only because it \emph{reuses} the $S$/$T$ counting
argument (4.4) from Theorem 4.3.  In Lean that argument has to exist somewhere
concrete --- so this lemma, not Dirac, is the right place to write it out, and
Dirac then follows from the closure machinery.

Expanded, (4.4) is: from a Hamilton cycle of $G + uv$ that must use $uv$, extract
a Hamilton path $v_{1} \dots v_\nu$ in $G$ with $v_{1} = u$, $v_\nu = v$.  Put
$S = {v_{i} | u ~ v_{i+1}}$ and $T = {v_{i} | v_{i} ~ v}$.  Then $v_\nu \notin S \cup T$ gives
$|S \cup T| < \nu$, and $S \cap T = \emptyset$ because a common $v_{i}$ would close the Hamilton
cycle $v_{1} \dots v_{i} v_\nu v_{\nu-1} \dots v_{i+1} v_{1}$ in $G$.  Hence
$d(u) + d(v) = |S| + |T| < \nu$.

namespace SimpleGraph

    (hdeg : Fintype.card V ≤ G.degree u + G.degree v) :
    G.IsHamiltonian ↔ (G ⊔ SimpleGraph.edge u v).IsHamiltonian := sorry
end SimpleGraph

Definitions:
- A walk is internally disjoint from a subgraph $H$: no \emph{internal} vertex lies in $H$. The walk may start and end on $H$, but between those endpoints it
must stay entirely outside $H$.  This is what makes the bridge relation an
equivalence, and it is why a bridge is a maximal chunk of the graph hanging off
$H$ and touching it only at its attachment points.

\texttt{p.support.tail.dropLast} is the walk's interior --- drop the
first vertex (\texttt{tail}) and the last (\texttt{dropLast}).  \textbf{!} This is \textbf{not} the repo's
\texttt{InternallyDisjoint} (\texttt{TwoConnected.lean:58}), which relates a walk to another
\emph{walk}; here the second argument is a \texttt{Subgraph}.  A walk of length $\le 1$ has empty
interior and so is vacuously internally disjoint from everything --- which is
intended, and is what makes \texttt{bridgeRel} reflexive on single edges.
- B&M's relation $~$ on $E(G) \ E(H)$: $e_{1} ~ e_{2}$ iff joined by a walk internally disjoint from $H$\dots. Two edges outside $H$ are related when you can travel from one to the
other without passing through $H$.  Grouping edges into classes carves
$G - E(H)$ into the pieces that hang off $H$ --- those pieces are the bridges.

\texttt{Relation.EqvGen} wraps the book's raw condition in its
reflexive--symmetric--transitive closure, which \emph{discharges} the book's "it is easy
to verify" rather than proving it: whatever the raw relation does, the closure is
an equivalence by construction.  This is a deliberate trade --- the file gains an
equivalence for free, at the cost that \texttt{bridgeRel} is a priori coarser than $\sim$.
It is not actually coarser (the book's $\sim$ really is an equivalence), but nothing
here proves that, so do not appeal to "\texttt{bridgeRel e f} gives a single connecting
walk" --- it gives a \emph{chain} of them.  Several skeletons below rely on this
distinction.
- The bridge of $H$ in $G$ containing the edge $e$: the subgraph induced by $e$'s $~$-class. A bridge is one of the connected pieces remaining when $H$ is
removed, together with the attachment points where it touches $H$.  The three
"immediate" facts quoted above are \texttt{bridgeOf\_connected},
\texttt{exists\_path\_internallyDisjoint} and \texttt{bridge\_inter\_subset\_cycle} below --- none of
them is actually immediate once $\sim$ is a closure.  In planar graph theory bridges
carry the argument: theorem 9.8 says inner bridges of a cycle avoid one another,
theorem 9.9 that a bridge avoiding every outer bridge is transferable, and together
these drive Kuratowski's theorem 9.10.

Indexed by a \emph{representative edge} $e$ rather than by a class,
so "the bridge containing $e$"; two edges give the same bridge exactly when
\texttt{bridgeRel H e f}.  Built with \texttt{Subgraph.mk} directly --- \textbf{not} with
\texttt{SimpleGraph.toSubgraph} (\texttt{Subgraph.lean:559}), which is \emph{spanning} and would put
every vertex of $G$ into every bridge.  Note \texttt{verts} is the union of the class's
edges, so it automatically includes the attachment points.

\textbf{!} Because \texttt{bridgeRel} is reflexive for \emph{any} $e$ (it is an \texttt{EqvGen}), \texttt{bridgeOf H e}
is nonempty even for an $e$ that is not an edge of $G$ at all --- it then has two
vertices and no edges.  Statements about bridges must therefore carry
\texttt{e $\in$ G.edgeSet \textbackslash\{\} H.edgeSet} explicitly.  Two of them below originally omitted it and
were false as a result; both now carry it (see the module header).

Statement: bridgeOf_connected. A bridge is one connected lump: its edges all lie in one $\sim$-class,
and $\sim$ relates edges precisely when a walk avoiding $H$'s interior joins them.

Together with \texttt{exists\_path\_internallyDisjoint} this is one of
two facts B&M wave through and that everything downstream (theorems 9.6, 9.7 and
exercise 9.4.3) actually consumes.  Step 3 is the real content and is worth
extracting as a lemma about \texttt{bridgeRel} chains, since the same induction is needed
for the companion result.
formal_statement:
import Mathlib

open scoped Classical

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
def Walk.InternallyDisjointFrom {V : Type*} {G : SimpleGraph V}
    (H : G.Subgraph) {u v : V} (p : G.Walk u v) : Prop :=
  ∀ x ∈ p.support.tail.dropLast, x ∉ H.verts
end SimpleGraph

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
def bridgeRel {V : Type*} (G : SimpleGraph V) (H : G.Subgraph) :
    Sym2 V → Sym2 V → Prop :=
  Relation.EqvGen fun e₁ e₂ =>
    e₁ ∈ G.edgeSet \ H.edgeSet ∧ e₂ ∈ G.edgeSet \ H.edgeSet ∧
    ∃ (u v : V) (p : G.Walk u v), p.InternallyDisjointFrom H ∧
      p.edges.head? = some e₁ ∧ p.edges.getLast? = some e₂
end SimpleGraph

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
def bridgeOf {V : Type*} (G : SimpleGraph V) (H : G.Subgraph) (e : Sym2 V) :
    G.Subgraph where
  verts := {x | ∃ f, G.bridgeRel H e f ∧ x ∈ f}
  Adj u v := G.Adj u v ∧ G.bridgeRel H e s(u, v)
  adj_sub h := h.1
  edge_vert h := ⟨_, h.2, Sym2.mem_mk_left _ _⟩
  symm u v h := ⟨h.1.symm, by rw [Sym2.eq_swap]; exact h.2⟩
end SimpleGraph

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
theorem bridgeOf_connected {V : Type*} (G : SimpleGraph V) (H : G.Subgraph) (e : Sym2 V)
    (he : e ∈ G.edgeSet \ H.edgeSet) :
    ((G.bridgeOf H e).coe).Connected := sorry
end SimpleGraph

formal_statement:
import Mathlib

open scoped Classical

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
def Walk.InternallyDisjointFrom {V : Type*} {G : SimpleGraph V}
    (H : G.Subgraph) {u v : V} (p : G.Walk u v) : Prop :=
  ∀ x ∈ p.support.tail.dropLast, x ∉ H.verts
end SimpleGraph

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
def bridgeRel {V : Type*} (G : SimpleGraph V) (H : G.Subgraph) :
    Sym2 V → Sym2 V → Prop :=
  Relation.EqvGen fun e₁ e₂ =>
    e₁ ∈ G.edgeSet \ H.edgeSet ∧ e₂ ∈ G.edgeSet \ H.edgeSet ∧
    ∃ (u v : V) (p : G.Walk u v), p.InternallyDisjointFrom H ∧
      p.edges.head? = some e₁ ∧ p.edges.getLast? = some e₂
end SimpleGraph

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
def bridgeOf {V : Type*} (G : SimpleGraph V) (H : G.Subgraph) (e : Sym2 V) :
    G.Subgraph where
  verts := {x | ∃ f, G.bridgeRel H e f ∧ x ∈ f}
  Adj u v := G.Adj u v ∧ G.bridgeRel H e s(u, v)
  adj_sub h := h.1
  edge_vert h := ⟨_, h.2, Sym2.mem_mk_left _ _⟩
  symm u v h := ⟨h.1.symm, by rw [Sym2.eq_swap]; exact h.2⟩
end SimpleGraph

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
theorem bridge_tripod_of_three_attachments
    {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] {G : SimpleGraph V}
    {u : V} {c : G.Walk u u} (hc : c.IsCycle) (e : Sym2 V)
    (he : e ∈ G.edgeSet \ c.toSubgraph.edgeSet)
    {v₁ v₂ v₃ : V} (h₁₂ : v₁ ≠ v₂) (h₁₃ : v₁ ≠ v₃) (h₂₃ : v₂ ≠ v₃)
    (ha : ∀ i ∈ ({v₁, v₂, v₃} : Set V),
      i ∈ (G.bridgeOf c.toSubgraph e).verts ∩ c.toSubgraph.verts) :
    ∃ (v₀ : V), v₀ ∈ (G.bridgeOf c.toSubgraph e).verts \ c.toSubgraph.verts ∧
      ∃ (P₁ : G.Walk v₀ v₁) (P₂ : G.Walk v₀ v₂) (P₃ : G.Walk v₀ v₃),
        P₁.IsPath ∧ P₂.IsPath ∧ P₃.IsPath ∧
        (∀ x, x ∈ P₁.support → x ∈ P₂.support → x = v₀) ∧
        (∀ x, x ∈ P₁.support → x ∈ P₃.support → x = v₀) ∧
        (∀ x, x ∈ P₂.support → x ∈ P₃.support → x = v₀) := sorry
end SimpleGraph

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
theorem brooks_chromaticNumber_le_maxDegree
    {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] [Nonempty V] {G : SimpleGraph V} [DecidableRel G.Adj]

informal_statement:
Definitions:
- $G$ is critical: $\chi(H) < \chi(G)$ for every proper subgraph $H \subset G$. A critical graph is "minimally" $k$-chromatic: remove any vertex or
any edge and the chromatic number drops.  Critical graphs are useful precisely
because they carry the whole difficulty of a colouring problem --- every
$k$-chromatic graph contains a $k$-critical subgraph, so statements about
$k$-chromatic graphs reduce to the critical case, which is how corollary 8.1.1,
Brooks' theorem 8.4 and theorem 8.5 all begin.

The quantifier ranges over \texttt{G.Subgraph}, not over the order
on \texttt{SimpleGraph V}.  This is load-bearing (Scaffolding judgement 1): the
\texttt{SimpleGraph V} order can only \emph{remove edges}, never vertices, whereas the book's
"proper subgraph" includes $G - v$.  Under the weaker order $\bot$ on two vertices
would be vacuously 1-critical --- it has no proper edge-subgraph --- contradicting
exercise 8.1.7, which says the only 1-critical graph is $K_{1}$.
- $G$ is $k$-critical: $k$-chromatic and critical. $k$-critical graphs are the irreducible witnesses to needing $k$
colours.  Exercise 8.1.7 classifies the small cases completely --- the only
1-critical graph is $K_{1}$, the only 2-critical graph is $K_{2}$, and the 3-critical
graphs are exactly the odd cycles --- and Brooks' theorem 8.4 consumes precisely
that classification to get its standing hypothesis $k \ge 4$.

\texttt{G.chromaticNumber = k} compares an $\mathbb{N}\infty$ with a coerced $\mathbb{N}$,
so $k$-chromaticity here also carries the information that $\chi(G) \ne \top$.

Statement: brooks_iff_edge_bound. Theorem 8.1 already gives $2\varepsilon \ge \nu(k-1)$ for a $k$-critical graph; the
exercise's content is the extra $+1$, which says the bound is never \emph{exactly}
attained --- not every vertex can have degree exactly $k - 1$.  That is precisely
Brooks in disguise: a $(k-1)$-regular critical graph would have $\chi = k = \Delta + 1$,
which Brooks forbids outside the two exceptional families.

Both sides are pinned to \texttt{Type} (not \texttt{Type*}) so that the two
quantifications range over the same universe and the $\leftrightarrow$ is well-formed.  Note the
statement quantifies over graphs, so each direction \emph{instantiates} the assumed side
at a graph it constructs --- this is an equivalence of schemas, not of propositions
about one fixed $G$.
formal_statement:
import Mathlib

open scoped Classical

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
def IsCritical {V : Type*} (G : SimpleGraph V) : Prop :=
  ∀ H : G.Subgraph, H < ⊤ → H.coe.chromaticNumber < G.chromaticNumber
end SimpleGraph

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
def IsKCritical {V : Type*} (G : SimpleGraph V) (k : ℕ) : Prop :=
  G.chromaticNumber = k ∧ G.IsCritical
end SimpleGraph

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
theorem brooks_iff_edge_bound :
    (∀ {V : Type} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] [Nonempty V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj],
        G.Connected → (∀ n, Odd n → IsEmpty (G ≃g cycleGraph n)) → G ≠ ⊤ →
        G.chromaticNumber ≤ G.maxDegree)
    ↔
    (∀ {V : Type} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] [Nonempty V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
        {k : ℕ}, G.IsKCritical k → 4 ≤ k → G ≠ ⊤ →
        Fintype.card V * (k - 1) + 1 ≤ 2 * G.edgeFinset.card) := sorry
end SimpleGraph

Statement: card_farGraph_le. Two genuinely geometric inputs, neither in Mathlib:
1. \textbf{Any four points in the plane determine an angle $\ge 90^{\circ}$} --- a convex-hull

2. \textbf{The law of cosines consequence}: an angle $\ge 90^{\circ}$ at $x_{j}$ with both

formal_statement:

open scoped Finset

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
def farGraph {n : ℕ} (x : Fin n → EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin 2)) : SimpleGraph (Fin n) where

    [DecidableRel (farGraph x).Adj]

    #(farGraph x).edgeFinset ≤ n ^ 2 / 3 := sorry

informal_statement:
Ex 5.1.1(b): number of perfect matchings of $K_{n,n}$ is $n!$. Every vertex of $X$ may be matched to any vertex of $Y$, so a perfect matching is
exactly a bijection $X \to Y$.  There are $n!$ of those.

This is why the optimal assignment problem of \S{}5.5 has $n!$ candidate solutions
and brute force is hopeless --- the book makes exactly that point on p. 94.
formal_statement:
import Mathlib

theorem card_perfectMatching_completeBipartite (n : ℕ) :
    Nat.card {M : (completeBipartiteGraph (Fin n) (Fin n)).Subgraph // M.IsPerfectMatching}
      = n.factorial := sorry
end SimpleGraph

informal_statement:
Ex 5.1.1(b): number of perfect matchings of $K_{2n}$ is $(2n)! / (2^n n!)$. A perfect matching of $K_{2n}$ partitions $2n$ labelled objects into $n$
unordered pairs.  Lining them up gives $(2n)!$ arrangements; each matching arises
from $2^n \cdot n!$ of them (swap within each pair, permute the pairs).  So the count
is $(2n)! / (2^n \cdot n!)$, the double factorial $(2n-1)!! = 1 \cdot 3 \cdot 5 \cdots (2n-1)$.

\textbf{!} The Lean statement uses \textbf{natural-number division}.  It happens to be exact
here, but the proof cannot manipulate it as division --- it must establish
\texttt{Nat.card \dots \emph{ (2 \^{} n } n !) = (2 * n)!} and then divide, or the \texttt{Nat.div} will
obstruct every rewrite.
formal_statement:
import Mathlib

open scoped Pointwise

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
theorem card_perfectMatching_completeGraph (n : ℕ) :
    Nat.card {M : (⊤ : SimpleGraph (Fin (2 * n))).Subgraph // M.IsPerfectMatching}
      = (2 * n).factorial / (2 ^ n * n.factorial) := sorry
end SimpleGraph
