informal_statement:
card_simpleGraph_fin. A simple graph on a labelled vertex set is determined by which of the $C(n,2)$
possible edges are present.

\textbf{!} Mathlib has a \texttt{Fintype (SimpleGraph (Fin n))} instance but \textbf{no cardinality
lemma}, so this genuinely has to be proved.  The route is an equiv
\texttt{SimpleGraph (Fin n) $\simeq$ (Sym2 (Fin n) \textbackslash\{\} diagonal $\to$ Bool)}, or via
\texttt{Finset.powerset} on the non-diagonal \texttt{Sym2}s --- the \texttt{Sym2} bookkeeping is the
work, not the arithmetic.

informal_statement:
Definitions:
- The unit-distance graph on a finite point set in the plane. Join $i, j$ when \texttt{dist (x i) (x j) = 1}.  Carrier \texttt{EuclideanSpace $\mathbb{R}$ (Fin 2)}.

The geometry enters as a forbidden subgraph: two points have at most \textbf{two}
common unit-distance neighbours (two unit circles meet in $\le$ 2 points), so the
graph has no $K_{2,3}$, and 7.3.4(b) bounds $\varepsilon$.

\textbf{+} Fully defined, \texttt{symm} and \texttt{loopless} both discharged --- no \texttt{sorry}.

\textbf{!} The $i \ne j$ conjunct in \texttt{Adj} is doing real work: without it, \texttt{dist (x i) (x i)
= 0 $\ne$ 1} would still exclude loops, but only if the $x i$ are \emph{distinct points}.
Since $x$ is not assumed injective, two indices may carry the same point, and
$i \ne j$ is what keeps the graph simple in that case.

Statement: card_unitDistanceGraph_le_of_diam_one. In a diameter-1 set, a pair at distance exactly $1$ is a \emph{diameter pair}.  The
key geometric fact: two diameter pairs must cross or share a point --- if $ab$ and
$cd$ were disjoint diameters, one of the four cross distances would exceed $1$.

That crossing property forces the diameter graph to have $\le n$ edges.

Contrast exercise 7.3.4(c), where without the diameter restriction the bound is
of order $n^{3/2}$; bounding the diameter collapses it to \textbf{linear}.
formal_statement:
import Mathlib

open scoped Finset

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
def unitDistanceGraph {n : ℕ} (x : Fin n → EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin 2)) : SimpleGraph (Fin n) where
  Adj i j := i ≠ j ∧ Dist.dist (x i) (x j) = 1
  symm := by rintro i j ⟨h1, h2⟩; exact ⟨h1.symm, by rwa [_root_.dist_comm]⟩
  loopless := by rintro i ⟨h, -⟩; exact h rfl
end SimpleGraph

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
theorem card_unitDistanceGraph_le_of_diam_one
    {n : ℕ} (x : Fin n → EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin 2))
    [DecidableRel (unitDistanceGraph x).Adj]
    (hdiam : Metric.diam (Set.range x) = 1) :
    #(unitDistanceGraph x).edgeFinset ≤ n := sorry
end SimpleGraph

card_unitDistanceGraph_le_of_diam_one. In a diameter-1 set, a pair at distance exactly $1$ is a \emph{diameter pair}.  The
key geometric fact: two diameter pairs must cross or share a point --- if $ab$ and
$cd$ were disjoint diameters, one of the four cross distances would exceed $1$.

That crossing property forces the diameter graph to have $\le n$ edges.

Definitions:
- The number of spanning trees $\tau(G)$: the number of tree subgraphs $T \le G$ on the full vertex set. \textbf{!} $\tau(G)$ counts the \emph{distinct} spanning trees, \textbf{not} the
non-isomorphic ones.  B&M stress the difference: $K_{6}$ has six non-isomorphic spanning
trees (figure 2.1) but $6^{4} = 1296$ distinct ones.  $\tau$ satisfies deletion--contraction
(theorem 2.8) and, for complete graphs, Cayley's formula (theorem 2.9); the general
determinant formula is chapter 12's matrix-tree theorem.

"Spanning" is automatic: a \texttt{T : SimpleGraph W} lives on the whole
vertex type, so \texttt{T $\le$ H $\land$ T.IsTree} already means a spanning tree.  \textbf{!} \texttt{IsTree} bundles
\texttt{Connected}, which requires \texttt{Nonempty W} --- so on an empty carrier $\tau = 0$.  That is
where \texttt{cayley} fails at $n = 0$.

Statement: cayley. \textbf{!} B&M caution that $n^{n-2}$ counts \emph{distinct} spanning trees, not
non-isomorphic ones: $K_{6}$ has six non-isomorphic ones but $6^{4} = 1296$ distinct.

four steps are from scratch --- the largest single item in the chapter.

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]

  Nat.card {T : SimpleGraph W // T ≤ H ∧ T.IsTree}
end SimpleGraph

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
theorem cayley (n : ℕ) :
    numSpanningTrees (⊤ : SimpleGraph (Fin n)) = n ^ (n - 2) := sorry
end SimpleGraph

informal_statement:
chromaticIndex_le_four_of_maxDegree_three. The edge chromatic number $\chi'(G)$ is the chromatic number of the line
graph $L(G)$, whose vertices are the edges of $G$ with adjacency "shares an end".
So Brooks' \emph{vertex}-colouring theorem yields an \emph{edge}-colouring bound, recovering
for cubic graphs what Vizing's theorem 6.2 gives in general.

Two departures from the book, both weakenings.  (i) $\chi'$ is
spelled as \texttt{$\chi$(lineGraph)}; there is no separate \texttt{chromaticIndex} here.  (ii) The
book says \emph{loopless}, which in B&M permits parallel edges; \texttt{SimpleGraph} has none,
so this is the simple-graph case only.  With multiplicities the degree count in
step 1 is unchanged, but \texttt{lineGraph} would have to be redefined, so the weakening
is deliberate.  Note also that the exercise is stated with $\Delta = 3$ exactly, not
$\Delta \le 3$; only $\le$ is used.

    (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj] (h : G.maxDegree = 3) :
    (G.lineGraph).chromaticNumber ≤ 4 := sorry
end SimpleGraph

informal_statement:
chromaticNumber_ge_of_card_edges. Many edges force many colours: each colour class is edge-free, so
large classes leave too little room for edges.  Equality holds exactly for
balanced complete multipartite graphs, where every non-edge is inside a class and
all classes have the same size.

Stated multiplicatively over $\mathbb{R}$ --- $\nu^{2}/(\nu^{2} - 2\varepsilon)$ would need
division and a proof that the denominator is nonzero.  (It always is: $G$ simple
gives $2\varepsilon \le \nu(\nu-1) < \nu^{2}$, so $\nu^{2} - 2\varepsilon \ge \nu > 0$ whenever $V$ is nonempty, whence
the \texttt{[Nonempty V]} hypothesis.)  $\chi$ is replaced by an arbitrary $k$ with
\texttt{G.Colorable k}, dodging $\mathbb{N}\infty$; this is equivalent to the book's statement, since
the right-hand side is monotone in $k$ and $\chi$ is the least colourable $k$.

title: chromaticNumber_ge_of_card_edges
statement_informal:
chromaticNumber_ge_of_card_edges. Many edges force many colours: each colour class is edge-free, so
large classes leave too little room for edges.  Equality holds exactly for
balanced complete multipartite graphs, where every non-edge is inside a class and
all classes have the same size.

Stated multiplicatively over $\mathbb{R}$ --- $\nu^{2}/(\nu^{2} - 2\varepsilon)$ would need
division and a proof that the denominator is nonzero.  (It always is: $G$ simple
gives $2\varepsilon \le \nu(\nu-1) < \nu^{2}$, so $\nu^{2} - 2\varepsilon \ge \nu > 0$ whenever $V$ is nonempty, whence
the \texttt{[Nonempty V]} hypothesis.)  $\chi$ is replaced by an arbitrary $k$ with
\texttt{G.Colorable k}, dodging $\mathbb{N}\infty$; this is equivalent to the book's statement, since
the right-hand side is monotone in $k$ and $\chi$ is the least colourable $k$.

edge running between them.  The book's $G + H$ (disjoint union) is Mathlib's
$\oplus g$, and "joining each vertex of $G$ to each vertex of $H$" is exactly

and \texttt{loopless} are inherited and need no proof.

Statement: chromaticNumber_join. No colour can be used on both sides of a join, so the two palettes are
forced to be disjoint and the chromatic numbers simply add.  This makes joins a
convenient way to build graphs of prescribed chromatic number, and is why the wheel

carriers), so it is ordinary addition, but the casts still need care --- extracting
$a$, $b$ as naturals up front, as in step 1, keeps the arithmetic in $\mathbb{N}$.
\texttt{[Nonempty $\alpha$]}, \texttt{[Nonempty $\beta$]} ensure both sides genuinely contribute.

informal_statement:
chromaticNumber_le_five_of_odd_cycles_meet. Odd cycles are the sole obstruction to 2-colourability, so if they
all pile up on one shortest cycle, only a bounded amount of extra colour is needed
to handle them.  Minimality in step 2 is what makes the cycle \emph{induced}, and hence
3-colourable rather than merely small.

The hypothesis quantifies over all pairs of closed walks that
are cycles of odd length, and asks for a common \emph{support} vertex.  Note $h$ is
also applied with $p = q$ in step 2's minimality argument, where it is vacuous ---
the content is only in the disjointness contradiction of step 4.
formal_statement:
import Mathlib

open scoped Classical

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
theorem chromaticNumber_le_five_of_odd_cycles_meet {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V]
    (G : SimpleGraph V)
    (h : ∀ (u w : V) (p : G.Walk u u) (q : G.Walk w w), p.IsCycle → q.IsCycle →
          Odd p.length → Odd q.length → ∃ x, x ∈ p.support ∧ x ∈ q.support) :
    G.chromaticNumber ≤ 5 := sorry
end SimpleGraph

informal_statement:
chromaticNumber_le_maxDegree_add_one. Colour the vertices one at a time in any order: when a vertex's turn
comes it has at most $\Delta$ neighbours, so at most $\Delta$ colours are forbidden and one
of $\Delta + 1$ is always free.  The book observes the bound *is sometimes very much
greater than the actual value* --- bipartite graphs are 2-chromatic with arbitrarily
large $\Delta$ --- making it weaker than Vizing's edge analogue (theorem 6.2) in one
sense; and weaker in a second sense too, since \emph{many} graphs satisfy $\chi' = \Delta + 1$
whereas Brooks' theorem 8.4 shows only two families satisfy $\chi = \Delta + 1$.

The book's route is recorded because it is the book's, but the
direct route is preferred: it avoids depending on \texttt{exists\_isKCritical\_subgraph}
and \texttt{IsKCritical.minDegree\_ge}, both of which are substantially harder than this
corollary.  This is the cheapest genuine win in the file --- a good first fill.

    {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj] :
    G.chromaticNumber ≤ G.maxDegree + 1 := sorry

informal_statement:
Definitions:
- $\pi_k(G)$, the number of distinct proper $k$-colourings. Count the proper colourings as \emph{labelled} objects, not up to
permutation of the colours --- the triangle example is exactly the warning against
quotienting.  Birkhoff (1912) introduced this counting approach as a possible
route to the four-colour conjecture.

\texttt{Nat.card (G.Coloring (Fin k))} rather than \texttt{Fintype.card}:
the two agree over a \texttt{Fintype}, but \texttt{Nat.card} needs no instance, which lets the
\S{}8.4 statements elaborate over \texttt{Subgraph} and component carriers without bespoke
\texttt{Fintype} derivations.  A \texttt{G.Coloring (Fin k)} is a function on vertices, so
distinctness is pointwise --- precisely the book's criterion.

Statement: chromaticPolynomial_coeff_card_sub_one. The second coefficient of the chromatic polynomial simply counts the
edges.  The mechanism is that each deletion--contraction step peels off exactly one
copy of the contracted graph's leading term, and the contracted graph has degree
one less --- so the $k^{\nu-1}$ coefficient decrements once per edge.  This is a first
small step toward the general question of which polynomials are chromatic, and it
is what makes exercise 8.4.2(b) possible.

$p$ is a hypothesis rather than a construction, which is why
step 1 is needed at all --- without uniqueness there is no link between the $p$ given
here and the one corollary 8.6 builds.  That uniqueness lemma is worth stating once
and reusing in exercises 8.4.2(b) and 8.4.8.
formal_statement:
import Mathlib

open scoped Classical

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
noncomputable def numColorings {V : Type*} (G : SimpleGraph V) (k : ℕ) : ℕ :=
  Nat.card (G.Coloring (Fin k))
end SimpleGraph

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
theorem chromaticPolynomial_coeff_card_sub_one {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] [Nonempty V]
    (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj] {p : Polynomial ℤ}
    (hp : ∀ k : ℕ, p.eval (k : ℤ) = (G.numColorings k : ℤ)) :
    p.coeff (Fintype.card V - 1) = -(G.edgeFinset.card : ℤ) := sorry
end SimpleGraph

Statement: chromaticPolynomial_no_root_gt_card. $\pi_k(G)$ counts colourings, so it is positive at every integer
$k \ge \chi(G)$, and $\chi(G) \le \nu$ always.  The exercise strengthens this from integers to
all reals: beyond $\nu$ the polynomial has no zero whatsoever.  The book notes that
the roots of chromatic polynomials \emph{exhibit an unexpected regularity} for planar
graphs, citing Tutte (1970) on their connection with the golden ratio.

Over $\mathbb{R}$ here (not $\mathbb{Z}$ as in corollary 8.6), since the claim is
about real roots; $hp$ ties $p$ to the integer-valued counting function at naturals
only, which is exactly what step 1 needs.  Step 2 is the substantial piece and is of
independent interest --- it is the standard proof that $\pi_k$ is a polynomial at all,
and an alternative to corollary 8.6's induction.

import Mathlib

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]

end SimpleGraph

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
theorem chromaticPolynomial_no_root_gt_card {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] [Nonempty V]
    (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj] {p : Polynomial ℝ}
    (hp : ∀ k : ℕ, p.eval (k : ℝ) = (G.numColorings k : ℝ))
    {x : ℝ} (hx : p.eval x = 0) :
    x ≤ Fintype.card V := sorry
end SimpleGraph

informal_statement:
Definitions:
- join. $G \lor H$, rebuilt on Mathlib: within-side edges from $\oplus g$, all cross
edges from \texttt{completeBipartiteGraph}. \texttt{symm}/\texttt{loopless} are inherited from $\sqcup$.

Lay the two graphs side by side keeping all their own edges, then add every
edge running between them.  The book's $G + H$ (disjoint union) is Mathlib's
$\oplus g$, and "joining each vertex of $G$ to each vertex of $H$" is exactly
\texttt{completeBipartiteGraph V W}, so

    join G H = (G $\oplus$g H) $\sqcup$ completeBipartiteGraph V W

on carrier $V \oplus W$.  Building it as a $\sqcup$ of two existing graphs means \texttt{symm}
and \texttt{loopless} are inherited and need no proof.

The building block of the graphs \texttt{Cmn} below.
- The sorted (ascending) degree sequence of $G$. Simply list how many neighbours each vertex has, smallest first.

Degree is written \texttt{Nat.card (G.neighborSet v)} rather than \texttt{G.degree v}, so the
definition works for any graph on a \texttt{Fintype} without threading a
\texttt{DecidableRel G.Adj} instance; the two agree when $V$ is finite.

The book indexes from $1$ ($d_{1} \le \dots \le d_\nu$); the Lean list is $0$-indexed, so the
book's $d_m$ is \texttt{degreeSequence.getD (m - 1) 0}.  Statements below that quote
Theorem 4.5 must account for that shift.

Chv\'atal's Theorem 4.5 reads hamiltonicity off this list alone; Theorem 4.6 and
Corollary 4.6 compare two such lists via \texttt{DegreeMajorised}.
- $C_{m,n} = K_m \lor (K_m^c + K_{n-2m})$, with $+$ the Mathlib disjoint sum $\oplus g$. Take $m$ "hub" vertices forming a complete graph, $m$ isolated vertices, and a
complete graph on the remaining $n - 2m$; then join every hub to everything
else.  Carrier \texttt{Fin m $\oplus$ (Fin m $\oplus$ Fin (n - 2 * m))}, with $K_m^{c} = \bot$ on \texttt{Fin m}.

Degrees: the $m$ hubs have degree $n - 1$, the $m$ isolated vertices have degree
$m$, and the remaining $n - 2m$ have degree $n - m - 1$.  That is the degree
sequence Theorem 4.6 majorises against.

\textbf{!} The side condition $1 \le m < n/2$ is \textbf{not} carried in the type.  For $m = 0$
or $2m > n$ the definition still elaborates (with $n - 2 * m$ truncating to $0$)
but no longer matches the book's figure.  Callers must supply the bound.
- $G$ is degree-majorised by $H$: same order, and every sorted-degree entry of $G$ is $\le$ the\dots. Line up both degree sequences in increasing order and compare entry by entry;
$G$ is degree-majorised by $H$ when $H$ wins or ties at every position.

Quantifying over \emph{all} $i : \mathbb{N}$ with \texttt{getD i 0} rather than over \texttt{Fin $\nu$} is
deliberate: past the end of both lists the comparison is $0 \le 0$, so the extra
indices are harmless and no bounds proof has to be threaded through.

Statement: Thm 4.6: a nonhamiltonian simple graph with $\nu \ge 3$ is degree-majorised by some $C_{m,\nu}$. The family ${C_{m,\nu}}$ consists of the \textbf{degree-maximal} nonhamiltonian graphs:
any nonhamiltonian graph has degrees dominated, position by position, by one of
them.

Corollary 4.6 --- bounding the edge count of a nonhamiltonian graph reduces to
computing $\varepsilon(C_{m,\nu})$.
formal_statement:
import Mathlib

open scoped Classical

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
def join {V W : Type*} (G : SimpleGraph V) (H : SimpleGraph W) : SimpleGraph (V ⊕ W) :=
  (G ⊕g H) ⊔ completeBipartiteGraph V W
end SimpleGraph

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
noncomputable def degreeSequence {V : Type*} [Fintype V] (G : SimpleGraph V) : List ℕ :=
  (Finset.univ.val.map fun v => Nat.card (G.neighborSet v)).sort (· ≤ ·)
end SimpleGraph

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
def Cmn (m n : ℕ) : SimpleGraph (Fin m ⊕ (Fin m ⊕ Fin (n - 2 * m))) :=
  (⊤ : SimpleGraph (Fin m)).join
    ((⊥ : SimpleGraph (Fin m)) ⊕g (⊤ : SimpleGraph (Fin (n - 2 * m))))
end SimpleGraph

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
def DegreeMajorised {V W : Type*} [Fintype V] [Fintype W]
    (G : SimpleGraph V) (H : SimpleGraph W) : Prop :=
  Fintype.card V = Fintype.card W ∧
    ∀ i : ℕ, G.degreeSequence.getD i 0 ≤ H.degreeSequence.getD i 0
end SimpleGraph

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
theorem chvatal_degree_majorised (hν : 3 ≤ Fintype.card V) (hnh : ¬ G.IsHamiltonian) :
    ∃ m : ℕ, 0 < m ∧ 2 * m < Fintype.card V ∧
      DegreeMajorised G (Cmn m (Fintype.card V)) := sorry
end SimpleGraph
title: Thm 4.6: a nonhamiltonian simple graph with $\nu \ge 3$ is degree-majorised by some $C_{m,\nu}$

definitions.informal:
Line up both degree sequences in increasing order and compare entry by entry;
$G$ is degree-majorised by $H$ when $H$ wins or ties at every position.

Quantifying over \emph{all} $i : \mathbb{N}$ with \texttt{getD i 0} rather than over \texttt{Fin $\nu$} is
deliberate: past the end of both lists the comparison is $0 \le 0$, so the extra
indices are harmless and no bounds proof has to be threaded through.

informal_statement:
Definitions:
- A vertex cut: a proper subset $S$ whose deletion leaves $G$ disconnected. $V'$ is a \texttt{Finset V}, and "$G - V'$ is disconnected" is
\texttt{$\lnot$ (G.induce (↑S)$^{c}$).Connected}.  The conjunct \texttt{↑S $\subset$ Set.univ} records that a
vertex cut is a \emph{proper} subset: without it $S = V$ would qualify vacuously,
since Mathlib's \texttt{Connected} is false on the empty induced graph.

A $k$-vertex cut is the pair \texttt{G.IsVertexCut S $\land$ S.card = k}; that is exactly
what \texttt{vertexConnectivity} minimises over.
- Vertex connectivity $\kappa(G)$. The book's case split is on "$G$ has a pair of distinct nonadjacent vertices";
the Lean split is on the equivalent "$G$ has a vertex cut at all", which is the
condition the two branches actually need.  So
\item some cut exists $\Rightarrow$ \texttt{$\kappa$ = sInf \{S.card | G.IsVertexCut S\}};
\item no cut exists (the complete graphs) $\Rightarrow$ $\kappa = \nu - 1$.

\texttt{sInf} on $\mathbb{N}$ is Mathlib's \texttt{Nat.sInf}, with \texttt{sInf $\emptyset$ = 0}; the $if$ guard means
that fallback is never reached here.  Natural subtraction makes $\nu - 1 = 0$
when $V$ is empty, matching "trivial $\Rightarrow$ $\kappa = 0$".

Statement: chvatal_erdos_hamiltonian. $\alpha$ is the independence number and $\kappa$ the connectivity, so the
hypothesis says the graph is at least as well connected as it is "spread out".  This
is one of the most elegant sufficient conditions for hamiltonicity known, and the
whole bridge apparatus of \S{}9.4 that survives in this file exists to reach it --- it is
the prize of the surviving combinatorial core.

\textbf{!} \texttt{h$\nu$ : 3 $\le$ Fintype.card V} is \textbf{load-bearing} and is \emph{not} in
B&M --- the statement is false without it.  $K_{2}$ has $\alpha = 1$ and $\kappa = 1$, so $\alpha \le \kappa$
holds, yet $K_{2}$ has no Hamilton cycle, there being no cycle of length two.  ($K_{1}$ is
similar.)  Step 5 is where most of the work sits; step 4's cut argument is the part
most likely to need its own supporting lemma.
formal_statement:
import Mathlib

open scoped Classical

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
def IsVertexCut (G : SimpleGraph V) (S : Finset V) : Prop :=
  (↑S : Set V) ⊂ Set.univ ∧ ¬ (G.induce ((↑S : Set V)ᶜ)).Connected
end SimpleGraph

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
noncomputable def vertexConnectivity (G : SimpleGraph V) : ℕ :=
  if ∃ S : Finset V, G.IsVertexCut S then
    sInf {n : ℕ | ∃ S : Finset V, G.IsVertexCut S ∧ S.card = n}
  else
    Fintype.card V - 1
end SimpleGraph

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
theorem chvatal_erdos_hamiltonian
    {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
    (hν : 3 ≤ Fintype.card V)
    (hconn : G.Connected)
    (h : G.indepNum ≤ G.vertexConnectivity) :
    G.IsHamiltonian := sorry
end SimpleGraph

informal_statement:
Thm 4.5 (counting form): the Chv\'atal degree condition implies hamiltonicity. \textbf{!} The hypothesis is formalised in \textbf{counting form}, not by indexing the sorted
degree sequence.  The book's $d_m \le m$ says "at least $m$ vertices have degree
$\le m$", and $d_{\nu-m} < \nu - m$ says "at least $\nu - m$ vertices have degree
$< \nu - m$" --- precisely the two \texttt{Finset.filter} cardinalities in \texttt{hcond}.  This
avoids all $1$- versus $0$-indexing hazards around \texttt{degreeSequence}, at the cost
of no longer looking like the book's inequality.

The book's $m < \nu/2$ is written $2 * m < \nu$, and $m \ge 1$ is made explicit
(the book's $m$ is a degree $d'(u)$, and $m = 0$ is excluded by connectivity
considerations implicit in "as large as possible").
formal_statement:
import Mathlib

open scoped Classical

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
theorem chvatal_hamiltonian (hν : 3 ≤ Fintype.card V)
    (hcond : ∀ m : ℕ, 1 ≤ m → 2 * m < Fintype.card V →
      ¬ (m ≤ (Finset.univ.filter fun v => G.degree v ≤ m).card ∧
         Fintype.card V - m ≤
           (Finset.univ.filter fun v => G.degree v < Fintype.card V - m).card)) :
    G.IsHamiltonian := sorry
end SimpleGraph

Ex 4.2.4*: Chv\'atal's Hamilton-path degree condition (counting form). The Hamilton-\emph{path} counterpart of Theorem 4.5, with thresholds shifted by one.
Formalised in counting form, exactly as Theorem 4.5 is --- see the note there on
why indexing the sorted sequence is avoided.

Note the strict $d_m < m$ here versus $d_m \le m$ in Theorem 4.5; the \texttt{hcond}

import Mathlib

open scoped Classical

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
theorem chvatal_hamiltonian_path (hν : 2 ≤ Fintype.card V)
    (hcond : ∀ m : ℕ, 1 ≤ m → 2 * m < Fintype.card V + 1 →
      ¬ (m ≤ (Finset.univ.filter fun v => G.degree v < m).card ∧
         Fintype.card V - m + 1 ≤
           (Finset.univ.filter fun v => G.degree v < Fintype.card V - m).card)) :
    ∃ (a b : V) (p : G.Walk a b), p.IsHamiltonian := sorry
end SimpleGraph

informal_statement:
Definitions:
- The generalised Ramsey number $r(G_{1},\dots,G_m)$ over Mathlib's containment $\sqsubseteq$. Instead of a monochromatic \emph{complete} subgraph, a monochromatic copy of a
prescribed graph.  All $G_{i}$ complete recovers \texttt{ramseyNumberMulti}.

"Subgraph isomorphic to $G_{i}$" is Mathlib's containment $\sqsubseteq$, and the colour-$i$
graph is \texttt{fromEdgeSet \{e | $\chi$ e = i $\land$ $\lnot$ e.IsDiag\}} --- the \texttt{$\lnot$ IsDiag} guard being
what stops the diagonal from creating spurious loops.

\textbf{!} Same \texttt{sInf $\emptyset$ = 0} trap again, with \textbf{no} existence lemma for this notion
either.  So all four generalised-Ramsey results below are vacuous as stated.

\textbf{!} The graphs are indexed by \texttt{W : Fin m $\to$ Type*}, so each $G_{i}$ may live on a
different carrier --- flexible, but it means \texttt{![pathGraph 4, pathGraph 4]} below
must elaborate its motive carefully.

Statement: chvatal_tree_complete. One of the cleanest results in generalised Ramsey theory: the answer depends on
the tree only through its \textbf{number of vertices}, not its shape.

\emph{Lower bound.}  Partition $(m-1)(n-1)$ points into $n-1$ groups of $m-1$; red
inside groups, blue between.  Red is a disjoint union of $K_{m-1}$s, too small
for a tree on $m$ vertices; blue is complete $(n-1)$-partite, so its largest
clique has $n-1$ vertices --- no $K_{n}$.

\emph{Upper bound.}  On $(m-1)(n-1) + 1$ points, if blue has no $K_{n}$ then Tur\'an-type
reasoning gives red minimum degree $\ge m-1$ somewhere, and the sub-lemma embeds
$T$.

\textbf{!} Same heterogeneous-carrier spelling as part (b).

\textbf{!} The upper bound's "Tur\'an-type reasoning" is genuinely \S{}7.3's Theorem 7.9 ---
so this exercise depends on the \emph{next} section, not just on \S{}7.2.
formal_statement:
import Mathlib

open scoped Finset

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
noncomputable def generalisedRamseyNumber {m : ℕ} {W : Fin m → Type*}
    (F : ∀ i, SimpleGraph (W i)) : ℕ :=
  sInf {n | ∀ χ : Sym2 (Fin n) → Fin m,
    ∃ i, F i ⊑ SimpleGraph.fromEdgeSet {e | χ e = i ∧ ¬ e.IsDiag}}
end SimpleGraph

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
theorem chvatal_tree_complete
    {W : Type} [Fintype W] {T : SimpleGraph W} (hT : T.IsTree)
    {m n : ℕ} (hm : Fintype.card W = m) (hn : 1 ≤ n) :
    generalisedRamseyNumber (W := ![W, Fin n])
        (Fin.cons T (Fin.cons (⊤ : SimpleGraph (Fin n)) finZeroElim))
      = (m - 1) * (n - 1) + 1 := sorry
end SimpleGraph

informal_statement:
compl_connected_of_not_connected. Every pair is joined in $G^{c}$ by a path of length at most $2$, so $G^{c}$ is
connected --- indeed of diameter $\le 2$.  Equivalently: \textbf{at least one of $G$, $G^{c}$ is
always connected}.

\textbf{!} Steps 2--3 need $u \ne w$ and $v \ne w$, which follow from them being
in different components; and "different components" must be extracted from
\texttt{$\lnot$ Connected} --- \texttt{Preconnected} failing gives an unreachable pair.

theorem compl_connected_of_not_connected [Nonempty V] (h : ¬ G.Connected) :
    Gᶜ.Connected := sorry
end SimpleGraph

compl_diam_lt_of_diam_gt. A graph and its complement cannot both be "spread out": if $G$ is very

disconnected graph, so \texttt{3 < G.diam} silently carries "$G$ is connected" --- worth

informal_statement:
Definitions:
- A $k$-factor: a $k$-regular spanning subgraph. Keep every vertex, and select edges so each vertex retains exactly $k$.  A
$1$-factor is precisely a perfect matching; a $2$-factor is a spanning union of
disjoint cycles.

Degree is written \texttt{(H.neighborSet v).ncard} rather than \texttt{H.degree v} --- equal in
value, but avoiding the \texttt{Fintype}/\texttt{DecidableRel} instance juggling that
\texttt{Subgraph.degree} would drag in on every use.
- $G$ is $k$-factorable: it decomposes into edge-disjoint $k$-factors. The edges of $G$ partition into groups, each a $k$-regular spanning subgraph.
The book's $G = H_{1} \cup \dots \cup H_n$ becomes $(\bigsqcup i, H i) = \top$ in the \texttt{Subgraph} lattice,
where $\top$ is $G$ viewed as a subgraph of itself.

Being $1$-factorable means the edges split into perfect matchings: $K_{n,n}$ and
$K_{2n}$ are (exercise 5.1.5(a)(i)), the Petersen graph is not
(exercise 5.1.5(a)(ii)).

$1$-factorability is exactly proper edge colouring with $\Delta$ colours: each factor
is a colour class.  So exercise 5.1.5(a)(ii) is the statement that the Petersen
graph has chromatic index $4$, which reappears in \texttt{EdgeColourings.lean}.

Statement: Ex 5.1.5(a)(i): $K_{n,n}$ is 1-factorable. Label both sides by \texttt{ZMod n}; for each $i$, let $H_{i}$ join $x_a$ to $y_{a+i}$ for
every $a$.  Each $H_{i}$ is a 1-factor, distinct $i$ give edge-disjoint matchings,
and every edge $x_a y_b$ occurs in exactly the one with $i = b - a$.

In chapter 6's language: $K_{n,n}$ has chromatic index $n$, its minimum possible
value --- the round-robin schedule for $n$ workers and $n$ jobs.
formal_statement:
import Mathlib

open scoped Pointwise

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
def Subgraph.IsKFactor {V : Type*} {G : SimpleGraph V} (H : G.Subgraph) (k : ℕ) : Prop :=
  H.IsSpanning ∧ ∀ v, (H.neighborSet v).ncard = k
end SimpleGraph

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
def IsKFactorable {V : Type*} (G : SimpleGraph V) (k : ℕ) : Prop :=
  ∃ (n : ℕ) (H : Fin n → G.Subgraph), (∀ i, (H i).IsKFactor k) ∧
    (∀ i j, i ≠ j → Disjoint (H i).edgeSet (H j).edgeSet) ∧
    (⨆ i, H i) = ⊤
end SimpleGraph

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
theorem completeBipartite_one_factorable (n : ℕ) :
    (completeBipartiteGraph (Fin n) (Fin n)).IsKFactorable 1 := sorry
end SimpleGraph
title: Ex 5.1.5(a)(i): $K_{n,n}$ is 1-factorable

Statement: Ex 5.1.5(a)(i): $K_{2n}$ is 1-factorable. The classical round-robin schedule.  Fix one vertex at the centre and arrange the
other $2n - 1$ in a circle.  In round $i$, match the centre with circle vertex
$i$ and pair the remaining circle vertices symmetrically about the line through
it.  Rotating gives $2n - 1$ rounds, each a perfect matching, together using
every edge exactly once.

So $2n$ players can be scheduled in $2n - 1$ rounds with every pair meeting once.
This fails for odd order, where no perfect matching exists at all.

import Mathlib

open scoped Pointwise

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]

  H.IsSpanning ∧ ∀ v, (H.neighborSet v).ncard = k
end SimpleGraph

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
def IsKFactorable {V : Type*} (G : SimpleGraph V) (k : ℕ) : Prop :=
  ∃ (n : ℕ) (H : Fin n → G.Subgraph), (∀ i, (H i).IsKFactor k) ∧
    (∀ i j, i ≠ j → Disjoint (H i).edgeSet (H j).edgeSet) ∧
    (⨆ i, H i) = ⊤
end SimpleGraph

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
theorem completeGraph_even_one_factorable (n : ℕ) :

title: Ex 5.1.5(a)(i): $K_{2n}$ is 1-factorable
statement_informal:
Ex 5.1.5(a)(i): $K_{2n}$ is 1-factorable. The classical round-robin schedule.  Fix one vertex at the centre and arrange the
other $2n - 1$ in a circle.  In round $i$, match the centre with circle vertex
$i$ and pair the remaining circle vertices symmetrically about the line through
it.  Rotating gives $2n - 1$ rounds, each a perfect matching, together using
every edge exactly once.

So $2n$ players can be scheduled in $2n - 1$ rounds with every pair meeting once.
This fails for odd order, where no perfect matching exists at all.

definitions.title: A $k$-factor: a $k$-regular spanning subgraph
definitions.informal:
Keep every vertex, and select edges so each vertex retains exactly $k$.  A
$1$-factor is precisely a perfect matching; a $2$-factor is a spanning union of
disjoint cycles.

Degree is written \texttt{(H.neighborSet v).ncard} rather than \texttt{H.degree v} --- equal in
value, but avoiding the \texttt{Fintype}/\texttt{DecidableRel} instance juggling that
\texttt{Subgraph.degree} would drag in on every use.

definitions.title: $G$ is $k$-factorable: it decomposes into edge-disjoint $k$-factors
definitions.informal:
The edges of $G$ partition into groups, each a $k$-regular spanning subgraph.
The book's $G = H_{1} \cup \dots \cup H_n$ becomes $(\bigsqcup i, H i) = \top$ in the \texttt{Subgraph} lattice,
where $\top$ is $G$ viewed as a subgraph of itself.

Being $1$-factorable means the edges split into perfect matchings: $K_{n,n}$ and
$K_{2n}$ are (exercise 5.1.5(a)(i)), the Petersen graph is not
(exercise 5.1.5(a)(ii)).

$1$-factorability is exactly proper edge colouring with $\Delta$ colours: each factor
is a colour class.  So exercise 5.1.5(a)(ii) is the statement that the Petersen
graph has chromatic index $4$, which reappears in \texttt{EdgeColourings.lean}.

informal_statement:
Definitions:

Statement: Ex 5.1.6*: $K_{2n+1}$ decomposes into $n$ connected 2-factors (Walecki). A connected 2-factor is precisely a Hamilton cycle --- a spanning connected
2-regular subgraph must be one cycle through every vertex.  So this asks for a
decomposition of $K_{2n+1}$'s edges into Hamilton cycles.

The count works: $K_{2n+1}$ has $n(2n+1)$ edges and each Hamilton cycle uses
$2n + 1$, so exactly $n$ cycles are needed.

The odd-order companion to 5.1.5(a)(i): odd complete graphs decompose into
Hamilton cycles, even ones into perfect matchings.
formal_statement:
import Mathlib

open scoped Pointwise

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
def Subgraph.IsKFactor {V : Type*} {G : SimpleGraph V} (H : G.Subgraph) (k : ℕ) : Prop :=
  H.IsSpanning ∧ ∀ v, (H.neighborSet v).ncard = k
end SimpleGraph

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
theorem completeGraph_odd_two_factorable (n : ℕ) (hn : 1 ≤ n) :
    ∃ H : Fin n → (⊤ : SimpleGraph (Fin (2 * n + 1))).Subgraph,
      (∀ i, (H i).IsKFactor 2 ∧ (H i).Connected) ∧
      (∀ i j, i ≠ j → Disjoint (H i).edgeSet (H j).edgeSet) ∧ (⨆ i, H i) = ⊤ := sorry
end SimpleGraph
title: Ex 5.1.6*: $K_{2n+1}$ decomposes into $n$ connected 2-factors (Walecki)
statement_informal:

decomposition of $K_{2n+1}$'s edges into Hamilton cycles.

The count works: $K_{2n+1}$ has $n(2n+1)$ edges and each Hamilton cycle uses
$2n + 1$, so exactly $n$ cycles are needed.

The odd-order companion to 5.1.5(a)(i): odd complete graphs decompose into
Hamilton cycles, even ones into perfect matchings.

informal_statement:
components_deleteEdge. Deleting an edge only destroys connections, never creates them; and it
affects only the component containing $e$, which can break into at most the parts
reachable from each end.  An edge whose deletion \emph{does} raise the count is a \textbf{cut
edge}, the subject of \S{}2.3.  \textbf{!} Part (b), not stated here, notes the analogue fails for
\emph{vertex} deletion --- removing one vertex can create many components.
formal_statement:
import Mathlib

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
theorem components_deleteEdge {e : Sym2 V} (he : e ∈ G.edgeSet) :
    Fintype.card G.ConnectedComponent
        ≤ Fintype.card (G.deleteEdges {e}).ConnectedComponent ∧
      Fintype.card (G.deleteEdges {e}).ConnectedComponent
        ≤ Fintype.card G.ConnectedComponent + 1 := sorry
end SimpleGraph

with no edges across it.

The partition is a set $s$ with its complement, both required

      ∀ s : Set V, s.Nonempty → sᶜ.Nonempty → ∃ u v, u ∈ s ∧ v ∈ sᶜ ∧ G.Adj u v := sorry

informal_statement:
Definitions:
- $v$ is a cut vertex: $G$ is connected but deleting $v$ disconnects it. A \texttt{SimpleGraph} is loopless by construction, so the second (component-counting)
characterisation is the usable one and is what is taken as the definition here.
Specialising it to a \emph{connected} $G$ --- where $\omega(G) = 1$ --- turns
$\omega(G - v) > \omega(G)$ into "$G - v$ is disconnected", giving
\texttt{G.Connected $\land$ $\lnot$ (G.induce \{v\}$^{c}$).Connected}.

Folding \texttt{G.Connected} into the definition is what makes \texttt{IsBlock} below read as
the book's "connected graph that has no cut vertices".

Statement: connected_two_non_cutVertices. However tangled a connected graph is, there are always at least two
vertices you can delete without breaking it apart.
formal_statement:
import Mathlib

open scoped Classical

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
def IsCutVertex (G : SimpleGraph V) (v : V) : Prop :=
  G.Connected ∧ ¬ (G.induce ({v}ᶜ : Set V)).Connected
end SimpleGraph

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
theorem connected_two_non_cutVertices (hG : G.Connected) [Nontrivial V] :
    ∃ u v : V, u ≠ v ∧ ¬ G.IsCutVertex u ∧ ¬ G.IsCutVertex v := sorry
end SimpleGraph
title: connected_two_non_cutVertices
statement_informal:
connected_two_non_cutVertices. However tangled a connected graph is, there are always at least two
vertices you can delete without breaking it apart.

definitions.informal:
A \texttt{SimpleGraph} is loopless by construction, so the second (component-counting)
characterisation is the usable one and is what is taken as the definition here.
Specialising it to a \emph{connected} $G$ --- where $\omega(G) = 1$ --- turns
$\omega(G - v) > \omega(G)$ into "$G - v$ is disconnected", giving
\texttt{G.Connected $\land$ $\lnot$ (G.induce \{v\}$^{c}$).Connected}.

Folding \texttt{G.Connected} into the definition is what makes \texttt{IsBlock} below read as
the book's "connected graph that has no cut vertices".

informal_statement:
Definitions:
- An edge cut set: a set of edges whose deletion disconnects $G$. Split the vertices into two nonempty groups and collect the edges
running between them; deleting them severs every route from one group to the other.

B&M define an edge cut \emph{by its shape} $[S, \bar{S}]$; this takes the
operational characterisation --- a subset of \texttt{edgeSet} whose removal leaves $G$
disconnected --- which for \textbf{connected} $G$ describes the same collections.  \textbf{!} For
disconnected $G$ they diverge, and $\emptyset$ satisfies this predicate; that is the source of
the \texttt{IsBond} defect below.
- A bond (\S{}2.2): a minimal (nonempty) edge cut, i.e. An edge cut with nothing to spare --- remove all of it and the graph falls
apart, but put any single edge back and it is connected again.  Exercise 2.2.8
characterises when $[S, \bar{S}]$ is a bond: exactly when both $G[S]$ and $G[\bar{S}]$ are
connected.  Bonds are the notion \textbf{dual} to cycles, a duality chapter 12 develops in
full --- theorem 2.6 here is the mirror of theorem 2.5.

\textbf{\textbf{!} Defect: $\emptyset$ is a bond when $G$ is disconnected.}  The docstring above claims
nonemptiness is automatic because "deleting $\emptyset$ leaves $G$ connected" --- but that holds
only for connected $G$.  For disconnected $G$, \texttt{IsEdgeCutSet $\emptyset$} unfolds to
\texttt{$\lnot$ G.Connected}, which is true, and there is no $B' \subset \emptyset$ to test, so the minimality
clause is vacuous.  Hence \texttt{IsBond G $\emptyset$}, contradicting \emph{minimal \textbf{nonempty} edge cut}.

\emph{The repair:} add \texttt{B.Nonempty} as a conjunct, or carry \texttt{G.Connected} as a hypothesis
wherever \texttt{IsBond} is used (theorem 2.6 already does --- its \texttt{hG} is available).

Statement: cotree_bond. The exact mirror of theorem 2.5, with \emph{cycle} $\to$ \emph{bond} and *spanning
tree\emph{ $\to$ }cotree*.  \textbf{*} Chapter 12's \texttt{fundamentalBondVertexSet} is exactly the $S$ of
step 3, and cites this theorem by name.

\textbf{!} Both parts consume \texttt{IsBond}, whose $\emptyset$ defect is active
here --- but \texttt{hG : G.Connected} is available as a hypothesis, which is precisely the
condition under which the defect disappears.  Use it explicitly rather than relying on
it silently.
formal_statement:
import Mathlib

open scoped Classical

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
def IsEdgeCutSet (G : SimpleGraph V) (F : Set (Sym2 V)) : Prop :=
  F ⊆ G.edgeSet ∧ ¬ (G.deleteEdges F).Connected
end SimpleGraph

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
def IsBond (G : SimpleGraph V) (B : Set (Sym2 V)) : Prop :=
  G.IsEdgeCutSet B ∧ ∀ B' ⊂ B, (G.deleteEdges B').Connected
end SimpleGraph

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
theorem cotree_bond
    (T : SimpleGraph V) (hT : T.IsTree) (hle : T ≤ G) (hG : G.Connected)
    (e : Sym2 V) (he : e ∈ T.edgeSet) :
    (∀ B : Set (Sym2 V), G.IsBond B → ¬ B ⊆ G.edgeSet \ T.edgeSet) ∧
      (∃! B : Set (Sym2 V), G.IsBond B ∧ B ⊆ insert e (G.edgeSet \ T.edgeSet)) := sorry
end SimpleGraph
title: cotree_bond
statement_informal:
cotree_bond. The exact mirror of theorem 2.5, with \emph{cycle} $\to$ \emph{bond} and *spanning
tree\emph{ $\to$ }cotree*.  \textbf{*} Chapter 12's \texttt{fundamentalBondVertexSet} is exactly the $S$ of
step 3, and cites this theorem by name.

\textbf{!} Both parts consume \texttt{IsBond}, whose $\emptyset$ defect is active
here --- but \texttt{hG : G.Connected} is available as a hypothesis, which is precisely the
condition under which the defect disappears.  Use it explicitly rather than relying on
it silently.

informal_statement:
Definitions:
- The $k$-cube $Q_k$. The corners and edges of a $k$-dimensional cube: $k$-regular, bipartite (split by
the parity of the number of $1$s), $2^k$ vertices, $k\cdot 2^{k-1}$ edges.

Adjacency is the book's condition literally: $\exists! i, x i \ne y i$.

\textbf{!} Note this file defines \texttt{cube} directly as a structure, whereas
\texttt{GraphsAndSubgraphs.lean} defines the same graph as
\texttt{SimpleGraph.fromRel (fun x y => $\exists$! i, x i $\ne$ y i)}.  The two are equal but not
definitionally so, and neither imports the other.

Statement: Ex 5.1.1(a): every $k$-cube ($k \ge 2$) has a perfect matching. The $k$-cube is $k$-regular and bipartite (sides given by the parity of the
number of $1$s), so for $k \ge 2$ Corollary 5.2 applies.
formal_statement:
import Mathlib

open scoped Pointwise

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
def cube (k : ℕ) : SimpleGraph (Fin k → Bool) where
  Adj x y := ∃! i, x i ≠ y i
  symm := by sorry
  loopless := by sorry
end SimpleGraph

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
theorem cube_isPerfectMatching (k : ℕ) (hk : 2 ≤ k) :
    ∃ M : (cube k).Subgraph, M.IsPerfectMatching := sorry
end SimpleGraph

statement_informal:

Definitions:
- The (3,5)-Ramsey graph: \texttt{ZMod 13}, adjacent iff the difference is a cubic residue. A circulant on \texttt{ZMod 13}.  ${1, 5, 8, 12}$ is closed under negation
($-1 = 12$, $-5 = 8$), which is exactly what makes \texttt{symm} hold --- so unlike most
\texttt{def}s in this repo, \texttt{symm} and \texttt{loopless} are \textbf{genuinely discharged}, by
\texttt{decide}.

\textbf{+} Fully defined, no \texttt{sorry} --- one of the few complete constructions in the
directory.

informal_statement:
cutEdge_iff_no_cycle. Cut edges are exactly the edges lying on no cycle: an edge on a cycle has
a detour around it, while an edge on no cycle is the sole link between the two sides it
joins.

Mathlib's \texttt{IsBridge} is B&M's \emph{cut edge}.  Note the conclusion
carries \texttt{G.Adj v w} as a conjunct, which \texttt{IsBridge} includes --- a non-edge is not a
bridge.
formal_statement:
import Mathlib

open scoped Classical

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
theorem cutEdge_iff_no_cycle (v w : V) :
    G.IsBridge s(v, w) ↔
      G.Adj v w ∧ ∀ (u : V) (c : G.Walk u u), c.IsCycle → s(v, w) ∉ c.edges := sorry
end SimpleGraph

Corollary 4.6 compare two such lists via \texttt{DegreeMajorised}.
- $G$ is degree-majorised by $H$: same order, and every sorted-degree entry of $G$ is $\le$ the\dots. Line up both degree sequences in increasing order and compare entry by entry;

import Mathlib

open scoped Classical
open scoped Finset

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
noncomputable def degreeSequence {V : Type*} [Fintype V] (G : SimpleGraph V) : List ℕ :=
  (Finset.univ.val.map fun v => Nat.card (G.neighborSet v)).sort (· ≤ ·)
end SimpleGraph

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
def DegreeMajorised {V W : Type*} [Fintype V] [Fintype W]
    (G : SimpleGraph V) (H : SimpleGraph W) : Prop :=
  Fintype.card V = Fintype.card W ∧
    ∀ i : ℕ, G.degreeSequence.getD i 0 ≤ H.degreeSequence.getD i 0
end SimpleGraph

    {V : Type*} [Fintype V] {G : SimpleGraph V} [DecidableRel G.Adj] {m : ℕ} (hm : 1 ≤ m)
    (h : G.CliqueFree (m + 1)) :

      H.IsCompleteMultipartite ∧ DegreeMajorised G H ∧

Statement: degreeMajorised_of_forall_degree_le. (absent from Mathlib).  *If $d_G(v) \le d_H(v)$ for
every vertex $v$, then $G$ is degree-majorised by $H$.*

Degree-majorisation compares \emph{sorted} sequences entrywise.  Pointwise domination
survives sorting: the $i$-th smallest degree of $G$ cannot exceed the $i$-th
smallest of $H$.

\textbf{!} \textbf{Two problems with this as stated.}

1. \texttt{degreeSequence} in this file is \textbf{unsorted}, so "sorting preserves
   domination" is not what the predicate says --- the entrywise comparison is
   against \texttt{Finset.univ.toList}'s arbitrary order.  With both graphs on the same
   $V$ that order is at least \emph{the same} on both sides, so pointwise domination
   does happen to give the conclusion --- but only by accident of the shared
   carrier, not because the lemma is right.
2. It is stated for \texttt{G H : SimpleGraph V} on the \textbf{same} carrier, whereas
   Theorem 7.8 needs it across different carriers ($G$ on $V$, $H$ on $W$).  So
   it does not actually discharge the step it was extracted for.

informal_statement:
descartes_construction. Mycielski's construction (theorem 8.7) removes triangles but still
leaves 5-cycles.  Descartes' construction is stronger --- it keeps the girth at six
or more, so the graphs have no short cycles at all, and yet the chromatic number
still climbs without bound.  Blanche Descartes (1954) gave the original recursive
construction; the book calls Mycielski's the \emph{easier} one, which is why \S{}8.5 proves
theorem 8.7 in the text and relegates this to a starred exercise.

The conclusion is $\ge k + 1$, not $= k + 1$: the construction
gives a lower bound and the exercise asks only for that.  Likewise \texttt{6 $\le$ girth}
rather than $= 6$.  Step 1 is most of the Lean work --- the indexed family of copies
and the per-copy matching bijection have to be built explicitly, and \texttt{Fintype}
instances derived for the resulting carrier.
formal_statement:
import Mathlib

open scoped Classical

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
theorem descartes_construction {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] [Nonempty V]
    (G : SimpleGraph V) {k : ℕ} (hk : 2 ≤ k)
    (hchrom : G.chromaticNumber = k) (hgirth : 6 ≤ G.girth) :
    ∃ (W : Type) (_ : Fintype W) (H : SimpleGraph W),
      (k + 1 : ℕ∞) ≤ H.chromaticNumber ∧ 6 ≤ H.girth := sorry
end SimpleGraph

Ex 5.2.8(a): a (rectangular) doubly stochastic matrix is necessarily square. Sum every entry two ways.  By rows: $1$ each, so $m$ in total.  By columns: $1$
each, so $n$.  Hence $m = n$.

type*, so the literal statement would be vacuous.  This version takes a genuinely
rectangular \texttt{Matrix m n $\mathbb{R}$} with the two summation hypotheses given explicitly,
which is what the exercise actually asks.

informal_statement:
Definitions:
- An edge cut: a set of edges of $G$ whose deletion leaves $G$ disconnected. Rather than carry the book's $[S, \bar{S}]$ presentation, the definition is taken in
its \emph{operative} form --- a set of edges whose removal disconnects $G$:
\texttt{↑F $\subseteq$ G.edgeSet $\land$ $\lnot$ (G.deleteEdges ↑F).Connected}.

The two agree on what is minimised: every $[S, \bar{S}]$ disconnects $G$, and every
disconnecting edge set contains one (take $S$ a component of $G - F$).  Since
\texttt{edgeConnectivity} only ever asks for the \emph{minimum} size, the coarser form is
equivalent for all purposes in this chapter.
- Edge connectivity $\kappa'(G)$: the minimum size of an edge cut (\texttt{sInf $\emptyset$ = 0}). \texttt{$\kappa$' = sInf \{F.card | G.IsEdgeCut F\}}, with no $if$ guard: the book's special
case "$G$ trivial $\Rightarrow$ $\kappa' = 0$" is already delivered by \texttt{Nat.sInf $\emptyset$ = 0}, since a
trivial graph is connected and so admits no edge cut at all.  That convention is
used directly in \texttt{edgeConnectivity\_le\_minDegree}.

Statement: edgeCard_ge_of_kEdgeConnected. a $k$-edge-connected graph satisfies $k\nu \le 2\varepsilon$.

Stated multiplicatively as $k\nu \le 2\varepsilon$ to stay in the natural numbers and avoid
division.

By Theorem 3.1, $k \le \kappa' \le \delta$, so every vertex has degree at least $k$.  Summing
over all $\nu$ vertices gives $\sum_v d(v) \ge k\nu$, and handshaking (Theorem 1.1) says
that sum equals $2\varepsilon$.  Hence $2\varepsilon \ge k\nu$.

A network that survives any $k$ link failures must give every station at least
$k$ links, so it cannot be sparse --- this is exactly the lower bound
$f(m, n) \ge \lceil mn/2\rceil$ of (3.1), which \S{}3.3 shows the Harary graphs attain.
formal_statement:
import Mathlib

open scoped Classical

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
def IsEdgeCut (G : SimpleGraph V) (F : Finset (Sym2 V)) : Prop :=
  (↑F : Set (Sym2 V)) ⊆ G.edgeSet ∧ ¬ (G.deleteEdges (↑F : Set (Sym2 V))).Connected
end SimpleGraph

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
noncomputable def edgeConnectivity (G : SimpleGraph V) : ℕ :=
  sInf {n : ℕ | ∃ F : Finset (Sym2 V), G.IsEdgeCut F ∧ F.card = n}
end SimpleGraph

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
theorem edgeCard_ge_of_kEdgeConnected (k : ℕ) (h : k ≤ G.edgeConnectivity) :
    k * Fintype.card V ≤ 2 * G.edgeFinset.card := sorry
end SimpleGraph

Ex 6.2.6(a) \textbf{!} BLOCKED (Vizing): $\chi'(G \square K_{2}) = \Delta(G \square K_{2})$. The book's "product" is exactly Mathlib's \texttt{boxProd}, written $\square$.

corresponding vertices, so every degree rises by one and
$\Delta(G \square K_{2}) = \Delta(G) + 1$.

Vizing gives $G$ a proper $(\Delta(G)+1)$-colouring.  Use it on both copies, then
colour the connecting matching edges by recycling --- each vertex of a copy already
omits at least one of the $\Delta(G)+1$ colours, and the two copies can be arranged to
omit \emph{different} ones, so each matching edge finds a free colour.

Ex 6.2.1*: $\chi'(K_{2n}) = 2n- 1$. $K_{2n}$ has $\Delta = 2n - 1$, so (6.1) gives $\chi' \ge 2n - 1$.  For the upper bound use
the round-robin schedule of exercise 5.1.5(a)(i): the edges partition into
$2n - 1$ perfect matchings, and colouring each with its own colour is proper.

informal_statement:
Ex 6.2.1*: $\chi'(K_{2n- 1}) = 2n- 1$ (explicit colouring --- bypasses Vizing). $K_{2n-1}$ has odd order, so no colour class is a perfect matching and each
misses a vertex.  With $\varepsilon = (2n-1)(n-1)$ and classes of size $\le n - 1$, at least
$2n - 1$ colours are needed --- one more than $\Delta = 2n - 2$.  So odd complete graphs
sit on the \textbf{upper} side of Vizing's dichotomy.

The explicit colouring: place the vertices at the corners of a regular
$(2n-1)$-gon and colour each edge by the axis of symmetry it is perpendicular to.
Each class is a matching of $n - 1$ edges missing one vertex, and there are
$2n - 1$ axes.

Concretely in \texttt{ZMod (2n-1)}: colour $s(a, b)$ by $a + b$.  Two edges at a shared
vertex get different sums because $2$ is invertible mod an odd number --- which is
exactly where oddness enters.

informal_statement:
Theorem 6.1 (K\"onig) \textbf{!} BLOCKED: if $G$ is bipartite then $\chi' = \Delta$. Contrapositive: if $\chi' > \Delta$, an optimal $\Delta$-colouring cannot be proper, so by
(6.3) some $u$ has $c(u) < d(u)$ --- a colour missing while another repeats.  That
is Lemma 6.1.2's hypothesis, which forces an odd cycle, so $G$ is not bipartite.

\textbf{!} The book's "Clearly, $u$ satisfies the hypothesis of lemma 6.1.2" compresses a
real step.  From $c(u) < d(u)$ one gets \emph{some} colour repeated at $u$; getting a
colour \emph{not represented} at $u$ needs the pigeonhole $c(u) < d(u) \le \Delta$ --- i.e.
that only $\Delta$ colours are available and fewer than $d(u)$ are used.  With
$d(u) \le \Delta$ this is tight and worth isolating.

\textbf{!} The odd cycle produced by Lemma 6.1.2 lives in \texttt{twoColourSubgraph C i j}, a
\emph{subgraph} of $G$.  Transporting it to an odd cycle of $G$ (to contradict
bipartiteness) requires a walk-level map along \texttt{twoColourSubgraph $\le$ G}, which is
not stated in this file.

informal_statement:
Definitions:
- Edge subdivision: replace $e = uv$ by a length-2 path through a new vertex. Subdivision grows the vertex set by one, so unlike edge deletion it *changes the
carrier type*: \texttt{V $\oplus$ Unit}, with \texttt{Sum.inr ()} the new midpoint.  Adjacency:
\item \texttt{inl x \textasciitilde{} inl y} iff \texttt{G.Adj x y} and $s(x, y) \ne e$ --- the old edges, minus $e$;
\item \texttt{inl x \textasciitilde{} inr \_} iff $x \in e$               --- the two new half-edges;
\item \texttt{inr \_ \textasciitilde{} inr \_} never                     --- no loop at the midpoint.

Corollary 3.2.2 only, via the book's remark that *"the class of blocks with at
least three vertices is closed under the operation of subdivision"*.  That
closure property is itself unproved here, which is the main obstacle to
\texttt{block\_edges\_on\_common\_cycle}.

Statement: Ex 6.2.3(b)(i) \textbf{!} BLOCKED: subdividing one edge of an even-order $k$-regular graph ($k \ge 2$)\dots. Start from $k$-regular on $2n$ vertices, $\varepsilon = kn$.  Subdividing inserts a
degree-$2$ vertex: $2n + 1$ vertices --- now odd --- and $kn + 1$ edges, with $\Delta$
still $k$ provided $k \ge 2$.  Part (a) then applies since
$kn + 1 > kn = n\Delta$.

A single subdivision flips the parity of the vertex count and pushes the graph
from the lower to the upper side of Vizing's dichotomy.

\textbf{!} $hk : 2 \le k$ is load-bearing: at $k = 1$ the new degree-$2$ vertex would
\emph{raise} $\Delta$ to $2$, and the count $n\Delta$ would change with it, breaking the
application of part (a).
formal_statement:
import Mathlib

open scoped Classical

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
noncomputable def subdivide (G : SimpleGraph V) (e : Sym2 V) : SimpleGraph (V ⊕ Unit) where
  Adj a b := match a, b with
    | Sum.inl x, Sum.inl y => G.Adj x y ∧ s(x, y) ≠ e
    | Sum.inl x, Sum.inr _ => x ∈ e
    | Sum.inr _, Sum.inl y => y ∈ e
    | Sum.inr _, Sum.inr _ => False
  symm := by
    rintro (x | _) (y | _) hab
    · exact ⟨hab.1.symm, by rw [Sym2.eq_swap]; exact hab.2⟩
    · exact hab
    · exact hab
    · exact hab
  loopless := by
    rintro (x | _) hx
    · exact G.loopless x hx.1
    · exact hx
end SimpleGraph

variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]

    {k : ℕ} (hk : 2 ≤ k) (hreg : G.IsRegularOfDegree k) (heven : Even (Fintype.card V))
    {u v : V} (huv : G.Adj u v) [DecidableRel (G.subdivide huv).Adj] :
    (G.subdivide huv).lineGraph.chromaticNumber = ((G.subdivide huv).maxDegree + 1 : ℕ) := sorry

informal_statement:
Definitions:
- An edge cut: a set of edges of $G$ whose deletion leaves $G$ disconnected. Rather than carry the book's $[S, \bar{S}]$ presentation, the definition is taken in
its \emph{operative} form --- a set of edges whose removal disconnects $G$:
\texttt{↑F $\subseteq$ G.edgeSet $\land$ $\lnot$ (G.deleteEdges ↑F).Connected}.

The two agree on what is minimised: every $[S, \bar{S}]$ disconnects $G$, and every
disconnecting edge set contains one (take $S$ a component of $G - F$).  Since
\texttt{edgeConnectivity} only ever asks for the \emph{minimum} size, the coarser form is
equivalent for all purposes in this chapter.
- Edge connectivity $\kappa'(G)$: the minimum size of an edge cut (\texttt{sInf $\emptyset$ = 0}). \texttt{$\kappa$' = sInf \{F.card | G.IsEdgeCut F\}}, with no $if$ guard: the book's special
case "$G$ trivial $\Rightarrow$ $\kappa' = 0$" is already delivered by \texttt{Nat.sInf $\emptyset$ = 0}, since a
trivial graph is connected and so admits no edge cut at all.  That convention is
used directly in \texttt{edgeConnectivity\_le\_minDegree}.

Statement: edgeConnectivity_le_minDegree. , second inequality: $\kappa' \le \delta$.

If $G$ is trivial then $\kappa' = 0 \le \delta$.  Otherwise take $v$ with $d(v) = \delta$; the
$\delta$ edges incident with $v$ form an edge cut, since deleting them isolates $v$.
Hence $\kappa' \le d(v) = \delta$.
formal_statement:
import Mathlib

open scoped Classical

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
def IsEdgeCut (G : SimpleGraph V) (F : Finset (Sym2 V)) : Prop :=
  (↑F : Set (Sym2 V)) ⊆ G.edgeSet ∧ ¬ (G.deleteEdges (↑F : Set (Sym2 V))).Connected
end SimpleGraph

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
noncomputable def edgeConnectivity (G : SimpleGraph V) : ℕ :=
  sInf {n : ℕ | ∃ F : Finset (Sym2 V), G.IsEdgeCut F ∧ F.card = n}
end SimpleGraph

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
theorem edgeConnectivity_le_minDegree [Nonempty V] :
    G.edgeConnectivity ≤ G.minDegree := sorry
end SimpleGraph

Hence $\kappa' \le d(v) = \delta$.

The two agree on what is minimised: every $[S, \bar{S}]$ disconnects $G$, and every
disconnecting edge set contains one (take $S$ a component of $G - F$).  Since
\texttt{edgeConnectivity} only ever asks for the \emph{minimum} size, the coarser form is
equivalent for all purposes in this chapter.

definitions.title: Edge connectivity $\kappa'(G)$: the minimum size of an edge cut (\texttt{sInf $\emptyset$ = 0})
definitions.informal:
\texttt{$\kappa$' = sInf \{F.card | G.IsEdgeCut F\}}, with no $if$ guard: the book's special
case "$G$ trivial $\Rightarrow$ $\kappa' = 0$" is already delivered by \texttt{Nat.sInf $\emptyset$ = 0}, since a
trivial graph is connected and so admits no edge cut at all.  That convention is
used directly in \texttt{edgeConnectivity\_le\_minDegree}.

informal_statement:
edge_in_cycle_of_closed_trail. A closed trail may revisit vertices, so it need not be a cycle; the
claim is that it can be pared down to one through any chosen edge.  \textbf{!} The analogous
statement for \emph{walks} is \textbf{false} --- a walk may traverse the same edge back and forth
with no cycle present --- which is why \texttt{ht : c.IsTrail} (distinct edges) is a hypothesis
and not decoration.

\texttt{hpos : 0 < c.length} excludes the trivial closed walk, for which
$he$ would be unsatisfiable anyway but which would otherwise complicate step 1.

import Mathlib

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
theorem edge_in_cycle_of_closed_trail {u : V} (c : G.Walk u u)
    (ht : c.IsTrail) (hpos : 0 < c.length) {e : Sym2 V} (he : e ∈ c.edges) :
    ∃ (v : V) (d : G.Walk v v), d.IsCycle ∧ e ∈ d.edges := sorry
end SimpleGraph

informal_statement:
Definitions:
- \texttt{IsRamseyBound n k l}: every graph on $n$ vertices has a $k$-clique or an $l$-indep set.\dots. \texttt{IsRamseyBound n k l} says $n$ is already large enough for that conclusion:
\texttt{$\forall$ G : SimpleGraph (Fin n), ($\exists$ s, G.IsNClique k s) $\lor$ ($\exists$ t, G.IsNIndepSet l t)}.

Fixing the carrier as \texttt{Fin n} rather than quantifying over all $n$-element types
is what makes \texttt{ramseyNumber} an \texttt{sInf} over $\mathbb{N}$ below.

Total disorder is impossible: any sufficiently large graph contains one kind of
order or the other.
- The Ramsey number $r(k, l)$. The exact threshold at which order becomes unavoidable.

\textbf{!} \textbf{\texttt{sInf $\emptyset$ = 0} is a live trap} until \texttt{exists\_isRamseyBound} is proved: without
it every \texttt{ramseyNumber k l} could silently be $0$, and every theorem below would
be about the wrong number.  That existence result is therefore not optional
scaffolding --- it gates the meaning of the definition itself.

Statement: eighteen_le_ramseyNumber_four_four. Seventeen vertices do not suffice, so the threshold is $\ge 18$ --- and with the
upper bound, exactly $18$, the largest value in the book's table.

\textbf{!} As with $r(3,5)$, only the lower bound is stated here, and the upper bound
would need $r(3,4) = 9$ --- itself unstated and requiring the strict form of
Theorem 7.4.
formal_statement:
import Mathlib

open scoped Finset

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
def IsRamseyBound (n k l : ℕ) : Prop :=
  ∀ G : SimpleGraph (Fin n), (∃ s, G.IsNClique k s) ∨ (∃ t, G.IsNIndepSet l t)
end SimpleGraph

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
noncomputable def ramseyNumber (k l : ℕ) : ℕ :=
  sInf {n | SimpleGraph.IsRamseyBound n k l}
end SimpleGraph

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
theorem eighteen_le_ramseyNumber_four_four : 18 ≤ SimpleGraph.ramseyNumber 4 4 := sorry
end SimpleGraph
title: eighteen_le_ramseyNumber_four_four
statement_informal:

would need $r(3,4) = 9$ --- itself unstated and requiring the strict form of
Theorem 7.4.

informal_statement:
Ex 4.2.8: Erd\H{o}s' edge bound $\nu \ge 6\delta$, $\varepsilon > C(\nu-\delta,2) + \delta^{2}$\dots. Corollary 4.6 gives a sufficient edge count taking no account of the minimum
degree.  Erd\H{o}s' refinement: when $\delta$ is known and small relative to $\nu$, a weaker
count suffices --- $C(\nu-\delta, 2) + \delta^{2}$ rather than $C(\nu-1, 2) + 1$.

The shape of the bound reflects the extremal configuration: a clique on $\nu - \delta$
vertices with $\delta$ low-degree vertices attached, the densest way to be
nonhamiltonian while holding the minimum degree at $\delta$.  $\nu \ge 6\delta$ keeps $\delta$
genuinely small.
formal_statement:
import Mathlib

open scoped Classical

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
theorem erdos_hamiltonian (hν : 6 * G.minDegree ≤ Fintype.card V)
    (hε : (Fintype.card V - G.minDegree).choose 2 + G.minDegree ^ 2 < G.edgeFinset.card) :
    G.IsHamiltonian := sorry
end SimpleGraph

informal_statement:
Definitions:
- $G$ is eulerian: it has a closed Euler trail (an Euler tour). \texttt{$\exists$ u, $\exists$ p : G.Walk u u, p.IsEulerian} --- a closed walk using every edge exactly
once.  Mathlib's \texttt{Walk.IsEulerian} is defined via \texttt{List.count} on \texttt{p.edges},
which is why \texttt{[DecidableEq V]} is genuinely required here and not merely
convenient.

Note the book's three-way vocabulary collapses in Lean: \texttt{IsEulerian} already
implies \texttt{IsTrail}, so "closed Euler trail" and "Euler tour" are the same
predicate on a \texttt{Walk u u}.

Statement: Thm 4.1: a nonempty connected graph is eulerian iff it has no odd-degree vertex. Every visit to a vertex consumes one edge coming in and one going out, so the
edges at each vertex must pair up.

The ($\Leftarrow$) direction is a \emph{minimal counterexample} argument.  In Lean that is
strong induction on $\varepsilon(G)$ --- the book's "choose such a graph with as few edges
as possible" --- generalised over the graph, since $G'$ is a different graph on
(the subtype of) the same vertex type.
formal_statement:
import Mathlib

open scoped Classical

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
def IsEulerianGraph {V : Type*} [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) : Prop :=
  ∃ (u : V) (p : G.Walk u u), p.IsEulerian
end SimpleGraph

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
theorem euler_tour_iff_no_odd_degree
    (hne : G.edgeSet.Nonempty) (hconn : G.Connected) :
    G.IsEulerianGraph ↔ ∀ v, Even (G.degree v) := sorry
end SimpleGraph
title: Thm 4.1: a nonempty connected graph is eulerian iff it has no odd-degree vertex
statement_informal:
Thm 4.1: a nonempty connected graph is eulerian iff it has no odd-degree vertex. Every visit to a vertex consumes one edge coming in and one going out, so the
edges at each vertex must pair up.

The ($\Leftarrow$) direction is a \emph{minimal counterexample} argument.  In Lean that is

as possible" --- generalised over the graph, since $G'$ is a different graph on
(the subtype of) the same vertex type.

definitions.informal:
\texttt{$\exists$ u, $\exists$ p : G.Walk u u, p.IsEulerian} --- a closed walk using every edge exactly
once.  Mathlib's \texttt{Walk.IsEulerian} is defined via \texttt{List.count} on \texttt{p.edges},
which is why \texttt{[DecidableEq V]} is genuinely required here and not merely
convenient.

Note the book's three-way vocabulary collapses in Lean: \texttt{IsEulerian} already

informal_statement:
Cor 4.1: a connected graph has an Euler trail iff at most two vertices have odd degree. By Corollary 1.1 the number of odd-degree vertices is always even, so "at most
two" means exactly $0$ or $2$.

This is the precise answer to the K\"onigsberg question and to exercise 4.1.1: a
figure can be drawn "without lifting the pen and without retracing" exactly when
it is connected and has at most two odd-degree vertices.
formal_statement:
import Mathlib

open scoped Classical

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
theorem euler_trail_iff_le_two_odd (hconn : G.Connected) :
    (∃ (u v : V) (p : G.Walk u v), p.IsEulerian) ↔
      (Finset.univ.filter fun v => Odd (G.degree v)).card ≤ 2 := sorry
end SimpleGraph
title: Cor 4.1: a connected graph has an Euler trail iff at most two vertices have odd degree
statement_informal:
Cor 4.1: a connected graph has an Euler trail iff at most two vertices have odd degree. By Corollary 1.1 the number of odd-degree vertices is always even, so "at most
two" means exactly $0$ or $2$.

figure can be drawn "without lifting the pen and without retracing" exactly when

informal_statement:
even_card_odd_degree. A sum of odd numbers is even precisely when there is an even number of
terms.  This tiny corollary is what \S{}1.9 uses to derive Sperner's lemma, and through
it Brouwer's fixed-point theorem --- the chapter's most striking application.
formal_statement:
import Mathlib

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
theorem even_card_odd_degree :
    Even (Finset.univ.filter (fun v => Odd (G.degree v))).card := sorry
end SimpleGraph
title: even_card_odd_degree
statement_informal:
even_card_odd_degree. A sum of odd numbers is even precisely when there is an even number of

informal_statement:
Ex 4.1.4: no odd degree $\Rightarrow$ an edge-disjoint decomposition into cycles. Even degrees everywhere means no "loose ends".  Peel cycles off one at a time:
removing a cycle subtracts $2$ from the degree of each vertex it visits, so all
degrees stay even and the argument repeats until no edges are left.

"$E(G) = \bigcup E(C_{i})$ with the $C_{i}$ edge-disjoint" is rendered as the single
$\exists!$ statement --- every edge lies in exactly one of the cycles --- which packages
covering and disjointness together.

Note this needs \textbf{no connectivity hypothesis}: it is the local content of
Euler's theorem.  Connectivity is what additionally lets the cycles be spliced
into one tour (Theorem 4.1).
formal_statement:
import Mathlib

open scoped Classical

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
theorem even_degree_cycle_decomposition (h : ∀ v, Even (G.degree v)) :
    ∃ cs : Finset (Σ u : V, G.Walk u u),
      (∀ c ∈ cs, c.2.IsCycle) ∧
      ∀ e ∈ G.edgeSet, ∃! c : (Σ u : V, G.Walk u u), c ∈ cs ∧ e ∈ c.2.edges := sorry
end SimpleGraph
title: Ex 4.1.4: no odd degree $\Rightarrow$ an edge-disjoint decomposition into cycles
statement_informal:
Ex 4.1.4: no odd degree $\Rightarrow$ an edge-disjoint decomposition into cycles. Even degrees everywhere means no "loose ends".  Peel cycles off one at a time:
removing a cycle subtracts $2$ from the degree of each vertex it visits, so all

informal_statement:
exists_balanced_matching_decomposition. \textbf{!} In the book's notation $[x]$ is the \textbf{floor} and ${x}$ the \textbf{ceiling} --- the
opposite of the modern convention for ${}$.  So (6.5) reads
$\lfloor\varepsilon/p\rfloor \le |M_{i}| \le \lceil\varepsilon/p\rceil$, rendered here as
\texttt{G.edgeFinset.card / p $\le$ \dots $\le$ (G.edgeFinset.card + p - 1) / p} in $\mathbb{N}$ division.

\textbf{!} The book's "repeatedly applying lemma 6.3 ... we eventually obtain" is an
induction whose \textbf{termination is not argued}.  In Lean it needs an explicit
measure --- e.g. $\sum_{i} |M_{i}|^{2}$, which strictly decreases on each rebalancing since
moving an edge from a larger to a smaller class reduces the sum of squares.
Supplying that measure is a real part of the formalisation the book skips.
formal_statement:
import Mathlib

open scoped Classical

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
theorem exists_balanced_matching_decomposition
    {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
    (hbip : G.IsBipartite) {p : ℕ} (hp : G.maxDegree ≤ p) (hp0 : 0 < p) :
    ∃ M : Fin p → Set (Sym2 V),
      (∀ i, ∃ S : G.Subgraph, S.IsMatching ∧ S.edgeSet = M i) ∧
      (Pairwise fun i j => Disjoint (M i) (M j)) ∧
      (⋃ i, M i) = G.edgeSet ∧
      ∀ i, G.edgeFinset.card / p ≤ (M i).ncard ∧
           (M i).ncard ≤ (G.edgeFinset.card + p - 1) / p := sorry
end SimpleGraph
title: exists_balanced_matching_decomposition
statement_informal:

\texttt{G.edgeFinset.card / p $\le$ \dots $\le$ (G.edgeFinset.card + p - 1) / p} in $\mathbb{N}$ division.

\textbf{!} The book's "repeatedly applying lemma 6.3 ... we eventually obtain" is an
induction whose \textbf{termination is not argued}.  In Lean it needs an explicit

informal_statement:
exists_bipartite_spanning_subgraph. Split the vertices in two and keep only the crossing edges --- automatically
bipartite and spanning --- choosing the split to maximise crossings.  Then no vertex can
have more than half its edges inside its own part, or moving it would improve the
split.

Conclusion in the cleared form $d_G(v) \le 2 d_H(v)$ to stay in $\mathbb{N}$.
\textbf{!} Step 3's $i - c \le 0$ must be argued in $\mathbb{Z}$ or by \texttt{Nat.le\_of\_add\_le\_add}, not by
$\mathbb{N}$-subtraction.
formal_statement:
import Mathlib

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
theorem exists_bipartite_spanning_subgraph :
    ∃ H : SimpleGraph V, H ≤ G ∧ H.Colorable 2 ∧
      ∀ v, G.degree v ≤ 2 * (H.neighborSet v).ncard := sorry
end SimpleGraph
title: exists_bipartite_spanning_subgraph
statement_informal:
exists_bipartite_spanning_subgraph. Split the vertices in two and keep only the crossing edges --- automatically
bipartite and spanning --- choosing the split to maximise crossings.  Then no vertex can
