informal_statement:
Definitions:
- A walk is internally disjoint from a subgraph $H$: no \emph{internal} vertex lies in $H$. The walk may start and end on $H$, but between those endpoints it
must stay entirely outside $H$.  This is what makes the bridge relation an
equivalence, and it is why a bridge is a maximal chunk of the graph hanging off
$H$ and touching it only at its attachment points.

\texttt{p.support.tail.dropLast} is the walk's interior --- drop the
first vertex (\texttt{tail}) and the last (\texttt{dropLast}).  \textbf{!} This is \textbf{not} the repo's
\texttt{InternallyDisjoint} (\texttt{TwoConnected.lean:58}), which relates a walk to another
\emph{walk}; here the second argument is a \texttt{Subgraph}.  A walk of length $\le 1$ has empty
interior and so is vacuously internally disjoint from everything --- which is
intended, and is what makes \texttt{bridgeRel} reflexive on single edges.
- A longest cycle. A cycle no shorter than any other cycle of $G$.  This is the standard
extremal device: assume the longest cycle is not a Hamilton cycle, then derive a
contradiction from the structure of the bridges hanging off it.  That is exactly how
Chv\'atal--Erd\H{o}s is proved below.

\textbf{!} Not \texttt{girth}/\texttt{egirth}, which are the \emph{shortest} cycle --- the
opposite extremum.  The maximality clause quantifies over cycles at \emph{every} base
point $w$, not just at $u$, which is what makes it a genuine global maximum.  Note
the definition does not assert existence: \texttt{IsLongestCycle} is a hypothesis to be
supplied, and producing one requires knowing $G$ has a cycle at all.
- B&M's relation $~$ on $E(G) \ E(H)$: $e_{1} ~ e_{2}$ iff joined by a walk internally disjoint from $H$\dots. Two edges outside $H$ are related when you can travel from one to the
other without passing through $H$.  Grouping edges into classes carves
$G - E(H)$ into the pieces that hang off $H$ --- those pieces are the bridges.

\texttt{Relation.EqvGen} wraps the book's raw condition in its
reflexive--symmetric--transitive closure, which \emph{discharges} the book's "it is easy
to verify" rather than proving it: whatever the raw relation does, the closure is
an equivalence by construction.  This is a deliberate trade --- the file gains an
equivalence for free, at the cost that \texttt{bridgeRel} is a priori coarser than $\sim$.
It is not actually coarser (the book's $\sim$ really is an equivalence), but nothing
here proves that, so do not appeal to "\texttt{bridgeRel e f} gives a single connecting
walk" --- it gives a \emph{chain} of them.  Several skeletons below rely on this
distinction.
- The bridge of $H$ in $G$ containing the edge $e$: the subgraph induced by $e$'s $~$-class. A bridge is one of the connected pieces remaining when $H$ is
removed, together with the attachment points where it touches $H$.  The three
"immediate" facts quoted above are \texttt{bridgeOf\_connected},
\texttt{exists\_path\_internallyDisjoint} and \texttt{bridge\_inter\_subset\_cycle} below --- none of
them is actually immediate once $\sim$ is a closure.  In planar graph theory bridges
carry the argument: theorem 9.8 says inner bridges of a cycle avoid one another,
theorem 9.9 that a bridge avoiding every outer bridge is transferable, and together
these drive Kuratowski's theorem 9.10.

Indexed by a \emph{representative edge} $e$ rather than by a class,
so "the bridge containing $e$"; two edges give the same bridge exactly when
\texttt{bridgeRel H e f}.  Built with \texttt{Subgraph.mk} directly --- \textbf{not} with
\texttt{SimpleGraph.toSubgraph} (\texttt{Subgraph.lean:559}), which is \emph{spanning} and would put
every vertex of $G$ into every bridge.  Note \texttt{verts} is the union of the class's
edges, so it automatically includes the attachment points.

\textbf{!} Because \texttt{bridgeRel} is reflexive for \emph{any} $e$ (it is an \texttt{EqvGen}), \texttt{bridgeOf H e}
is nonempty even for an $e$ that is not an edge of $G$ at all --- it then has two
vertices and no edges.  Statements about bridges must therefore carry
\texttt{e $\in$ G.edgeSet \textbackslash\{\} H.edgeSet} explicitly.  Two of them below originally omitted it and
were false as a result; both now carry it (see the module header).

Statement: exists_bridge_off_longest_cycle. Since $G$ is not hamiltonian the longest cycle misses some vertex;
connectivity joins that vertex to the cycle, and the joining path's edges lie in a
bridge that therefore reaches off $C$.  This is the setup for the whole exercise ---
that bridge is the object whose attachments part (ii) constrains, and Chv\'atal--Erd\H{o}s
falls out of those constraints.

Note this is the \emph{only} one of the three 9.4.3 statements that
carries \texttt{hnh}; part (ii) as stated below drops it, which is where its defect comes
from.
formal_statement:
import Mathlib

open scoped Classical

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
def Walk.InternallyDisjointFrom {V : Type*} {G : SimpleGraph V}
    (H : G.Subgraph) {u v : V} (p : G.Walk u v) : Prop :=
  ∀ x ∈ p.support.tail.dropLast, x ∉ H.verts
end SimpleGraph

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
def Walk.IsLongestCycle {V : Type*} {G : SimpleGraph V} {u : V}
    (c : G.Walk u u) : Prop :=
  c.IsCycle ∧ ∀ (w : V) (c' : G.Walk w w), c'.IsCycle → c'.length ≤ c.length
end SimpleGraph

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
def bridgeRel {V : Type*} (G : SimpleGraph V) (H : G.Subgraph) :
    Sym2 V → Sym2 V → Prop :=
  Relation.EqvGen fun e₁ e₂ =>
    e₁ ∈ G.edgeSet \ H.edgeSet ∧ e₂ ∈ G.edgeSet \ H.edgeSet ∧
    ∃ (u v : V) (p : G.Walk u v), p.InternallyDisjointFrom H ∧
      p.edges.head? = some e₁ ∧ p.edges.getLast? = some e₂
end SimpleGraph

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
def bridgeOf {V : Type*} (G : SimpleGraph V) (H : G.Subgraph) (e : Sym2 V) :
    G.Subgraph where
  verts := {x | ∃ f, G.bridgeRel H e f ∧ x ∈ f}
  Adj u v := G.Adj u v ∧ G.bridgeRel H e s(u, v)
  adj_sub h := h.1
  edge_vert h := ⟨_, h.2, Sym2.mem_mk_left _ _⟩
  symm u v h := ⟨h.1.symm, by rw [Sym2.eq_swap]; exact h.2⟩
end SimpleGraph

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
theorem exists_bridge_off_longest_cycle
    {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] {G : SimpleGraph V} (hconn : G.Connected)
    (hnh : ¬ G.IsHamiltonian) {u : V} {c : G.Walk u u} (hc : c.IsLongestCycle) :
    ∃ e ∈ G.edgeSet \ c.toSubgraph.edgeSet,
      ((G.bridgeOf c.toSubgraph e).verts \ c.toSubgraph.verts).Nonempty := sorry

title: exists_bridge_off_longest_cycle
statement_informal:
exists_bridge_off_longest_cycle. Since $G$ is not hamiltonian the longest cycle misses some vertex;
connectivity joins that vertex to the cycle, and the joining path's edges lie in a
bridge that therefore reaches off $C$.  This is the setup for the whole exercise ---
that bridge is the object whose attachments part (ii) constrains, and Chv\'atal--Erd\H{o}s
falls out of those constraints.

Note this is the \emph{only} one of the three 9.4.3 statements that
carries \texttt{hnh}; part (ii) as stated below drops it, which is where its defect comes
from.

definitions.title: A walk is internally disjoint from a subgraph $H$: no \emph{internal} vertex lies in $H$
definitions.informal:
The walk may start and end on $H$, but between those endpoints it
must stay entirely outside $H$.  This is what makes the bridge relation an
equivalence, and it is why a bridge is a maximal chunk of the graph hanging off
$H$ and touching it only at its attachment points.

\texttt{p.support.tail.dropLast} is the walk's interior --- drop the
first vertex (\texttt{tail}) and the last (\texttt{dropLast}).  \textbf{!} This is \textbf{not} the repo's
\texttt{InternallyDisjoint} (\texttt{TwoConnected.lean:58}), which relates a walk to another
\emph{walk}; here the second argument is a \texttt{Subgraph}.  A walk of length $\le 1$ has empty
interior and so is vacuously internally disjoint from everything --- which is
intended, and is what makes \texttt{bridgeRel} reflexive on single edges.

definitions.title: A longest cycle
definitions.informal:
A cycle no shorter than any other cycle of $G$.  This is the standard
extremal device: assume the longest cycle is not a Hamilton cycle, then derive a
contradiction from the structure of the bridges hanging off it.  That is exactly how
Chv\'atal--Erd\H{o}s is proved below.

\textbf{!} Not \texttt{girth}/\texttt{egirth}, which are the \emph{shortest} cycle --- the
opposite extremum.  The maximality clause quantifies over cycles at \emph{every} base
point $w$, not just at $u$, which is what makes it a genuine global maximum.  Note
the definition does not assert existence: \texttt{IsLongestCycle} is a hypothesis to be
supplied, and producing one requires knowing $G$ has a cycle at all.

definitions.title: B&M's relation $~$ on $E(G) \ E(H)$: $e_{1} ~ e_{2}$ iff joined by a walk internally disjoint from $H$\dots
definitions.informal:
Two edges outside $H$ are related when you can travel from one to the
other without passing through $H$.  Grouping edges into classes carves
$G - E(H)$ into the pieces that hang off $H$ --- those pieces are the bridges.

\texttt{Relation.EqvGen} wraps the book's raw condition in its
reflexive--symmetric--transitive closure, which \emph{discharges} the book's "it is easy
to verify" rather than proving it: whatever the raw relation does, the closure is
an equivalence by construction.  This is a deliberate trade --- the file gains an
equivalence for free, at the cost that \texttt{bridgeRel} is a priori coarser than $\sim$.
It is not actually coarser (the book's $\sim$ really is an equivalence), but nothing
here proves that, so do not appeal to "\texttt{bridgeRel e f} gives a single connecting
walk" --- it gives a \emph{chain} of them.  Several skeletons below rely on this
distinction.

definitions.title: The bridge of $H$ in $G$ containing the edge $e$: the subgraph induced by $e$'s $~$-class
definitions.informal:
A bridge is one of the connected pieces remaining when $H$ is
removed, together with the attachment points where it touches $H$.  The three
"immediate" facts quoted above are \texttt{bridgeOf\_connected},
\texttt{exists\_path\_internallyDisjoint} and \texttt{bridge\_inter\_subset\_cycle} below --- none of
them is actually immediate once $\sim$ is a closure.  In planar graph theory bridges
carry the argument: theorem 9.8 says inner bridges of a cycle avoid one another,
theorem 9.9 that a bridge avoiding every outer bridge is transferable, and together
these drive Kuratowski's theorem 9.10.

Indexed by a \emph{representative edge} $e$ rather than by a class,
so "the bridge containing $e$"; two edges give the same bridge exactly when
\texttt{bridgeRel H e f}.  Built with \texttt{Subgraph.mk} directly --- \textbf{not} with
\texttt{SimpleGraph.toSubgraph} (\texttt{Subgraph.lean:559}), which is \emph{spanning} and would put
every vertex of $G$ into every bridge.  Note \texttt{verts} is the union of the class's
edges, so it automatically includes the attachment points.

\textbf{!} Because \texttt{bridgeRel} is reflexive for \emph{any} $e$ (it is an \texttt{EqvGen}), \texttt{bridgeOf H e}
is nonempty even for an $e$ that is not an edge of $G$ at all --- it then has two
vertices and no edges.  Statements about bridges must therefore carry
\texttt{e $\in$ G.edgeSet \textbackslash\{\} H.edgeSet} explicitly.  Two of them below originally omitted it and
were false as a result; both now carry it (see the module header).

informal_statement:
exists_chromaticNumber_ge_girth_six. High chromatic number is compatible not merely with triangle-freeness
(theorem 8.7) but with the complete absence of short cycles.  Locally such a graph
looks like a tree --- every small neighbourhood is acyclic and trivially
2-colourable --- yet globally it resists any bounded number of colours.  Chromatic
number is a genuinely global invariant.

The conclusion is the honest $\ge$ form ($k \le \chi$, \texttt{6 $\le$ girth})
rather than the book's "$k$-chromatic of girth six".  Two reasons: part (a) delivers
only a lower bound on $\chi$, and \texttt{girth = 6} exactly would additionally require
exhibiting a 6-cycle, which the construction does not obviously do.  Step 3's
instantiation at $m$ rather than $k$ is the small manoeuvre that lets the $\ge$
induction feed part (a)'s $=$ hypothesis.
formal_statement:

open scoped Classical

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
theorem exists_chromaticNumber_ge_girth_six (k : ℕ) (hk : 2 ≤ k) :
    ∃ (W : Type) (_ : Fintype W) (H : SimpleGraph W),
      (k : ℕ∞) ≤ H.chromaticNumber ∧ 6 ≤ H.girth := sorry
end SimpleGraph

informal_statement:
Definitions:
- $\pi_k(G)$, the number of distinct proper $k$-colourings. Count the proper colourings as \emph{labelled} objects, not up to
permutation of the colours --- the triangle example is exactly the warning against
quotienting.  Birkhoff (1912) introduced this counting approach as a possible
route to the four-colour conjecture.

\texttt{Nat.card (G.Coloring (Fin k))} rather than \texttt{Fintype.card}:
the two agree over a \texttt{Fintype}, but \texttt{Nat.card} needs no instance, which lets the
\S{}8.4 statements elaborate over \texttt{Subgraph} and component carriers without bespoke
\texttt{Fintype} derivations.  A \texttt{G.Coloring (Fin k)} is a function on vertices, so
distinctness is pointwise --- precisely the book's criterion.

Statement: exists_chromaticPolynomial. This is what justifies calling $\pi_k(G)$ the \textbf{chromatic polynomial}.
The book notes that \emph{no one has yet discovered which polynomials are chromatic}:
Read (1968) conjectured the coefficients must first rise then fall in absolute
value, but even that plus this corollary is not sufficient --- $k^{4} - 3k^{3} + 3k^{2}$
satisfies all of them yet is no graph's chromatic polynomial (exercise 8.4.2(b)).

\texttt{[Nonempty V]} is load-bearing, as step 2 shows: for $\nu = 0$ the
empty graph has $\pi_k = 1$, whose constant term is $1$, not $0$.  The alternation is
encoded as \texttt{$\forall$ i, 0 $\le$ (-1)\^{}($\nu$ - i) * p.coeff i} rather than as an explicit sum with
non-negative $a_{i}$, which is equivalent and much easier to carry through step 5.
formal_statement:
import Mathlib

open scoped Classical

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
noncomputable def numColorings {V : Type*} (G : SimpleGraph V) (k : ℕ) : ℕ :=
  Nat.card (G.Coloring (Fin k))
end SimpleGraph

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
theorem exists_chromaticPolynomial
    {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] [Nonempty V] (G : SimpleGraph V) :
    ∃ p : Polynomial ℤ,
      (∀ k : ℕ, p.eval (k : ℤ) = (G.numColorings k : ℤ)) ∧
      p.natDegree = Fintype.card V ∧
      p.leadingCoeff = 1 ∧
      p.coeff 0 = 0 ∧
      ∀ i, 0 ≤ (-1 : ℤ) ^ (Fintype.card V - i) * p.coeff i := sorry
end SimpleGraph

informal_statement:
Ex 5.2.9: a common transversal of the left and right cosets of a subgroup (P. Hall). Left and right cosets each partition $H$ into $n = [H : K]$ blocks of size $|K|$.
The claim: one list of $n$ elements represents \emph{both} partitions simultaneously.

Hall again --- put left cosets on one side, right cosets on the other, joining \texttt{aK}
to \texttt{Kb} when they intersect.  All cosets having size $|K|$ makes this graph
regular, so Corollary 5.2 gives a perfect matching; choosing an element from each
matched intersection is the common transversal.

\textbf{!} The Lean rendering states the two conclusions as \texttt{Function.Bijective} of the
maps $i \mapsto h_{i} \textbullet{} K$ and $i \mapsto op h_{i} \textbullet{} K$ into \texttt{Set H}.  The note in the file flags
this shape as provisional, and it is worth scrutiny: bijectivity onto \emph{what}
codomain is left implicit (it is \texttt{Set H}, not the set of cosets), so as written
the maps are into a far larger type than intended and the statement may be
stronger --- or simply wrong --- relative to the exercise.  Recheck before proving.
formal_statement:
import Mathlib

open scoped Pointwise

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
theorem exists_common_coset_transversal {H : Type*} [Group H] [Fintype H] [DecidableEq H]
    (K : Subgroup H) [DecidablePred (· ∈ K)] :
    ∃ (n : ℕ) (h : Fin n → H),
      Function.Bijective (fun i => (h i : H) • (K : Set H)) ∧
      Function.Bijective (fun i => MulOpposite.op (h i : H) • (K : Set H)) := sorry
end SimpleGraph

informal_statement:
exists_cycle_of_edgeCard_ge. Each edge added to a forest either joins two different components ---
possible at most $\nu - 1$ times --- or joins two already-connected vertices, immediately
closing a cycle.  \textbf{!} Part (b), due to P\'osa and not stated here, strengthens this:
$\varepsilon \ge \nu + 4$ forces two \textbf{edge-disjoint} cycles.

\textbf{+} \textbf{Hypothesis repaired.}  Step 2 needs $\omega \ge 1$, i.e.
\texttt{Nonempty V}.  Without it the statement is \textbf{false} on an empty carrier, where
$\nu = \varepsilon = 0$ so $h$ holds vacuously while no cycle exists (indeed no vertex $v$ exists
to base one at).  \texttt{[Nonempty V]} has been added; it is not in B&M only because the
book's graphs are nonempty by convention.

theorem exists_cycle_of_edgeCard_ge [Nonempty V]
    (h : Fintype.card V ≤ G.edgeFinset.card) :
    ∃ (v : V) (c : G.Walk v v), c.IsCycle := sorry
end SimpleGraph

informal_statement:
exists_cycle_of_minDegree_ge_two. If every vertex offers a second way out you can never get stuck, so
walking forward must eventually revisit a vertex, and the first revisit closes a
cycle.  \textbf{*} Contrapositively, \textbf{an acyclic graph always has a vertex of degree $\le$ 1} ---
used repeatedly in chapter 2's theory of trees, and by chapter 12's lemma 12.2.1.

informal_statement:
Definitions:
- An edge cut: a set of edges of $G$ whose deletion leaves $G$ disconnected. Rather than carry the book's $[S, \bar{S}]$ presentation, the definition is taken in
its \emph{operative} form --- a set of edges whose removal disconnects $G$:
\texttt{↑F $\subseteq$ G.edgeSet $\land$ $\lnot$ (G.deleteEdges ↑F).Connected}.

The two agree on what is minimised: every $[S, \bar{S}]$ disconnects $G$, and every
disconnecting edge set contains one (take $S$ a component of $G - F$).  Since
\texttt{edgeConnectivity} only ever asks for the \emph{minimum} size, the coarser form is
equivalent for all purposes in this chapter.
- Edge connectivity $\kappa'(G)$: the minimum size of an edge cut (\texttt{sInf $\emptyset$ = 0}). \texttt{$\kappa$' = sInf \{F.card | G.IsEdgeCut F\}}, with no $if$ guard: the book's special
case "$G$ trivial $\Rightarrow$ $\kappa' = 0$" is already delivered by \texttt{Nat.sInf $\emptyset$ = 0}, since a
trivial graph is connected and so admits no edge cut at all.  That convention is
used directly in \texttt{edgeConnectivity\_le\_minDegree}.

Statement: Successor step, part 1: from a minimum edge cut of size $k + 1$, deleting one of its edges drops the edge\dots. Indices are shifted by one to stay in $\mathbb{N}$: the book's $\kappa'(G) = k$ with
$\kappa'(H) = k - 1$ is stated here as $\kappa'(G) = k + 1$ with $\kappa'(G - e) = k$, which
avoids truncated subtraction entirely.

Take $F$ realising $\kappa'(G) = k + 1$; it is nonempty, so pick $e \in F$.  Then
$F \ {e}$ is an edge cut of $G - e$ of size $k$, giving $\kappa'(G - e) \le k$; and
$\kappa'(G - e) \ge k$, because a smaller cut of $G - e$ together with $e$ would be a
cut of $G$ of size $< k + 1$, contradicting minimality.
formal_statement:
import Mathlib

open scoped Classical

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
def IsEdgeCut (G : SimpleGraph V) (F : Finset (Sym2 V)) : Prop :=
  (↑F : Set (Sym2 V)) ⊆ G.edgeSet ∧ ¬ (G.deleteEdges (↑F : Set (Sym2 V))).Connected
end SimpleGraph

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
noncomputable def edgeConnectivity (G : SimpleGraph V) : ℕ :=
  sInf {n : ℕ | ∃ F : Finset (Sym2 V), G.IsEdgeCut F ∧ F.card = n}
end SimpleGraph

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
theorem exists_deleteEdge_edgeConnectivity_eq
    (G' : SimpleGraph V) (k : ℕ) (h : G'.edgeConnectivity = k + 1) :
    ∃ e ∈ G'.edgeSet, (G'.deleteEdges {e}).edgeConnectivity = k := sorry
end SimpleGraph
title: Successor step, part 1: from a minimum edge cut of size $k + 1$, deleting one of its edges drops the edge\dots

$\kappa'(H) = k - 1$ is stated here as $\kappa'(G) = k + 1$ with $\kappa'(G - e) = k$, which
avoids truncated subtraction entirely.

Take $F$ realising $\kappa'(G) = k + 1$; it is nonempty, so pick $e \in F$.  Then
$F \ {e}$ is an edge cut of $G - e$ of size $k$, giving $\kappa'(G - e) \le k$; and
$\kappa'(G - e) \ge k$, because a smaller cut of $G - e$ together with $e$ would be a
cut of $G$ of size $< k + 1$, contradicting minimality.

informal_statement:
Definitions:
- Colour $i$ is \emph{represented} at $v$: some edge incident with $v$ has colour $i$. A $k$-edge colouring is a plain function \texttt{C : G.edgeSet $\to$ Fin k}, deliberately
\textbf{not} assumed proper --- that is the whole point, since Lemma 6.1.2, Theorem 6.1
and Vizing's Theorem 6.2 all operate on improper colourings and repair them.

"Represented at $v$" is \texttt{$\exists$ e, ↑e $\in$ G.incidenceSet v $\land$ C e = i}.

\textbf{!} Note this file uses \textbf{two different} colouring encodings.  Here a colouring is
a raw function \texttt{G.edgeSet $\to$ Fin k}; but \texttt{IsUniquelyEdgeColourable} below and the
\texttt{edgeChromaticNumber} results use Mathlib's \texttt{G.lineGraph.Coloring (Fin k)}, which
is proper by construction.  The two are not interchangeable, and any proof
crossing between \S{}6.1's machinery and a $\chi'$ statement must convert explicitly.

Statement: Ex 6.1.6 (Gupta) \textbf{!} BLOCKED: bipartite with $\delta > 0$ $\Rightarrow$ a $\delta$-edge colouring\dots. The \textbf{dual} of proper colouring.  Proper asks that no colour appear \emph{twice} at a
vertex, using $\Delta$ colours; this asks that every colour appear \emph{at least once} at
every vertex, using $\delta$ colours.  Since the least degree is $\delta$, that is the most
one could force everywhere.

The colouring is explicitly \textbf{not} required to be proper, so the statement is
about \texttt{IsRepresentedAt} rather than about \texttt{lineGraph.chromaticNumber} --- one of
the few places the raw-function encoding is the right one.

Exercise 6.2.8 is the simple-graph analogue with $\delta - 1$ colours; it is not
stated in this file.
formal_statement:
import Mathlib

open scoped Classical

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
def IsRepresentedAt {V : Type*} {G : SimpleGraph V} {k : ℕ}
    (C : G.edgeSet → Fin k) (i : Fin k) (v : V) : Prop :=
  ∃ e : G.edgeSet, (e : Sym2 V) ∈ G.incidenceSet v ∧ C e = i
end SimpleGraph

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
theorem exists_edge_colouring_all_represented_of_isBipartite
    {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
    (hbip : G.IsBipartite) (hδ : 0 < G.minDegree) :
    ∃ C : G.edgeSet → Fin G.minDegree,
      ∀ (v : V) (i : Fin G.minDegree), IsRepresentedAt C i v := sorry
end SimpleGraph

Statement: exists_farGraph_card_eq. The far-pairs graph of this configuration is \emph{exactly} the balanced complete
tripartite $T_{3,n}$, with $\lfloor n^{2}/3\rfloor$ edges --- so the Tur\'an bound is attained and

formal_statement:
import Mathlib

open scoped Finset

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
def farGraph {n : ℕ} (x : Fin n → EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin 2)) : SimpleGraph (Fin n) where
  Adj i j := i ≠ j ∧ 1 / Real.sqrt 2 < Dist.dist (x i) (x j)
  symm := by rintro i j ⟨h1, h2⟩; exact ⟨h1.symm, by rwa [_root_.dist_comm]⟩
  loopless := by rintro i ⟨h, -⟩; exact h rfl
end SimpleGraph

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
theorem exists_farGraph_card_eq (n : ℕ) :
    ∃ (x : Fin n → EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin 2)) (_ : DecidableRel (farGraph x).Adj),
      Metric.diam (Set.range x) = 1 ∧ #(farGraph x).edgeFinset = n ^ 2 / 3 := sorry
end SimpleGraph

informal_statement:
Definitions:
- $s$ is a maximal independent set of $G$ within $t$. $s$ is independent, lies inside $t$, and cannot be enlarged *within
$t$* without losing independence.

The book only ever says "maximal independent set of $G - X$"
for various $X$.  Rather than form the deleted graph, this relativises: $t$ is the
ambient set, and maximality is tested against subsets of $t$.  Taking
\texttt{t = Set.univ} recovers the plain notion.  This is the shape
\texttt{IsCanonicalColouring} needs, where each colour class must be maximal in what
remains after the earlier classes are removed.
- A canonical colouring, as a list of colour classes. Build the colour classes greedily, each time taking as large an
independent set as possible from what remains.  Exercise 8.6.3 shows this costs
nothing, so enumerating canonical colourings suffices to find $\chi(G)$ --- the basis
of the \S{}8.6 procedure for the storage problem, which the book concedes *is not
very efficient for large graphs*.

Stated as a \emph{static} condition on a list of classes, not as a
procedure: $L[i]$ is required to be maximal-independent in the complement of
$L[0] \cup \dots \cup L[i-1]$, which is what "maximal independent set of
$G - (V_{1} \cup \dots \cup V_{i-1})$" means.  The last two conjuncts say $L$ really is a
partition --- the classes cover $V$ and are pairwise disjoint.  A \texttt{List} rather than
a \texttt{Fin k $\to$ Set V} because the book's condition is inherently ordered, and because
exercise 8.6.3 concludes with \texttt{L.length $\le$ k} rather than $= k$ (a canonical
colouring may use fewer colours, which is precisely why the procedure finds $\chi$
rather than merely confirming $k$).

Statement: exists_isCanonicalColouring. Greedily enlarge the first colour class to a maximal independent set,
absorbing whatever later classes will give up; repeat on what remains.  Nothing is
lost: the result is canonical and uses no more colours than before.

\emph{Why this matters (\S{}8.6).}  The storage problem asks for the fewest warehouse
compartments so that incompatible chemicals are separated --- which is the chromatic
number of the incompatibility graph.  No good algorithm is known, so the book gives
an enumerative procedure: list the minimal coverings (equivalently, by theorem 7.1,
the maximal independent sets), then search over canonical colourings.  \textbf{This
exercise is what makes that search complete} --- restricting attention to canonical
colourings loses nothing.  The book's example (figure 8.11) has minimal coverings
${a,c,e,g}$, ${b,c,d,e,g}$, ${b,d,e,f}$, ${b,c,d,f}$, hence maximal independent sets
${b,d,f}$, ${a,f}$, ${a,c,g}$, ${a,e,g}$, and $\chi = 3$ via the canonical colouring
$({b,d,f}, {a,e,g}, {c})$.

\texttt{L.length $\le$ k}, not $= k$: a canonical colouring may use fewer
colours than the one it was built from, and that is precisely the point --- the least
length over canonical colourings \emph{is} $\chi(G)$, which is what the \S{}8.6 procedure
computes.  Step 1's strengthening is essential: the statement as given is not
directly inductive, because the recursive call is about a \emph{deleted} graph.
formal_statement:
import Mathlib

open scoped Classical

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
def IsMaximalIndepSetIn {V : Type*} (G : SimpleGraph V) (s t : Set V) : Prop :=
  s ⊆ t ∧ G.IsIndepSet s ∧ ∀ u, s ⊂ u → u ⊆ t → ¬ G.IsIndepSet u
end SimpleGraph

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
def IsCanonicalColouring {V : Type*} (G : SimpleGraph V) (L : List (Set V)) : Prop :=
  (∀ i (h : i < L.length),
      G.IsMaximalIndepSetIn (L.get ⟨i, h⟩) (Set.univ \ ⋃ j ∈ Finset.range i, L.getD j ∅)) ∧
  (⋃ s ∈ L, s) = Set.univ ∧ L.Pairwise Disjoint
end SimpleGraph

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
theorem exists_isCanonicalColouring {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V)
    {k : ℕ} (hk : G.Colorable k) :
    ∃ L : List (Set V), L.length ≤ k ∧ G.IsCanonicalColouring L := sorry
end SimpleGraph

informal_statement:
Definitions:
- $G$ is critical: $\chi(H) < \chi(G)$ for every proper subgraph $H \subset G$. A critical graph is "minimally" $k$-chromatic: remove any vertex or
any edge and the chromatic number drops.  Critical graphs are useful precisely
because they carry the whole difficulty of a colouring problem --- every
$k$-chromatic graph contains a $k$-critical subgraph, so statements about
$k$-chromatic graphs reduce to the critical case, which is how corollary 8.1.1,
Brooks' theorem 8.4 and theorem 8.5 all begin.

The quantifier ranges over \texttt{G.Subgraph}, not over the order
on \texttt{SimpleGraph V}.  This is load-bearing (Scaffolding judgement 1): the
\texttt{SimpleGraph V} order can only \emph{remove edges}, never vertices, whereas the book's
"proper subgraph" includes $G - v$.  Under the weaker order $\bot$ on two vertices
would be vacuously 1-critical --- it has no proper edge-subgraph --- contradicting
exercise 8.1.7, which says the only 1-critical graph is $K_{1}$.
- $G$ is $k$-critical: $k$-chromatic and critical. $k$-critical graphs are the irreducible witnesses to needing $k$
colours.  Exercise 8.1.7 classifies the small cases completely --- the only
1-critical graph is $K_{1}$, the only 2-critical graph is $K_{2}$, and the 3-critical
graphs are exactly the odd cycles --- and Brooks' theorem 8.4 consumes precisely
that classification to get its standing hypothesis $k \ge 4$.

\texttt{G.chromaticNumber = k} compares an $\mathbb{N}\infty$ with a coerced $\mathbb{N}$,
so $k$-chromaticity here also carries the information that $\chi(G) \ne \top$.

Statement: exists_isKCritical_four. The excluded case $n = 5$ is exactly exercise 8.1.9(b): no
$k$-critical graph has $k + 1$ vertices, so no 4-critical graph has five.  The
book's figure 8.2 (the Gr\"otzsch graph) is another witness, for $n = 11$.

The carrier is pinned to \texttt{Fin n}, so each construction must be
transported along an explicit equivalence --- \texttt{Fin 1 $\oplus$ Fin (n-1) $\simeq$ Fin n} for case 2,
and the Haj\'os single-carrier encoding of exercise 8.1.11 for case 3.  That
transport, rather than the graph theory, is most of the Lean work here; a reusable
"\texttt{IsKCritical} transfers along $$\simeq$g$" lemma is worth having first.

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
def IsCritical {V : Type*} (G : SimpleGraph V) : Prop :=
  ∀ H : G.Subgraph, H < ⊤ → H.coe.chromaticNumber < G.chromaticNumber
end SimpleGraph

variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
def IsKCritical {V : Type*} (G : SimpleGraph V) (k : ℕ) : Prop :=
  G.chromaticNumber = k ∧ G.IsCritical
end SimpleGraph

theorem exists_isKCritical_four (n : ℕ) (hn : n = 4 ∨ 6 ≤ n) :
    ∃ G : SimpleGraph (Fin n), G.IsKCritical 4 := sorry
end SimpleGraph

Definitions:
- \texttt{IsRamseyBound n k l}: every graph on $n$ vertices has a $k$-clique or an $l$-indep set.\dots. \texttt{IsRamseyBound n k l} says $n$ is already large enough for that conclusion:
\texttt{$\forall$ G : SimpleGraph (Fin n), ($\exists$ s, G.IsNClique k s) $\lor$ ($\exists$ t, G.IsNIndepSet l t)}.

Fixing the carrier as \texttt{Fin n} rather than quantifying over all $n$-element types
is what makes \texttt{ramseyNumber} an \texttt{sInf} over $\mathbb{N}$ below.

Total disorder is impossible: any sufficiently large graph contains one kind of
order or the other.

Statement: exists_isRamseyBound. No matter how a graph is drawn, if it is large enough it cannot avoid \emph{both} a
big clique and a big independent set.

The book can be informal about existence because $r(k,l)$ is only ever used
comparatively.  In Lean, \texttt{ramseyNumber} is \texttt{sInf} over a set that this lemma
proves nonempty --- so \textbf{until this is proved, every \texttt{ramseyNumber} in the file is
provably $0$} and every result below is vacuous.  It gates all of \S{}7.2 and, via
Schur, \S{}7.4.

Definitions:
- A vertex cut: a proper subset $S$ whose deletion leaves $G$ disconnected. $V'$ is a \texttt{Finset V}, and "$G - V'$ is disconnected" is
\texttt{$\lnot$ (G.induce (↑S)$^{c}$).Connected}.  The conjunct \texttt{↑S $\subset$ Set.univ} records that a
vertex cut is a \emph{proper} subset: without it $S = V$ would qualify vacuously,
since Mathlib's \texttt{Connected} is false on the empty induced graph.

A $k$-vertex cut is the pair \texttt{G.IsVertexCut S $\land$ S.card = k}; that is exactly
what \texttt{vertexConnectivity} minimises over.

import Mathlib

open scoped Classical

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
def IsVertexCut (G : SimpleGraph V) (S : Finset V) : Prop :=
  (↑S : Set V) ⊂ Set.univ ∧ ¬ (G.induce ((↑S : Set V)ᶜ)).Connected
end SimpleGraph

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
theorem exists_isVertexCut_singleton_of_isBridge
    (G' : SimpleGraph V) (hconn : G'.Connected) (h3 : 3 ≤ Fintype.card V)
    {u v : V} (hbr : G'.IsBridge s(u, v)) :
    ∃ w : V, G'.IsVertexCut {w} := sorry
end SimpleGraph

definitions.title: A vertex cut: a proper subset $S$ whose deletion leaves $G$ disconnected
definitions.informal:
$V'$ is a \texttt{Finset V}, and "$G - V'$ is disconnected" is
\texttt{$\lnot$ (G.induce (↑S)$^{c}$).Connected}.  The conjunct \texttt{↑S $\subset$ Set.univ} records that a
vertex cut is a \emph{proper} subset: without it $S = V$ would qualify vacuously,
since Mathlib's \texttt{Connected} is false on the empty induced graph.

A $k$-vertex cut is the pair \texttt{G.IsVertexCut S $\land$ S.card = k}; that is exactly
what \texttt{vertexConnectivity} minimises over.

informal_statement:
Ex 5.2.6(b): simple, $|X| = |Y| = n$, $\varepsilon > (k- 1)n$ $\Rightarrow$ a matching of size $k$. By the defect formula, a maximum matching smaller than $k$ forces some $S \subseteq X$
with large $|S| - |N(S)|$.  Every edge meeting $S$ then ends inside the small set
$N(S)$, and simplicity caps the total edge count at $(k-1)n$ --- contradiction.

Equivalently, via K\"onig: a covering of size $< k$ caps $\varepsilon$ at $(k-1)n$, since
each covering vertex has degree at most $n$.
formal_statement:
import Mathlib

open scoped Pointwise

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
theorem exists_matching_card_eq_of_card_edges_gt
    {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
    {X Y : Set V} (hbip : G.IsBipartiteWith X Y) {n k : ℕ}
    (hX : X.ncard = n) (hY : Y.ncard = n)
    (hε : (k - 1) * n < G.edgeFinset.card) :
    ∃ M : G.Subgraph, M.IsMatching ∧ M.edgeSet.ncard = k := sorry
end SimpleGraph

informal_statement:
exists_min_weight_spanningTree. Assign each edge a weight and each spanning tree the total; the connector
problem asks for the least, and theorem 2.10 guarantees Kruskal's greedy procedure ---
repeatedly take the cheapest edge not closing a cycle --- always finds one.

\textbf{!} The algorithm is a \emph{procedure}, not a proposition, so what is
stated is the mathematical target it attains: \textbf{existence} of a minimum-weight
spanning tree.  That is strictly weaker than theorem 2.10, which asserts the *greedy
output* is optimal --- the exchange argument quoted above is not exercised by the
skeleton, which is a three-line finiteness argument instead.  Formalising the real
theorem would need Kruskal's algorithm defined first.  Weights are $\mathbb{R}$-valued, matching
B&M's remark that the algorithm is valid for arbitrary real weights.
formal_statement:
import Mathlib

open scoped Classical

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
theorem exists_min_weight_spanningTree (hG : G.Connected) (w : Sym2 V → ℝ) :
    ∃ T : SimpleGraph V, T ≤ G ∧ T.IsTree ∧
      ∀ T' : SimpleGraph V, T' ≤ G → T'.IsTree →
        ∑ e ∈ T.edgeFinset, w e ≤ ∑ e ∈ T'.edgeFinset, w e := sorry
end SimpleGraph

informal_statement:
Definitions:
- A walk is internally disjoint from a subgraph $H$: no \emph{internal} vertex lies in $H$. The walk may start and end on $H$, but between those endpoints it
must stay entirely outside $H$.  This is what makes the bridge relation an
equivalence, and it is why a bridge is a maximal chunk of the graph hanging off
$H$ and touching it only at its attachment points.

\texttt{p.support.tail.dropLast} is the walk's interior --- drop the
first vertex (\texttt{tail}) and the last (\texttt{dropLast}).  \textbf{!} This is \textbf{not} the repo's
\texttt{InternallyDisjoint} (\texttt{TwoConnected.lean:58}), which relates a walk to another
\emph{walk}; here the second argument is a \texttt{Subgraph}.  A walk of length $\le 1$ has empty
interior and so is vacuously internally disjoint from everything --- which is
intended, and is what makes \texttt{bridgeRel} reflexive on single edges.
- B&M's relation $~$ on $E(G) \ E(H)$: $e_{1} ~ e_{2}$ iff joined by a walk internally disjoint from $H$\dots. Two edges outside $H$ are related when you can travel from one to the
other without passing through $H$.  Grouping edges into classes carves
$G - E(H)$ into the pieces that hang off $H$ --- those pieces are the bridges.

\texttt{Relation.EqvGen} wraps the book's raw condition in its
reflexive--symmetric--transitive closure, which \emph{discharges} the book's "it is easy
to verify" rather than proving it: whatever the raw relation does, the closure is
an equivalence by construction.  This is a deliberate trade --- the file gains an
equivalence for free, at the cost that \texttt{bridgeRel} is a priori coarser than $\sim$.
It is not actually coarser (the book's $\sim$ really is an equivalence), but nothing
here proves that, so do not appeal to "\texttt{bridgeRel e f} gives a single connecting
walk" --- it gives a \emph{chain} of them.  Several skeletons below rely on this
distinction.
- The bridge of $H$ in $G$ containing the edge $e$: the subgraph induced by $e$'s $~$-class. A bridge is one of the connected pieces remaining when $H$ is
removed, together with the attachment points where it touches $H$.  The three
"immediate" facts quoted above are \texttt{bridgeOf\_connected},
\texttt{exists\_path\_internallyDisjoint} and \texttt{bridge\_inter\_subset\_cycle} below --- none of
them is actually immediate once $\sim$ is a closure.  In planar graph theory bridges
carry the argument: theorem 9.8 says inner bridges of a cycle avoid one another,
theorem 9.9 that a bridge avoiding every outer bridge is transferable, and together
these drive Kuratowski's theorem 9.10.

Indexed by a \emph{representative edge} $e$ rather than by a class,
so "the bridge containing $e$"; two edges give the same bridge exactly when
\texttt{bridgeRel H e f}.  Built with \texttt{Subgraph.mk} directly --- \textbf{not} with
\texttt{SimpleGraph.toSubgraph} (\texttt{Subgraph.lean:559}), which is \emph{spanning} and would put
every vertex of $G$ into every bridge.  Note \texttt{verts} is the union of the class's
edges, so it automatically includes the attachment points.

\textbf{!} Because \texttt{bridgeRel} is reflexive for \emph{any} $e$ (it is an \texttt{EqvGen}), \texttt{bridgeOf H e}
is nonempty even for an $e$ that is not an edge of $G$ at all --- it then has two
vertices and no edges.  Statements about bridges must therefore carry
\texttt{e $\in$ G.edgeSet \textbackslash\{\} H.edgeSet} explicitly.  Two of them below originally omitted it and
were false as a result; both now carry it (see the module header).

Statement: exists_path_internallyDisjoint. Not only is a bridge connected, but the connection can be made without
re-entering $H$.  This is the form actually used downstream: theorem 9.7 needs
$(v_{1},v_{2})$-paths inside a bridge avoiding the cycle internally, and the dropped
theorem 9.8 needs the same to reach its Jordan-curve contradiction.

The path is asked for as a \texttt{G.Walk}, not a walk in the bridge.
That is equivalent and more convenient: a walk in $G$ between two bridge vertices
that is internally disjoint from $H$ automatically has all its edges in the bridge's
class.  Note the trans case in step 1 is the reason this is genuinely harder than
\texttt{bridgeOf\_connected} and not a corollary of it.
formal_statement:
import Mathlib

open scoped Classical

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
def Walk.InternallyDisjointFrom {V : Type*} {G : SimpleGraph V}
    (H : G.Subgraph) {u v : V} (p : G.Walk u v) : Prop :=
  ∀ x ∈ p.support.tail.dropLast, x ∉ H.verts
end SimpleGraph

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
def bridgeRel {V : Type*} (G : SimpleGraph V) (H : G.Subgraph) :
    Sym2 V → Sym2 V → Prop :=
  Relation.EqvGen fun e₁ e₂ =>
    e₁ ∈ G.edgeSet \ H.edgeSet ∧ e₂ ∈ G.edgeSet \ H.edgeSet ∧
    ∃ (u v : V) (p : G.Walk u v), p.InternallyDisjointFrom H ∧
      p.edges.head? = some e₁ ∧ p.edges.getLast? = some e₂
end SimpleGraph

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
def bridgeOf {V : Type*} (G : SimpleGraph V) (H : G.Subgraph) (e : Sym2 V) :
    G.Subgraph where
  verts := {x | ∃ f, G.bridgeRel H e f ∧ x ∈ f}
  Adj u v := G.Adj u v ∧ G.bridgeRel H e s(u, v)
  adj_sub h := h.1
  edge_vert h := ⟨_, h.2, Sym2.mem_mk_left _ _⟩
  symm u v h := ⟨h.1.symm, by rw [Sym2.eq_swap]; exact h.2⟩
end SimpleGraph

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
theorem exists_path_internallyDisjoint {V : Type*} (G : SimpleGraph V) (H : G.Subgraph)
    (e : Sym2 V) (he : e ∈ G.edgeSet \ H.edgeSet) :
    ∀ u ∈ (G.bridgeOf H e).verts, ∀ v ∈ (G.bridgeOf H e).verts,
      ∃ p : G.Walk u v, p.IsPath ∧ p.InternallyDisjointFrom H := sorry
end SimpleGraph

informal_statement:
exists_rebalanced_matchings. Swapping roles along $P$ moves exactly one edge from the larger matching to the
smaller, leaving the union unchanged.  Repeated application \emph{balances} a family
of matchings --- in \S{}6.3's timetabling reading, spreading lessons evenly across
periods so fewer classrooms are needed at once.

$|M'| = |M| - 1$ is stated additively as \texttt{M'.ncard + 1 = M.ncard} to avoid $\mathbb{N}$
subtraction.

Matchings are carried as \texttt{Set (Sym2 V)} together with an existential witness
\texttt{$\exists$ S : G.Subgraph, S.IsMatching $\land$ S.edgeSet = M}, rather than as subgraphs
directly --- which makes the set operations $\$, $\cup$ in the book's formulas
literal, at the cost of re-deriving the subgraph witness for $M'$ and $N'$.
formal_statement:
import Mathlib

open scoped Classical

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
theorem exists_rebalanced_matchings
    {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] {G : SimpleGraph V}
    {M N : Set (Sym2 V)} (hM : ∃ SM : G.Subgraph, SM.IsMatching ∧ SM.edgeSet = M)
    (hN : ∃ SN : G.Subgraph, SN.IsMatching ∧ SN.edgeSet = N)
    (hdisj : Disjoint M N) (hlt : N.ncard < M.ncard) :
    ∃ M' N' : Set (Sym2 V),
      (∃ SM' : G.Subgraph, SM'.IsMatching ∧ SM'.edgeSet = M') ∧
      (∃ SN' : G.Subgraph, SN'.IsMatching ∧ SN'.edgeSet = N') ∧
      Disjoint M' N' ∧
      M'.ncard + 1 = M.ncard ∧ N'.ncard = N.ncard + 1 ∧ M' ∪ N' = M ∪ N := sorry
end SimpleGraph

informal_statement:
Ex 6.1.3(a): every bipartite $G$ has a $\Delta$-regular bipartite supergraph \textbf{!} carrier change. Pad until every vertex has degree exactly $\Delta$.  Enlarge the smaller side with
isolated vertices so the sides match; then repeatedly join a deficient vertex on
each side --- both sides have equal total deficiency, so such a pair always exists.

\textbf{!} Carrier changes, so the statement produces a new type $W$ together with an
embedding $G \hookrightarrow g H$.

\textbf{!} \textbf{The $\hookrightarrow g$ here is a \texttt{RelEmbedding}, i.e. an \emph{induced} embedding} --- the same
trap that sank the original statement of exercise 1.4.1 in
\texttt{GraphsAndSubgraphs.lean} (recorded in
\texttt{GraphTheory/ExtractionArchive/MathlibDuplicates.md}, entry 5).
It demands \texttt{H.Adj (f a) (f b) $\leftrightarrow$ G.Adj a b}, so the padding edges must never join
two images of $G$-vertices.  The two-disjoint-copies construction respects this;
the naive "add edges between deficient vertices of $G$ itself" does \textbf{not}, and
would make the statement false.  Worth checking carefully before proving.

Part (b) is the alternative proof of Theorem 6.1: a $\Delta$-regular bipartite graph
is 1-factorable (exercise 5.2.3(a)), hence properly $\Delta$-edge colourable, and
restricting to $G$ gives $\chi'(G) \le \Delta$.

\textbf{+} \textbf{This route avoids Lemma 6.1.1 and the Euler theorem entirely}, so it is the
recommended path to Theorem 6.1 in Lean --- see the note there.

import Mathlib

open scoped Classical

namespace SimpleGraph

theorem exists_regular_bipartite_supergraph
    {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
    (hbip : G.IsBipartite) :
    ∃ (W : Type) (_ : Fintype W) (H : SimpleGraph W) (_ : DecidableRel H.Adj) (_ : G ↪g H),
      H.IsBipartite ∧ H.IsRegularOfDegree G.maxDegree := sorry
end SimpleGraph

informal_statement:
Definitions:
- A $k$-factor: a $k$-regular spanning subgraph. Keep every vertex, and select edges so each vertex retains exactly $k$.  A
$1$-factor is precisely a perfect matching; a $2$-factor is a spanning union of
disjoint cycles.

Degree is written \texttt{(H.neighborSet v).ncard} rather than \texttt{H.degree v} --- equal in
value, but avoiding the \texttt{Fintype}/\texttt{DecidableRel} instance juggling that
\texttt{Subgraph.degree} would drag in on every use.

definitions.informal:

$1$-factor is precisely a perfect matching; a $2$-factor is a spanning union of

informal_statement:
exists_triangleFree_chromaticNumber_eq. One might expect a graph needing many colours to contain a large
clique --- after all, a clique's vertices must all differ.  This theorem says the
converse fails badly: chromatic number can be arbitrarily high with no triangle at
all.  Starting from $K_{2}$, the construction gives a triangle-free $k$-chromatic graph
on $3\cdot 2^{k-2} - 1$ vertices --- the 5-cycle for $k = 3$, the Gr\"otzsch graph for
$k = 4$.  The book adds that Erd\H{o}s (1961) proved by the probabilistic method that
for any $k, l \ge 2$ there is a graph of girth $k$ and chromatic number $l$, and that
Descartes' construction (exercise 8.5.2) already achieves girth $6$.

Self-contained: everything needed is the local \texttt{mycielskian}
def, and step 5's recolouring is the only delicate part.  The carrier is
existentially quantified, so each induction step may change it --- which is exactly
what \texttt{mycielskian} does (\texttt{W $\mapsto$ W $\oplus$ W $\oplus$ Unit}).  Note the "without loss of
generality" in the book's step 5 is a genuine permutation of the palette and must
be performed explicitly.
formal_statement:
import Mathlib

open scoped Classical

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
theorem exists_triangleFree_chromaticNumber_eq
    (k : ℕ) (hk : 0 < k) :
    ∃ (V : Type) (_ : Fintype V) (G : SimpleGraph V),
      G.CliqueFree 3 ∧ G.chromaticNumber = k := sorry
end SimpleGraph

informal_statement:
Definitions:
- Colour $i$ is \emph{represented} at $v$: some edge incident with $v$ has colour $i$. A $k$-edge colouring is a plain function \texttt{C : G.edgeSet $\to$ Fin k}, deliberately
\textbf{not} assumed proper --- that is the whole point, since Lemma 6.1.2, Theorem 6.1
and Vizing's Theorem 6.2 all operate on improper colourings and repair them.

"Represented at $v$" is \texttt{$\exists$ e, ↑e $\in$ G.incidenceSet v $\land$ C e = i}.

\textbf{!} Note this file uses \textbf{two different} colouring encodings.  Here a colouring is
a raw function \texttt{G.edgeSet $\to$ Fin k}; but \texttt{IsUniquelyEdgeColourable} below and the
\texttt{edgeChromaticNumber} results use Mathlib's \texttt{G.lineGraph.Coloring (Fin k)}, which
is proper by construction.  The two are not interchangeable, and any proof
crossing between \S{}6.1's machinery and a $\chi'$ statement must convert explicitly.

Statement: exists_two_edge_colouring_both_represented. An Euler tour threads through every vertex; alternating colours along it means
any vertex with room for two edges sees both.  Odd cycles are the sole exception,
since alternation around an odd cycle must repeat somewhere.

\textbf{!} "is not an odd cycle" is a statement about $G$ \textbf{itself}, not about containing
one.  Hence the clause \texttt{p.edges.toFinset = G.edgeFinset} in \texttt{hnotodd} is
load-bearing: it says the cycle exhausts $G$.  Dropping it would make the
hypothesis far too strong (excluding every graph with an odd cycle anywhere) and
the lemma useless for Lemma 6.1.2, which applies it to two-coloured components.
formal_statement:
import Mathlib

open scoped Classical

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
def IsRepresentedAt {V : Type*} {G : SimpleGraph V} {k : ℕ}
    (C : G.edgeSet → Fin k) (i : Fin k) (v : V) : Prop :=
  ∃ e : G.edgeSet, (e : Sym2 V) ∈ G.incidenceSet v ∧ C e = i
end SimpleGraph

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
theorem exists_two_edge_colouring_both_represented
    {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
    (hconn : G.Connected)
    (hnotodd : ¬ ∃ (u : V) (p : G.Walk u u),
      p.IsCycle ∧ Odd p.length ∧ p.edges.toFinset = G.edgeFinset) :
    ∃ C : G.edgeSet → Fin 2,
      ∀ v : V, 2 ≤ G.degree v → ∀ i : Fin 2, IsRepresentedAt C i v := sorry
end SimpleGraph

informal_statement:
Definitions:
- Two $u$--$v$ walks are internally disjoint if they share no internal vertex. Specialised to a family of \emph{two} $u$--$v$ walks.  "$x$ is an internal vertex of
$p$" is \texttt{x $\in$ p.support $\land$ x $\ne$ u $\land$ x $\ne$ v}, so "no $x$ is internal to both" becomes

    $\forall$ x, x $\in$ p.support $\to$ x $\in$ q.support $\to$ x = u $\lor$ x = v.

\textbf{!} Note this does \textbf{not} forbid $p = q$.  For adjacent $u, v$ the single edge
satisfies it with $p = q$, its only vertices being the two endpoints.  Theorem
3.2 as stated therefore cannot yield a cycle, which is why Corollary 3.2.1 is
derived from the edge-disjointness-carrying strengthening
\texttt{exists\_two\_internally\_disjoint\_paths\_of\_two\_connected} rather than from
\texttt{two\_connected\_iff\_two\_internally\_disjoint\_paths} directly.
- A vertex cut: a proper subset $S$ whose deletion leaves $G$ disconnected. $V'$ is a \texttt{Finset V}, and "$G - V'$ is disconnected" is
\texttt{$\lnot$ (G.induce (↑S)$^{c}$).Connected}.  The conjunct \texttt{↑S $\subset$ Set.univ} records that a
vertex cut is a \emph{proper} subset: without it $S = V$ would qualify vacuously,
since Mathlib's \texttt{Connected} is false on the empty induced graph.

A $k$-vertex cut is the pair \texttt{G.IsVertexCut S $\land$ S.card = k}; that is exactly
what \texttt{vertexConnectivity} minimises over.
- Vertex connectivity $\kappa(G)$. The book's case split is on "$G$ has a pair of distinct nonadjacent vertices";
the Lean split is on the equivalent "$G$ has a vertex cut at all", which is the
condition the two branches actually need.  So
\item some cut exists $\Rightarrow$ \texttt{$\kappa$ = sInf \{S.card | G.IsVertexCut S\}};
\item no cut exists (the complete graphs) $\Rightarrow$ $\kappa = \nu - 1$.

\texttt{sInf} on $\mathbb{N}$ is Mathlib's \texttt{Nat.sInf}, with \texttt{sInf $\emptyset$ = 0}; the $if$ guard means
that fallback is never reached here.  Natural subtraction makes $\nu - 1 = 0$
when $V$ is empty, matching "trivial $\Rightarrow$ $\kappa = 0$".

Statement: exists_two_internally_disjoint_paths_of_two_connected. , strengthened to carry the edge-disjointness that
Corollary 3.2.1 needs.

\texttt{InternallyDisjoint p q} as defined in this file does \emph{not} forbid $p = q$: for
adjacent $u, v$ the single edge satisfies it with $p = q$, since its only
vertices are the two endpoints.  So Theorem 3.2 \emph{as stated} cannot yield a cycle,
and the book's one-line derivation of Corollary 3.2.1 does not go through.
Adding \texttt{p.edges.Disjoint q.edges} to the conclusion repairs this; the book gets
it for free because its $d(u,v) = 1$ case produces a genuine \emph{cycle}
via theorem 2.3, not merely two paths.
formal_statement:
import Mathlib

open scoped Classical

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
def InternallyDisjoint {u v : V} (p q : G.Walk u v) : Prop :=
  ∀ x : V, x ∈ p.support → x ∈ q.support → x = u ∨ x = v
end SimpleGraph

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
def IsVertexCut (G : SimpleGraph V) (S : Finset V) : Prop :=
  (↑S : Set V) ⊂ Set.univ ∧ ¬ (G.induce ((↑S : Set V)ᶜ)).Connected
end SimpleGraph

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
noncomputable def vertexConnectivity (G : SimpleGraph V) : ℕ :=
  if ∃ S : Finset V, G.IsVertexCut S then
    sInf {n : ℕ | ∃ S : Finset V, G.IsVertexCut S ∧ S.card = n}
  else
    Fintype.card V - 1
end SimpleGraph

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
theorem exists_two_internally_disjoint_paths_of_two_connected
    (hk : 2 ≤ G.vertexConnectivity) (h : 3 ≤ Fintype.card V)
    {u v : V} (huv : u ≠ v) :
    ∃ p q : G.Walk u v, p.IsPath ∧ q.IsPath ∧
      G.InternallyDisjoint p q ∧ p.edges.Disjoint q.edges := sorry
end SimpleGraph

informal_statement:
Definitions:
- $G$ contains a subdivision of $K_{4}$: four distinct branch vertices joined pairwise by six paths,\dots. A "topological $K_{4}$": four \textbf{branch vertices}, each of the six pairs
joined by a path, the six paths sharing no interior vertices with one another or
with the branch vertices.  Drawn on paper it is $K_{4}$ with beads threaded onto its
edges.

The book says "obtainable from $K_{4}$ by subdividing edges",
which is a statement about an abstract graph; what a \emph{containment} claim needs is
the witness form above --- six \texttt{Walk}s in $G$ with disjointness conditions.  The two
are equivalent, and only this direction is ever used.  The three side conditions
say, in order: the branch vertices are distinct; each of the six walks is a path;
no path's interior meets a branch vertex; and no two paths' interiors meet.
\texttt{support.tail.dropLast} is the interior of a walk (drop both endpoints).

Statement: fourChromatic_hasK4Subdivision. This is the case $k = 4$ of Haj\'os' conjecture, settled by Dirac
(1952).  The book notes the conjecture in general is *known to be a very difficult
problem*, and mentions Hadwiger's related conjecture, whose case $k = 5$ Wagner
showed equivalent to the four-colour conjecture of chapter 9.

Step 1's monotonicity lemma is what licenses the book's
"without loss of generality" and should be built first --- without it the reduction
to the critical subgraph is not available.  The induction in step 2 is on the
carrier's cardinality, but cases A and B produce graphs on \emph{different carriers}
(subgraph coercions), so the induction is cleanest stated over all graphs on all
carriers of bounded size rather than over subgraphs of a fixed $G$.
formal_statement:
import Mathlib

open scoped Classical

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
def HasK4Subdivision {V : Type*} (G : SimpleGraph V) : Prop :=
  ∃ (a b c d : V) (pab : G.Walk a b) (pac : G.Walk a c) (pad : G.Walk a d)
    (pbc : G.Walk b c) (pbd : G.Walk b d) (pcd : G.Walk c d),
    [a, b, c, d].Nodup ∧
    (pab.IsPath ∧ pac.IsPath ∧ pad.IsPath ∧ pbc.IsPath ∧ pbd.IsPath ∧ pcd.IsPath) ∧
    (∀ p ∈ [pab.support.tail.dropLast, pac.support.tail.dropLast, pad.support.tail.dropLast,
            pbc.support.tail.dropLast, pbd.support.tail.dropLast, pcd.support.tail.dropLast],
       ∀ x ∈ p, x ∉ ({a, b, c, d} : Set V)) ∧
    (List.Pairwise (fun p q => ∀ x ∈ p, x ∉ q)
      [pab.support.tail.dropLast, pac.support.tail.dropLast, pad.support.tail.dropLast,
       pbc.support.tail.dropLast, pbd.support.tail.dropLast, pcd.support.tail.dropLast])
end SimpleGraph

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
theorem fourChromatic_hasK4Subdivision
    {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] [Nonempty V] {G : SimpleGraph V}
    (h : G.chromaticNumber = 4) :
    G.HasK4Subdivision := sorry
end SimpleGraph

informal_statement:
Definitions:
- \texttt{IsRamseyBound n k l}: every graph on $n$ vertices has a $k$-clique or an $l$-indep set.\dots. \texttt{IsRamseyBound n k l} says $n$ is already large enough for that conclusion:
\texttt{$\forall$ G : SimpleGraph (Fin n), ($\exists$ s, G.IsNClique k s) $\lor$ ($\exists$ t, G.IsNIndepSet l t)}.

Fixing the carrier as \texttt{Fin n} rather than quantifying over all $n$-element types
is what makes \texttt{ramseyNumber} an \texttt{sInf} over $\mathbb{N}$ below.

Total disorder is impossible: any sufficiently large graph contains one kind of
order or the other.
- The Ramsey number $r(k, l)$. The exact threshold at which order becomes unavoidable.

\textbf{!} \textbf{\texttt{sInf $\emptyset$ = 0} is a live trap} until \texttt{exists\_isRamseyBound} is proved: without
it every \texttt{ramseyNumber k l} could silently be $0$, and every theorem below would
be about the wrong number.  That existence result is therefore not optional
scaffolding --- it gates the meaning of the definition itself.

Statement: fourteen_le_ramseyNumber_three_five. Thirteen vertices do not suffice, so the threshold is $\ge 14$.

\textbf{!} The book's upper bound chain routes through $r(3,4) = 9$, which itself needs
the \textbf{strict} form of Theorem 7.4 ($r(3,3)$ and $r(2,4)$ both even).  Neither
$r(3,4) = 9$ nor its ingredients are stated in this file, so the exact value
$r(3,5) = 14$ is not reachable from what is here even once everything is proved.
formal_statement:
import Mathlib

open scoped Finset

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
def IsRamseyBound (n k l : ℕ) : Prop :=
  ∀ G : SimpleGraph (Fin n), (∃ s, G.IsNClique k s) ∨ (∃ t, G.IsNIndepSet l t)
end SimpleGraph

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
noncomputable def ramseyNumber (k l : ℕ) : ℕ :=
  sInf {n | SimpleGraph.IsRamseyBound n k l}
end SimpleGraph

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
theorem fourteen_le_ramseyNumber_three_five : 14 ≤ SimpleGraph.ramseyNumber 3 5 := sorry
end SimpleGraph

gallai_two_per_class. The hypothesis provides \emph{some} colouring, possibly using far more

import Mathlib

open scoped Finset

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
noncomputable def generalisedRamseyNumber {m : ℕ} {W : Fin m → Type*}
    (F : ∀ i, SimpleGraph (W i)) : ℕ :=
  sInf {n | ∀ χ : Sym2 (Fin n) → Fin m,
    ∃ i, F i ⊑ SimpleGraph.fromEdgeSet {e | χ e = i ∧ ¬ e.IsDiag}}
end SimpleGraph

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
theorem generalisedRamsey_tree_star
    {W : Type} [Fintype W] {T : SimpleGraph W} (hT : T.IsTree)
    {m n : ℕ} (hm : Fintype.card W = m) (hdvd : (m - 1) ∣ (n - 1)) :
    generalisedRamseyNumber (W := ![W, Fin 1 ⊕ Fin n])
        (Fin.cons T (Fin.cons (completeBipartiteGraph (Fin 1) (Fin n)) finZeroElim))
      = m + n - 1 := sorry
end SimpleGraph

informal_statement:
Definitions:
- $G$ is critical: $\chi(H) < \chi(G)$ for every proper subgraph $H \subset G$. A critical graph is "minimally" $k$-chromatic: remove any vertex or
any edge and the chromatic number drops.  Critical graphs are useful precisely
because they carry the whole difficulty of a colouring problem --- every
$k$-chromatic graph contains a $k$-critical subgraph, so statements about
$k$-chromatic graphs reduce to the critical case, which is how corollary 8.1.1,
Brooks' theorem 8.4 and theorem 8.5 all begin.

The quantifier ranges over \texttt{G.Subgraph}, not over the order
on \texttt{SimpleGraph V}.  This is load-bearing (Scaffolding judgement 1): the
\texttt{SimpleGraph V} order can only \emph{remove edges}, never vertices, whereas the book's
"proper subgraph" includes $G - v$.  Under the weaker order $\bot$ on two vertices
would be vacuously 1-critical --- it has no proper edge-subgraph --- contradicting
exercise 8.1.7, which says the only 1-critical graph is $K_{1}$.
- $G$ is $k$-critical: $k$-chromatic and critical. $k$-critical graphs are the irreducible witnesses to needing $k$
colours.  Exercise 8.1.7 classifies the small cases completely --- the only
1-critical graph is $K_{1}$, the only 2-critical graph is $K_{2}$, and the 3-critical
graphs are exactly the odd cycles --- and Brooks' theorem 8.4 consumes precisely
that classification to get its standing hypothesis $k \ge 4$.

\texttt{G.chromaticNumber = k} compares an $\mathbb{N}\infty$ with a coerced $\mathbb{N}$,
so $k$-chromaticity here also carries the information that $\chi(G) \ne \top$.

Statement: hajos_construction. Glue two $k$-critical graphs at a single vertex $v$, delete one edge
at $v$ from each, and join the two orphaned endpoints $v_{1}$, $v_{2}$ by a new edge; the
result is again $k$-critical.  Step 1 is the heart: the new edge forces $v_{1}$ and
$v_{2}$ apart, so $v$ must agree with one of them, and that agreement is exactly what
repairs the deleted edge on that side.  The \textbf{Haj\'os construction} matters because,
iterated from $K_k$, it generates \emph{every} graph with chromatic number at least $k$
--- a complete but impractical characterisation.

The outline's binder ${k v v_{1} v_{2} : _}$ cannot elaborate
(heterogeneous types under one hole), so the statement uses explicit
${k : \mathbb{N}} {v v_{1} v_{2} : V}$.  Both graphs live on \textbf{one} carrier $V$; "exactly one
vertex in common" is \texttt{hmeet : G$_{1}$.support $\cap$ G$_{2}$.support = \{v\}}, and each $G_{i}$'s real
content is \texttt{G$_{i}$.induce G$_{i}$.support}, which is why the hypotheses are stated about the
induced graphs rather than about $G_{1}$, $G_{2}$ directly.  Edge deletion is \texttt{\textbackslash\{\} edge}
and edge addition is \texttt{$\sqcup$ edge}.
formal_statement:
import Mathlib

open scoped Classical

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
def IsCritical {V : Type*} (G : SimpleGraph V) : Prop :=
  ∀ H : G.Subgraph, H < ⊤ → H.coe.chromaticNumber < G.chromaticNumber
end SimpleGraph

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
def IsKCritical {V : Type*} (G : SimpleGraph V) (k : ℕ) : Prop :=
  G.chromaticNumber = k ∧ G.IsCritical
end SimpleGraph

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
theorem hajos_construction {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] [Nonempty V]
    {G₁ G₂ : SimpleGraph V} {k : ℕ} {v v₁ v₂ : V}
    (h₁ : (G₁.induce G₁.support).IsKCritical k) (h₂ : (G₂.induce G₂.support).IsKCritical k)
    (hmeet : G₁.support ∩ G₂.support = {v})
    (he₁ : G₁.Adj v v₁) (he₂ : G₂.Adj v v₂) :
    IsKCritical
      (((G₁ \ SimpleGraph.edge v v₁) ⊔ (G₂ \ SimpleGraph.edge v v₂)) ⊔ SimpleGraph.edge v₁ v₂)
      k := sorry
end SimpleGraph

informal_statement:
Thm 5.2 (Hall): a bipartite $G$ has a matching saturating $X$ iff $|N(S)| \ge |S|$. Hall's condition: no set of vertices on the $X$ side may collectively have too
few neighbours.  Colloquially --- no group of $k$ workers may be jointly qualified
for fewer than $k$ jobs.

$N(S)$ is written \texttt{$\bigcup$ v $\in$ S, G.neighborSet v}, and the inequality is stated as
\texttt{S.ncard $\le$ ($\bigcup$ \dots).ncard} --- the book's $|N(S)| \ge |S|$ with sides swapped.
formal_statement:
import Mathlib

open scoped Pointwise

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
theorem hall_bipartite_matching
    {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
    {X Y : Set V} (hbip : G.IsBipartiteWith X Y) :
    (∃ M : G.Subgraph, M.IsMatching ∧ X ⊆ M.verts) ↔
      ∀ S ⊆ X, S.ncard ≤ (⋃ v ∈ S, G.neighborSet v).ncard := sorry
end SimpleGraph
title: Thm 5.2 (Hall): a bipartite $G$ has a matching saturating $X$ iff $|N(S)| \ge |S|$
statement_informal:

few neighbours.  Colloquially --- no group of $k$ workers may be jointly qualified

informal_statement:
Definitions:
- $G$ is Hamilton-connected: every ordered pair is joined by a Hamilton path (Ex 4.2.11). Not merely that \emph{some} spanning path exists, but that both endpoints may be
prescribed arbitrarily: \texttt{$\forall$ u v, u $\ne$ v $\to$ $\exists$ p : G.Walk u v, p.IsHamiltonian}.

Substantially stronger than being hamiltonian, and correspondingly forces many
edges --- part (a) is \texttt{hamiltonConnected\_edge\_bound} below, part (b) is
\texttt{exists\_extremal\_hamiltonConnected}.

The book's $[x]$ here denotes the ceiling, so $[\tfrac{1}{2}(3\nu+1)]$ is $(3 * \nu + 1 + 1) / 2$
in natural-number division.

Statement: Ex 4.2.11(a): a Hamilton-connected graph satisfies $3\nu + 1 \le 2\varepsilon$ (Moon). Hamilton-connectedness demands a spanning path between \emph{every} pair, forcing many
edges.  Every vertex must have degree at least $3$: a degree-$2$ vertex has both
its edges forced into any spanning path through it as an interior vertex, leaving
no way to make it an endpoint of a spanning path to a third vertex.  Summing
$d(v) \ge 3$ and applying handshaking gives $2\varepsilon \ge 3\nu$, and a parity refinement
pushes this to $2\varepsilon \ge 3\nu + 1$.

Formalised as $3\nu + 1 \le 2\varepsilon$ to stay in the natural numbers and avoid the ceiling.

\textbf{!} The Lean signature omits the book's $\nu \ge 4$.  It is needed: for $\nu = 3$,
$\top$ on three vertices is Hamilton-connected with $\varepsilon = 3$, but $3\nu + 1 = 10 > 6 = 2\varepsilon$.
So the statement as written is \textbf{false at $\nu = 3$} and \texttt{4 $\le$ Fintype.card V} must
be added.
formal_statement:
import Mathlib

open scoped Classical

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
def IsHamiltonConnected {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) : Prop :=
  ∀ u v : V, u ≠ v → ∃ p : G.Walk u v, p.IsHamiltonian
end SimpleGraph

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
theorem hamiltonConnected_edge_bound (hν : 4 ≤ Fintype.card V)
    (h : G.IsHamiltonConnected) :
    3 * Fintype.card V + 1 ≤ 2 * G.edgeFinset.card := sorry
end SimpleGraph

informal_statement:
Definitions:
- One Bondy--Chv\'atal closure step: add a nonadjacent pair whose degree sum is $\ge$ $\nu$. Look for two vertices not yet joined but which between them already have at
least $\nu$ neighbours; Lemma 4.4.1 says adding the edge changes nothing about
hamiltonicity, so add it.  Repeat until no such pair is left.

\texttt{ClosureStep G H} captures a \emph{single} such addition, \texttt{H = G $\sqcup$ edge u v}.  The
closure is then reached by \texttt{Relation.ReflTransGen ClosureStep}, and "no such pair
remains" is expressed at the use site as $H = \top$ or as the absence of a further
step, rather than by a fixpoint operator.

Defining $c(G)$ as a function presupposes Lemma 4.4.2 --- that the result is
independent of the order in which edges are added --- and that lemma is itself one
of the chapter's results.  Positing the fixpoint would therefore assume what the
chapter sets out to prove.  Using the step relation keeps the development honest;
the price is that statements below quantify over \texttt{ReflTransGen ClosureStep}
chains instead of mentioning $c(G)$ directly.

Degree is \texttt{Nat.card (G.neighborSet $\cdot$)} so the relation is well-typed for
arbitrary graphs on $V$ without a \texttt{DecidableRel} instance.

Statement: Thm 4.4 (honest restatement): reachability by closure steps preserves hamiltonicity. Stated in the file's "honest restatement" form: instead of positing a closure
operator, it says that if $H$ is reachable from $G$ by any finite chain of
\texttt{ClosureStep}s, then $G$ is hamiltonian exactly when $H$ is.  Taking $H$ to admit
no further step recovers the book's statement.

This restatement is what lets the file skip Lemma 4.4.2 entirely --- see below.

The book must prove $c(G)$ well defined before Theorem 4.4 can even be stated;
its proof (\S{}4.2, p. 64) is the argument:

Because this file quantifies over \texttt{ReflTransGen ClosureStep} chains rather than
naming a closure, \textbf{Lemma 4.4.2 is not needed and is not formalised}: the
statement above holds for \emph{every} chain, confluent or not.  It would only be
required if a \texttt{closure : SimpleGraph V $\to$ SimpleGraph V} function were introduced.
formal_statement:
import Mathlib

open scoped Classical

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
def ClosureStep (G H : SimpleGraph V) : Prop :=
  ∃ u v : V, ¬ G.Adj u v ∧ u ≠ v ∧
    Fintype.card V ≤ Nat.card (G.neighborSet u) + Nat.card (G.neighborSet v) ∧
    H = G ⊔ SimpleGraph.edge u v
end SimpleGraph

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
theorem hamiltonian_iff_of_closureSteps {G H : SimpleGraph V}
    (h : Relation.ReflTransGen ClosureStep G H) :
    G.IsHamiltonian ↔ H.IsHamiltonian := sorry
end SimpleGraph

definitions.title: One Bondy--Chv\'atal closure step: add a nonadjacent pair whose degree sum is $\ge$ $\nu$
definitions.informal:
Look for two vertices not yet joined but which between them already have at
least $\nu$ neighbours; Lemma 4.4.1 says adding the edge changes nothing about
hamiltonicity, so add it.  Repeat until no such pair is left.

\texttt{ClosureStep G H} captures a \emph{single} such addition, \texttt{H = G $\sqcup$ edge u v}.  The
closure is then reached by \texttt{Relation.ReflTransGen ClosureStep}, and "no such pair
remains" is expressed at the use site as $H = \top$ or as the absence of a further
step, rather than by a fixpoint operator.

Defining $c(G)$ as a function presupposes Lemma 4.4.2 --- that the result is
independent of the order in which edges are added --- and that lemma is itself one
of the chapter's results.  Positing the fixpoint would therefore assume what the
chapter sets out to prove.  Using the step relation keeps the development honest;
the price is that statements below quantify over \texttt{ReflTransGen ClosureStep}
chains instead of mentioning $c(G)$ directly.

Degree is \texttt{Nat.card (G.neighborSet $\cdot$)} so the relation is well-typed for
arbitrary graphs on $V$ without a \texttt{DecidableRel} instance.

import Mathlib

open scoped Classical

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
def ClosureStep (G H : SimpleGraph V) : Prop :=
  ∃ u v : V, ¬ G.Adj u v ∧ u ≠ v ∧
    Fintype.card V ≤ Nat.card (G.neighborSet u) + Nat.card (G.neighborSet v) ∧
    H = G ⊔ SimpleGraph.edge u v
end SimpleGraph

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
theorem hamiltonian_of_closureSteps_top (hν : 3 ≤ Fintype.card V)
    (h : Relation.ReflTransGen ClosureStep G ⊤) :
    G.IsHamiltonian := sorry
end SimpleGraph

(a) --- so (a) was a hidden prerequisite with no declaration.  The triage
(\texttt{log/graphtheory-EXERCISE\_TRIAGE.md} \S{}A.3) recorded this as a fidelity gap and
recommended stating (a).  Nothing here is invented: the statement is the book's
own, quoted above.

renders its sequence --- via a sorting equiv $\sigma$ on \texttt{Fin $\nu$} making the degrees

informal_statement:
Ex 4.2.3: a Hamilton path implies $\omega(G - S) \le |S| + 1$. The path analogue of Theorem 4.2.  Deleting $k$ vertices from a \emph{path} breaks it
into at most $k + 1$ pieces --- one more than for a cycle, because a path has two
loose ends rather than being closed up.  The Hamilton path $P$ is a spanning
subgraph of $G$, so $\omega(G - S) \le \omega(P - S) \le |S| + 1$.

The extra $+1$ is the price of not closing the cycle, making the condition
weaker --- as it must be, since a Hamilton path is weaker than a Hamilton cycle.

    (hG : ∃ (a b : V) (p : G.Walk a b), p.IsHamiltonian)
    (S : Finset V) (hS : S.Nonempty) (hSne : S ≠ Finset.univ) :
    Nat.card ((⊤ : G.Subgraph).deleteVerts ↑S).coe.ConnectedComponent ≤ S.card + 1 := sorry
end SimpleGraph

informal_statement:
Thm 4.2: if $G$ is hamiltonian then $\omega(G - S) \le |S|$ for every nonempty proper $S$. A hamiltonian graph is held together by a single cycle through every vertex, and
a cycle is hard to shatter: removing $k$ vertices from it leaves at most $k$
arcs.

$G - S$ is rendered as \texttt{(($\top$ : G.Subgraph).deleteVerts ↑S).coe}, so the component
count is \texttt{Nat.card} of \emph{that} graph's \texttt{ConnectedComponent}.  Using the \texttt{Subgraph}
API rather than \texttt{G.induce (↑S)$^{c}$} is what lets the "spanning subgraph" step be
stated at all, since $C - S$ and $G - S$ then live over the same vertex set.
formal_statement:

open scoped Classical

variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
theorem hamiltonian_toughness (hG : G.IsHamiltonian) (S : Finset V)
    (hS : S.Nonempty) (hSne : S ≠ Finset.univ) :
    Nat.card ((⊤ : G.Subgraph).deleteVerts ↑S).coe.ConnectedComponent ≤ S.card := sorry
end SimpleGraph

informal_statement:
Definitions:
- The Harary graph $H_{m,n}$ on vertex set \texttt{ZMod n} (a circulant). Arrange $n$ stations in a circle and link each to its $r$ nearest neighbours on
each side, adding long-range links across the circle when $m$ is odd.  The
carrier is \texttt{ZMod n}, which makes the book's "addition taken modulo $n$" literal.

The three cases are a single $if$-cascade on $m \% 2$ and $n \% 2$; Case 1 is the
base and Cases 2--3 are $\sqcup$ with an extra chord relation.

Statement: Edge count / optimality: $H_{m,n}$ has $\lceil mn/2\rceil$ edges. The book's ${x}$ is the ceiling $\lceil x\rceil$, so ${mn/2}$ is written as the
natural-number division $(m * n + 1) / 2$.

Only $\varepsilon(H_{m,n}) = \lceil mn/2\rceil$ is formalised.  The optimality conclusions
$f(m,n) = \lceil mn/2\rceil$ and $g(m,n) = \lceil mn/2\rceil$ are \emph{not} stated in this file, since
$f$ and $g$ (least edge counts over all $m$-connected graphs) are not defined
here.

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
def hararyGraph (m n : ℕ) : SimpleGraph (ZMod n) := sorry
end SimpleGraph

    [DecidableRel (hararyGraph m n).Adj] (hmn : m < n) :
