informal_statement:
Definitions:
- A vertex cut: a proper subset $S$ whose deletion leaves $G$ disconnected. $V'$ is a \texttt{Finset V}, and "$G - V'$ is disconnected" is
\texttt{$\lnot$ (G.induce (↑S)$^{c}$).Connected}.  The conjunct \texttt{↑S $\subset$ Set.univ} records that a
vertex cut is a \emph{proper} subset: without it $S = V$ would qualify vacuously,
since Mathlib's \texttt{Connected} is false on the empty induced graph.

A $k$-vertex cut is the pair \texttt{G.IsVertexCut S $\land$ S.card = k}; that is exactly
what \texttt{vertexConnectivity} minimises over.
- The Harary graph $H_{m,n}$ on vertex set \texttt{ZMod n} (a circulant). Arrange $n$ stations in a circle and link each to its $r$ nearest neighbours on
each side, adding long-range links across the circle when $m$ is odd.  The
carrier is \texttt{ZMod n}, which makes the book's "addition taken modulo $n$" literal.

The three cases are a single $if$-cascade on $m \% 2$ and $n \% 2$; Case 1 is the
base and Cases 2--3 are $\sqcup$ with an extra chord relation.
- Vertex connectivity $\kappa(G)$. The book's case split is on "$G$ has a pair of distinct nonadjacent vertices";
the Lean split is on the equivalent "$G$ has a vertex cut at all", which is the
condition the two branches actually need.  So
\item some cut exists $\Rightarrow$ \texttt{$\kappa$ = sInf \{S.card | G.IsVertexCut S\}};
\item no cut exists (the complete graphs) $\Rightarrow$ $\kappa = \nu - 1$.

\texttt{sInf} on $\mathbb{N}$ is Mathlib's \texttt{Nat.sInf}, with \texttt{sInf $\emptyset$ = 0}; the $if$ guard means
that fallback is never reached here.  Natural subtraction makes $\nu - 1 = 0$
when $V$ is empty, matching "trivial $\Rightarrow$ $\kappa = 0$".

Statement: hararyGraph_isConnectivity. (Harary, 1962).

The book proves only the even case; the odd case is exercise 3.3.1, so a full
Lean proof of the statement as given must supply it.

Note the two "clearly"/"without loss of generality" steps carry real weight in
Lean: the WLOG needs $|V' \cap S| + |V' \cap T| \le |V'| + 2 < 2r + 2$, and the
"sequence of distinct vertices ... difference at most $r$" is a greedy
construction requiring an explicit induction on the arc.
formal_statement:
import Mathlib

open scoped Classical

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
def IsVertexCut (G : SimpleGraph V) (S : Finset V) : Prop :=
  (↑S : Set V) ⊂ Set.univ ∧ ¬ (G.induce ((↑S : Set V)ᶜ)).Connected
end SimpleGraph

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
def hararyGraph (m n : ℕ) : SimpleGraph (ZMod n) := sorry
end SimpleGraph

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
noncomputable def vertexConnectivity (G : SimpleGraph V) : ℕ :=
  if ∃ S : Finset V, G.IsVertexCut S then
    sInf {n : ℕ | ∃ S : Finset V, G.IsVertexCut S ∧ S.card = n}
  else
    Fintype.card V - 1
end SimpleGraph

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
theorem hararyGraph_isConnectivity (m n : ℕ) [NeZero n] (hmn : m < n) :
    (hararyGraph m n).vertexConnectivity = m := sorry
end SimpleGraph

informal_statement:
Definitions:
- $G$ contains a subdivision of $K_{4}$: four distinct branch vertices joined pairwise by six paths,\dots. A "topological $K_{4}$": four \textbf{branch vertices}, each of the six pairs
joined by a path, the six paths sharing no interior vertices with one another or
with the branch vertices.  Drawn on paper it is $K_{4}$ with beads threaded onto its
edges.

The book says "obtainable from $K_{4}$ by subdividing edges",
which is a statement about an abstract graph; what a \emph{containment} claim needs is
the witness form above --- six \texttt{Walk}s in $G$ with disjointness conditions.  The two
are equivalent, and only this direction is ever used.  The three side conditions
say, in order: the branch vertices are distinct; each of the six walks is a path;
no path's interior meets a branch vertex; and no two paths' interiors meet.
\texttt{support.tail.dropLast} is the interior of a walk (drop both endpoints).

Statement: hasK4Subdivision_of_card_edges. Enough edges relative to vertices force the graph to be locally rich
enough to contain four branch vertices and six connecting paths.  The invariant in
step 2 is the whole trick: deleting a low-degree vertex is "free" with respect to
the quantity $2\nu - \varepsilon$, so the stripping can be run to completion without ever
losing the hypothesis.  Part (b) shows $2\nu - 2$ is exactly the right threshold.

Restated additively as $2\nu \le \varepsilon + 2$ rather than $\varepsilon \ge 2\nu - 2$, to
keep $\mathbb{N}$-subtraction out.  Step 2's bookkeeping is the $\mathbb{N}$-arithmetic core and is worth
isolating: \texttt{(G.induce \{v\}$^{c}$).edgeFinset.card + G.degree v = G.edgeFinset.card}.
formal_statement:
import Mathlib

open scoped Classical

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
def HasK4Subdivision {V : Type*} (G : SimpleGraph V) : Prop :=
  ∃ (a b c d : V) (pab : G.Walk a b) (pac : G.Walk a c) (pad : G.Walk a d)
    (pbc : G.Walk b c) (pbd : G.Walk b d) (pcd : G.Walk c d),
    [a, b, c, d].Nodup ∧
    (pab.IsPath ∧ pac.IsPath ∧ pad.IsPath ∧ pbc.IsPath ∧ pbd.IsPath ∧ pcd.IsPath) ∧
    (∀ p ∈ [pab.support.tail.dropLast, pac.support.tail.dropLast, pad.support.tail.dropLast,
            pbc.support.tail.dropLast, pbd.support.tail.dropLast, pcd.support.tail.dropLast],
       ∀ x ∈ p, x ∉ ({a, b, c, d} : Set V)) ∧
    (List.Pairwise (fun p q => ∀ x ∈ p, x ∉ q)
      [pab.support.tail.dropLast, pac.support.tail.dropLast, pad.support.tail.dropLast,
       pbc.support.tail.dropLast, pbd.support.tail.dropLast, pcd.support.tail.dropLast])
end SimpleGraph

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
theorem hasK4Subdivision_of_card_edges {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V]
    (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
    (hv : 4 ≤ Fintype.card V) (he : 2 * Fintype.card V ≤ G.edgeFinset.card + 2) :
    G.HasK4Subdivision := sorry
end SimpleGraph

joined by a path, the six paths sharing no interior vertices with one another or
with the branch vertices.  Drawn on paper it is $K_{4}$ with beads threaded onto its
edges.

The book says "obtainable from $K_{4}$ by subdividing edges",
which is a statement about an abstract graph; what a \emph{containment} claim needs is
the witness form above --- six \texttt{Walk}s in $G$ with disjointness conditions.  The two
are equivalent, and only this direction is ever used.  The three side conditions
say, in order: the branch vertices are distinct; each of the six walks is a path;
no path's interior meets a branch vertex; and no two paths' interiors meet.
\texttt{support.tail.dropLast} is the interior of a walk (drop both endpoints).

import Mathlib

open scoped Classical

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
def HasK4Subdivision {V : Type*} (G : SimpleGraph V) : Prop :=
  ∃ (a b c d : V) (pab : G.Walk a b) (pac : G.Walk a c) (pad : G.Walk a d)
    (pbc : G.Walk b c) (pbd : G.Walk b d) (pcd : G.Walk c d),
    [a, b, c, d].Nodup ∧
    (pab.IsPath ∧ pac.IsPath ∧ pad.IsPath ∧ pbc.IsPath ∧ pbd.IsPath ∧ pcd.IsPath) ∧
    (∀ p ∈ [pab.support.tail.dropLast, pac.support.tail.dropLast, pad.support.tail.dropLast,
            pbc.support.tail.dropLast, pbd.support.tail.dropLast, pcd.support.tail.dropLast],
       ∀ x ∈ p, x ∉ ({a, b, c, d} : Set V)) ∧
    (List.Pairwise (fun p q => ∀ x ∈ p, x ∉ q)
      [pab.support.tail.dropLast, pac.support.tail.dropLast, pad.support.tail.dropLast,
       pbc.support.tail.dropLast, pbd.support.tail.dropLast, pcd.support.tail.dropLast])
end SimpleGraph

    (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj] (hv : 4 ≤ Fintype.card V)
    (h : (Finset.univ.filter fun v => G.degree v < 3).card ≤ 1) :
    G.HasK4Subdivision := sorry
end SimpleGraph

informal_statement:
Definitions:
- Ex 1.2.10: the $k$-cube --- vertices are $k$-bit strings, adjacent iff they differ in exactly one coordinate. Each vertex is a binary string of length $k$, equivalently a corner of a
$k$-dimensional cube; two corners are joined when their descriptions agree everywhere
but one position.  For $k = 3$ this is literally the corners and edges of an ordinary
cube --- the book's figure 1.4b.

Mathlib has no named hypercube graph, so this is built here.
Tuples are \texttt{Fin k $\to$ Bool}; "differ in exactly one coordinate" is $\exists! i, x i \ne y i$.
\texttt{SimpleGraph.fromRel} symmetrises the relation and removes the diagonal, which is
what makes the result a \texttt{SimpleGraph} without a separate looplessness proof --- at the
cost that \texttt{Adj} unfolds to $x \ne y \land (R x y \lor R y x)$, as the \texttt{hypercube\_bipartite}
proof has to unpack.

Statement: hypercube_bipartite. Split the tuples by the parity of their number of $1$s; an edge flips
exactly one entry and so changes that parity, making every edge cross between the
classes.

Bipartiteness as \texttt{Colorable 2}, with \texttt{ZMod 2} as the palette and
\texttt{simpa} bridging to \texttt{Fin 2}.
formal_statement:
import Mathlib

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
def hypercube (k : ℕ) : SimpleGraph (Fin k → Bool) :=
  SimpleGraph.fromRel (fun x y => ∃! i, x i ≠ y i)
end SimpleGraph

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
theorem hypercube_bipartite (k : ℕ) : (hypercube k).Colorable 2 := sorry
end SimpleGraph

Definitions:
- A covering $K$: every edge has an end in $K$. A set of vertices touching every edge.  Theorem 7.1 says coverings and
independent sets are exactly complementary.

\textbf{!} Duplicated from \texttt{Matchings.lean}, textually identical.  Neither file imports the
other; see \texttt{log/graphtheory-ISSUES.md} \S{}F.
- The covering number $\beta(G)$. The fewest vertices touching every edge.  $\alpha$ is Mathlib's \texttt{indepNum}; only $\beta$
needs defining here.

\textbf{+} No \texttt{sInf $\emptyset$ = 0} pitfall: \texttt{Set.univ} is always a covering, so the set being
minimised is never empty.  Contrast \texttt{edgeCoveringNumber} below, where the trap is

Statement: indepNum_add_coveringNumber. The largest independent set and the smallest covering are exact complements:
choosing one is the same problem as choosing the other.
formal_statement:
import Mathlib

open scoped Finset

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
def IsCovering {V : Type*} (G : SimpleGraph V) (K : Set V) : Prop :=
  ∀ ⦃u v : V⦄, G.Adj u v → u ∈ K ∨ v ∈ K
end SimpleGraph

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
noncomputable def coveringNumber {V : Type*} (G : SimpleGraph V) : ℕ :=
  sInf {n | ∃ K : Set V, G.IsCovering K ∧ K.ncard = n}
end SimpleGraph

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
theorem indepNum_add_coveringNumber {V : Type*} [Fintype V] (G : SimpleGraph V) :
    G.indepNum + G.coveringNumber = Fintype.card V := sorry
end SimpleGraph

informal_statement:
Definitions:
- The composition (lexicographic product) $G(H)$. Replace each vertex of $G$ by a copy of $H$.  Vertices in \emph{different} copies are
joined iff the corresponding $G$-vertices are adjacent; within one copy, iff
adjacent in $H$.  The $G$-structure dominates --- hence the alternative name
\emph{lexicographic product}.

\textbf{+} Fully defined, \texttt{symm} and \texttt{loopless} both discharged --- no \texttt{sorry}.

\textbf{!} Distinct from chapter 6's \texttt{boxProd} ($G \square H$), where within-copy and
across-copy edges are treated symmetrically.  Composition is not commutative.

Parts (b) and (c) of the exercise, to multiply Ramsey lower bounds.

Statement: indepNum_composition_le. Let $S$ be independent in $G[H]$.  Its first-coordinate projection is independent
in $G$ (two $S$-vertices in different copies force those $G$-vertices
non-adjacent), so at most $\alpha(G)$ copies are touched; within each, at most $\alpha(H)$
vertices.  Multiply.
formal_statement:
import Mathlib

open scoped Finset

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
def composition {V W : Type*} (G : SimpleGraph V) (H : SimpleGraph W) :
    SimpleGraph (V × W) where
  Adj p q := G.Adj p.1 q.1 ∨ (p.1 = q.1 ∧ H.Adj p.2 q.2)
  symm := by
    rintro ⟨u, v⟩ ⟨u', v'⟩ (h | ⟨h1, h2⟩)
    · exact Or.inl h.symm
    · exact Or.inr ⟨h1.symm, h2.symm⟩
  loopless := by
    rintro ⟨u, v⟩ (h | ⟨-, h⟩)
    · exact G.loopless u h
    · exact H.loopless v h
end SimpleGraph

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
theorem indepNum_composition_le {V W : Type*} [Fintype V] [Fintype W]
    (G : SimpleGraph V) (H : SimpleGraph W) :
    (G.composition H).indepNum ≤ G.indepNum * H.indepNum := sorry
end SimpleGraph
title: indepNum_composition_le
statement_informal:
indepNum_composition_le. Let $S$ be independent in $G[H]$.  Its first-coordinate projection is independent
in $G$ (two $S$-vertices in different copies force those $G$-vertices
non-adjacent), so at most $\alpha(G)$ copies are touched; within each, at most $\alpha(H)$
vertices.  Multiply.

informal_statement:
Definitions:
- An edge covering $L$: every vertex is an end of some edge of $L$. A set of edges touching every vertex.  The \texttt{L $\subseteq$ G.edgeSet} conjunct is the book's
"subset of $E$", which matters here --- without it $L$ could contain non-edges and
cover trivially.

The existence caveat is what forces the $\delta > 0$ hypothesis on Theorem 7.2; see
\texttt{edgeCoveringNumber} below.
- The edge covering number $\beta'(G)$. The fewest edges touching every vertex.

\textbf{!} \textbf{\texttt{sInf $\emptyset$ = 0} is a live trap here}, unlike \texttt{coveringNumber}.  When $\delta = 0$ no
edge covering exists, the set being minimised is empty, and Lean's convention
silently returns $0$ --- a value the book would call undefined.  That is precisely
why Theorem 7.2 carries $\delta > 0$, and why any lemma about $\beta'$ must either assume
it or handle the degenerate case explicitly.

Statement: indepNum_eq_edgeCoveringNumber. K\"onig's min-max equality transported across the two Gallai identities.  The book
introduces it with (\S{}7.1, p. 110):
formal_statement:
import Mathlib

open scoped Finset

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
def IsEdgeCovering {V : Type*} (G : SimpleGraph V) (L : Set (Sym2 V)) : Prop :=
  L ⊆ G.edgeSet ∧ ∀ v : V, ∃ e ∈ L, v ∈ e
end SimpleGraph

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
noncomputable def edgeCoveringNumber {V : Type*} (G : SimpleGraph V) : ℕ :=
  sInf {n | ∃ L : Set (Sym2 V), G.IsEdgeCovering L ∧ L.ncard = n}
end SimpleGraph

namespace SimpleGraph

    {V : Type*} [Fintype V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
    {X Y : Set V} (hbip : G.IsBipartiteWith X Y) (hδ : 0 < G.minDegree) :
    G.indepNum = G.edgeCoveringNumber := sorry
end SimpleGraph

Statement: isBipartite_iff_forall_subgraph_indepNum_eq_edgeCoveringNumber. ($\Rightarrow$) Theorem 7.3 applied subgraph-wise, every subgraph of a bipartite graph being
bipartite.

($\Leftarrow$) Contrapositive: an odd cycle $H$ on $2k+1$ vertices has $\delta(H) = 2 > 0$,
$\alpha(H) = k$ and $\beta'(H) = k + 1$, so the equality fails there.

So the identity $\alpha = \beta'$ --- which Theorem 7.3 gives for bipartite graphs ---
actually \emph{characterises} them.

\textbf{!} The instance binders \texttt{[Fintype H.verts] $\to$ [DecidableRel H.coe.Adj] $\to$} sit
\textbf{inside} the $\forall H$, as hypotheses rather than instance arguments.  That is
unusual and means a user must supply them explicitly at each application; it also
means the ($\Leftarrow$) direction gets to \emph{assume} them for its witness, which is harmless
here but worth noticing.

definitions.title: An edge covering $L$: every vertex is an end of some edge of $L$
definitions.informal:
A set of edges touching every vertex.  The \texttt{L $\subseteq$ G.edgeSet} conjunct is the book's
"subset of $E$", which matters here --- without it $L$ could contain non-edges and
cover trivially.

The existence caveat is what forces the $\delta > 0$ hypothesis on Theorem 7.2; see
\texttt{edgeCoveringNumber} below.

definitions.title: The edge covering number $\beta'(G)$
definitions.informal:
The fewest edges touching every vertex.

\textbf{!} \textbf{\texttt{sInf $\emptyset$ = 0} is a live trap here}, unlike \texttt{coveringNumber}.  When $\delta = 0$ no
edge covering exists, the set being minimised is empty, and Lean's convention
silently returns $0$ --- a value the book would call undefined.  That is precisely
why Theorem 7.2 carries $\delta > 0$, and why any lemma about $\beta'$ must either assume
it or handle the degenerate case explicitly.

informal_statement:
isBipartite_iff_forall_subgraph_two_mul_indepNum_le. ($\Rightarrow$) Every subgraph of a bipartite graph is bipartite, and the larger side of a
bipartition is an independent set with at least half the vertices.

($\Leftarrow$) If $G$ were not bipartite it would contain an odd cycle (Thm 1.2).  That
cycle on $2k+1$ vertices has $\alpha = k$, and $2k < 2k+1$, so the condition fails at
that subgraph.

Stated as $\nu(H) \le 2\cdot\alpha(H)$ to avoid division.

"Subgraph $H$ of $G$" is \texttt{H : G.Subgraph}, which carries its own \texttt{verts} --- so
$\nu(H)$ genuinely shrinks and the odd-cycle witness is expressible.  \texttt{H.coe} is
the subgraph viewed as a \texttt{SimpleGraph ↥H.verts}, and \texttt{H.verts.ncard} is used in
place of \texttt{Fintype.card ↥H.verts} to avoid an instance that \texttt{[Fintype V]} alone
does not supply.

open scoped Finset

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
theorem isBipartite_iff_forall_subgraph_two_mul_indepNum_le
    {V : Type*} [Fintype V] (G : SimpleGraph V) :
    -- NOTE: outline wrote `Fintype.card H.verts`; using `H.verts.ncard` avoids requiring a
    -- `Fintype ↥H.verts` instance (not synthesizable from `[Fintype V]` alone).
    G.IsBipartite ↔ ∀ H : G.Subgraph, H.verts.ncard ≤ 2 * H.coe.indepNum := sorry
end SimpleGraph

informal_statement:
isContained_completeBipartite_of_card_edgeFinset_gt. Generalises 7.3.4 from $K_{2,m}$ to $K_{m,m}$.  Count \emph{stars} --- a vertex with $m$
of its neighbours --- two ways: each $v$ contributes $C(d(v), m)$, and each
$m$-set can be the leaf-set of $\le m-1$ stars unless a $K_{m,m}$ appears.
Convexity converts the degree sum into an edge count.

The exponent $2 - 1/m$ is the point: forbidding a complete \emph{bipartite} subgraph
caps $\varepsilon$ at strictly sub-quadratic order, unlike Tur\'an's constant fraction of
$\nu^{2}$.  Whether the exponent is tight for every $m$ is the \textbf{Zarankiewicz
problem}, still open.

\textbf{!} The \texttt{rpow} exponent varies with $m$, so this is irreducibly real-valued; and
$(m - 1 : \mathbb{R})$ with $hm : 1 \le m$ means the base can be $0$ at $m = 1$, where
$0 ^ (1/1) = 0$ --- check that boundary case does not make the hypothesis vacuous.
formal_statement:
import Mathlib

open scoped Finset

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
theorem isContained_completeBipartite_of_card_edgeFinset_gt
    {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] {G : SimpleGraph V} [DecidableRel G.Adj]
    {m : ℕ} (hm : 1 ≤ m)
    (h : ((m - 1 : ℝ)) ^ ((1 : ℝ) / m) * (Fintype.card V : ℝ) ^ (2 - (1 : ℝ) / m) / 2
           + ((m : ℝ) - 1) * (Fintype.card V : ℝ) / 2 < (#G.edgeFinset : ℝ)) :
    completeBipartiteGraph (Fin m) (Fin m) ⊑ G := sorry
end SimpleGraph

informal_statement:
isContained_completeBipartite_two_of_card_edgeFinset_gt. Convert part (a)'s degree condition into an edge count.  By convexity,
$\sum_v C(d(v),2)$ is minimised at fixed $\varepsilon$ when all degrees equal $2\varepsilon/\nu$, so
$\sum_v C(d(v),2) \ge \nu \cdot C(2\varepsilon/\nu, 2)$; demanding this exceed $(m-1)C(\nu,2)$ and solving
for $\varepsilon$ gives the threshold.

A genuinely \textbf{sub-quadratic} threshold ($\nu^{3/2}$), unlike Tur\'an's for cliques.

\textbf{!} Real-valued with \texttt{rpow} exponents, so the proof leaves $\mathbb{N}$ early.  Mathlib's
\texttt{inner\_mul\_le\_norm\_mul\_norm} or \texttt{Finset.inner\_mul\_le\_norm\_mul\_norm} /
\texttt{sq\_sum\_le\_card\_mul\_sum\_sq} supply the convexity step; \texttt{Finset.inner\_card\_le\_...}
is the usual shape for "sum of $C(d_{v},2)$ versus the average".

import Mathlib

open scoped Finset

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
theorem isContained_completeBipartite_two_of_card_edgeFinset_gt
    {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] {G : SimpleGraph V} [DecidableRel G.Adj]
    {m : ℕ} (hm : 2 ≤ m)
    (h : ((m - 1 : ℝ)) ^ ((1 : ℝ) / 2) * (Fintype.card V : ℝ) ^ ((3 : ℝ) / 2) / 2
           + (Fintype.card V : ℝ) / 4 < (#G.edgeFinset : ℝ)) :
    completeBipartiteGraph (Fin 2) (Fin m) ⊑ G := sorry
end SimpleGraph

informal_statement:
isContained_completeBipartite_two_of_sum_choose_gt. Double-count \textbf{cherries} (paths of length two).  Each $v$ centres $C(d(v),2)$ of
them, so the total is $\sum_v C(d(v),2)$; each is determined by its two \emph{endpoints},
an unordered pair from $C(\nu,2)$.  If no pair had $m$ common neighbours, each pair
would host $\le m-1$ cherries, capping the total at $(m-1)C(\nu,2)$.

The prototype for K\H{o}v\'ari--S\'os--Tur\'an (exercise 7.3.5).
formal_statement:
import Mathlib

open scoped Finset

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
theorem isContained_completeBipartite_two_of_sum_choose_gt
    {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] {G : SimpleGraph V} [DecidableRel G.Adj]
    {m : ℕ} (hm : 2 ≤ m)
    (h : (m - 1) * (Fintype.card V).choose 2 < ∑ v : V, (G.degree v).choose 2) :
    completeBipartiteGraph (Fin 2) (Fin m) ⊑ G := sorry
end SimpleGraph

informal_statement:
Definitions:
- $G$ is uniquely $k$-edge-colourable: any two proper $k$-edge colourings agree up to a permutation of the\dots. Colours are arbitrary labels, so what a colouring really determines is the
partition into colour classes.  Unique colourability means that partition is
forced, and any two proper colourings differ only by renaming --- which is what the
permutation $\sigma$ expresses.

Proper $k$-edge colourings are rendered as \texttt{G.lineGraph.Coloring (Fin k)}, using
Mathlib's line graph: adjacent \emph{edges} of $G$ become adjacent \emph{vertices} of
\texttt{G.lineGraph}, so a proper vertex colouring there is a proper edge colouring
here.

\textbf{!} "Induce the same partition" and "differ by a permutation of colours" are
equivalent only when every colour is actually \emph{used}.  If $k$ exceeds the number
of classes, two colourings can induce the same partition while no single $\sigma$
relates them pointwise --- and conversely $\sigma$ may permute unused colours freely.
For the intended application ($k = 3$, 3-regular, so all three classes nonempty)
this is harmless, but the definition is not faithful in general.

Statement: Ex 6.2.5: every uniquely 3-edge-colourable 3-regular graph is hamiltonian. In a cubic graph a proper 3-edge colouring splits the edges into three perfect
matchings.  Any \emph{two} of them form a spanning 2-regular subgraph --- a disjoint
union of even cycles.  If that union had more than one cycle, swapping the two
colours around a single cycle would give a genuinely different partition,
contradicting uniqueness.  So each pair of classes is a \emph{single} spanning cycle,
i.e. a Hamilton cycle.

\textbf{!} \textbf{\texttt{hcol} is mandatory.}  \texttt{IsUniquelyEdgeColourable} quantifies over proper
3-colourings; if none exists the condition holds \textbf{vacuously}, and the statement
would then assert that every cubic graph with no 3-edge-colouring is
hamiltonian --- false, the Petersen graph being a counterexample ($\chi' = 4$,
nonhamiltonian).  Requiring \texttt{G.lineGraph.Colorable 3} rules that out.
formal_statement:
import Mathlib

open scoped Classical

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
def IsUniquelyEdgeColourable {V : Type*} (G : SimpleGraph V) (k : ℕ) : Prop :=
  ∀ C C' : G.lineGraph.Coloring (Fin k), ∃ σ : Equiv.Perm (Fin k), ∀ e, C' e = σ (C e)
end SimpleGraph

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
theorem isHamiltonian_of_uniquely_three_edge_colourable
    {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
    (hreg : G.IsRegularOfDegree 3) (huniq : G.IsUniquelyEdgeColourable 3)
    (hcol : G.lineGraph.Colorable 3) :
    ∃ (u : V) (p : G.Walk u u), p.IsHamiltonianCycle := sorry
end SimpleGraph

import Mathlib

namespace SimpleGraph

informal_statement:
Definitions:
- $G$ is critical: $\chi(H) < \chi(G)$ for every proper subgraph $H \subset G$. A critical graph is "minimally" $k$-chromatic: remove any vertex or
any edge and the chromatic number drops.  Critical graphs are useful precisely
because they carry the whole difficulty of a colouring problem --- every
$k$-chromatic graph contains a $k$-critical subgraph, so statements about
$k$-chromatic graphs reduce to the critical case, which is how corollary 8.1.1,
Brooks' theorem 8.4 and theorem 8.5 all begin.

The quantifier ranges over \texttt{G.Subgraph}, not over the order
on \texttt{SimpleGraph V}.  This is load-bearing (Scaffolding judgement 1): the
\texttt{SimpleGraph V} order can only \emph{remove edges}, never vertices, whereas the book's
"proper subgraph" includes $G - v$.  Under the weaker order $\bot$ on two vertices
would be vacuously 1-critical --- it has no proper edge-subgraph --- contradicting
exercise 8.1.7, which says the only 1-critical graph is $K_{1}$.
- $G$ is $k$-critical: $k$-chromatic and critical. $k$-critical graphs are the irreducible witnesses to needing $k$
colours.  Exercise 8.1.7 classifies the small cases completely --- the only
1-critical graph is $K_{1}$, the only 2-critical graph is $K_{2}$, and the 3-critical
graphs are exactly the odd cycles --- and Brooks' theorem 8.4 consumes precisely
that classification to get its standing hypothesis $k \ge 4$.

\texttt{G.chromaticNumber = k} compares an $\mathbb{N}\infty$ with a coerced $\mathbb{N}$,
so $k$-chromaticity here also carries the information that $\chi(G) \ne \top$.

Statement: isKCritical_one_iff. A 1-chromatic graph has no edges and at least one vertex.
Criticality forces exactly one --- with two or more vertices, deleting one leaves a
graph still needing one colour, so the chromatic number would not drop.

\texttt{$\top$ : SimpleGraph (Fin 1)} is $K_{1}$; on a single vertex the
complete and empty graphs coincide, which is what makes step 3 go through despite
$G$ being edgeless.  Note that without the \texttt{Subgraph}-lattice definition of
\texttt{IsCritical}, step 2 would fail: the edge-only order has no proper subgraph of $\bot$
to test, and every edgeless graph would count as 1-critical.
formal_statement:
import Mathlib

open scoped Classical

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
def IsCritical {V : Type*} (G : SimpleGraph V) : Prop :=
  ∀ H : G.Subgraph, H < ⊤ → H.coe.chromaticNumber < G.chromaticNumber
end SimpleGraph

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
def IsKCritical {V : Type*} (G : SimpleGraph V) (k : ℕ) : Prop :=
  G.chromaticNumber = k ∧ G.IsCritical
end SimpleGraph

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
theorem isKCritical_one_iff {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] [Nonempty V]
    {G : SimpleGraph V} :
    G.IsKCritical 1 ↔ Nonempty (G ≃g (⊤ : SimpleGraph (Fin 1))) := sorry
end SimpleGraph

Statement: isKCritical_three_iff_odd_cycle. An odd cycle is 3-chromatic and minimally so --- delete any edge or
vertex and it unrolls into a path, which is 2-colourable.  Conversely a 3-critical
graph cannot contain an odd cycle properly, and it must contain one, so it \emph{is}
one.  This classification is exactly what Brooks' theorem 8.4 consumes: its proof
observes that *since 1-critical and 2-critical graphs are complete and 3-critical
graphs are odd cycles, we have $k \ge 4$*.

"The only 3-critical graphs are the odd cycles" is up to
isomorphism, hence \texttt{Nonempty (G $\simeq$g cycleGraph n)} rather than an equality.  Steps
3--5 are the same three moves used in \texttt{isKCritical\_two\_iff} (with an edge in place
of an odd cycle); factoring out "a subgraph attaining $\chi(G)$ must be $\top$" as a
lemma about \texttt{IsCritical} pays for itself across all three cases of 8.1.7.

import Mathlib

open scoped Finset
open scoped Pointwise

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
def IsCovering {V : Type*} (G : SimpleGraph V) (K : Set V) : Prop :=
  ∀ ⦃u v : V⦄, G.Adj u v → u ∈ K ∨ v ∈ K
end SimpleGraph

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
def Subgraph.IsMaximumMatching {V : Type*} {G : SimpleGraph V} (M : G.Subgraph) : Prop :=
  M.IsMatching ∧ ∀ M' : G.Subgraph, M'.IsMatching → M'.edgeSet.ncard ≤ M.edgeSet.ncard
end SimpleGraph

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
def IsMinimumCovering {V : Type*} (G : SimpleGraph V) (K : Set V) : Prop :=
  G.IsCovering K ∧ ∀ K' : Set V, G.IsCovering K' → K.ncard ≤ K'.ncard
end SimpleGraph

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
theorem isMaximumMatching_and_isMinimumCovering_of_card_eq
    {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] {G : SimpleGraph V}
    {M : G.Subgraph} (hM : M.IsMatching) {K : Set V} (hK : G.IsCovering K)
    (hcard : M.edgeSet.ncard = K.ncard) :
    M.IsMaximumMatching ∧ G.IsMinimumCovering K := sorry
end SimpleGraph

informal_statement:
Definitions:
- Colour $i$ is \emph{represented} at $v$: some edge incident with $v$ has colour $i$. A $k$-edge colouring is a plain function \texttt{C : G.edgeSet $\to$ Fin k}, deliberately
\textbf{not} assumed proper --- that is the whole point, since Lemma 6.1.2, Theorem 6.1
and Vizing's Theorem 6.2 all operate on improper colourings and repair them.

"Represented at $v$" is \texttt{$\exists$ e, ↑e $\in$ G.incidenceSet v $\land$ C e = i}.

\textbf{!} Note this file uses \textbf{two different} colouring encodings.  Here a colouring is
a raw function \texttt{G.edgeSet $\to$ Fin k}; but \texttt{IsUniquelyEdgeColourable} below and the
\texttt{edgeChromaticNumber} results use Mathlib's \texttt{G.lineGraph.Coloring (Fin k)}, which
is proper by construction.  The two are not interchangeable, and any proof
crossing between \S{}6.1's machinery and a $\chi'$ statement must convert explicitly.
- $G(E_i \cup E_j)$, the subgraph on the edges coloured $i$ or $j$. Erase every edge except those coloured $i$ or $j$:
\texttt{fromEdgeSet \{e | $\exists$ h : e $\in$ G.edgeSet, C ⟨e,h⟩ = i $\lor$ C ⟨e,h⟩ = j\}}.

If the colouring is proper this leaves maximum degree $2$ --- a disjoint union of
paths and cycles alternating between the two colours.  Recolouring inside such a
component is the fundamental move of the chapter; Lemma 6.1.2 says the only
components resisting improvement in an \emph{optimal} colouring are odd cycles.

\textbf{!} The book's $G[\cdot]$ is edge-induced, so isolated vertices are irrelevant to it.
Mathlib's \texttt{fromEdgeSet} keeps the full vertex type $V$, so the resulting graph
has isolated vertices wherever neither colour appears.  This matters when
speaking of "the component containing $u$": in the Lean rendering that component
is a single vertex when $u$ meets neither colour, whereas the book's $G[E_{i} \cup E_{j}]$
would not contain $u$ at all.
- $c(v)$: the number of distinct colours represented at $v$. $c(v)$ counts the \emph{distinct} colours on edges at $v$, as
\texttt{(univ.filter fun i => IsRepresentedAt C i v).card}.

Two edges at $v$ sharing a colour drop $c(v)$ below $d(v)$; the colouring is
proper exactly when $c(v) = d(v)$ everywhere --- that is \texttt{numColoursAt\_le\_degree}
and \texttt{isProper\_iff\_numColoursAt\_eq\_degree} below.

$\sum_v c(v)$ is the potential function the whole chapter maximises.
- An optimal $k$-edge colouring: one that cannot be improved, where an improvement strictly increases $\sum\dots. Among all $k$-edge colourings --- proper or not --- prefer those spreading colours
most widely, measured by $\sum_v c(v)$.  Rendered directly as
\texttt{$\forall$ C', $\sum$ v, numColoursAt C' v $\le$ $\sum$ v, numColoursAt C v}, i.e. $C$ attains the
maximum.

Since $c(v) \le d(v)$ with equality everywhere iff proper, a proper colouring is
automatically optimal.  The chapter's strategy is the converse direction: start
from an optimal colouring and show that if it were \emph{not} proper it could be
improved after all.

\textbf{!} Note this is a static extremal condition, not a procedure --- no improvement
algorithm is defined here.  Existence of an optimal colouring (needed by
Theorem 6.1 and Vizing) follows from finiteness of the colouring space but is
\textbf{not stated as a lemma anywhere in this file}, and both proofs will need it.

Statement: isOddCycle_component_of_isOptimalEdgeColouring. A wasted colour at $u$ --- one missing, another doubled --- is an opportunity to
improve; the only structure blocking the repair is an odd cycle, whose
alternation cannot work out.

\textbf{!} "represented at least twice at $u$" counts \textbf{edges}, not colours, so $hj$ is
\texttt{2 $\le$ (univ.filter fun e => ↑e $\in$ G.incidenceSet u $\land$ C e = j).card} rather than
anything phrased via \texttt{numColoursAt}.

\textbf{!} The conclusion "the component \emph{is} an odd cycle" is stated as: there is an odd
cycle $p$ at $u$ in \texttt{twoColourSubgraph C i j} whose support coincides with the
component's \texttt{supp}.  The membership form \texttt{$\forall$ w, w $\in$ p.support $\leftrightarrow$ w $\in$ (\dots).supp} is
used instead of a set equality to avoid a \texttt{Fintype (ConnectedComponent.supp)}
obligation that does not synthesize.

import Mathlib

open scoped Classical

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
def IsRepresentedAt {V : Type*} {G : SimpleGraph V} {k : ℕ}
    (C : G.edgeSet → Fin k) (i : Fin k) (v : V) : Prop :=
  ∃ e : G.edgeSet, (e : Sym2 V) ∈ G.incidenceSet v ∧ C e = i
end SimpleGraph

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
noncomputable def twoColourSubgraph {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V]
    {G : SimpleGraph V} [DecidableRel G.Adj] {k : ℕ} (C : G.edgeSet → Fin k) (i j : Fin k) :
    SimpleGraph V :=
  fromEdgeSet {e | ∃ h : e ∈ G.edgeSet, C ⟨e, h⟩ = i ∨ C ⟨e, h⟩ = j}
end SimpleGraph

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
noncomputable def numColoursAt {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V]
    {G : SimpleGraph V} [DecidableRel G.Adj] {k : ℕ} (C : G.edgeSet → Fin k) (v : V) : ℕ :=
  (Finset.univ.filter fun i => IsRepresentedAt C i v).card
end SimpleGraph

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
def IsOptimalEdgeColouring {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V]
    {G : SimpleGraph V} [DecidableRel G.Adj] {k : ℕ} (C : G.edgeSet → Fin k) : Prop :=
  ∀ C' : G.edgeSet → Fin k, ∑ v, numColoursAt C' v ≤ ∑ v, numColoursAt C v
end SimpleGraph

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
theorem isOddCycle_component_of_isOptimalEdgeColouring
    {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] {G : SimpleGraph V} [DecidableRel G.Adj]
    {k : ℕ} {C : G.edgeSet → Fin k} (hC : IsOptimalEdgeColouring C)
    {u : V} {i j : Fin k}
    (hi : ¬ IsRepresentedAt C i u)
    (hj : 2 ≤ (Finset.univ.filter
      fun e : G.edgeSet => (e : Sym2 V) ∈ G.incidenceSet u ∧ C e = j).card) :
    ∃ p : (twoColourSubgraph C i j).Walk u u,
      p.IsCycle ∧ Odd p.length ∧
      ∀ w, w ∈ p.support ↔ w ∈ ((twoColourSubgraph C i j).connectedComponentMk u).supp := sorry
end SimpleGraph

def IsRepresentedAt {V : Type*} {G : SimpleGraph V} {k : ℕ}
    (C : G.edgeSet → Fin k) (i : Fin k) (v : V) : Prop :=
  ∃ e : G.edgeSet, (e : Sym2 V) ∈ G.incidenceSet v ∧ C e = i
end SimpleGraph

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
noncomputable def numColoursAt {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V]
    {G : SimpleGraph V} [DecidableRel G.Adj] {k : ℕ} (C : G.edgeSet → Fin k) (v : V) : ℕ :=
  (Finset.univ.filter fun i => IsRepresentedAt C i v).card
end SimpleGraph

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
theorem isProper_iff_numColoursAt_eq_degree
    {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] {G : SimpleGraph V} [DecidableRel G.Adj]
    {k : ℕ} (C : G.edgeSet → Fin k) :
    (∀ e₁ e₂, G.lineGraph.Adj e₁ e₂ → C e₁ ≠ C e₂) ↔ ∀ v, numColoursAt C v = G.degree v := sorry
end SimpleGraph
title: (6.3): $C$ is proper $\iff$ equality holds in (6.3) at every vertex
statement_informal:
(6.3): $C$ is proper $\iff$ equality holds in (6.3) at every vertex. Two edges are adjacent exactly when they meet at a vertex, so "no two adjacent
edges share a colour" is "at every vertex the incident edges carry distinct
colours" --- i.e. $c(v) = d(v)$.

Properness is stated directly as
\texttt{$\forall$ e$_{1}$ e$_{2}$, G.lineGraph.Adj e$_{1}$ e$_{2}$ $\to$ C e$_{1}$ $\ne$ C e$_{2}$} rather than by packaging $C$ as a
\texttt{lineGraph.Coloring}, since $C$ here is a bare function.

This equivalence is the bridge turning "make the colouring proper" into the
numerical goal "maximise $\sum_v c(v)$", which is what optimality is about.

definitions.title: Colour $i$ is \emph{represented} at $v$: some edge incident with $v$ has colour $i$
definitions.informal:
A $k$-edge colouring is a plain function \texttt{C : G.edgeSet $\to$ Fin k}, deliberately
\textbf{not} assumed proper --- that is the whole point, since Lemma 6.1.2, Theorem 6.1
and Vizing's Theorem 6.2 all operate on improper colourings and repair them.

"Represented at $v$" is \texttt{$\exists$ e, ↑e $\in$ G.incidenceSet v $\land$ C e = i}.

\textbf{!} Note this file uses \textbf{two different} colouring encodings.  Here a colouring is
a raw function \texttt{G.edgeSet $\to$ Fin k}; but \texttt{IsUniquelyEdgeColourable} below and the
\texttt{edgeChromaticNumber} results use Mathlib's \texttt{G.lineGraph.Coloring (Fin k)}, which
is proper by construction.  The two are not interchangeable, and any proof
crossing between \S{}6.1's machinery and a $\chi'$ statement must convert explicitly.

definitions.title: $c(v)$: the number of distinct colours represented at $v$
definitions.informal:
$c(v)$ counts the \emph{distinct} colours on edges at $v$, as
\texttt{(univ.filter fun i => IsRepresentedAt C i v).card}.

Two edges at $v$ sharing a colour drop $c(v)$ below $d(v)$; the colouring is
proper exactly when $c(v) = d(v)$ everywhere --- that is \texttt{numColoursAt\_le\_degree}
and \texttt{isProper\_iff\_numColoursAt\_eq\_degree} below.

$\sum_v c(v)$ is the potential function the whole chapter maximises.

informal_statement:
Definitions:
- \texttt{IsRamseyBound n k l}: every graph on $n$ vertices has a $k$-clique or an $l$-indep set.\dots. \texttt{IsRamseyBound n k l} says $n$ is already large enough for that conclusion:
\texttt{$\forall$ G : SimpleGraph (Fin n), ($\exists$ s, G.IsNClique k s) $\lor$ ($\exists$ t, G.IsNIndepSet l t)}.

Fixing the carrier as \texttt{Fin n} rather than quantifying over all $n$-element types
is what makes \texttt{ramseyNumber} an \texttt{sInf} over $\mathbb{N}$ below.

Total disorder is impossible: any sufficiently large graph contains one kind of
order or the other.

Statement: isRamseyBound_mono. A bigger graph contains a smaller one: restrict a graph on $m$ vertices to any
$n$ of them, get a $k$-clique or $l$-independent set there, and it survives in
the larger graph.
formal_statement:
import Mathlib

open scoped Finset

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
def IsRamseyBound (n k l : ℕ) : Prop :=
  ∀ G : SimpleGraph (Fin n), (∃ s, G.IsNClique k s) ∨ (∃ t, G.IsNIndepSet l t)
end SimpleGraph

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
theorem isRamseyBound_mono {n m k l : ℕ} (hnm : n ≤ m) (h : SimpleGraph.IsRamseyBound n k l) :
    SimpleGraph.IsRamseyBound m k l := sorry
end SimpleGraph
title: isRamseyBound_mono

open scoped Finset

informal_statement:
Ex 5.3.3: a tree has a perfect matching iff $o(G - v) = 1$ for every vertex $v$. Tutte's condition quantifies over all $S$, but for trees the singletons already
decide it.

($\Rightarrow$) The partner of $v$ lies in one component of $G - v$, and a parity count shows
exactly one component is odd.

($\Leftarrow$) $o(G - v) = 1$ for every $v$ is Tutte's condition at singletons, and
acyclicity makes that enough: build greedily from the leaves, each leaf forced to
match its unique neighbour.

Combined with exercise 5.1.2, a tree's perfect matching --- when it exists --- is
unique and locally detectable.
formal_statement:
import Mathlib

open scoped Pointwise

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
theorem isTree_perfectMatching_iff
    {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] {G : SimpleGraph V} (hG : G.IsTree) :
    (∃ M : G.Subgraph, M.IsPerfectMatching) ↔
      ∀ v : V, ((⊤ : G.Subgraph).deleteVerts {v}).coe.oddComponents.ncard = 1 := sorry
end SimpleGraph
title: Ex 5.3.3: a tree has a perfect matching iff $o(G - v) = 1$ for every vertex $v$

informal_statement:
Ex 5.1.2: a tree has at most one perfect matching. Suppose a tree had two perfect matchings $M \ne M'$.  Every vertex meets at most
one edge of each, so every vertex of $M \Delta M'$ has degree one or two and its
components are alternating paths and even cycles.  Both matchings being perfect,
no vertex is an endpoint of such a path, so only cycles occur --- impossible in an
acyclic graph.  Hence $M \Delta M' = \emptyset$.
formal_statement:
import Mathlib

open scoped Pointwise

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
theorem isTree_subsingleton_perfectMatching
    {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] {G : SimpleGraph V} (hG : G.IsTree)
    {M M' : G.Subgraph} (hM : M.IsPerfectMatching) (hM' : M'.IsPerfectMatching) :
    M = M' := sorry
end SimpleGraph
title: Ex 5.1.2: a tree has at most one perfect matching

informal_statement:
Definitions:
- join. $G \lor H$, rebuilt on Mathlib: within-side edges from $\oplus g$, all cross
edges from \texttt{completeBipartiteGraph}. \texttt{symm}/\texttt{loopless} are inherited from $\sqcup$.

Lay the two graphs side by side keeping all their own edges, then add every
edge running between them.  The book's $G + H$ (disjoint union) is Mathlib's
$\oplus g$, and "joining each vertex of $G$ to each vertex of $H$" is exactly
\texttt{completeBipartiteGraph V W}, so

    join G H = (G $\oplus$g H) $\sqcup$ completeBipartiteGraph V W

on carrier $V \oplus W$.  Building it as a $\sqcup$ of two existing graphs means \texttt{symm}
and \texttt{loopless} are inherited and need no proof.

The building block of the graphs \texttt{Cmn} below.
- $G$ is critical: $\chi(H) < \chi(G)$ for every proper subgraph $H \subset G$. A critical graph is "minimally" $k$-chromatic: remove any vertex or
any edge and the chromatic number drops.  Critical graphs are useful precisely
because they carry the whole difficulty of a colouring problem --- every
$k$-chromatic graph contains a $k$-critical subgraph, so statements about
$k$-chromatic graphs reduce to the critical case, which is how corollary 8.1.1,
Brooks' theorem 8.4 and theorem 8.5 all begin.

The quantifier ranges over \texttt{G.Subgraph}, not over the order
on \texttt{SimpleGraph V}.  This is load-bearing (Scaffolding judgement 1): the
\texttt{SimpleGraph V} order can only \emph{remove edges}, never vertices, whereas the book's
"proper subgraph" includes $G - v$.  Under the weaker order $\bot$ on two vertices
would be vacuously 1-critical --- it has no proper edge-subgraph --- contradicting
exercise 8.1.7, which says the only 1-critical graph is $K_{1}$.

Statement: join_isCritical_iff. By part (a) the join's chromatic number is the sum, so a drop on one
side is a drop for the join.  This yields a construction for critical graphs of
large chromatic number: join known critical graphs.  For instance $K_{1} \lor C_{5}$ is
4-critical, $C_{5}$ being 3-critical (exercise 8.1.7) --- this is exactly the family
exercise 8.1.12 asks for.

Step 4 is the one that would be missed by reasoning only about
"remove a vertex or a within-side edge"; the subgraph lattice of a join contains
subgraphs that are not themselves joins, and they must be handled.
formal_statement:
import Mathlib

open scoped Classical

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
def join {V W : Type*} (G : SimpleGraph V) (H : SimpleGraph W) : SimpleGraph (V ⊕ W) :=
  (G ⊕g H) ⊔ completeBipartiteGraph V W
end SimpleGraph

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
def IsCritical {V : Type*} (G : SimpleGraph V) : Prop :=
  ∀ H : G.Subgraph, H < ⊤ → H.coe.chromaticNumber < G.chromaticNumber
end SimpleGraph

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
theorem join_isCritical_iff {α β : Type*} [Fintype α] [Fintype β] [Nonempty α] [Nonempty β]
    (G : SimpleGraph α) (H : SimpleGraph β) :
    (G.join H).IsCritical ↔ G.IsCritical ∧ H.IsCritical := sorry
end SimpleGraph
title: join_isCritical_iff
statement_informal:
join_isCritical_iff. By part (a) the join's chromatic number is the sum, so a drop on one
side is a drop for the join.  This yields a construction for critical graphs of
large chromatic number: join known critical graphs.  For instance $K_{1} \lor C_{5}$ is
4-critical, $C_{5}$ being 3-critical (exercise 8.1.7) --- this is exactly the family
exercise 8.1.12 asks for.

Step 4 is the one that would be missed by reasoning only about
"remove a vertex or a within-side edge"; the subgraph lattice of a join contains
subgraphs that are not themselves joins, and they must be handled.

informal_statement:
Definitions:
- A vertex cut: a proper subset $S$ whose deletion leaves $G$ disconnected. $V'$ is a \texttt{Finset V}, and "$G - V'$ is disconnected" is
\texttt{$\lnot$ (G.induce (↑S)$^{c}$).Connected}.  The conjunct \texttt{↑S $\subset$ Set.univ} records that a
vertex cut is a \emph{proper} subset: without it $S = V$ would qualify vacuously,
since Mathlib's \texttt{Connected} is false on the empty induced graph.

A $k$-vertex cut is the pair \texttt{G.IsVertexCut S $\land$ S.card = k}; that is exactly
what \texttt{vertexConnectivity} minimises over.
- $G$ is critical: $\chi(H) < \chi(G)$ for every proper subgraph $H \subset G$. A critical graph is "minimally" $k$-chromatic: remove any vertex or
any edge and the chromatic number drops.  Critical graphs are useful precisely
because they carry the whole difficulty of a colouring problem --- every
$k$-chromatic graph contains a $k$-critical subgraph, so statements about
$k$-chromatic graphs reduce to the critical case, which is how corollary 8.1.1,
Brooks' theorem 8.4 and theorem 8.5 all begin.

The quantifier ranges over \texttt{G.Subgraph}, not over the order
on \texttt{SimpleGraph V}.  This is load-bearing (Scaffolding judgement 1): the
\texttt{SimpleGraph V} order can only \emph{remove edges}, never vertices, whereas the book's
"proper subgraph" includes $G - v$.  Under the weaker order $\bot$ on two vertices
would be vacuously 1-critical --- it has no proper edge-subgraph --- contradicting
exercise 8.1.7, which says the only 1-critical graph is $K_{1}$.
- $G$ is $k$-critical: $k$-chromatic and critical. $k$-critical graphs are the irreducible witnesses to needing $k$
colours.  Exercise 8.1.7 classifies the small cases completely --- the only
1-critical graph is $K_{1}$, the only 2-critical graph is $K_{2}$, and the 3-critical
graphs are exactly the odd cycles --- and Brooks' theorem 8.4 consumes precisely
that classification to get its standing hypothesis $k \ge 4$.

\texttt{G.chromaticNumber = k} compares an $\mathbb{N}\infty$ with a coerced $\mathbb{N}$,
so $k$-chromaticity here also carries the information that $\chi(G) \ne \top$.

Statement: kCritical_two_vertex_cut_degree_sum. This inequality is precisely what Brooks' theorem uses to dispose of
the 2-vertex-cut case: combined with $d(u), d(v) \le \Delta$ it forces $2\Delta \ge 3k - 5$,
which for $k \ge 4$ already gives $k \le \Delta$.

Stated additively as $3k \le d(u) + d(v) + 5$ rather than
$d(u) + d(v) \ge 3k - 5$, because $\mathbb{N}$-subtraction would truncate $3k - 5$ to $0$ for
$k \le 1$ and make the statement vacuous exactly where it should be informative.
Step 5 deserves care: if $u$ and $v$ had a common neighbour in $G_{2}$, contracting
would merge two edges into one and the degree identity would fail --- establish that
they do not, or weaken the identity to the inequality actually needed.

import Mathlib

open scoped Classical

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
def IsVertexCut (G : SimpleGraph V) (S : Finset V) : Prop :=
  (↑S : Set V) ⊂ Set.univ ∧ ¬ (G.induce ((↑S : Set V)ᶜ)).Connected
end SimpleGraph

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
def IsCritical {V : Type*} (G : SimpleGraph V) : Prop :=
  ∀ H : G.Subgraph, H < ⊤ → H.coe.chromaticNumber < G.chromaticNumber
end SimpleGraph

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
def IsKCritical {V : Type*} (G : SimpleGraph V) (k : ℕ) : Prop :=
  G.chromaticNumber = k ∧ G.IsCritical
end SimpleGraph

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
theorem kCritical_two_vertex_cut_degree_sum
    {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] [Nonempty V] {G : SimpleGraph V} [DecidableRel G.Adj]
    {k : ℕ} (hG : G.IsKCritical k) {u v : V} (huv : u ≠ v)
    (hcut : G.IsVertexCut ({u, v} : Finset V)) :
    3 * k ≤ G.degree u + G.degree v + 5 := sorry
end SimpleGraph

import Mathlib

open scoped Classical

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
def IsVertexCut (G : SimpleGraph V) (S : Finset V) : Prop :=
  (↑S : Set V) ⊂ Set.univ ∧ ¬ (G.induce ((↑S : Set V)ᶜ)).Connected
end SimpleGraph

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
def IsCritical {V : Type*} (G : SimpleGraph V) : Prop :=
  ∀ H : G.Subgraph, H < ⊤ → H.coe.chromaticNumber < G.chromaticNumber
end SimpleGraph

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
def Subgraph.IsType1 {V : Type*} {G : SimpleGraph V} (H : G.Subgraph)
    (u v : V) (hu : u ∈ H.verts) (hv : v ∈ H.verts) (k : ℕ) : Prop :=
  ∀ C : H.coe.Coloring (Fin (k - 1)), C ⟨u, hu⟩ = C ⟨v, hv⟩
end SimpleGraph

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
def Subgraph.IsType2 {V : Type*} {G : SimpleGraph V} (H : G.Subgraph)
    (u v : V) (hu : u ∈ H.verts) (hv : v ∈ H.verts) (k : ℕ) : Prop :=
  ∀ C : H.coe.Coloring (Fin (k - 1)), C ⟨u, hu⟩ ≠ C ⟨v, hv⟩
end SimpleGraph

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
def contractEdge {V : Type*} (G : SimpleGraph V) (u v : V) :
    SimpleGraph {x : V // x ≠ v} where
  Adj a b := a ≠ b ∧ (G.Adj a.1 b.1 ∨ (a.1 = u ∧ G.Adj v b.1) ∨ (b.1 = u ∧ G.Adj a.1 v))
  symm := by
    rintro a b ⟨hab, h | ⟨h₁, h₂⟩ | ⟨h₁, h₂⟩⟩
    · exact ⟨hab.symm, Or.inl h.symm⟩
    · exact ⟨hab.symm, Or.inr (Or.inr ⟨h₁, h₂.symm⟩)⟩
    · exact ⟨hab.symm, Or.inr (Or.inl ⟨h₁, h₂.symm⟩)⟩
  loopless := by rintro a ⟨h, -⟩; exact h rfl
end SimpleGraph

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
def uvComponent {V : Type*} [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) (u v : V)
    (c : (G.induce ({u, v}ᶜ : Set V)).ConnectedComponent) : G.Subgraph :=
  (⊤ : G.Subgraph).induce ((Subtype.val '' c.supp) ∪ {u, v})
end SimpleGraph

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
def IsKCritical {V : Type*} (G : SimpleGraph V) (k : ℕ) : Prop :=
  G.chromaticNumber = k ∧ G.IsCritical
end SimpleGraph

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
theorem kCritical_two_vertex_cut_structure
    {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] [Nonempty V] {G : SimpleGraph V}
    {k : ℕ} (hG : G.IsKCritical k) {u v : V} (huv : u ≠ v)
    (hcut : G.IsVertexCut ({u, v} : Finset V)) :
    ∃ (c₁ c₂ : (G.induce ({u, v}ᶜ : Set V)).ConnectedComponent) (_ : c₁ ≠ c₂),
      -- (i)
      G.uvComponent u v c₁ ⊔ G.uvComponent u v c₂ = ⊤ ∧
      (G.uvComponent u v c₁).IsType1 u v (by simp [uvComponent]) (by simp [uvComponent]) k ∧
      (G.uvComponent u v c₂).IsType2 u v (by simp [uvComponent]) (by simp [uvComponent]) k ∧
      -- (ii)
      ((G.uvComponent u v c₁).coe ⊔ SimpleGraph.edge
          ⟨u, by simp [uvComponent]⟩ ⟨v, by simp [uvComponent]⟩).IsKCritical k ∧
      ((G.uvComponent u v c₂).coe.contractEdge
          ⟨u, by simp [uvComponent]⟩ ⟨v, by simp [uvComponent]⟩).IsKCritical k := sorry
end SimpleGraph

kainen. Colour each side separately; the two colourings may clash across the
cut, but there are at most $n - 1$ cut edges and $n!$ ways to relabel one side's

would give $n \cdot (n-1)! = n!$, exactly enough to rule out every permutation.

namespace SimpleGraph

    {X : Set V} {n : ℕ}
    (hX : (G.induce X).Colorable n) (hY : (G.induce (Xᶜ)).Colorable n)
    (hcut : (G.edgeFinset.filter fun e => ∃ x ∈ X, ∃ y ∉ X, e = s(x, y)).card + 1 ≤ n) :

end SimpleGraph

Definitions:
- A covering $K$: every edge has an end in $K$. A set of vertices touching every edge.  Theorem 7.1 says coverings and
independent sets are exactly complementary.

\textbf{!} Duplicated from \texttt{Matchings.lean}, textually identical.  Neither file imports the
other; see \texttt{log/graphtheory-ISSUES.md} \S{}F.
- A maximum matching: a matching no larger than which exists. Mathlib supplies "matching" (\texttt{Subgraph.IsMatching}), "saturates"
(\texttt{v $\in$ M.verts}) and "perfect" (\texttt{Subgraph.IsPerfectMatching}), but has \textbf{no
matching-number notion}, so maximality has to be said by hand:

    M.IsMatching $\land$ $\forall$ M', M'.IsMatching $\to$ M'.edgeSet.ncard $\le$ M.edgeSet.ncard

This is a \emph{global} maximum, not a maximal matching (one admitting no extension).
The two genuinely differ, and Berge's Theorem 5.1 is exactly the tool that
certifies the global property from a local check.
- A minimum covering. Watch every edge using as few vertices as possible.  As with
\texttt{Subgraph.IsMaximumMatching}, minimality is spelled out by hand since Mathlib has
no covering-number notion.

Statement: Thm 5.3 (K\"onig): in a bipartite graph, max-matching size = min-covering size. The prototypical min-max theorem of combinatorics --- maximum packing equals
minimum cover.  Closely related to Hall's theorem: exercise 5.2.7 asks to derive
Hall from K\"onig, and its matrix form is exercise 5.2.5.

Note the Lean statement takes \emph{both} extremal objects as hypotheses (\texttt{hM}, \texttt{hK})

import Mathlib

open scoped Finset
open scoped Pointwise

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
def IsCovering {V : Type*} (G : SimpleGraph V) (K : Set V) : Prop :=
  ∀ ⦃u v : V⦄, G.Adj u v → u ∈ K ∨ v ∈ K
end SimpleGraph

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
def Subgraph.IsMaximumMatching {V : Type*} {G : SimpleGraph V} (M : G.Subgraph) : Prop :=
  M.IsMatching ∧ ∀ M' : G.Subgraph, M'.IsMatching → M'.edgeSet.ncard ≤ M.edgeSet.ncard
end SimpleGraph

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
def IsMinimumCovering {V : Type*} (G : SimpleGraph V) (K : Set V) : Prop :=
  G.IsCovering K ∧ ∀ K' : Set V, G.IsCovering K' → K.ncard ≤ K'.ncard
end SimpleGraph

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
theorem konig_matching_covering
    {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
    {X Y : Set V} (hbip : G.IsBipartiteWith X Y)
    {M : G.Subgraph} (hM : M.IsMaximumMatching)
    {K : Set V} (hK : G.IsMinimumCovering K) :
    M.edgeSet.ncard = K.ncard := sorry
end SimpleGraph

informal_statement:
Ex 5.2.5: K\"onig's theorem, matrix (line-cover) form. K\"onig's Theorem 5.3 in matrix dress.  A vertex per row and per column, joining
row $i$ to column $j$ when \texttt{A i j = true}.  Lines covering all the $1$s are a
vertex covering; $1$s no two sharing a line are a matching.

The \texttt{IsLeast}/\texttt{IsGreatest} hypotheses supply the two optima as \emph{given}, so this
statement only has to equate them.  "No two in the same line" is rendered as the
pair of \texttt{InjOn} conditions on \texttt{Prod.fst} and \texttt{Prod.snd}.

import Mathlib

open scoped Pointwise

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
theorem konig_matrix {m n : ℕ} (A : Matrix (Fin m) (Fin n) Bool)
    {c : ℕ} (hc : IsLeast {k | ∃ (R : Finset (Fin m)) (C : Finset (Fin n)),
        R.card + C.card = k ∧ ∀ i j, A i j = true → i ∈ R ∨ j ∈ C} c)
    {d : ℕ} (hd : IsGreatest {k | ∃ S : Finset (Fin m × Fin n), S.card = k ∧
        (∀ p ∈ S, A p.1 p.2 = true) ∧ (S : Set (Fin m × Fin n)).InjOn Prod.fst ∧
        (S : Set (Fin m × Fin n)).InjOn Prod.snd} d) :
    c = d := sorry
end SimpleGraph
title: Ex 5.2.5: K\"onig's theorem, matrix (line-cover) form
statement_informal:
Ex 5.2.5: K\"onig's theorem, matrix (line-cover) form. K\"onig's Theorem 5.3 in matrix dress.  A vertex per row and per column, joining
row $i$ to column $j$ when \texttt{A i j = true}.  Lines covering all the $1$s are a
vertex covering; $1$s no two sharing a line are a matching.

The \texttt{IsLeast}/\texttt{IsGreatest} hypotheses supply the two optima as \emph{given}, so this
statement only has to equate them.  "No two in the same line" is rendered as the
pair of \texttt{InjOn} conditions on \texttt{Prod.fst} and \texttt{Prod.snd}.

informal_statement:
Definitions:
- A maximum matching: a matching no larger than which exists. Mathlib supplies "matching" (\texttt{Subgraph.IsMatching}), "saturates"
(\texttt{v $\in$ M.verts}) and "perfect" (\texttt{Subgraph.IsPerfectMatching}), but has \textbf{no
matching-number notion}, so maximality has to be said by hand:

    M.IsMatching $\land$ $\forall$ M', M'.IsMatching $\to$ M'.edgeSet.ncard $\le$ M.edgeSet.ncard

This is a \emph{global} maximum, not a maximal matching (one admitting no extension).
The two genuinely differ, and Berge's Theorem 5.1 is exactly the tool that
certifies the global property from a local check.

Statement: Ex 5.2.6(a): the K\"onig--Ore defect formula (stated additively to avoid $\mathbb{N}$ subtraction). Hall's theorem says a matching saturating $X$ exists exactly when
$|S| - |N(S)| \le 0$ for all $S \subseteq X$.  The defect formula quantifies failure: the
largest $|S| - |N(S)|$, the \textbf{deficiency}, is exactly how many vertices of $X$
a maximum matching must leave unsaturated.  Hall is the zero-deficiency case.

Formalised additively as \texttt{|M| + deficiency = |X|} to avoid $\mathbb{N}$ subtraction on the
outside.

\textbf{!} But the \emph{inner} \texttt{S.ncard - ($\bigcup$ \dots).ncard} is still natural subtraction, so it
truncates to $0$ exactly when Hall's condition holds at $S$ --- which is what makes
the $\bigsqcup$ compute the book's \texttt{max\{\dots\}} correctly only because the book's max is
also effectively taken against $0$ (via $S = \emptyset$).  This is a happy accident
rather than a faithful rendering, and is worth re-checking when the proof is
attempted.
formal_statement:
import Mathlib

open scoped Pointwise

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
def Subgraph.IsMaximumMatching {V : Type*} {G : SimpleGraph V} (M : G.Subgraph) : Prop :=
  M.IsMatching ∧ ∀ M' : G.Subgraph, M'.IsMatching → M'.edgeSet.ncard ≤ M.edgeSet.ncard
end SimpleGraph

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
theorem konig_ore_defect
    {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
    {X Y : Set V} (hbip : G.IsBipartiteWith X Y)
    {M : G.Subgraph} (hM : M.IsMaximumMatching) :
    M.edgeSet.ncard + (⨆ S ∈ {S | S ⊆ X}, (S.ncard - (⋃ v ∈ S, G.neighborSet v).ncard))
      = X.ncard := sorry
end SimpleGraph

informal_statement:
lineGraph_colorable_three_of_isHamiltonian_of_three_regular. A cubic hamiltonian graph splits into an even cycle plus a perfect
matching; two colours alternate around the cycle and the third takes the matching.

\emph{Why this matters (\S{}9.7).}  Tait (1880) showed the four-colour conjecture equivalent
to "every simple 3-regular 3-connected planar graph has a Tait colouring" (theorem
9.12(iii)), and then \emph{by mistakenly assuming that every such graph is hamiltonian},
gave a "proof" of the conjecture using exactly this exercise.  Over half a century
later Tutte (1946) exhibited a nonhamiltonian 3-regular 3-connected planar graph,
invalidating the argument.  So this exercise is sound; only Tait's extra assumption
was not.

A Tait colouring is spelled \texttt{G.lineGraph.Colorable 3}, needing
no new definitions --- \texttt{lineGraph} has the edges of $G$ as vertices, adjacent when
they share an end, so a proper colouring of it \emph{is} a proper edge colouring of $G$.
Step 3's parity assignment is the fiddly part: it needs a function from an edge of
$c$ to its index along $c$, which \texttt{c.edges} provides as a list position.
formal_statement:
import Mathlib

open scoped Classical

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
theorem lineGraph_colorable_three_of_isHamiltonian_of_three_regular
    {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
    (hreg : G.IsRegularOfDegree 3)
    {a : V} {c : G.Walk a a} (hc : c.IsHamiltonianCycle) :
    G.lineGraph.Colorable 3 := sorry
end SimpleGraph

lineGraph_edgeCard. Two edges are adjacent in the edge graph exactly when they share an end;
simplicity makes that end unique, so the count localises at each vertex.

\textbf{!} Step 1's uniqueness is where \emph{simplicity} is spent --- with
parallel edges two edges could share both ends and be counted twice.  Part (b) of the
exercise, not stated here, notes the edge graph of $K_{5}$ is the complement of the
Petersen graph.

    G.lineGraph.edgeFinset.card = ∑ v, (G.degree v).choose 2 := sorry
end SimpleGraph

informal_statement:
Definitions:
- An edge covering $L$: every vertex is an end of some edge of $L$. A set of edges touching every vertex.  The \texttt{L $\subseteq$ G.edgeSet} conjunct is the book's
"subset of $E$", which matters here --- without it $L$ could contain non-edges and
cover trivially.

The existence caveat is what forces the $\delta > 0$ hypothesis on Theorem 7.2; see
\texttt{edgeCoveringNumber} below.
- The matching number $\alpha'(G)$. An \texttt{sSup} over matching sizes --- the edge analogue of $\alpha$.  Bounded above by
$\varepsilon$, so the supremum is attained; as with \texttt{coveringNumber} that attainment is not
packaged and must be re-derived at each use.
- The edge covering number $\beta'(G)$. The fewest edges touching every vertex.

\textbf{!} \textbf{\texttt{sInf $\emptyset$ = 0} is a live trap here}, unlike \texttt{coveringNumber}.  When $\delta = 0$ no
edge covering exists, the set being minimised is empty, and Lean's convention
silently returns $0$ --- a value the book would call undefined.  That is precisely
why Theorem 7.2 carries $\delta > 0$, and why any lemma about $\beta'$ must either assume
it or handle the degenerate case explicitly.

Statement: matchingNumber_add_edgeCoveringNumber. The striking parallel with Corollary 7.1 --- even though matchings and edge
coverings are \textbf{not} complementary the way independent sets and coverings are.
The book is explicit about this (\S{}7.1, p. 110):
formal_statement:
import Mathlib

open scoped Finset

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
def IsEdgeCovering {V : Type*} (G : SimpleGraph V) (L : Set (Sym2 V)) : Prop :=
  L ⊆ G.edgeSet ∧ ∀ v : V, ∃ e ∈ L, v ∈ e
end SimpleGraph

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
noncomputable def matchingNumber {V : Type*} (G : SimpleGraph V) : ℕ :=
  sSup {n | ∃ M : G.Subgraph, M.IsMatching ∧ M.edgeSet.ncard = n}
end SimpleGraph

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
noncomputable def edgeCoveringNumber {V : Type*} (G : SimpleGraph V) : ℕ :=
  sInf {n | ∃ L : Set (Sym2 V), G.IsEdgeCovering L ∧ L.ncard = n}
end SimpleGraph

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
theorem matchingNumber_add_edgeCoveringNumber
    {V : Type*} [Fintype V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
    (hδ : 0 < G.minDegree) :
    G.matchingNumber + G.edgeCoveringNumber = Fintype.card V := sorry
end SimpleGraph

Statement: (5.5): for any matching $M$ and covering $K$, $|M| \le |K|$. The edges of a matching are pairwise disjoint and the covering must contain an
endpoint of each; since no two matching edges share an endpoint, the chosen
endpoints are distinct, so $K$ has at least $|M|$ elements.

informal_statement:
minDegree_le_five_of_card_edge_le. A planar graph cannot be everywhere dense: Euler's formula caps its
edge count at $3\nu - 6$, so the average degree is below $6$ and some vertex has
degree at most $5$.  This is the fact driving the five-colour theorem 9.11 --- every
planar graph has a vertex of degree at most five to induct on --- and it is why the
arithmetic core was worth salvaging even though the planarity around it was not.

\textbf{!} This is \textbf{not} corollary 9.5.3 as the book states it.
Planarity is replaced by the hypothesis $h\varepsilon$, which corollary 9.5.2 (dropped, being
unstatable without faces) would have supplied.  Ship it under the name
\texttt{minDegree\_le\_five\_of\_card\_edge\_le}, never as \texttt{planar\_minDegree\_le\_five}: the
theorem proved is the arithmetic half only.  Stated additively ($\varepsilon + 6 \le 3\nu$) to
dodge truncated $\mathbb{N}$-subtraction.

Worth knowing while filling: \textbf{\texttt{h$\nu$ : 3 $\le$ Fintype.card V} is unused.}  Steps 1--4
never mention $\nu$ except through the two inequalities $2\varepsilon + 12 \le 6\nu$ and
$6\nu \le 2\varepsilon$, whose contradiction is independent of the size of $\nu$.  The book needs
its $\nu = 1, 2$ caveat because it invokes corollary 9.5.2, which carries $\nu \ge 3$;
once that corollary is replaced by the raw hypothesis $h\varepsilon$, the caveat evaporates.
$h\nu$ is kept only so the statement still reads as the book's; do not go looking for
a place to use it.
formal_statement:
import Mathlib

open scoped Classical

theorem minDegree_le_five_of_card_edge_le
    {V : Type*} [Fintype V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
    (hν : 3 ≤ Fintype.card V)
    (hε : G.edgeFinset.card + 6 ≤ 3 * Fintype.card V) :
    G.minDegree ≤ 5 := sorry
end SimpleGraph

informal_statement:
Definitions:
- $G$ is critical: $\chi(H) < \chi(G)$ for every proper subgraph $H \subset G$. A critical graph is "minimally" $k$-chromatic: remove any vertex or
any edge and the chromatic number drops.  Critical graphs are useful precisely
because they carry the whole difficulty of a colouring problem --- every
$k$-chromatic graph contains a $k$-critical subgraph, so statements about
$k$-chromatic graphs reduce to the critical case, which is how corollary 8.1.1,
Brooks' theorem 8.4 and theorem 8.5 all begin.

The quantifier ranges over \texttt{G.Subgraph}, not over the order
on \texttt{SimpleGraph V}.  This is load-bearing (Scaffolding judgement 1): the
\texttt{SimpleGraph V} order can only \emph{remove edges}, never vertices, whereas the book's
"proper subgraph" includes $G - v$.  Under the weaker order $\bot$ on two vertices
would be vacuously 1-critical --- it has no proper edge-subgraph --- contradicting
exercise 8.1.7, which says the only 1-critical graph is $K_{1}$.
- mycielskian. on \texttt{V $\oplus$ V $\oplus$ Unit}: \texttt{inl} = the old graph, \texttt{inr $\circ$ inl} = the
shadows $u_{i}$ (joined to $v_{i}$'s neighbours), \texttt{inr $\circ$ inr} = the apex (joined to every shadow).
\textbf{!} MISSING from Mathlib.

Each original vertex $v_{i}$ gets a \textbf{shadow} $u_{i}$ attached to $v_{i}$'s
neighbourhood but \emph{not} to $v_{i}$ itself, and a single \textbf{apex} $v$ is joined to all
the shadows.  The construction preserves triangle-freeness while raising the
chromatic number by exactly one; starting from $K_{2}$ it yields the 5-cycle, then
the Gr\"otzsch graph, and in general a triangle-free $k$-chromatic graph on
$3\cdot 2^{k-2} - 1$ vertices.  Theorem 8.7 is the proof that it does this.

Carrier \texttt{V $\oplus$ V $\oplus$ Unit}: \texttt{inl a} is the original $v_a$,
\texttt{inr (inl a)} its shadow $u_a$, \texttt{inr (inr ())} the apex.  Reading the \texttt{Adj} match
against the book: \texttt{inl}--\texttt{inl} copies $G$; \texttt{inl}--\texttt{inr $\circ$ inl} joins $u_a$ to the
neighbours of $v_a$ (note \texttt{G.Adj a b}, not $a = b$, so $u_a$ is \emph{not} joined to
$v_a$); \texttt{inr $\circ$ inl}--\texttt{inr $\circ$ inr} joins every shadow to the apex.  Everything else
is \texttt{False}, which in particular leaves the shadows independent and the apex
nonadjacent to the original vertices.
- $G$ is $k$-critical: $k$-chromatic and critical. $k$-critical graphs are the irreducible witnesses to needing $k$
colours.  Exercise 8.1.7 classifies the small cases completely --- the only
1-critical graph is $K_{1}$, the only 2-critical graph is $K_{2}$, and the 3-critical
graphs are exactly the odd cycles --- and Brooks' theorem 8.4 consumes precisely
that classification to get its standing hypothesis $k \ge 4$.

\texttt{G.chromaticNumber = k} compares an $\mathbb{N}\infty$ with a coerced $\mathbb{N}$,
so $k$-chromaticity here also carries the information that $\chi(G) \ne \top$.
- The Mycielski tower $G_{2} = K_{2}, G_{3}, G_{4}, \dots$. Iterate Mycielski's construction from a single edge.  The book
records the first few: $G_{2} = K_{2}$, $G_{3}$ is the 5-cycle, $G_{4}$ is the Gr\"otzsch graph
of figure 8.2.  Exercise 8.5.1 strengthens theorem 8.7 for this particular tower:
each $G_k$ is not merely $k$-chromatic but $k$-\emph{critical}.

open scoped Classical

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
def IsCritical {V : Type*} (G : SimpleGraph V) : Prop :=
  ∀ H : G.Subgraph, H < ⊤ → H.coe.chromaticNumber < G.chromaticNumber
end SimpleGraph

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
def mycielskian {V : Type*} (G : SimpleGraph V) : SimpleGraph (V ⊕ V ⊕ Unit) where
  Adj
    | .inl a,        .inl b        => G.Adj a b
    | .inl a,        .inr (.inl b) => G.Adj a b
    | .inr (.inl a), .inl b        => G.Adj a b
    | .inr (.inl _), .inr (.inr _) => True
    | .inr (.inr _), .inr (.inl _) => True
    | _,             _             => False
  symm := by rintro (a | a | a) (b | b | b) <;> simp_all [G.adj_comm]
  loopless := by rintro (a | a | a) <;> simp
end SimpleGraph

definitions.title: $G$ is critical: $\chi(H) < \chi(G)$ for every proper subgraph $H \subset G$
definitions.informal:
A critical graph is "minimally" $k$-chromatic: remove any vertex or
any edge and the chromatic number drops.  Critical graphs are useful precisely
because they carry the whole difficulty of a colouring problem --- every
$k$-chromatic graph contains a $k$-critical subgraph, so statements about
$k$-chromatic graphs reduce to the critical case, which is how corollary 8.1.1,
Brooks' theorem 8.4 and theorem 8.5 all begin.

The quantifier ranges over \texttt{G.Subgraph}, not over the order
on \texttt{SimpleGraph V}.  This is load-bearing (Scaffolding judgement 1): the
\texttt{SimpleGraph V} order can only \emph{remove edges}, never vertices, whereas the book's
"proper subgraph" includes $G - v$.  Under the weaker order $\bot$ on two vertices
would be vacuously 1-critical --- it has no proper edge-subgraph --- contradicting
exercise 8.1.7, which says the only 1-critical graph is $K_{1}$.

definitions.title: mycielskian
definitions.informal:
on \texttt{V $\oplus$ V $\oplus$ Unit}: \texttt{inl} = the old graph, \texttt{inr $\circ$ inl} = the
shadows $u_{i}$ (joined to $v_{i}$'s neighbours), \texttt{inr $\circ$ inr} = the apex (joined to every shadow).
\textbf{!} MISSING from Mathlib.

Each original vertex $v_{i}$ gets a \textbf{shadow} $u_{i}$ attached to $v_{i}$'s
neighbourhood but \emph{not} to $v_{i}$ itself, and a single \textbf{apex} $v$ is joined to all
the shadows.  The construction preserves triangle-freeness while raising the
chromatic number by exactly one; starting from $K_{2}$ it yields the 5-cycle, then
the Gr\"otzsch graph, and in general a triangle-free $k$-chromatic graph on
$3\cdot 2^{k-2} - 1$ vertices.  Theorem 8.7 is the proof that it does this.

Carrier \texttt{V $\oplus$ V $\oplus$ Unit}: \texttt{inl a} is the original $v_a$,
\texttt{inr (inl a)} its shadow $u_a$, \texttt{inr (inr ())} the apex.  Reading the \texttt{Adj} match
against the book: \texttt{inl}--\texttt{inl} copies $G$; \texttt{inl}--\texttt{inr $\circ$ inl} joins $u_a$ to the
neighbours of $v_a$ (note \texttt{G.Adj a b}, not $a = b$, so $u_a$ is \emph{not} joined to
$v_a$); \texttt{inr $\circ$ inl}--\texttt{inr $\circ$ inr} joins every shadow to the apex.  Everything else
is \texttt{False}, which in particular leaves the shadows independent and the apex
nonadjacent to the original vertices.

informal_statement:
Ex 4.2.10: a $2k$-regular graph on $4k+1$ vertices is hamiltonian (Nash-Williams). Such a graph has $\delta = \Delta = 2k$ and $\nu = 4k + 1 = 2\delta + 1$, one vertex above the
threshold $\nu \ge 2\delta$ of Dirac's cycle remark.  That remark yields a cycle of length
at least $2\delta = 4k$ --- missing at most one vertex --- and regularity plus parity then
force the cycle to pick up the last vertex too.

\textbf{!} The Lean signature omits the book's $k \ge 1$.  At $k = 0$ the statement reads
"every $0$-regular graph on $1$ vertex is hamiltonian", which is false in
Mathlib: a Hamilton cycle needs length $\ge 3$, so the one-vertex graph is not
\texttt{IsHamiltonian}.  The hypothesis $1 \le k$ must be added.

informal_statement:
Definitions:
- A vertex cut: a proper subset $S$ whose deletion leaves $G$ disconnected. $V'$ is a \texttt{Finset V}, and "$G - V'$ is disconnected" is
\texttt{$\lnot$ (G.induce (↑S)$^{c}$).Connected}.  The conjunct \texttt{↑S $\subset$ Set.univ} records that a
vertex cut is a \emph{proper} subset: without it $S = V$ would qualify vacuously,
since Mathlib's \texttt{Connected} is false on the empty induced graph.

A $k$-vertex cut is the pair \texttt{G.IsVertexCut S $\land$ S.card = k}; that is exactly
what \texttt{vertexConnectivity} minimises over.
- $\alpha$-critical: deleting any edge raises the independence number. Every edge matters for $\alpha$: removing any one lets a larger independent set
appear, so an $\alpha$-critical graph has no $\alpha$-redundant edges.

$G - e$ is \texttt{G.deleteEdges \{e\}}, on the same vertex type --- so $\nu$ is unchanged,
which is what makes the equivalence with $\beta$-criticality (below) exact.

Statement: no_cutVertex_of_isAlphaCritical. Suppose $v$ is a cut vertex, so $G - v$ splits.  Independent sets can be chosen
per component, and one shows some edge at $v$ is deletable without increasing
$\alpha$ --- contradicting criticality, where \emph{every} deletion must raise it.

So $\alpha$-criticality forces a structure that cannot be pieced together at a single
articulation point.
formal_statement:
import Mathlib

open scoped Classical
open scoped Finset

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
def IsVertexCut (G : SimpleGraph V) (S : Finset V) : Prop :=
  (↑S : Set V) ⊂ Set.univ ∧ ¬ (G.induce ((↑S : Set V)ᶜ)).Connected
end SimpleGraph

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
def IsAlphaCritical {V : Type*} [Fintype V] (G : SimpleGraph V) : Prop :=
  ∀ e ∈ G.edgeSet, G.indepNum < (G.deleteEdges {e}).indepNum
end SimpleGraph

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
theorem no_cutVertex_of_isAlphaCritical
    {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] {G : SimpleGraph V}
    (hconn : G.Connected) (hcrit : G.IsAlphaCritical) (v : V) :
    ¬ G.IsVertexCut {v} := sorry
end SimpleGraph
title: no_cutVertex_of_isAlphaCritical
statement_informal:
no_cutVertex_of_isAlphaCritical. Suppose $v$ is a cut vertex, so $G - v$ splits.  Independent sets can be chosen
per component, and one shows some edge at $v$ is deletable without increasing
$\alpha$ --- contradicting criticality, where \emph{every} deletion must raise it.

So $\alpha$-criticality forces a structure that cannot be pieced together at a single
articulation point.

open scoped Classical
open scoped Finset

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
def IsCovering {V : Type*} (G : SimpleGraph V) (K : Set V) : Prop :=
  ∀ ⦃u v : V⦄, G.Adj u v → u ∈ K ∨ v ∈ K
