namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]

  sInf {n | ∃ K : Set V, G.IsCovering K ∧ K.ncard = n}

colours.  Exercise 8.1.7 classifies the small cases completely --- the only
1-critical graph is $K_{1}$, the only 2-critical graph is $K_{2}$, and the 3-critical
graphs are exactly the odd cycles --- and Brooks' theorem 8.4 consumes precisely
that classification to get its standing hypothesis $k \ge 4$.

\texttt{G.chromaticNumber = k} compares an $\mathbb{N}\infty$ with a coerced $\mathbb{N}$,
so $k$-chromaticity here also carries the information that $\chi(G) \ne \top$.

informal_statement:
nonempty_iso_iff. B&M's general isomorphism needs two bijections, one on vertices and one
on edges, respecting incidence.  For \emph{simple} graphs the edge bijection carries no
information --- at most one edge joins any pair --- so an adjacency-preserving vertex
bijection already induces it.  This is precisely why Mathlib can define $G $\simeq$g H$ as
an equivalence of vertex types with \texttt{G.Adj u v $\leftrightarrow$ H.Adj ($\theta$ u) ($\theta$ v)}, and this
exercise is the justification for using it throughout the file.
formal_statement:
import Mathlib

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
theorem nonempty_iso_iff {W : Type*} (H : SimpleGraph W) :
    Nonempty (G ≃g H) ↔ ∃ θ : V ≃ W, ∀ u v, G.Adj u v ↔ H.Adj (θ u) (θ v) := sorry
end SimpleGraph

informal_statement:
Definitions:
- A vertex cut: a proper subset $S$ whose deletion leaves $G$ disconnected. $V'$ is a \texttt{Finset V}, and "$G - V'$ is disconnected" is
\texttt{$\lnot$ (G.induce (↑S)$^{c}$).Connected}.  The conjunct \texttt{↑S $\subset$ Set.univ} records that a
vertex cut is a \emph{proper} subset: without it $S = V$ would qualify vacuously,
since Mathlib's \texttt{Connected} is false on the empty induced graph.

A $k$-vertex cut is the pair \texttt{G.IsVertexCut S $\land$ S.card = k}; that is exactly
what \texttt{vertexConnectivity} minimises over.
- Vertex connectivity $\kappa(G)$. The book's case split is on "$G$ has a pair of distinct nonadjacent vertices";
the Lean split is on the equivalent "$G$ has a vertex cut at all", which is the
condition the two branches actually need.  So
\item some cut exists $\Rightarrow$ \texttt{$\kappa$ = sInf \{S.card | G.IsVertexCut S\}};
\item no cut exists (the complete graphs) $\Rightarrow$ $\kappa = \nu - 1$.

\texttt{sInf} on $\mathbb{N}$ is Mathlib's \texttt{Nat.sInf}, with \texttt{sInf $\emptyset$ = 0}; the $if$ guard means
that fallback is never reached here.  Natural subtraction makes $\nu - 1 = 0$
when $V$ is empty, matching "trivial $\Rightarrow$ $\kappa = 0$".

Statement: Ex 4.2.1(a): not 2-connected (with $\nu \ge 3$) $\Rightarrow$ nonhamiltonian (restated on the repo\dots. A graph that is not 2-connected is either disconnected or has a cut vertex $v$.
Disconnected: no cycle reaches every vertex.  Cut vertex: take $S = {v}$ in
Theorem 4.2 --- deleting $v$ leaves at least two components, so
$\omega(G - S) \ge 2 > 1 = |S|$, violating the necessary condition.

A Hamilton cycle visits every vertex and returns, which needs two independent
routes out of every vertex --- exactly 2-connectivity.  Necessary but far from
sufficient (the Petersen graph is 3-connected and nonhamiltonian).

Stated against this file's local \texttt{vertexConnectivity}, not the one in
\texttt{Connectivity.lean} --- see the warning on that definition above.
formal_statement:
import Mathlib

open scoped Classical

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
def IsVertexCut (G : SimpleGraph V) (S : Finset V) : Prop :=
  (↑S : Set V) ⊂ Set.univ ∧ ¬ (G.induce ((↑S : Set V)ᶜ)).Connected
end SimpleGraph

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
noncomputable def vertexConnectivity (G : SimpleGraph V) : ℕ :=
  if ∃ S : Finset V, G.IsVertexCut S then
    sInf {n : ℕ | ∃ S : Finset V, G.IsVertexCut S ∧ S.card = n}
  else
    Fintype.card V - 1
end SimpleGraph

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
theorem nonhamiltonian_of_not_two_connected (hν : 3 ≤ Fintype.card V)
    (h : ¬ (2 ≤ G.vertexConnectivity)) : ¬ G.IsHamiltonian := sorry
end SimpleGraph

informal_statement:
Ex 4.2.1(b): an unbalanced bipartite graph is nonhamiltonian. Every edge crosses between $X$ and $Y$, so a cycle alternates sides and uses
equally many vertices from each.  A Hamilton cycle uses \emph{all} vertices, forcing
$|X| = |Y|$.

This is why the book's Herschel graph is nonhamiltonian:

(\S{}4.2, p. 61.)  Equivalently, apply Theorem 4.2 with $S$ the smaller side.
formal_statement:
import Mathlib

open scoped Classical

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
theorem nonhamiltonian_of_unbalanced_bipartite {X Y : Finset V}
    (hb : G.IsBipartiteWith ↑X ↑Y) (hne : X.card ≠ Y.card) : ¬ G.IsHamiltonian := sorry
end SimpleGraph

informal_statement:
nordhaus_gaddum. A graph and its complement cannot both be hard to colour: an edge
missing from $G$ is present in $G^{c}$, so the two compete for the same $\nu - 1$
adjacencies at each vertex.  Equality holds for complete graphs, where
$\chi(K_{n}) = n$ and $\chi(K_{n}^{c}) = 1$.  This is the archetypal Nordhaus--Gaddum inequality,
of which many analogues are known for other graph parameters.

The addition is in $\mathbb{N}\infty$, where subtraction is badly behaved ---
hence step 1, which moves the whole argument into $\mathbb{N}$ before any arithmetic.  Step
3's index gymnastics (reverse, then complement) is the fiddliest part and is worth
isolating as its own lemma about the two sorted sequences.
formal_statement:
import Mathlib

open scoped Classical

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
theorem nordhaus_gaddum {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V]
    (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj] :
    G.chromaticNumber + Gᶜ.chromaticNumber ≤ (Fintype.card V : ℕ∞) + 1 := sorry
end SimpleGraph

informal_statement:
not_both_card_edge_le_of_eleven_le. Planarity forces sparsity, and a graph and its complement cannot both
be sparse: between them they must carry \emph{every} possible edge, and $C(\nu,2)$ outgrows
$2(3\nu-6)$ at exactly $\nu = 11$.  Part (b) of the exercise confirms the bound is
sharp in spirit --- there is a simple planar graph on $\nu = 8$ vertices whose
complement is also planar.

\textbf{!} This is \textbf{not} exercise 9.3.3(a) as stated.  "Planar" is
replaced by the corollary-9.5.2 edge bound on \emph{both} sides, so what is proved is
that the two bounds are jointly unsatisfiable --- the arithmetic obstruction, with
the topology stripped out.  The conclusion is therefore a negated conjunction
rather than "$G^{c}$ is nonplanar".
formal_statement:
import Mathlib

open scoped Classical

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
theorem not_both_card_edge_le_of_eleven_le
    {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V)
    [DecidableRel G.Adj] [DecidableRel Gᶜ.Adj]
    (hν : 11 ≤ Fintype.card V) :
    ¬ (G.edgeFinset.card + 6 ≤ 3 * Fintype.card V ∧
       Gᶜ.edgeFinset.card + 6 ≤ 3 * Fintype.card V) := sorry
end SimpleGraph

informal_statement:
Definitions:
- $G \cdot uv$: contract the edge $uv$ by identifying $v$ into $u$. Pull the edge $uv$ tight until $u$ and $v$ merge into a single
vertex, which inherits the neighbours of both.  Contraction appears twice in this
chapter: in theorem 8.3, where $G_{2} \cdot uv$ is shown to be $k$-critical, and in
theorem 8.6, the deletion--contraction recursion for the chromatic polynomial ---
which the book notes *bears a close resemblance to the recursion formula for
$\tau(G)$* in theorem 2.8.

Identification is realised by \emph{dropping} $v$ from the carrier
and re-pointing its edges at $u$, so the carrier is ${x : V // x \ne v}$ and the
merged vertex is $u$.  The $a \ne b$ conjunct in \texttt{Adj} restores looplessness: the
book's contraction of a multigraph may create loops and parallel edges, and
taking the underlying simple graph is exactly what discarding them means.  This
is harmless for both uses --- theorem 8.6 is stated for simple $G$, and colourings
never see loops or multiplicities.
- $\pi_k(G)$, the number of distinct proper $k$-colourings. Count the proper colourings as \emph{labelled} objects, not up to
permutation of the colours --- the triangle example is exactly the warning against
quotienting.  Birkhoff (1912) introduced this counting approach as a possible
route to the four-colour conjecture.

\texttt{Nat.card (G.Coloring (Fin k))} rather than \texttt{Fintype.card}:
the two agree over a \texttt{Fintype}, but \texttt{Nat.card} needs no instance, which lets the
\S{}8.4 statements elaborate over \texttt{Subgraph} and component carriers without bespoke
\texttt{Fintype} derivations.  A \texttt{G.Coloring (Fin k)} is a function on vertices, so
distinctness is pointwise --- precisely the book's criterion.

Statement: numColorings_add_contract. Classify the $k$-colourings of $G - e$ by whether they give $u$ and
$v$ the same colour: the "same" ones are the colourings of $G \cdot e$, the "different"
ones are the colourings of $G$.  The book notes the recursion *bears a close
resemblance to the recursion formula for $\tau(G)$* in theorem 2.8, and that it can be
run in either direction --- reducing to empty graphs (efficient for sparse $G$) or to
complete graphs (efficient for dense $G$), as illustrated in figure 8.9.

Stated additively, $\pi_k(G) + \pi_k(G\cdot e) = \pi_k(G-e)$, to stay in
$\mathbb{N}$ --- the book's headline form has a subtraction.  Happily this \emph{is} how B&M's own
proof ends, so the Lean statement is the more faithful of the two.  Steps 2 and 3
are the only real work; step 1 is bookkeeping and step 4 is $rw$.
formal_statement:
import Mathlib

open scoped Classical

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
def contractEdge {V : Type*} (G : SimpleGraph V) (u v : V) :
    SimpleGraph {x : V // x ≠ v} where
  Adj a b := a ≠ b ∧ (G.Adj a.1 b.1 ∨ (a.1 = u ∧ G.Adj v b.1) ∨ (b.1 = u ∧ G.Adj a.1 v))
  symm := by
    rintro a b ⟨hab, h | ⟨h₁, h₂⟩ | ⟨h₁, h₂⟩⟩
    · exact ⟨hab.symm, Or.inl h.symm⟩
    · exact ⟨hab.symm, Or.inr (Or.inr ⟨h₁, h₂.symm⟩)⟩
    · exact ⟨hab.symm, Or.inr (Or.inl ⟨h₁, h₂.symm⟩)⟩
  loopless := by rintro a ⟨h, -⟩; exact h rfl
end SimpleGraph

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
noncomputable def numColorings {V : Type*} (G : SimpleGraph V) (k : ℕ) : ℕ :=
  Nat.card (G.Coloring (Fin k))
end SimpleGraph

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
theorem numColorings_add_contract
    {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) {u v : V} (h : G.Adj u v) (k : ℕ) :
    G.numColorings k + (G.contractEdge u v).numColorings k
      = (G \ SimpleGraph.edge u v).numColorings k := sorry
end SimpleGraph

resemblance to the recursion formula for $\tau(G)$* in theorem 2.8, and that it can be
run in either direction --- reducing to empty graphs (efficient for sparse $G$) or to

Stated additively, $\pi_k(G) + \pi_k(G\cdot e) = \pi_k(G-e)$, to stay in

Statement: numColorings_cycleGraph. Sanity checks: at $k = 2$ the formula gives $1 + (-1)^{n}$, which is $2$
for even $n$ and $0$ for odd $n$ --- matching that even cycles are bipartite (two
2-colourings) and odd cycles are not (none).  The $(-1)^{n}$ term is precisely where
the parity of the cycle enters, and it is what makes odd cycles the exceptional
family throughout this chapter.

Stated over $\mathbb{Z}$ with a cast on the left, because
$(k-1)^{n} + (-1)^{n}(k-1)$ is not a natural number expression --- the $(-1)^{n}$ term is
genuinely negative for odd $n$.  The base case is $n = 3$ rather than $n = 0$
because \texttt{cycleGraph n} is only a cycle for $n \ge 3$, and because contracting an edge
of $C_{3}$ would leave a multi-edge, which \texttt{contractEdge} silently simplifies.
formal_statement:
import Mathlib

open scoped Classical

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
noncomputable def numColorings {V : Type*} (G : SimpleGraph V) (k : ℕ) : ℕ :=
  Nat.card (G.Coloring (Fin k))
end SimpleGraph

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
theorem numColorings_cycleGraph (n k : ℕ) (hn : 3 ≤ n) :
    ((cycleGraph n).numColorings k : ℤ)
      = ((k : ℤ) - 1)^n + (-1)^n * ((k : ℤ) - 1) := sorry
end SimpleGraph

Statement: numColorings_eq_prod_components. No edge joins different components, so their colourings are entirely
independent: a colouring of $G$ is precisely a choice of colouring for each
component, and the count multiplies.  This is the chromatic-polynomial version of
\texttt{$\chi$(G) = max $\chi$(G$_{i}$)}, and one of the formulae the book lists as *facilitating the
calculation of chromatic polynomials*.

Step 2 is the same "components are independent" equivalence used
by \texttt{IsCritical.connected} (in its \texttt{sup} form) --- worth building once in a shared
place and specialising twice, since the counting and the $\chi$ versions differ only
in what is applied to the resulting family.

open scoped Classical

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
theorem numColorings_eq_prod_components {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V]
    (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj] (k : ℕ) :
    G.numColorings k = ∏ c : G.ConnectedComponent, (G.induce c.supp).numColorings k := sorry
end SimpleGraph

Statement: numColorings_of_isTree. Root the tree anywhere and colour outward: the root takes any of the
$k$ colours, and every other vertex is reached across exactly one edge from its
already-coloured parent, so it avoids just that one colour.  The formula reflects
the structure exactly --- $\nu - 1$ edges, each imposing precisely one constraint, with
no cycles to make the constraints interact.

$(k - 1)$ is $\mathbb{N}$-subtraction, harmless because at $k = 0$ both
sides are $0$ for a nonempty tree.  Consumed by exercises 8.4.3(b) (as the spanning
tree bound) and 8.4.4 (as the deleted-edge case of the cycle).

Statement: numColorings_union_mul_inter. A gluing formula.  A colouring of the union is a pair of colourings of
the parts agreeing on the overlap; because the overlap is \emph{complete}, its vertices
must take distinct colours, which makes the two sides' colourings matchable in a
uniform number of ways.  Together with exercise 8.4.6 (components multiply) this is
one of the practical tools for computing chromatic polynomials by decomposition.

Phrased on the \texttt{Subgraph} lattice --- $\sqcup$ and $\sqcap$ of \texttt{G.Subgraph}
--- because \texttt{SimpleGraph V} has no notion of union/intersection with differing vertex
sets.  \texttt{hcomp : (G' $\sqcap$ H').coe = $\top$} says the overlap is complete *as a graph on its
own vertex set*.  Note that the book's identity is stated multiplicatively precisely
to avoid the division that step 5 also avoids.

informal_statement:
Definitions:
- Colour $i$ is \emph{represented} at $v$: some edge incident with $v$ has colour $i$. A $k$-edge colouring is a plain function \texttt{C : G.edgeSet $\to$ Fin k}, deliberately
\textbf{not} assumed proper --- that is the whole point, since Lemma 6.1.2, Theorem 6.1
and Vizing's Theorem 6.2 all operate on improper colourings and repair them.

"Represented at $v$" is \texttt{$\exists$ e, ↑e $\in$ G.incidenceSet v $\land$ C e = i}.

\textbf{!} Note this file uses \textbf{two different} colouring encodings.  Here a colouring is
a raw function \texttt{G.edgeSet $\to$ Fin k}; but \texttt{IsUniquelyEdgeColourable} below and the
\texttt{edgeChromaticNumber} results use Mathlib's \texttt{G.lineGraph.Coloring (Fin k)}, which
is proper by construction.  The two are not interchangeable, and any proof
crossing between \S{}6.1's machinery and a $\chi'$ statement must convert explicitly.
- $c(v)$: the number of distinct colours represented at $v$. $c(v)$ counts the \emph{distinct} colours on edges at $v$, as
\texttt{(univ.filter fun i => IsRepresentedAt C i v).card}.

Two edges at $v$ sharing a colour drop $c(v)$ below $d(v)$; the colouring is
proper exactly when $c(v) = d(v)$ everywhere --- that is \texttt{numColoursAt\_le\_degree}
and \texttt{isProper\_iff\_numColoursAt\_eq\_degree} below.

$\sum_v c(v)$ is the potential function the whole chapter maximises.

Statement: (6.3): $c(v) \le d(v)$. $c(v)$ counts distinct colours on the $d(v)$ edges at $v$; distinct colours
cannot outnumber the edges carrying them.  Strict exactly when two edges at $v$
repeat a colour.

import Mathlib

open scoped Classical

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
def IsRepresentedAt {V : Type*} {G : SimpleGraph V} {k : ℕ}
    (C : G.edgeSet → Fin k) (i : Fin k) (v : V) : Prop :=
  ∃ e : G.edgeSet, (e : Sym2 V) ∈ G.incidenceSet v ∧ C e = i
end SimpleGraph

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
noncomputable def numColoursAt {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V]
    {G : SimpleGraph V} [DecidableRel G.Adj] {k : ℕ} (C : G.edgeSet → Fin k) (v : V) : ℕ :=
  (Finset.univ.filter fun i => IsRepresentedAt C i v).card
end SimpleGraph

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
theorem numColoursAt_le_degree
    {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] {G : SimpleGraph V} [DecidableRel G.Adj]
    {k : ℕ} (C : G.edgeSet → Fin k) (v : V) :

title: (6.3): $c(v) \le d(v)$
statement_informal:

cannot outnumber the edges carrying them.  Strict exactly when two edges at $v$
repeat a colour.

definitions.informal:
A $k$-edge colouring is a plain function \texttt{C : G.edgeSet $\to$ Fin k}, deliberately
\textbf{not} assumed proper --- that is the whole point, since Lemma 6.1.2, Theorem 6.1
and Vizing's Theorem 6.2 all operate on improper colourings and repair them.

"Represented at $v$" is \texttt{$\exists$ e, ↑e $\in$ G.incidenceSet v $\land$ C e = i}.

\textbf{!} Note this file uses \textbf{two different} colouring encodings.  Here a colouring is
a raw function \texttt{G.edgeSet $\to$ Fin k}; but \texttt{IsUniquelyEdgeColourable} below and the
\texttt{edgeChromaticNumber} results use Mathlib's \texttt{G.lineGraph.Coloring (Fin k)}, which
is proper by construction.  The two are not interchangeable, and any proof
crossing between \S{}6.1's machinery and a $\chi'$ statement must convert explicitly.

definitions.title: $c(v)$: the number of distinct colours represented at $v$
definitions.informal:
$c(v)$ counts the \emph{distinct} colours on edges at $v$, as
\texttt{(univ.filter fun i => IsRepresentedAt C i v).card}.

Two edges at $v$ sharing a colour drop $c(v)$ below $d(v)$; the colouring is
proper exactly when $c(v) = d(v)$ everywhere --- that is \texttt{numColoursAt\_le\_degree}
and \texttt{isProper\_iff\_numColoursAt\_eq\_degree} below.

$\sum_v c(v)$ is the potential function the whole chapter maximises.

informal_statement:
Definitions:
- contract. $G \cdot e$ (\S{}2.4).  Mathlib has no edge contraction for \texttt{SimpleGraph}.
NOTE: a genuine contraction identifies the ends of $e$ and therefore changes the carrier
type (to $|V| - 1$ vertices).  Here it is \emph{stubbed on the same carrier} $V$ as a placeholder,
purely so that the deletion--contraction recurrence (Theorem 2.8) can be typed.

Think of $e = uv$ as a string pulled tight until $u$ and $v$ merge;
everything attached to either is now attached to the merged vertex, and $e$
disappears.  For a link, $\nu(G\cdot e) = \nu - 1$, $\varepsilon(G\cdot e) = \varepsilon - 1$, $\omega(G\cdot e) = \omega$ --- so
contracting an edge of a tree again yields a tree, which is what makes
deletion--contraction work.

\textbf{\textbf{!} Defective on two counts.}
1. \emph{\texttt{sorry} body.}  $G \cdot e$ is an opaque graph, so theorem 2.8 relates opaque
   quantities and asserts nothing.
2. \emph{Wrong carrier.}  A genuine contraction has $\nu - 1$ vertices; this is stubbed on
   the \textbf{same} carrier $V$ purely so theorem 2.8 can be typed.  Even given an honest
   body on $V$, the identity $\nu(G\cdot e) = \nu - 1$ could not hold.

\emph{The repair} is to move to the quotient carrier ${x : V // x \ne v}$ with $v$'s
incidences re-pointed at $u$, exactly as chapter 10's \texttt{Digraph.contractEdge} does ---
that definition is honest and complete, and can be transcribed.
- The number of spanning trees $\tau(G)$: the number of tree subgraphs $T \le G$ on the full vertex set. \textbf{!} $\tau(G)$ counts the \emph{distinct} spanning trees, \textbf{not} the
non-isomorphic ones.  B&M stress the difference: $K_{6}$ has six non-isomorphic spanning
trees (figure 2.1) but $6^{4} = 1296$ distinct ones.  $\tau$ satisfies deletion--contraction
(theorem 2.8) and, for complete graphs, Cayley's formula (theorem 2.9); the general
determinant formula is chapter 12's matrix-tree theorem.

"Spanning" is automatic: a \texttt{T : SimpleGraph W} lives on the whole
vertex type, so \texttt{T $\le$ H $\land$ T.IsTree} already means a spanning tree.  \textbf{!} \texttt{IsTree} bundles
\texttt{Connected}, which requires \texttt{Nonempty W} --- so on an empty carrier $\tau = 0$.  That is
where \texttt{cayley} fails at $n = 0$.

Statement: numSpanningTrees_deletion_contraction. Iterating the recursion reduces any graph to trivial ones and so computes
$\tau$ --- though B&M note it is impractical for large graphs, which is what motivates
chapter 12's determinant formula.

\textbf{\textbf{!} Currently vacuous.}  \texttt{contract} has a \texttt{sorry} body, so $G \cdot e$ is opaque and this
statement relates opaque quantities.  Worse, \texttt{contract} is a \textbf{same-carrier}
placeholder, so even an honest body on $V$ could not satisfy $\nu(G\cdot e) = \nu - 1$ and step
3's bijection would be false.  Repair \texttt{contract} on the quotient carrier first --- see its
docstring.

import Mathlib

open scoped Classical

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
noncomputable def contract (G : SimpleGraph V) (e : Sym2 V) : SimpleGraph V := sorry
end SimpleGraph

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
noncomputable def numSpanningTrees {W : Type*} (H : SimpleGraph W) : ℕ :=
  Nat.card {T : SimpleGraph W // T ≤ H ∧ T.IsTree}
end SimpleGraph

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
theorem numSpanningTrees_deletion_contraction (e : Sym2 V) (he : e ∈ G.edgeSet) :
    G.numSpanningTrees =
      (G.deleteEdges {e}).numSpanningTrees + (G.contract e).numSpanningTrees := sorry
end SimpleGraph

informal_statement:
Ex 4.1.5: exactly $2k$ odd-degree vertices $\Rightarrow$ $k$ edge-disjoint covering trails. By Corollary 1.1 the odd-degree vertices come in pairs, so there are $k$ pairs.
Pair them up and add $k$ new edges joining the members of each pair; every vertex
of the enlarged graph then has even degree, so Theorem 4.1 gives an Euler tour.
Deleting the $k$ added edges cuts that tour into exactly $k$ trails, which are
edge-disjoint and between them cover every edge of $G$.

The practical reading: a road network with $2k$ awkward junctions needs $k$
separate pen-strokes; one Euler trail is the case $k = 1$.
formal_statement:
import Mathlib

open scoped Classical

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
theorem odd_vertices_trail_cover (k : ℕ) (hk : 0 < k) (hconn : G.Connected)
    (h : (Finset.univ.filter fun v => Odd (G.degree v)).card = 2 * k) :
    ∃ ts : Finset (Σ p : V × V, G.Walk p.1 p.2),
      ts.card = k ∧ (∀ t ∈ ts, t.2.IsTrail) ∧
      ∀ e ∈ G.edgeSet, ∃! t : (Σ p : V × V, G.Walk p.1 p.2), t ∈ ts ∧ e ∈ t.2.edges := sorry
end SimpleGraph

informal_statement:
Definitions:
- Feasible vertex labelling: $l x + l y \ge w s(x,y)$. Assign a label to every vertex so the two labels at an edge's ends sum to at
least its weight.  Weights are carried as \texttt{w : Sym2 V $\to$ $\mathbb{R}$} rather than
$V \to V \to \mathbb{R}$, which makes symmetry automatic.

Labels are the dual objects to matchings: $\sum_v l(v)$ upper-bounds the weight of
any perfect matching, and Theorem 5.5 says a matching attaining that bound is
optimal.

\textbf{!} The existence claim (5.12) is \textbf{not} stated as a lemma anywhere in this file,
though the Kuhn--Munkres algorithm needs it as its starting point.
- The equality subgraph $G_l$. Keep only the edges that are "tight" for the labelling --- those whose weight
exactly uses up the sum of the labels at their ends.  As the Kuhn--Munkres
algorithm adjusts labels the equality subgraph changes, and the algorithm stops
once some equality subgraph contains a perfect matching.

Representing weights as \texttt{Sym2 V $\to$ $\mathbb{R}$} makes $l x + l y = w s(x,y)$ symmetric in
$x, y$ definitionally, which is why the \texttt{symm} obligation is routine.
- Weight of a matching. \texttt{$\sum^{f}$ e $\in$ M.edgeSet, w e}, using the \emph{finsum} $\sum^{f}$ rather than \texttt{Finset.sum} so that
no \texttt{Fintype (M.edgeSet)} instance has to be threaded through --- \texttt{M.edgeSet} is a
\texttt{Set}, and finsum handles the finiteness side condition implicitly.

In the personnel-assignment setting $w(x_{i}y_{j})$ is the effectiveness of worker $X_{i}$
in job $Y_{j}$, and $w(M)$ the total effectiveness of assignment $M$.
- An optimal matching: a max-weight perfect matching. Among all assignments of each worker to a distinct job, the one of greatest total
effectiveness.  Maximality is spelled out by hand, as with
\texttt{Subgraph.IsMaximumMatching}.

Statement: Thm 5.5: a perfect matching in the equality subgraph is an optimal matching of $G$. Weak duality certifying optimality again: $\sum_v l(v)$ bounds every perfect
matching from above, and one attaining the bound must be best.  This is the
foundation of the Kuhn--Munkres algorithm, which alternates the Hungarian method
inside $G_l$ with label adjustments that grow $G_l$.

The conclusion transports $M$ along \texttt{Hom.ofLE} from \texttt{equalitySubgraph w G l} up
to $G$, since the two live over different graphs.
formal_statement:
import Mathlib

open scoped Pointwise

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
def IsFeasibleLabelling {V : Type*} (w : Sym2 V → ℝ) (X Y : Set V) (l : V → ℝ) : Prop :=
  ∀ x ∈ X, ∀ y ∈ Y, w s(x, y) ≤ l x + l y
end SimpleGraph

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
def equalitySubgraph {V : Type*} (w : Sym2 V → ℝ) (G : SimpleGraph V) (l : V → ℝ) :
    SimpleGraph V where
  Adj x y := G.Adj x y ∧ l x + l y = w s(x, y)
  symm := by sorry
  loopless := by sorry
end SimpleGraph

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
noncomputable def matchingWeight {V : Type*} (w : Sym2 V → ℝ) {G : SimpleGraph V}
    (M : G.Subgraph) : ℝ :=
  ∑ᶠ e ∈ M.edgeSet, w e
end SimpleGraph

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
def IsOptimalMatching {V : Type*} (w : Sym2 V → ℝ) (G : SimpleGraph V) (M : G.Subgraph) : Prop :=
  M.IsPerfectMatching ∧
    ∀ M' : G.Subgraph, M'.IsPerfectMatching → matchingWeight w M' ≤ matchingWeight w M
end SimpleGraph

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
theorem optimal_of_perfectMatching_equalitySubgraph
    {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (w : Sym2 V → ℝ) (G : SimpleGraph V)
    {X Y : Set V} (hbip : G.IsBipartiteWith X Y) (hcov : X ∪ Y = Set.univ)
    (l : V → ℝ) (hl : IsFeasibleLabelling w X Y l)
    {M : (equalitySubgraph w G l).Subgraph} (hM : M.IsPerfectMatching) :
    IsOptimalMatching w G
      (M.map (Hom.ofLE (by sorry : equalitySubgraph w G l ≤ G))) := sorry
end SimpleGraph
title: Thm 5.5: a perfect matching in the equality subgraph is an optimal matching of $G$
statement_informal:

matching from above, and one attaining the bound must be best.  This is the

informal_statement:
Cor 4.6a: $\varepsilon > C(\nu- 1,2) + 1$ implies hamiltonicity. Enough edges guarantee a spanning cycle, and this pins down exactly how many
"enough" is: a nonhamiltonian graph has at most $C(\nu-1, 2) + 1$ edges.

"By theorem 1.1" is the handshaking lemma --- degree majorisation transfers to an
edge-count inequality because $2\varepsilon = \sum d(v)$.

\textbf{!} The book's algebra is over $\mathbb{Q}$ (note the $\tfrac{1}{2}$); in $\mathbb{N}$ the identity
$\tfrac{1}{2}(m^{2} + (\nu-2m)(\nu-m-1) + m(\nu-1)) = C(\nu-1,2) + 1 - \tfrac{1}{2}(m-1)(m-2) - (m-1)(\nu-2m-1)$
involves subtraction that truncates.  Either clear denominators and work with
$2\varepsilon$ throughout, or cast to $\mathbb{Z}$/$\mathbb{Q}$ for the identity and cast back.  The latter
is likely cleaner.
formal_statement:
import Mathlib

open scoped Classical

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
theorem ore_bondy_edge_bound (hν : 3 ≤ Fintype.card V)
    (hε : (Fintype.card V - 1).choose 2 + 1 < G.edgeFinset.card) :
    G.IsHamiltonian := sorry
end SimpleGraph
title: Cor 4.6a: $\varepsilon > C(\nu- 1,2) + 1$ implies hamiltonicity

informal_statement:
Definitions:
- join. $G \lor H$, rebuilt on Mathlib: within-side edges from $\oplus g$, all cross
edges from \texttt{completeBipartiteGraph}. \texttt{symm}/\texttt{loopless} are inherited from $\sqcup$.

Lay the two graphs side by side keeping all their own edges, then add every
edge running between them.  The book's $G + H$ (disjoint union) is Mathlib's
$\oplus g$, and "joining each vertex of $G$ to each vertex of $H$" is exactly
\texttt{completeBipartiteGraph V W}, so

    join G H = (G $\oplus$g H) $\sqcup$ completeBipartiteGraph V W

on carrier $V \oplus W$.  Building it as a $\sqcup$ of two existing graphs means \texttt{symm}
and \texttt{loopless} are inherited and need no proof.

The building block of the graphs \texttt{Cmn} below.
- $C_{m,n} = K_m \lor (K_m^c + K_{n-2m})$, with $+$ the Mathlib disjoint sum $\oplus g$. Take $m$ "hub" vertices forming a complete graph, $m$ isolated vertices, and a
complete graph on the remaining $n - 2m$; then join every hub to everything
else.  Carrier \texttt{Fin m $\oplus$ (Fin m $\oplus$ Fin (n - 2 * m))}, with $K_m^{c} = \bot$ on \texttt{Fin m}.

Degrees: the $m$ hubs have degree $n - 1$, the $m$ isolated vertices have degree
$m$, and the remaining $n - 2m$ have degree $n - m - 1$.  That is the degree
sequence Theorem 4.6 majorises against.

\textbf{!} The side condition $1 \le m < n/2$ is \textbf{not} carried in the type.  For $m = 0$
or $2m > n$ the definition still elaborates (with $n - 2 * m$ truncating to $0$)
but no longer matches the book's figure.  Callers must supply the bound.

Statement: Cor 4.6b: the extremal nonhamiltonian graphs at $C(\nu- 1,2)+1$ edges are $C_{1,\nu}$ (and $C_{2,5}$). The equality analysis of the first half.  The final inequality is tight only when
both subtracted terms $\tfrac{1}{2}(m-1)(m-2)$ and $(m-1)(\nu-2m-1)$ vanish, which happens
only for $m = 1$, or $m = 2$ together with $\nu = 5$.

So the bound is attained by exactly one graph for each $\nu$, plus one sporadic
extra at $\nu = 5$: the densest nonhamiltonian simple graphs there are.

\textbf{!} The book's closing "which is easily seen to imply that $G \cong C_{1,\nu}$" is
the hardest step to formalise, and it is \textbf{not} easy in Lean.  Degree sequence
does not in general determine a graph up to isomorphism; the implication holds
here only because of the specific structure of $C_{1,\nu}$ and $C_{2,5}$, and
recovering an explicit $$\simeq$g$ requires constructing the vertex bijection by hand.
formal_statement:
import Mathlib

open scoped Classical

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
def join {V W : Type*} (G : SimpleGraph V) (H : SimpleGraph W) : SimpleGraph (V ⊕ W) :=
  (G ⊕g H) ⊔ completeBipartiteGraph V W
end SimpleGraph

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
def Cmn (m n : ℕ) : SimpleGraph (Fin m ⊕ (Fin m ⊕ Fin (n - 2 * m))) :=
  (⊤ : SimpleGraph (Fin m)).join
    ((⊥ : SimpleGraph (Fin m)) ⊕g (⊤ : SimpleGraph (Fin (n - 2 * m))))
end SimpleGraph

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
theorem ore_bondy_extremal (hν : 3 ≤ Fintype.card V) (hnh : ¬ G.IsHamiltonian)
    (hε : G.edgeFinset.card = (Fintype.card V - 1).choose 2 + 1) :
    Nonempty (G ≃g Cmn 1 (Fintype.card V)) ∨
      (Fintype.card V = 5 ∧ Nonempty (G ≃g Cmn 2 5)) := sorry
end SimpleGraph

definitions.title: $C_{m,n} = K_m \lor (K_m^c + K_{n-2m})$, with $+$ the Mathlib disjoint sum $\oplus g$
definitions.informal:
Take $m$ "hub" vertices forming a complete graph, $m$ isolated vertices, and a
complete graph on the remaining $n - 2m$; then join every hub to everything
else.  Carrier \texttt{Fin m $\oplus$ (Fin m $\oplus$ Fin (n - 2 * m))}, with $K_m^{c} = \bot$ on \texttt{Fin m}.

Degrees: the $m$ hubs have degree $n - 1$, the $m$ isolated vertices have degree
$m$, and the remaining $n - 2m$ have degree $n - m - 1$.  That is the degree
sequence Theorem 4.6 majorises against.

\textbf{!} The side condition $1 \le m < n/2$ is \textbf{not} carried in the type.  For $m = 0$
or $2m > n$ the definition still elaborates (with $n - 2 * m$ truncating to $0$)
but no longer matches the book's figure.  Callers must supply the bound.

informal_statement:
Definitions:
- A walk is internally disjoint from a subgraph $H$: no \emph{internal} vertex lies in $H$. The walk may start and end on $H$, but between those endpoints it
must stay entirely outside $H$.  This is what makes the bridge relation an
equivalence, and it is why a bridge is a maximal chunk of the graph hanging off
$H$ and touching it only at its attachment points.

\texttt{p.support.tail.dropLast} is the walk's interior --- drop the
first vertex (\texttt{tail}) and the last (\texttt{dropLast}).  \textbf{!} This is \textbf{not} the repo's
\texttt{InternallyDisjoint} (\texttt{TwoConnected.lean:58}), which relates a walk to another
\emph{walk}; here the second argument is a \texttt{Subgraph}.  A walk of length $\le 1$ has empty
interior and so is vacuously internally disjoint from everything --- which is
intended, and is what makes \texttt{bridgeRel} reflexive on single edges.
- Position of a vertex along a cycle (index into its support). Walking around the cycle from its base point, this records how many
steps it takes to reach $x$.  Comparing indices is how "cyclic order" is expressed
here.

\textbf{!} Mathlib's \texttt{CircularOrder}/\texttt{Btw}/\texttt{SBtw} are order classes on a
\emph{type} and do not apply to the support list of a particular cycle, so they are no
help.  \textbf{!} \texttt{List.idxOf} silently returns the list's \texttt{length} for an absent element,
so every use must be guarded by \texttt{x $\in$ c.support} --- unguarded, all missing vertices
quietly share one position past the end.  Note also that this is genuinely
\emph{linear}, not cyclic: it is measured from $c$'s base point, so \texttt{InCyclicOrder}
below expresses a cyclic condition only up to the choice of that base point.
- Four vertices in cyclic order on $c$. Travelling once round the cycle, the four vertices are met in that
order.  This is the configuration making two bridges \emph{skew}: each bridge's two
attachments separate the other's, so drawn inside the same region their connecting
paths would have to cross --- which is precisely the Jordan-curve contradiction in
theorem 9.8.

Rendered as a chain of strict \texttt{cycleIdx} inequalities, i.e. as
a \emph{linear} order from $c$'s base point rather than a genuinely cyclic one.  This is
weaker than the book's phrase: the book's "cyclic order $u, u', v, v'$" is invariant
under rotation, whereas this version distinguishes rotations.  It suffices for
\texttt{Skew}, which existentially quantifies over which attachment plays which role and so
recovers rotation-invariance, but do not reuse \texttt{InCyclicOrder} where genuine
rotation-invariance is needed.
- Forward distance along $c$ from $a$ to $x$, in steps, wrapping at the base point. Stand at $a$ and walk forwards around the cycle; this counts the steps
until $x$ is reached.  Unlike \texttt{cycleIdx} --- which is measured from $c$'s own base
point and so is merely linear --- this is genuinely cyclic: it is what lets an arc
"wrap round" past the base point.

\textbf{!} Guard uses by \texttt{a, x $\in$ c.support}.  \texttt{cycleIdx} returns
\texttt{c.support.length} for an absent vertex, which here yields a meaningless distance.
For $a$ on the cycle the $\mathbb{N}$-subtraction never truncates: \texttt{cycleIdx a $\le$ c.length}
(the base point occurs first at index $0$), so \texttt{cycleIdx x + c.length $\ge$ cycleIdx a}.
The \texttt{\% c.length} is what performs the wraparound; for a degenerate $c$ of length $0$
it is the identity ($n \% 0 = n$ in Lean), which is harmless since every use site
carries \texttt{hc : c.IsCycle}.
- B&M's relation $~$ on $E(G) \ E(H)$: $e_{1} ~ e_{2}$ iff joined by a walk internally disjoint from $H$\dots. Two edges outside $H$ are related when you can travel from one to the
other without passing through $H$.  Grouping edges into classes carves
$G - E(H)$ into the pieces that hang off $H$ --- those pieces are the bridges.

\texttt{Relation.EqvGen} wraps the book's raw condition in its
reflexive--symmetric--transitive closure, which \emph{discharges} the book's "it is easy
to verify" rather than proving it: whatever the raw relation does, the closure is
an equivalence by construction.  This is a deliberate trade --- the file gains an
equivalence for free, at the cost that \texttt{bridgeRel} is a priori coarser than $\sim$.
It is not actually coarser (the book's $\sim$ really is an equivalence), but nothing
here proves that, so do not appeal to "\texttt{bridgeRel e f} gives a single connecting
walk" --- it gives a \emph{chain} of them.  Several skeletons below rely on this
distinction.
- $x$ lies on the closed arc of $c$ running forwards from $a$ to $b$. Walking forwards from $a$, you meet $x$ no later than $b$.  Both
endpoints count as being on the arc, matching the book's segments, which share their
endpoints with the neighbouring segments and so are edge-disjoint but not
vertex-disjoint.

Stated via \texttt{cycleDist}, so the wraparound is handled: the arc
from $a$ to $b$ may pass through $c$'s base point.  The \texttt{x $\in$ c.support} conjunct is
the guard that keeps vertices off the cycle out, since \texttt{cycleDist} would otherwise
give them a spurious finite distance.
- The bridge of $H$ in $G$ containing the edge $e$: the subgraph induced by $e$'s $~$-class. A bridge is one of the connected pieces remaining when $H$ is
removed, together with the attachment points where it touches $H$.  The three
"immediate" facts quoted above are \texttt{bridgeOf\_connected},
\texttt{exists\_path\_internallyDisjoint} and \texttt{bridge\_inter\_subset\_cycle} below --- none of
them is actually immediate once $\sim$ is a closure.  In planar graph theory bridges
carry the argument: theorem 9.8 says inner bridges of a cycle avoid one another,
theorem 9.9 that a bridge avoiding every outer bridge is transferable, and together
these drive Kuratowski's theorem 9.10.

Indexed by a \emph{representative edge} $e$ rather than by a class,
so "the bridge containing $e$"; two edges give the same bridge exactly when
\texttt{bridgeRel H e f}.  Built with \texttt{Subgraph.mk} directly --- \textbf{not} with
\texttt{SimpleGraph.toSubgraph} (\texttt{Subgraph.lean:559}), which is \emph{spanning} and would put
every vertex of $G$ into every bridge.  Note \texttt{verts} is the union of the class's
edges, so it automatically includes the attachment points.

\textbf{!} Because \texttt{bridgeRel} is reflexive for \emph{any} $e$ (it is an \texttt{EqvGen}), \texttt{bridgeOf H e}
is nonempty even for an $e$ that is not an edge of $G$ at all --- it then has two
vertices and no edges.  Statements about bridges must therefore carry
\texttt{e $\in$ G.edgeSet \textbackslash\{\} H.edgeSet} explicitly.  Two of them below originally omitted it and
were false as a result; both now carry it (see the module header).
- Vertices of attachment of the bridge of $e$ to the cycle traced by $c$: $V(B) \cap V(C)$. The points at which the bridge touches down onto the cycle.  Almost
everything in \S{}9.4 is a statement about how two bridges' attachment sets interleave
around $C$ --- \texttt{Overlaps}, \texttt{Skew} and the segments below are all built on this one
set.

Specialised to \texttt{H = c.toSubgraph} for a closed walk $c$, since
\S{}9.4 only ever needs bridges of a \emph{cycle}.  A \texttt{Set V}, not a \texttt{Finset}, so that
\texttt{.ncard} is used for $k$ (see theorem 9.6's conclusion).  "$B$ is a $k$-bridge"
is spelled \texttt{(G.attach c e).ncard = k}, and "$B$ and $B'$ are equivalent" is
\texttt{G.attach c e = G.attach c e'}.
- $a$ and $b$ are consecutive vertices of attachment of the bridge of $e$: both are attachments, and no\dots. The arc from $a$ forwards to $b$ is then exactly one \textbf{segment} of the
bridge --- an arc of $C$ with attachments at both ends and none in between.  Ranging
over all consecutive pairs recovers the book's partition of $C$.

"No attachment strictly between" is phrased as: every attachment
on the closed arc is one of the two endpoints.  This is what makes the segments
partition $C$ rather than merely cover it.  The definition does not require the
bridge to have $k \ge 2$ attachments; with fewer, no pair satisfies it, and \texttt{Avoids}
below is then false for want of a witness --- which is the right answer, since a
$0$- or $1$-bridge has no segments to contain anything.
- Two bridges of a cycle are skew: they have attachments $a, a', b, b'$ occurring in that cyclic order on\dots. The two bridges interleave around the cycle.  In a plane graph this is
fatal for two bridges on the same side: their connecting paths would have to cross,
contradicting the Jordan curve theorem --- which is exactly the (dropped) proof of
theorem 9.8.

The book asks for \emph{four distinct} vertices; the Lean version
requires only $a \ne b$ and $a' \ne b'$.  The remaining distinctness is implied by the
strict \texttt{cycleIdx} chain in \texttt{InCyclicOrder}, since distinct indices force distinct
vertices --- provided all four lie on \texttt{c.support}, which the \texttt{attach} memberships
supply.  Rotation-invariance is recovered by the existential over which attachment
plays which role, compensating for \texttt{InCyclicOrder} being measured from $c$'s base
point.
- Two bridges of a cycle avoid one another: all the attachments of one lie in a single segment of the other. Cut the cycle at one bridge's attachment points, producing arcs; the
two bridges avoid each other when the second's attachments all fall inside a single
arc, so both can be drawn on the same side of $C$ without crossing.

The disjunction mirrors the book's "of one bridge \dots of the
other", which is not symmetric on its face --- the definition says only that \emph{some}
assignment of the two roles works.  A segment of the bridge of $e$ is the arc
\texttt{OnArc a b} for $a$, $b$ consecutive attachments of $e$.
- Two bridges of a cycle overlap: they do not avoid one another. Neither bridge's attachments fit inside a single segment of the other,
so drawn on the same side of $C$ they would be forced to cross.  Theorem 9.8 says
this cannot happen for two inner (or two outer) bridges of a plane graph, and
theorem 9.6 says overlapping comes in only two shapes.

\textbf{\textbf{!} Repaired --- previously \texttt{sorry}.}  This definition formerly had the body
\texttt{Prop := sorry}, making it an \emph{opaque, unspecified} proposition and rendering
\texttt{overlap\_imp\_skew\_or\_equivalent\_three\_bridge} (theorem 9.6) vacuous: with \texttt{Overlaps}
opaque, that theorem said nothing about bridges and "proving" it would have
established nothing.  It also violated the project convention
(\texttt{.claude/CLAUDE.md}): \emph{never \texttt{sorry} in a \texttt{def}} --- a \texttt{sorry}-ed proof is an honest
debt, a \texttt{sorry}-ed definition is a silent change of meaning.

It is now the honest negation of \texttt{Avoids}, built on the segment machinery above
(\texttt{cycleDist} $\to$ \texttt{OnArc} $\to$ \texttt{ConsecutiveAttach} $\to$ \texttt{Avoids}), which is the layer B&M
assume when they speak of segments.  \textbf{!} \texttt{[DecidableEq V]} had to be added to the
signature, since \texttt{cycleIdx} needs it; every use site already had the instance.

Statement: overlap_imp_skew_or_equivalent_three_bridge. Overlapping comes in exactly two flavours.  This dichotomy is what the
dropped theorem 9.8 disposes of --- the skew case by the Jordan curve theorem, the
equivalent-3-bridge case by the tripod of theorem 9.7.  It is the reason theorem 9.7
exists at all.

"Equivalent 3-bridges" is rendered as the conjunction
\texttt{attach c e = attach c e' $\land$ (attach c e).ncard = 3}, matching the book's definition
of equivalent $k$-bridges.  Steps 2--4 all reduce to arc arithmetic on \texttt{cycleIdx},
so the segment machinery built for \texttt{Overlaps} will carry most of them.
formal_statement:
import Mathlib

open scoped Classical

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
def Walk.InternallyDisjointFrom {V : Type*} {G : SimpleGraph V}
    (H : G.Subgraph) {u v : V} (p : G.Walk u v) : Prop :=
  ∀ x ∈ p.support.tail.dropLast, x ∉ H.verts
end SimpleGraph

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
def Walk.cycleIdx {V : Type*} [DecidableEq V] {G : SimpleGraph V} {u : V}
    (c : G.Walk u u) (x : V) : ℕ := List.idxOf x c.support
end SimpleGraph

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
def Walk.InCyclicOrder {V : Type*} [DecidableEq V] {G : SimpleGraph V} {u : V}
    (c : G.Walk u u) (a b d e : V) : Prop :=
  c.cycleIdx a < c.cycleIdx b ∧ c.cycleIdx b < c.cycleIdx d ∧ c.cycleIdx d < c.cycleIdx e
end SimpleGraph

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
def Walk.cycleDist {V : Type*} [DecidableEq V] {G : SimpleGraph V} {u : V}
    (c : G.Walk u u) (a x : V) : ℕ :=
  (c.cycleIdx x + c.length - c.cycleIdx a) % c.length
end SimpleGraph

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
def bridgeRel {V : Type*} (G : SimpleGraph V) (H : G.Subgraph) :
    Sym2 V → Sym2 V → Prop :=
  Relation.EqvGen fun e₁ e₂ =>
    e₁ ∈ G.edgeSet \ H.edgeSet ∧ e₂ ∈ G.edgeSet \ H.edgeSet ∧
    ∃ (u v : V) (p : G.Walk u v), p.InternallyDisjointFrom H ∧
      p.edges.head? = some e₁ ∧ p.edges.getLast? = some e₂
end SimpleGraph

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
def Walk.OnArc {V : Type*} [DecidableEq V] {G : SimpleGraph V} {u : V}
    (c : G.Walk u u) (a b x : V) : Prop :=
  x ∈ c.support ∧ c.cycleDist a x ≤ c.cycleDist a b
end SimpleGraph

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
def bridgeOf {V : Type*} (G : SimpleGraph V) (H : G.Subgraph) (e : Sym2 V) :
    G.Subgraph where
  verts := {x | ∃ f, G.bridgeRel H e f ∧ x ∈ f}
  Adj u v := G.Adj u v ∧ G.bridgeRel H e s(u, v)
  adj_sub h := h.1
  edge_vert h := ⟨_, h.2, Sym2.mem_mk_left _ _⟩
  symm u v h := ⟨h.1.symm, by rw [Sym2.eq_swap]; exact h.2⟩
end SimpleGraph

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
def attach {V : Type*} (G : SimpleGraph V) {u : V} (c : G.Walk u u) (e : Sym2 V) : Set V :=
  (G.bridgeOf c.toSubgraph e).verts ∩ c.toSubgraph.verts
end SimpleGraph

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
def ConsecutiveAttach {V : Type*} [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) {u : V}
    (c : G.Walk u u) (e : Sym2 V) (a b : V) : Prop :=
  a ∈ G.attach c e ∧ b ∈ G.attach c e ∧ a ≠ b ∧
    ∀ x ∈ G.attach c e, c.OnArc a b x → x = a ∨ x = b
end SimpleGraph

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
def Skew {V : Type*} [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) {u : V}
    (c : G.Walk u u) (e e' : Sym2 V) : Prop :=
  ∃ a b a' b', a ≠ b ∧ a' ≠ b' ∧
    a ∈ G.attach c e ∧ b ∈ G.attach c e ∧
    a' ∈ G.attach c e' ∧ b' ∈ G.attach c e' ∧
    c.InCyclicOrder a a' b b'
end SimpleGraph

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
def Avoids {V : Type*} [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) {u : V}
    (c : G.Walk u u) (e e' : Sym2 V) : Prop :=
  (∃ a b, G.ConsecutiveAttach c e a b ∧ ∀ x ∈ G.attach c e', c.OnArc a b x) ∨
  (∃ a b, G.ConsecutiveAttach c e' a b ∧ ∀ x ∈ G.attach c e, c.OnArc a b x)
end SimpleGraph

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
def Overlaps {V : Type*} [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) {u : V}
    (c : G.Walk u u) (e e' : Sym2 V) : Prop := ¬ G.Avoids c e e'
end SimpleGraph

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
theorem overlap_imp_skew_or_equivalent_three_bridge
    {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] {G : SimpleGraph V}
    {u : V} {c : G.Walk u u} (hc : c.IsCycle) {e e' : Sym2 V}
    (hB : e ∈ G.edgeSet \ c.toSubgraph.edgeSet) (hB' : e' ∈ G.edgeSet \ c.toSubgraph.edgeSet)
    (hov : G.Overlaps c e e') :
    G.Skew c e e' ∨
      (G.attach c e = G.attach c e' ∧ (G.attach c e).ncard = 3) := sorry
end SimpleGraph

\texttt{.ncard} is used for $k$ (see theorem 9.6's conclusion).  "$B$ is a $k$-bridge"
is spelled \texttt{(G.attach c e).ncard = k}, and "$B$ and $B'$ are equivalent" is
\texttt{G.attach c e = G.attach c e'}.

definitions.title: $a$ and $b$ are consecutive vertices of attachment of the bridge of $e$: both are attachments, and no\dots
definitions.informal:
The arc from $a$ forwards to $b$ is then exactly one \textbf{segment} of the
bridge --- an arc of $C$ with attachments at both ends and none in between.  Ranging
over all consecutive pairs recovers the book's partition of $C$.

"No attachment strictly between" is phrased as: every attachment
on the closed arc is one of the two endpoints.  This is what makes the segments
partition $C$ rather than merely cover it.  The definition does not require the
bridge to have $k \ge 2$ attachments; with fewer, no pair satisfies it, and \texttt{Avoids}
below is then false for want of a witness --- which is the right answer, since a
$0$- or $1$-bridge has no segments to contain anything.

definitions.title: Two bridges of a cycle are skew: they have attachments $a, a', b, b'$ occurring in that cyclic order on\dots
definitions.informal:
The two bridges interleave around the cycle.  In a plane graph this is
fatal for two bridges on the same side: their connecting paths would have to cross,
contradicting the Jordan curve theorem --- which is exactly the (dropped) proof of
theorem 9.8.

The book asks for \emph{four distinct} vertices; the Lean version
requires only $a \ne b$ and $a' \ne b'$.  The remaining distinctness is implied by the
strict \texttt{cycleIdx} chain in \texttt{InCyclicOrder}, since distinct indices force distinct
vertices --- provided all four lie on \texttt{c.support}, which the \texttt{attach} memberships
supply.  Rotation-invariance is recovered by the existential over which attachment
plays which role, compensating for \texttt{InCyclicOrder} being measured from $c$'s base
point.

definitions.title: Two bridges of a cycle avoid one another: all the attachments of one lie in a single segment of the other
definitions.informal:
Cut the cycle at one bridge's attachment points, producing arcs; the
two bridges avoid each other when the second's attachments all fall inside a single
arc, so both can be drawn on the same side of $C$ without crossing.

The disjunction mirrors the book's "of one bridge \dots of the
other", which is not symmetric on its face --- the definition says only that \emph{some}
assignment of the two roles works.  A segment of the bridge of $e$ is the arc
\texttt{OnArc a b} for $a$, $b$ consecutive attachments of $e$.

definitions.title: Two bridges of a cycle overlap: they do not avoid one another
definitions.informal:
Neither bridge's attachments fit inside a single segment of the other,
so drawn on the same side of $C$ they would be forced to cross.  Theorem 9.8 says
this cannot happen for two inner (or two outer) bridges of a plane graph, and
theorem 9.6 says overlapping comes in only two shapes.

\textbf{\textbf{!} Repaired --- previously \texttt{sorry}.}  This definition formerly had the body
\texttt{Prop := sorry}, making it an \emph{opaque, unspecified} proposition and rendering
\texttt{overlap\_imp\_skew\_or\_equivalent\_three\_bridge} (theorem 9.6) vacuous: with \texttt{Overlaps}
opaque, that theorem said nothing about bridges and "proving" it would have
established nothing.  It also violated the project convention
(\texttt{.claude/CLAUDE.md}): \emph{never \texttt{sorry} in a \texttt{def}} --- a \texttt{sorry}-ed proof is an honest
debt, a \texttt{sorry}-ed definition is a silent change of meaning.

It is now the honest negation of \texttt{Avoids}, built on the segment machinery above
(\texttt{cycleDist} $\to$ \texttt{OnArc} $\to$ \texttt{ConsecutiveAttach} $\to$ \texttt{Avoids}), which is the layer B&M
assume when they speak of segments.  \textbf{!} \texttt{[DecidableEq V]} had to be added to the
signature, since \texttt{cycleIdx} needs it; every use site already had the instance.

informal_statement:
Ex 5.3.5(b): $\nu$ even, $\delta < \nu/2$, and a large edge count $\Rightarrow$ a perfect matching. An edge-count sufficient condition, in the spirit of Corollary 4.6 for
hamiltonicity.  The threshold is the edge count of the densest simple graph on
$\nu$ vertices with minimum degree $\delta$ that still violates Tutte's condition: a
$\delta$-set $S$ whose removal leaves too many odd components, plus as many edges as
can be packed around it.  Exceeding it leaves no room to violate Tutte.

Part (a) --- "characterise the maximal simple graphs which have no perfect
matching" --- has no propositional content and is dropped; the book's answer is
recorded in the dropped-items section at the end of this file.
formal_statement:
import Mathlib

open scoped Pointwise

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
theorem perfectMatching_of_card_edges_gt
    {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
    (hν : Even (Fintype.card V)) (hδ : 2 * G.minDegree < Fintype.card V)
    (hε : Nat.choose G.minDegree 2 + Nat.choose (Fintype.card V - 2 * G.minDegree - 1) 2
            + G.minDegree * (Fintype.card V - G.minDegree) < G.edgeFinset.card) :
    ∃ M : G.Subgraph, M.IsPerfectMatching := sorry
end SimpleGraph

informal_statement:
Definitions:
- An edge cut: a set of edges of $G$ whose deletion leaves $G$ disconnected. Rather than carry the book's $[S, \bar{S}]$ presentation, the definition is taken in
its \emph{operative} form --- a set of edges whose removal disconnects $G$:
\texttt{↑F $\subseteq$ G.edgeSet $\land$ $\lnot$ (G.deleteEdges ↑F).Connected}.

The two agree on what is minimised: every $[S, \bar{S}]$ disconnects $G$, and every
disconnecting edge set contains one (take $S$ a component of $G - F$).  Since
\texttt{edgeConnectivity} only ever asks for the \emph{minimum} size, the coarser form is
equivalent for all purposes in this chapter.
- Edge connectivity $\kappa'(G)$: the minimum size of an edge cut (\texttt{sInf $\emptyset$ = 0}). \texttt{$\kappa$' = sInf \{F.card | G.IsEdgeCut F\}}, with no $if$ guard: the book's special
case "$G$ trivial $\Rightarrow$ $\kappa' = 0$" is already delivered by \texttt{Nat.sInf $\emptyset$ = 0}, since a
trivial graph is connected and so admits no edge cut at all.  That convention is
used directly in \texttt{edgeConnectivity\_le\_minDegree}.

Statement: Ex 5.3.2: a $(k- 1)$-edge-connected $k$-regular graph with $\nu$ even has a perfect matching. Petersen's argument at general $k$.  For $S \subset V$ with odd components $G_{i}$ of
$G - S$ and $m_{i}$ the edges from $G_{i}$ to $S$: regularity gives
$m_{i} = k\nu(G_{i}) - 2\varepsilon(G_{i})$, of the same parity as $k\nu(G_{i})$.  Those edges form an edge
cut, so $(k-1)$-edge-connectivity gives $m_{i} \ge k - 1$, and parity upgrades that to
$m_{i} \ge k$ where needed.  Summing,
$k \cdot o(G - S) \le \sum m_{i} \le \sum_{v \in S} d(v) = k|S|$.

Corollary 5.4 is the case $k = 3$: a bridgeless cubic graph is 2-edge-connected.
formal_statement:
import Mathlib

open scoped Classical
open scoped Pointwise

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
def IsEdgeCut (G : SimpleGraph V) (F : Finset (Sym2 V)) : Prop :=
  (↑F : Set (Sym2 V)) ⊆ G.edgeSet ∧ ¬ (G.deleteEdges (↑F : Set (Sym2 V))).Connected
end SimpleGraph

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
noncomputable def edgeConnectivity (G : SimpleGraph V) : ℕ :=
  sInf {n : ℕ | ∃ F : Finset (Sym2 V), G.IsEdgeCut F ∧ F.card = n}
end SimpleGraph

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
theorem perfectMatching_of_edgeConnected_regular
    {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
    {k : ℕ} (hk : 0 < k) (hreg : G.IsRegularOfDegree k)
    (hconn : k - 1 ≤ G.edgeConnectivity) (hν : Even (Fintype.card V)) :
    ∃ M : G.Subgraph, M.IsPerfectMatching := sorry
end SimpleGraph
title: Ex 5.3.2: a $(k- 1)$-edge-connected $k$-regular graph with $\nu$ even has a perfect matching

Corollary 5.4 is the case $k = 3$: a bridgeless cubic graph is 2-edge-connected.

informal_statement:
Cor 5.4 (Petersen, 1891): every 3-regular graph without cut edges has a perfect matching. A double count per odd component, then Tutte.  The parity step is the crux:
$m_{i} = 3\nu(G_{i}) - 2\varepsilon(G_{i})$ is odd because $\nu(G_{i})$ is odd, and bridgelessness then
upgrades $m_{i} \ge 1$ to $m_{i} \ge 3$.

\textbf{!} The book's $\tfrac{1}{3} \sum m_{i} \le \tfrac{1}{3} \sum_{v \in S} d(v)$ is over $\mathbb{Q}$.  In $\mathbb{N}$ this should be
cleared to $3n \le \sum m_{i} \le 3|S|$ and divided only at the end, or done in $\mathbb{Z}$.

open scoped Pointwise

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
theorem petersen_three_regular_bridgeless
    {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
    (hreg : G.IsRegularOfDegree 3) (hbridge : ∀ e ∈ G.edgeSet, ¬ G.IsBridge e) :
    ∃ M : G.Subgraph, M.IsPerfectMatching := sorry
end SimpleGraph
title: Cor 5.4 (Petersen, 1891): every 3-regular graph without cut edges has a perfect matching
statement_informal:

upgrades $m_{i} \ge 1$ to $m_{i} \ge 3$.

informal_statement:
Definitions:
- An $m$-edge-colouring of $K_{n}$: a total function on unordered pairs. A total function \texttt{Sym2 (Fin n) $\to$ Fin m} --- colouring every pair, including the
diagonal, which is harmless since \texttt{IsRamseyBoundMulti} only inspects $s(u,v)$ for
$u \ne v$.

\textbf{!} \textbf{Not} Mathlib's \texttt{SimpleGraph.Coloring}, which colours \emph{vertices}.  Also not
chapter 6's \texttt{G.edgeSet $\to$ Fin k}, which is partial (defined only on actual edges);
here the host graph is $K_{n}$, so every pair is an edge and a total function is
right.

"One easily sees" that the two formulations agree for $m = 2$ --- but this file
\textbf{does not state that equivalence}, so \texttt{ramseyNumber} and \texttt{ramseyNumberMulti} at
$m = 2$ are formally unrelated.  Anything wanting to move between \S{}7.2's two
halves needs that bridge.
- \texttt{IsRamseyBoundMulti n c}: every $m$-edge-colouring of $K_{n}$ has, for some $i$, a set of $c i$\dots. Colour every pair of $n$ points with one of $m$ colours; once $n$ is large
enough, some colour $i$ covers all edges within some $k_{i}$ points.

The target sizes are a function \texttt{c : Fin m $\to$ $\mathbb{N}$} rather than a list, which makes
\texttt{Function.update c i (c i - 1)} the natural way to express "decrement the $i$-th
argument" in Theorem 7.7 below.
- The multicolour Ramsey number $r(k_{1},\dots,k_m)$. \textbf{!} Same \texttt{sInf $\emptyset$ = 0} trap as \texttt{ramseyNumber}, and \textbf{worse}: there is no
\texttt{exists\_isRamseyBoundMulti} anywhere in the file.  So every \texttt{ramseyNumberMulti}
is provably $0$ as things stand, which makes \texttt{ramseyMulti\_recursion},
\texttt{ramseyTriangle\_*} and Schur's theorem in \S{}7.4 all vacuous.

With $m = 2$ this should reduce to \texttt{ramseyNumber}, but that bridge is unstated
(see \texttt{EdgeColouring}).

$k_{1} = \dots = k_m = 3$ gives the sequence $r_{n}$ of exercise 7.2.3, which is what
Schur's theorem consumes in \S{}7.4.

Statement: ramseyMulti_le_multinomial. Iterating Theorem 7.7 gives exactly the multinomial recursion, as the two-colour
case gave binomials in Theorem 7.5.

With $m = 2$ this is Theorem 7.5, since $(k_{1}+k_{2})!/(k_{1}!k_{2}!) = C(k_{1}+k_{2}, k_{1})$.

\textbf{!} The division is exact but is $\mathbb{N}$ division in Lean; as with \texttt{card\_perfectMatching\_completeGraph}
in chapter 5, the proof should establish the \emph{multiplied} form
$r(\dots) * \prod k_{i}! \le (\sum k_{i})!$ and divide only at the end.
formal_statement:
import Mathlib

open scoped Finset

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
abbrev EdgeColouring (n m : ℕ) : Type := Sym2 (Fin n) → Fin m
end SimpleGraph

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
def IsRamseyBoundMulti {m : ℕ} (n : ℕ) (c : Fin m → ℕ) : Prop :=
  ∀ χ : EdgeColouring n m, ∃ i : Fin m, ∃ s : Finset (Fin n),
    #s = c i ∧ ∀ u ∈ s, ∀ v ∈ s, u ≠ v → χ s(u, v) = i
end SimpleGraph

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
noncomputable def ramseyNumberMulti {m : ℕ} (c : Fin m → ℕ) : ℕ :=
  sInf {n | IsRamseyBoundMulti n c}
end SimpleGraph

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
theorem ramseyMulti_le_multinomial {m : ℕ} (k : Fin m → ℕ) :
    ramseyNumberMulti (fun i => k i + 1) ≤ Nat.multinomial Finset.univ k := sorry
end SimpleGraph
title: ramseyMulti_le_multinomial
statement_informal:

\textbf{!} The division is exact but is $\mathbb{N}$ division in Lean; as with \texttt{card\_perfectMatching\_completeGraph}
in chapter 5, the proof should establish the \emph{multiplied} form
$r(\dots) * \prod k_{i}! \le (\sum k_{i})!$ and divide only at the end.

Statement: ramseyMulti_recursion. Generalises Theorem 7.4's recursion.  Fix $v$ in a large $K_{n}$ and classify the
other vertices by the colour of their edge to $v$.  If every colour class were
smaller than $r(\dots, k_{i}-1, \dots)$, the classes could not cover all vertices --- which is
exactly what the bound arranges.  Some class is then big enough for a
monochromatic complete subgraph, and $v$ extends it in colour $i$.

Stated additively ($+ m$ on the left, $+ 2$ on the right) to avoid the $\mathbb{N}$
subtraction $- m + 2$.

\textbf{!} \texttt{Function.update c i (c i - 1)} still has an inner $\mathbb{N}$ subtraction; $hc : \forall i, 2 \le c i$
keeps it from truncating.
formal_statement:
import Mathlib

open scoped Finset

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
abbrev EdgeColouring (n m : ℕ) : Type := Sym2 (Fin n) → Fin m
end SimpleGraph

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
def IsRamseyBoundMulti {m : ℕ} (n : ℕ) (c : Fin m → ℕ) : Prop :=
  ∀ χ : EdgeColouring n m, ∃ i : Fin m, ∃ s : Finset (Fin n),
    #s = c i ∧ ∀ u ∈ s, ∀ v ∈ s, u ≠ v → χ s(u, v) = i
end SimpleGraph

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
noncomputable def ramseyNumberMulti {m : ℕ} (c : Fin m → ℕ) : ℕ :=
  sInf {n | IsRamseyBoundMulti n c}
end SimpleGraph

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
theorem ramseyMulti_recursion {m : ℕ} (hm : 0 < m) (c : Fin m → ℕ) (hc : ∀ i, 2 ≤ c i) :
    ramseyNumberMulti c + m ≤
      (∑ i : Fin m, ramseyNumberMulti (Function.update c i (c i - 1))) + 2 := sorry
end SimpleGraph

definitions.title: An $m$-edge-colouring of $K_{n}$: a total function on unordered pairs
definitions.informal:
A total function \texttt{Sym2 (Fin n) $\to$ Fin m} --- colouring every pair, including the
diagonal, which is harmless since \texttt{IsRamseyBoundMulti} only inspects $s(u,v)$ for
$u \ne v$.

\textbf{!} \textbf{Not} Mathlib's \texttt{SimpleGraph.Coloring}, which colours \emph{vertices}.  Also not
chapter 6's \texttt{G.edgeSet $\to$ Fin k}, which is partial (defined only on actual edges);
here the host graph is $K_{n}$, so every pair is an edge and a total function is
right.

"One easily sees" that the two formulations agree for $m = 2$ --- but this file
\textbf{does not state that equivalence}, so \texttt{ramseyNumber} and \texttt{ramseyNumberMulti} at
$m = 2$ are formally unrelated.  Anything wanting to move between \S{}7.2's two
halves needs that bridge.

definitions.title: \texttt{IsRamseyBoundMulti n c}: every $m$-edge-colouring of $K_{n}$ has, for some $i$, a set of $c i$\dots
definitions.informal:
Colour every pair of $n$ points with one of $m$ colours; once $n$ is large
enough, some colour $i$ covers all edges within some $k_{i}$ points.

The target sizes are a function \texttt{c : Fin m $\to$ $\mathbb{N}$} rather than a list, which makes
\texttt{Function.update c i (c i - 1)} the natural way to express "decrement the $i$-th
argument" in Theorem 7.7 below.

definitions.title: The multicolour Ramsey number $r(k_{1},\dots,k_m)$
definitions.informal:
\textbf{!} Same \texttt{sInf $\emptyset$ = 0} trap as \texttt{ramseyNumber}, and \textbf{worse}: there is no
\texttt{exists\_isRamseyBoundMulti} anywhere in the file.  So every \texttt{ramseyNumberMulti}
is provably $0$ as things stand, which makes \texttt{ramseyMulti\_recursion},
\texttt{ramseyTriangle\_*} and Schur's theorem in \S{}7.4 all vacuous.

With $m = 2$ this should reduce to \texttt{ramseyNumber}, but that bridge is unstated
(see \texttt{EdgeColouring}).

$k_{1} = \dots = k_m = 3$ gives the sequence $r_{n}$ of exercise 7.2.3, which is what
Schur's theorem consumes in \S{}7.4.

informal_statement:
Definitions:
- \texttt{IsRamseyBound n k l}: every graph on $n$ vertices has a $k$-clique or an $l$-indep set.\dots. \texttt{IsRamseyBound n k l} says $n$ is already large enough for that conclusion:
\texttt{$\forall$ G : SimpleGraph (Fin n), ($\exists$ s, G.IsNClique k s) $\lor$ ($\exists$ t, G.IsNIndepSet l t)}.

Fixing the carrier as \texttt{Fin n} rather than quantifying over all $n$-element types
is what makes \texttt{ramseyNumber} an \texttt{sInf} over $\mathbb{N}$ below.

Total disorder is impossible: any sufficiently large graph contains one kind of
order or the other.
- The Ramsey number $r(k, l)$. The exact threshold at which order becomes unavoidable.

\textbf{!} \textbf{\texttt{sInf $\emptyset$ = 0} is a live trap} until \texttt{exists\_isRamseyBound} is proved: without
it every \texttt{ramseyNumber k l} could silently be $0$, and every theorem below would
be about the wrong number.  That existence result is therefore not optional
scaffolding --- it gates the meaning of the definition itself.

Statement: ramseyNumber_comm. Complementation swaps cliques and independent sets, so a graph with no $k$-clique
and no $l$-independent set becomes one with no $l$-clique and no $k$-independent
set.  The thresholds coincide.

Why the book's table is symmetric about its diagonal.

namespace SimpleGraph

namespace SimpleGraph

theorem ramseyNumber_comm (k l : ℕ) :
    SimpleGraph.ramseyNumber k l = SimpleGraph.ramseyNumber l k := sorry
end SimpleGraph

Statement: ramseyNumber_le_choose. $r(k, l) \le C(k + l - 2, k - 1)$.

Theorem 7.4's recursion is exactly Pascal's rule, so the Ramsey numbers are
dominated by binomial coefficients.  Setting $k = l$ gives roughly $r(k,k) \le 4^k$;
Theorem 7.6 gives $2^{k/2}$ below, and closing that gap is still open.

\textbf{!} Three $\mathbb{N}$ subtractions in the statement ($k + l - 2$, $k - 1$, and $m - 2$ in the
proof).  The Pascal step $C(m+n-3, m-1) + C(m+n-3, m-2) = C(m+n-2, m-1)$ is
\texttt{Nat.choose\_succ\_succ} only after the indices are massaged into \texttt{succ} form ---
budget for that.

suffices; and $l - 1$ does not, since $\bot$ on \texttt{Fin (l-1)} has no edge and no
$l$-element independent set.

title: ramseyNumber_two_left
statement_informal:

2-clique --- or there are none, and all $l$ vertices are independent.  So $l$
suffices; and $l - 1$ does not, since $\bot$ on \texttt{Fin (l-1)} has no edge and no
$l$-element independent set.

definitions.title: \texttt{IsRamseyBound n k l}: every graph on $n$ vertices has a $k$-clique or an $l$-indep set.\dots
definitions.informal:
\texttt{IsRamseyBound n k l} says $n$ is already large enough for that conclusion:
\texttt{$\forall$ G : SimpleGraph (Fin n), ($\exists$ s, G.IsNClique k s) $\lor$ ($\exists$ t, G.IsNIndepSet l t)}.

Fixing the carrier as \texttt{Fin n} rather than quantifying over all $n$-element types
is what makes \texttt{ramseyNumber} an \texttt{sInf} over $\mathbb{N}$ below.

Total disorder is impossible: any sufficiently large graph contains one kind of
order or the other.

it every \texttt{ramseyNumber k l} could silently be $0$, and every theorem below would
be about the wrong number.  That existence result is therefore not optional
scaffolding --- it gates the meaning of the definition itself.

informal_statement:
Definitions:
- An $m$-edge-colouring of $K_{n}$: a total function on unordered pairs. A total function \texttt{Sym2 (Fin n) $\to$ Fin m} --- colouring every pair, including the
diagonal, which is harmless since \texttt{IsRamseyBoundMulti} only inspects $s(u,v)$ for
$u \ne v$.

\textbf{!} \textbf{Not} Mathlib's \texttt{SimpleGraph.Coloring}, which colours \emph{vertices}.  Also not
chapter 6's \texttt{G.edgeSet $\to$ Fin k}, which is partial (defined only on actual edges);
here the host graph is $K_{n}$, so every pair is an edge and a total function is
right.

"One easily sees" that the two formulations agree for $m = 2$ --- but this file
\textbf{does not state that equivalence}, so \texttt{ramseyNumber} and \texttt{ramseyNumberMulti} at
$m = 2$ are formally unrelated.  Anything wanting to move between \S{}7.2's two
halves needs that bridge.
- \texttt{IsRamseyBoundMulti n c}: every $m$-edge-colouring of $K_{n}$ has, for some $i$, a set of $c i$\dots. Colour every pair of $n$ points with one of $m$ colours; once $n$ is large
enough, some colour $i$ covers all edges within some $k_{i}$ points.

The target sizes are a function \texttt{c : Fin m $\to$ $\mathbb{N}$} rather than a list, which makes
\texttt{Function.update c i (c i - 1)} the natural way to express "decrement the $i$-th
argument" in Theorem 7.7 below.
- The multicolour Ramsey number $r(k_{1},\dots,k_m)$. \textbf{!} Same \texttt{sInf $\emptyset$ = 0} trap as \texttt{ramseyNumber}, and \textbf{worse}: there is no
\texttt{exists\_isRamseyBoundMulti} anywhere in the file.  So every \texttt{ramseyNumberMulti}
is provably $0$ as things stand, which makes \texttt{ramseyMulti\_recursion},
\texttt{ramseyTriangle\_*} and Schur's theorem in \S{}7.4 all vacuous.

With $m = 2$ this should reduce to \texttt{ramseyNumber}, but that bridge is unstated
(see \texttt{EdgeColouring}).

$k_{1} = \dots = k_m = 3$ gives the sequence $r_{n}$ of exercise 7.2.3, which is what
Schur's theorem consumes in \S{}7.4.
- $r_{n} = r(3, \dots, 3)$ with $n$ colours. The least number of points such that any $n$-colouring of the pairs forces a
monochromatic \emph{triangle}.  $r_{2} = r(3,3) = 6$; Greenwood and Gleason showed
$r_{3} = 17$.

Exactly what Schur's theorem (\S{}7.4) consumes.

\textbf{!} Inherits \texttt{ramseyNumberMulti}'s missing existence lemma, so \texttt{ramseyTriangle n}
is currently provably $0$ for every $n$.

Statement: ramseyTriangle_le_factorial_exp. Unwinding $r_{n} \le n(r_{n-1} - 1) + 2$ from $r_{2} = 6$ and dividing by $n!$ gives a
telescoping sum of reciprocals $1/k!$, which converge to $e$.  Hence
$r_{n} - 1 \le n! e$.

$e$ appears precisely as $\sum 1/k!$.

import Mathlib

open scoped Finset

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
abbrev EdgeColouring (n m : ℕ) : Type := Sym2 (Fin n) → Fin m
end SimpleGraph

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
def IsRamseyBoundMulti {m : ℕ} (n : ℕ) (c : Fin m → ℕ) : Prop :=
  ∀ χ : EdgeColouring n m, ∃ i : Fin m, ∃ s : Finset (Fin n),
    #s = c i ∧ ∀ u ∈ s, ∀ v ∈ s, u ≠ v → χ s(u, v) = i
end SimpleGraph

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
noncomputable def ramseyNumberMulti {m : ℕ} (c : Fin m → ℕ) : ℕ :=
  sInf {n | IsRamseyBoundMulti n c}
end SimpleGraph

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
noncomputable def ramseyTriangle (n : ℕ) : ℕ := ramseyNumberMulti (fun _ : Fin n => 3)
end SimpleGraph

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
theorem ramseyTriangle_le_factorial_exp {n : ℕ} (hn : 2 ≤ n) :
    ramseyTriangle n ≤ ⌊(Nat.factorial n : ℝ) * Real.exp 1⌋₊ + 1 := sorry
end SimpleGraph

$e$ appears precisely as $\sum 1/k!$.
