title: ramseyTriangle_three_le
statement_informal:
ramseyTriangle_three_le. Part (a) at $n = 3$ with $r_{2} = 6$: $r_{3} \le 3(6-1) + 2 = 17$.  (Part (b) also gives
$\lfloor 6e\rfloor + 1 = 16 + 1 = 17$.)

So among any seventeen points, any 3-colouring of the pairs forces a
monochromatic triangle.

definitions.title: An $m$-edge-colouring of $K_{n}$: a total function on unordered pairs
definitions.informal:
A total function \texttt{Sym2 (Fin n) $\to$ Fin m} --- colouring every pair, including the
diagonal, which is harmless since \texttt{IsRamseyBoundMulti} only inspects $s(u,v)$ for
$u \ne v$.

\textbf{!} \textbf{Not} Mathlib's \texttt{SimpleGraph.Coloring}, which colours \emph{vertices}.  Also not
chapter 6's \texttt{G.edgeSet $\to$ Fin k}, which is partial (defined only on actual edges);
here the host graph is $K_{n}$, so every pair is an edge and a total function is
right.

"One easily sees" that the two formulations agree for $m = 2$ --- but this file
\textbf{does not state that equivalence}, so \texttt{ramseyNumber} and \texttt{ramseyNumberMulti} at
$m = 2$ are formally unrelated.  Anything wanting to move between \S{}7.2's two
halves needs that bridge.

definitions.title: \texttt{IsRamseyBoundMulti n c}: every $m$-edge-colouring of $K_{n}$ has, for some $i$, a set of $c i$\dots
definitions.informal:
Colour every pair of $n$ points with one of $m$ colours; once $n$ is large
enough, some colour $i$ covers all edges within some $k_{i}$ points.

The target sizes are a function \texttt{c : Fin m $\to$ $\mathbb{N}$} rather than a list, which makes
\texttt{Function.update c i (c i - 1)} the natural way to express "decrement the $i$-th
argument" in Theorem 7.7 below.

definitions.title: The multicolour Ramsey number $r(k_{1},\dots,k_m)$
definitions.informal:
\textbf{!} Same \texttt{sInf $\emptyset$ = 0} trap as \texttt{ramseyNumber}, and \textbf{worse}: there is no
\texttt{exists\_isRamseyBoundMulti} anywhere in the file.  So every \texttt{ramseyNumberMulti}
is provably $0$ as things stand, which makes \texttt{ramseyMulti\_recursion},
\texttt{ramseyTriangle\_*} and Schur's theorem in \S{}7.4 all vacuous.

With $m = 2$ this should reduce to \texttt{ramseyNumber}, but that bridge is unstated
(see \texttt{EdgeColouring}).

$k_{1} = \dots = k_m = 3$ gives the sequence $r_{n}$ of exercise 7.2.3, which is what
Schur's theorem consumes in \S{}7.4.

definitions.title: $r_{n} = r(3, \dots, 3)$ with $n$ colours
definitions.informal:
The least number of points such that any $n$-colouring of the pairs forces a
monochromatic \emph{triangle}.  $r_{2} = r(3,3) = 6$; Greenwood and Gleason showed
$r_{3} = 17$.

Exactly what Schur's theorem (\S{}7.4) consumes.

\textbf{!} Inherits \texttt{ramseyNumberMulti}'s missing existence lemma, so \texttt{ramseyTriangle n}
is currently provably $0$ for every $n$.

informal_statement:
Definitions:
- \texttt{IsRamseyBound n k l}: every graph on $n$ vertices has a $k$-clique or an $l$-indep set.\dots. \texttt{IsRamseyBound n k l} says $n$ is already large enough for that conclusion:
\texttt{$\forall$ G : SimpleGraph (Fin n), ($\exists$ s, G.IsNClique k s) $\lor$ ($\exists$ t, G.IsNIndepSet l t)}.

Fixing the carrier as \texttt{Fin n} rather than quantifying over all $n$-element types
is what makes \texttt{ramseyNumber} an \texttt{sInf} over $\mathbb{N}$ below.

Total disorder is impossible: any sufficiently large graph contains one kind of
order or the other.
- The Ramsey number $r(k, l)$. The exact threshold at which order becomes unavoidable.

\textbf{!} \textbf{\texttt{sInf $\emptyset$ = 0} is a live trap} until \texttt{exists\_isRamseyBound} is proved: without
it every \texttt{ramseyNumber k l} could silently be $0$, and every theorem below would
be about the wrong number.  That existence result is therefore not optional
scaffolding --- it gates the meaning of the definition itself.

Statement: ramsey_product_lower. Take $(k+1,k+1)$- and $(l+1,l+1)$-Ramsey graphs $G$, $H$ --- so $\omega, \alpha \le k$ and
$\le l$ respectively --- and form $G[H]$, which has the product vertex count.  Part
(a) gives $\alpha(G[H]) \le kl$; complementing gives $\omega(G[H]) \le kl$.  So $G[H]$ avoids
both a $(kl+1)$-clique and a $(kl+1)$-independent set.

Stated additively ($\dots + 1 \le r(\dots)$) to avoid $\mathbb{N}$ subtraction on the outside --- though
the two inner $- 1$s remain.

\textbf{!} The complement step needs $(G[H])^{c} \cong G^{c}[H^{c}]$, which is \textbf{true but not
obvious} and is not stated in this file.  Without it, part (a) bounds only $\alpha$
and the clique side has to be argued separately.

import Mathlib

open scoped Finset

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
def IsRamseyBound (n k l : ℕ) : Prop :=
  ∀ G : SimpleGraph (Fin n), (∃ s, G.IsNClique k s) ∨ (∃ t, G.IsNIndepSet l t)
end SimpleGraph

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
noncomputable def ramseyNumber (k l : ℕ) : ℕ :=
  sInf {n | SimpleGraph.IsRamseyBound n k l}
end SimpleGraph

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
theorem ramsey_product_lower {k l : ℕ} (hk : 1 ≤ k) (hl : 1 ≤ l) :
    (SimpleGraph.ramseyNumber (k + 1) (k + 1) - 1) * (SimpleGraph.ramseyNumber (l + 1) (l + 1) - 1)
      + 1 ≤ SimpleGraph.ramseyNumber (k * l + 1) (k * l + 1) := sorry
end SimpleGraph

Statement: ramsey_recursion_strict. The parity refinement that pins down $r(3,4) = 9$: $r(3,3) = 6$ and $r(2,4) = 4$
are both even, so $r(3,4) \le 6 + 4 - 1 = 9$.

\textbf{!} The book's "in particular, $v$ cannot be adjacent to precisely $r(k-1,l) - 1$
vertices" is the crux and compresses a parity computation: with both summands
even, $r(k-1,l) - 1$ is odd, so a vertex of even degree cannot have exactly that
degree.  That one configuration is precisely the one where neither (i) nor (ii)
holds, so ruling it out restores the case analysis.
formal_statement:

open scoped Finset

variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]

    (he₁ : Even (SimpleGraph.ramseyNumber k (l - 1)))
    (he₂ : Even (SimpleGraph.ramseyNumber (k - 1) l)) :
    SimpleGraph.ramseyNumber k l
      < SimpleGraph.ramseyNumber k (l - 1) + SimpleGraph.ramseyNumber (k - 1) l := sorry
end SimpleGraph

in $s$ witnesses reachability inside \texttt{G.induce s}.

      ∀ (hu : u ∈ s) (hv : v ∈ s), (G.induce s).Reachable ⟨u, hu⟩ ⟨v, hv⟩ := sorry

informal_statement:
Definitions:
- A $k$-factor: a $k$-regular spanning subgraph. Keep every vertex, and select edges so each vertex retains exactly $k$.  A
$1$-factor is precisely a perfect matching; a $2$-factor is a spanning union of
disjoint cycles.

Degree is written \texttt{(H.neighborSet v).ncard} rather than \texttt{H.degree v} --- equal in
value, but avoiding the \texttt{Fintype}/\texttt{DecidableRel} instance juggling that
\texttt{Subgraph.degree} would drag in on every use.
- $G$ is $k$-factorable: it decomposes into edge-disjoint $k$-factors. The edges of $G$ partition into groups, each a $k$-regular spanning subgraph.
The book's $G = H_{1} \cup \dots \cup H_n$ becomes $(\bigsqcup i, H i) = \top$ in the \texttt{Subgraph} lattice,
where $\top$ is $G$ viewed as a subgraph of itself.

Being $1$-factorable means the edges split into perfect matchings: $K_{n,n}$ and
$K_{2n}$ are (exercise 5.1.5(a)(i)), the Petersen graph is not
(exercise 5.1.5(a)(ii)).

$1$-factorability is exactly proper edge colouring with $\Delta$ colours: each factor
is a colour class.  So exercise 5.1.5(a)(ii) is the statement that the Petersen
graph has chromatic index $4$, which reappears in \texttt{EdgeColourings.lean}.

Statement: Ex 5.2.3(a): every $k$-regular bipartite graph ($k > 0$) is 1-factorable. Corollary 5.2 gives a perfect matching $M$.  Deleting its edges lowers every
degree by one, leaving a $(k-1)$-regular bipartite graph; iterate $k$ times.

In chapter 6's language this is $\chi'(G) = \Delta(G)$ for bipartite graphs --- K\"onig's
edge-colouring theorem.  In scheduling terms, a balanced workload always splits
into $k$ conflict-free rounds.
formal_statement:
import Mathlib

open scoped Pointwise

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
def Subgraph.IsKFactor {V : Type*} {G : SimpleGraph V} (H : G.Subgraph) (k : ℕ) : Prop :=
  H.IsSpanning ∧ ∀ v, (H.neighborSet v).ncard = k
end SimpleGraph

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
def IsKFactorable {V : Type*} (G : SimpleGraph V) (k : ℕ) : Prop :=
  ∃ (n : ℕ) (H : Fin n → G.Subgraph), (∀ i, (H i).IsKFactor k) ∧
    (∀ i j, i ≠ j → Disjoint (H i).edgeSet (H j).edgeSet) ∧
    (⨆ i, H i) = ⊤
end SimpleGraph

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
theorem regular_bipartite_one_factorable
    {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
    {X Y : Set V} (hbip : G.IsBipartiteWith X Y) {k : ℕ} (hk : 0 < k)
    (hreg : G.IsRegularOfDegree k) : G.IsKFactorable 1 := sorry
end SimpleGraph
title: Ex 5.2.3(a): every $k$-regular bipartite graph ($k > 0$) is 1-factorable

Statement: Ex 5.2.3(b)*: every $2k$-regular graph is 2-factorable (Petersen;. Every degree is even, so Theorem 4.1 gives each component an Euler tour.
Traverse it and orient each edge in the direction of travel; every vertex then

import Mathlib

open scoped Pointwise

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
def Subgraph.IsKFactor {V : Type*} {G : SimpleGraph V} (H : G.Subgraph) (k : ℕ) : Prop :=
  H.IsSpanning ∧ ∀ v, (H.neighborSet v).ncard = k
end SimpleGraph

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
def IsKFactorable {V : Type*} (G : SimpleGraph V) (k : ℕ) : Prop :=
  ∃ (n : ℕ) (H : Fin n → G.Subgraph), (∀ i, (H i).IsKFactor k) ∧
    (∀ i j, i ≠ j → Disjoint (H i).edgeSet (H j).edgeSet) ∧
    (⨆ i, H i) = ⊤
end SimpleGraph

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
theorem regular_two_factorable
    {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
    {k : ℕ} (hreg : G.IsRegularOfDegree (2 * k)) : G.IsKFactorable 2 := sorry
end SimpleGraph

$u \ne v$.

here the host graph is $K_{n}$, so every pair is an edge and a total function is
right.

\textbf{does not state that equivalence}, so \texttt{ramseyNumber} and \texttt{ramseyNumberMulti} at

argument" in Theorem 7.7 below.

$k_{1} = \dots = k_m = 3$ gives the sequence $r_{n}$ of exercise 7.2.3, which is what
Schur's theorem consumes in \S{}7.4.

Statement: schur. The classical bridge from Ramsey theory to additive number theory.  Schur's
original motivation was Fermat's Last Theorem mod $p$.

The book's motivating example (\S{}7.4, p. 120):

\textbf{!} Note "not necessarily distinct" --- so $x = y$ is allowed, and the Lean statement
correctly does not require distinctness.

\textbf{!} \texttt{hpart} says every $k \in [1, r_{n}]$ lies in exactly one part, and \texttt{hsub} that no

import Mathlib

open scoped Finset

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
abbrev EdgeColouring (n m : ℕ) : Type := Sym2 (Fin n) → Fin m
end SimpleGraph

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
def IsRamseyBoundMulti {m : ℕ} (n : ℕ) (c : Fin m → ℕ) : Prop :=
  ∀ χ : EdgeColouring n m, ∃ i : Fin m, ∃ s : Finset (Fin n),
    #s = c i ∧ ∀ u ∈ s, ∀ v ∈ s, u ≠ v → χ s(u, v) = i
end SimpleGraph

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
noncomputable def ramseyNumberMulti {m : ℕ} (c : Fin m → ℕ) : ℕ :=
  sInf {n | IsRamseyBoundMulti n c}
end SimpleGraph

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
noncomputable def ramseyTriangle (n : ℕ) : ℕ := ramseyNumberMulti (fun _ : Fin n => 3)
end SimpleGraph

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
theorem schur {n : ℕ} (hn : 1 ≤ n) (S : Fin n → Finset ℕ)
    (hpart : ∀ k ∈ Finset.Icc 1 (ramseyTriangle n), ∃! i, k ∈ S i)
    (hsub : ∀ i, S i ⊆ Finset.Icc 1 (ramseyTriangle n)) :
    ∃ i, ∃ x ∈ S i, ∃ y ∈ S i, ∃ z ∈ S i, x + y = z := sorry
end SimpleGraph

Definitions:
- The Schur number $s_{n}$. The exact threshold at which sum-free partitions become impossible.

\textbf{+} Unlike most \texttt{sInf}s in this chapter, nonemptiness here is supplied by \textbf{Theorem
7.10} ($s_{n} \le r_{n}$) --- so \texttt{schurNumber} is well defined as soon as Schur's theorem
is, without a separate existence lemma.

\textbf{!} But that inherits Theorem 7.10's own vacuity: while \texttt{ramseyTriangle n = 0},
Theorem 7.10 gives nothing and \texttt{schurNumber} falls back to \texttt{sInf $\emptyset$ = 0}.

Statement: schurNumber_lower_bound. Iterate $s_{n} \ge 3s_{n-1} - 1$ from $s_{3} = 14$; solving the linear recurrence gives
$s_{n} \ge (27\cdot 3^{n-3} + 1)/2$.

Cleared to $27\cdot 3^{n-3} + 1 \le 2s_{n}$.

Schur numbers grow at least exponentially with ratio $3$; the upper bound
$s_{n} \le r_{n} \le \lfloor n!e\rfloor + 1$ grows factorially, and the true rate is unknown.

informal_statement:
Definitions:
- \texttt{IsRamseyBound n k l}: every graph on $n$ vertices has a $k$-clique or an $l$-indep set.\dots. \texttt{IsRamseyBound n k l} says $n$ is already large enough for that conclusion:
\texttt{$\forall$ G : SimpleGraph (Fin n), ($\exists$ s, G.IsNClique k s) $\lor$ ($\exists$ t, G.IsNIndepSet l t)}.

Fixing the carrier as \texttt{Fin n} rather than quantifying over all $n$-element types
is what makes \texttt{ramseyNumber} an \texttt{sInf} over $\mathbb{N}$ below.

Total disorder is impossible: any sufficiently large graph contains one kind of
order or the other.
- The Ramsey number $r(k, l)$. The exact threshold at which order becomes unavoidable.

\textbf{!} \textbf{\texttt{sInf $\emptyset$ = 0} is a live trap} until \texttt{exists\_isRamseyBound} is proved: without
it every \texttt{ramseyNumber k l} could silently be $0$, and every theorem below would
be about the wrong number.  That existence result is therefore not optional
scaffolding --- it gates the meaning of the definition itself.

Statement: six_le_ramseyNumber_three_three. $C_{5}$ witnesses that five vertices do not force either structure, so the threshold
is $\ge 6$.  Combined with Thm 7.4 this is the exact value: among any six people,
three are mutual acquaintances or three mutual strangers.

\textbf{!} Only the \textbf{lower} bound is stated here; the file does not state $r(3,3) = 6$.
Same for $r(3,5)$ and $r(4,4)$ below --- all three exact values in the book's
worked examples are left unstated.
formal_statement:
import Mathlib

open scoped Finset

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
def IsRamseyBound (n k l : ℕ) : Prop :=
  ∀ G : SimpleGraph (Fin n), (∃ s, G.IsNClique k s) ∨ (∃ t, G.IsNIndepSet l t)
end SimpleGraph

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
noncomputable def ramseyNumber (k l : ℕ) : ℕ :=
  sInf {n | SimpleGraph.IsRamseyBound n k l}
end SimpleGraph

namespace SimpleGraph

statement_informal:
six_le_ramseyNumber_three_three. $C_{5}$ witnesses that five vertices do not force either structure, so the threshold

three are mutual acquaintances or three mutual strangers.

definitions.title: \texttt{IsRamseyBound n k l}: every graph on $n$ vertices has a $k$-clique or an $l$-indep set.\dots
definitions.informal:
\texttt{IsRamseyBound n k l} says $n$ is already large enough for that conclusion:
\texttt{$\forall$ G : SimpleGraph (Fin n), ($\exists$ s, G.IsNClique k s) $\lor$ ($\exists$ t, G.IsNIndepSet l t)}.

Fixing the carrier as \texttt{Fin n} rather than quantifying over all $n$-element types
is what makes \texttt{ramseyNumber} an \texttt{sInf} over $\mathbb{N}$ below.

Total disorder is impossible: any sufficiently large graph contains one kind of
order or the other.

definitions.title: The Ramsey number $r(k, l)$
definitions.informal:
The exact threshold at which order becomes unavoidable.

\textbf{!} \textbf{\texttt{sInf $\emptyset$ = 0} is a live trap} until \texttt{exists\_isRamseyBound} is proved: without

\textbf{fundamental cycle} of $e$ with respect to $T$.  \textbf{*} The engine of the exchange
argument for Kruskal's optimality (theorem 2.10), and of chapter 12's tree-basis of the
cycle space.

Lean holds only up to rotation and reflection of the walk, which is awkward to phrase
directly.  Chapter 12's \texttt{fundamentalCycle} needs the uniqueness half, so this gap
propagates there.

informal_statement:
Definitions:
- A walk is internally disjoint from a subgraph $H$: no \emph{internal} vertex lies in $H$. The walk may start and end on $H$, but between those endpoints it
must stay entirely outside $H$.  This is what makes the bridge relation an
equivalence, and it is why a bridge is a maximal chunk of the graph hanging off
$H$ and touching it only at its attachment points.

\texttt{p.support.tail.dropLast} is the walk's interior --- drop the
first vertex (\texttt{tail}) and the last (\texttt{dropLast}).  \textbf{!} This is \textbf{not} the repo's
\texttt{InternallyDisjoint} (\texttt{TwoConnected.lean:58}), which relates a walk to another
\emph{walk}; here the second argument is a \texttt{Subgraph}.  A walk of length $\le 1$ has empty
interior and so is vacuously internally disjoint from everything --- which is
intended, and is what makes \texttt{bridgeRel} reflexive on single edges.
- A longest cycle. A cycle no shorter than any other cycle of $G$.  This is the standard
extremal device: assume the longest cycle is not a Hamilton cycle, then derive a
contradiction from the structure of the bridges hanging off it.  That is exactly how
Chv\'atal--Erd\H{o}s is proved below.

\textbf{!} Not \texttt{girth}/\texttt{egirth}, which are the \emph{shortest} cycle --- the
opposite extremum.  The maximality clause quantifies over cycles at \emph{every} base
point $w$, not just at $u$, which is what makes it a genuine global maximum.  Note
the definition does not assert existence: \texttt{IsLongestCycle} is a hypothesis to be
supplied, and producing one requires knowing $G$ has a cycle at all.
- B&M's relation $~$ on $E(G) \ E(H)$: $e_{1} ~ e_{2}$ iff joined by a walk internally disjoint from $H$\dots. Two edges outside $H$ are related when you can travel from one to the
other without passing through $H$.  Grouping edges into classes carves
$G - E(H)$ into the pieces that hang off $H$ --- those pieces are the bridges.

\texttt{Relation.EqvGen} wraps the book's raw condition in its
reflexive--symmetric--transitive closure, which \emph{discharges} the book's "it is easy
to verify" rather than proving it: whatever the raw relation does, the closure is
an equivalence by construction.  This is a deliberate trade --- the file gains an
equivalence for free, at the cost that \texttt{bridgeRel} is a priori coarser than $\sim$.
It is not actually coarser (the book's $\sim$ really is an equivalence), but nothing
here proves that, so do not appeal to "\texttt{bridgeRel e f} gives a single connecting
walk" --- it gives a \emph{chain} of them.  Several skeletons below rely on this
distinction.
- The bridge of $H$ in $G$ containing the edge $e$: the subgraph induced by $e$'s $~$-class. A bridge is one of the connected pieces remaining when $H$ is
removed, together with the attachment points where it touches $H$.  The three
"immediate" facts quoted above are \texttt{bridgeOf\_connected},
\texttt{exists\_path\_internallyDisjoint} and \texttt{bridge\_inter\_subset\_cycle} below --- none of
them is actually immediate once $\sim$ is a closure.  In planar graph theory bridges
carry the argument: theorem 9.8 says inner bridges of a cycle avoid one another,
theorem 9.9 that a bridge avoiding every outer bridge is transferable, and together
these drive Kuratowski's theorem 9.10.

Indexed by a \emph{representative edge} $e$ rather than by a class,
so "the bridge containing $e$"; two edges give the same bridge exactly when
\texttt{bridgeRel H e f}.  Built with \texttt{Subgraph.mk} directly --- \textbf{not} with
\texttt{SimpleGraph.toSubgraph} (\texttt{Subgraph.lean:559}), which is \emph{spanning} and would put
every vertex of $G$ into every bridge.  Note \texttt{verts} is the union of the class's
edges, so it automatically includes the attachment points.

\textbf{!} Because \texttt{bridgeRel} is reflexive for \emph{any} $e$ (it is an \texttt{EqvGen}), \texttt{bridgeOf H e}
is nonempty even for an $e$ that is not an edge of $G$ at all --- it then has two
vertices and no edges.  Statements about bridges must therefore carry
\texttt{e $\in$ G.edgeSet \textbackslash\{\} H.edgeSet} explicitly.  Two of them below originally omitted it and
were false as a result; both now carry it (see the module header).
- Vertices of attachment of the bridge of $e$ to the cycle traced by $c$: $V(B) \cap V(C)$. The points at which the bridge touches down onto the cycle.  Almost
everything in \S{}9.4 is a statement about how two bridges' attachment sets interleave
around $C$ --- \texttt{Overlaps}, \texttt{Skew} and the segments below are all built on this one
set.

Specialised to \texttt{H = c.toSubgraph} for a closed walk $c$, since
\S{}9.4 only ever needs bridges of a \emph{cycle}.  A \texttt{Set V}, not a \texttt{Finset}, so that
\texttt{.ncard} is used for $k$ (see theorem 9.6's conclusion).  "$B$ is a $k$-bridge"
is spelled \texttt{(G.attach c e).ncard = k}, and "$B$ and $B'$ are equivalent" is
\texttt{G.attach c e = G.attach c e'}.

Statement: succ_attachments_not_adj. The successors of a bridge's attachment points form an *independent
set*.  That is exactly the leverage Chv\'atal--Erd\H{o}s needs: a bridge with many
attachments yields a large independent set, which $\alpha \le \kappa$ forbids.

Indices are into the walk (\texttt{c.getVert i}), so $i + 1$ is the
successor along $c$; the wraparound at the end of the support is handled by
\texttt{getVert} saturating, which is why step 3 must be phrased as two explicit arcs
rather than as index arithmetic mod $n$.
formal_statement:
import Mathlib

open scoped Classical

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
def Walk.InternallyDisjointFrom {V : Type*} {G : SimpleGraph V}
    (H : G.Subgraph) {u v : V} (p : G.Walk u v) : Prop :=
  ∀ x ∈ p.support.tail.dropLast, x ∉ H.verts
end SimpleGraph

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
def Walk.IsLongestCycle {V : Type*} {G : SimpleGraph V} {u : V}
    (c : G.Walk u u) : Prop :=
  c.IsCycle ∧ ∀ (w : V) (c' : G.Walk w w), c'.IsCycle → c'.length ≤ c.length
end SimpleGraph

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
def bridgeRel {V : Type*} (G : SimpleGraph V) (H : G.Subgraph) :
    Sym2 V → Sym2 V → Prop :=
  Relation.EqvGen fun e₁ e₂ =>
    e₁ ∈ G.edgeSet \ H.edgeSet ∧ e₂ ∈ G.edgeSet \ H.edgeSet ∧
    ∃ (u v : V) (p : G.Walk u v), p.InternallyDisjointFrom H ∧
      p.edges.head? = some e₁ ∧ p.edges.getLast? = some e₂
end SimpleGraph

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
def bridgeOf {V : Type*} (G : SimpleGraph V) (H : G.Subgraph) (e : Sym2 V) :
    G.Subgraph where
  verts := {x | ∃ f, G.bridgeRel H e f ∧ x ∈ f}
  Adj u v := G.Adj u v ∧ G.bridgeRel H e s(u, v)
  adj_sub h := h.1
  edge_vert h := ⟨_, h.2, Sym2.mem_mk_left _ _⟩
  symm u v h := ⟨h.1.symm, by rw [Sym2.eq_swap]; exact h.2⟩
end SimpleGraph

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
def attach {V : Type*} (G : SimpleGraph V) {u : V} (c : G.Walk u u) (e : Sym2 V) : Set V :=
  (G.bridgeOf c.toSubgraph e).verts ∩ c.toSubgraph.verts
end SimpleGraph

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
theorem succ_attachments_not_adj
    {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] {G : SimpleGraph V} (hconn : G.Connected)
    {u : V} {c : G.Walk u u} (hc : c.IsLongestCycle) {e : Sym2 V}
    (he : e ∈ G.edgeSet \ c.toSubgraph.edgeSet)
    (hoff : ((G.bridgeOf c.toSubgraph e).verts \ c.toSubgraph.verts).Nonempty) {i j : ℕ}
    (hi : c.getVert i ∈ G.attach c e) (hj : c.getVert j ∈ G.attach c e)
    (hij : c.getVert i ≠ c.getVert j) :
    ¬ G.Adj (c.getVert (i + 1)) (c.getVert (j + 1)) := sorry
end SimpleGraph

successor along $c$; the wraparound at the end of the support is handled by
\texttt{getVert} saturating, which is why step 3 must be phrased as two explicit arcs
rather than as index arithmetic mod $n$.

informal_statement:
szekeres_wilf. $D$ is the \textbf{degeneracy} of $G$.  Strip off a vertex of degree at
most $D$, repeatedly, recording the order; then colour the vertices back in reverse
order --- when a vertex is restored it has at most $D$ neighbours already present, so
one of $D + 1$ colours is free.  This refines $\chi \le \Delta + 1$ (corollary 8.1.2), since
$D \le \Delta$ always and often $D$ is far smaller: a tree has $D = 1$, giving $\chi \le 2$ no
matter how large $\Delta$ is.

"Induced subgraph" is indexed by \texttt{Finset V} (a vertex subset)
rather than by a \texttt{Subgraph}, since the book's maximum is over \emph{induced} subgraphs
only.  The \texttt{sup} includes $s = \emptyset$, whose \texttt{minDegree} is $0$ by Mathlib's
convention; this can only make $D$ larger and so weakens the bound harmlessly.
Note the induction in step 2 is the formal content of "repeatedly strip off" --- as
usual, the informal repetition becomes an induction on the size of what remains.
formal_statement:
import Mathlib

open scoped Classical

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
theorem szekeres_wilf {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V)
    [DecidableRel G.Adj] :
    G.chromaticNumber ≤ 1 + (Finset.univ.sup fun s : Finset V =>
      (G.induce (s : Set V)).minDegree) := sorry
end SimpleGraph

Reusable helper (\textbf{!} absent from Mathlib): $\top$ on $\ge$ 3 vertices is hamiltonian. In $K_{n}$ every pair of distinct vertices is adjacent, so any enumeration
$v_{1} v_{2} \dots v_n v_{1}$ is already a Hamilton cycle.  Three vertices are needed because
a cycle must have length at least three --- $K_{1}$ and $K_{2}$ have no cycle at all.

\textbf{!} Despite the book calling it "trivial", \textbf{Mathlib has no such lemma}, and it is
not trivial in Lean: it requires exhibiting a concrete cyclic enumeration of $V$
and proving the resulting walk is a cycle whose support is nodup and spans.

Build the embedding greedily.  A tree on $m$ vertices can be listed so each new
vertex attaches to exactly one already-placed vertex (peel leaves).  Placing the
$j$-th, its unique placed neighbour has $\ge m - 1$ neighbours in $G$, of which at
most $j - 1 \le m - 2$ are used --- a fresh image always exists.

The standard "minimum degree forces every small tree" lemma; it is what makes
tree-target Ramsey numbers exactly computable.

\textbf{!} $m$ is a free variable in the signature, tied to $W$ only through
\texttt{hm : Fintype.card W = m} --- so $m$ is determined but Lean will not infer it;
callers must supply it.
formal_statement:
import Mathlib

open scoped Finset

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
theorem tree_isContained_of_minDegree_le
    {V W : Type*} [Fintype V] [Fintype W] {G : SimpleGraph V} [DecidableRel G.Adj]
    {T : SimpleGraph W} (hT : T.IsTree) (hm : Fintype.card W = m)
    (hδ : m - 1 ≤ G.minDegree) :
    T ⊑ G := sorry
end SimpleGraph

informal_statement:
Definitions:
- $v$ is a cut vertex: $G$ is connected but deleting $v$ disconnects it. A \texttt{SimpleGraph} is loopless by construction, so the second (component-counting)
characterisation is the usable one and is what is taken as the definition here.
Specialising it to a \emph{connected} $G$ --- where $\omega(G) = 1$ --- turns
$\omega(G - v) > \omega(G)$ into "$G - v$ is disconnected", giving
\texttt{G.Connected $\land$ $\lnot$ (G.induce \{v\}$^{c}$).Connected}.

Folding \texttt{G.Connected} into the definition is what makes \texttt{IsBlock} below read as
the book's "connected graph that has no cut vertices".

Statement: tree_isCutVertex_iff_degree. In a tree the cut vertices are exactly the internal (non-leaf) vertices.

\textbf{!} Step 2's exercise 2.1.5 is the one real import; Mathlib's
\texttt{IsAcyclic} API may supply it more directly than reproving the book's route.
formal_statement:
import Mathlib

open scoped Classical

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
def IsCutVertex (G : SimpleGraph V) (v : V) : Prop :=
  G.Connected ∧ ¬ (G.induce ({v}ᶜ : Set V)).Connected
end SimpleGraph

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
theorem tree_isCutVertex_iff_degree (hG : G.IsTree) (v : V) :
    G.IsCutVertex v ↔ 1 < G.degree v := sorry
end SimpleGraph
title: tree_isCutVertex_iff_degree
statement_informal:
tree_isCutVertex_iff_degree. In a tree the cut vertices are exactly the internal (non-leaf) vertices.

informal_statement:
tree_two_leaves. A degree-one vertex of a tree is a \textbf{leaf}.  \textbf{!} B&M offer a more
illuminating alternative (exercise 2.1.2): take a longest path; both endpoints have
degree one, since an extra neighbour would either extend the path or close a cycle.
That route would be shorter in Lean too, if \texttt{exists\_path\_length\_of\_minDegree}-style
machinery from chapter 1 were available.
formal_statement:
import Mathlib

open scoped Classical

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
theorem tree_two_leaves (hG : G.IsTree) [Nontrivial V] :
    ∃ u v : V, u ≠ v ∧ G.degree u = 1 ∧ G.degree v = 1 := sorry
end SimpleGraph

informal_statement:
tree_unique_path. A tree has exactly enough edges to hold the vertices together and not one
more: connectivity gives at least one route between any two vertices, acyclicity
forbids a second, since two distinct routes always enclose a cycle.  \textbf{!} The converse
holds for loopless graphs (exercise 2.1.1), so "unique paths between all pairs" is an
equivalent definition of a tree --- that direction is not stated here.
formal_statement:
import Mathlib

open scoped Classical

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
theorem tree_unique_path (hG : G.IsTree) (u v : V) :
    ∃! p : G.Walk u v, p.IsPath := sorry
end SimpleGraph
title: tree_unique_path
statement_informal:

equivalent definition of a tree --- that direction is not stated here.

informal_statement:
triangle_of_card_edgeFinset_gt. Tur\'an at $m = 2$ --- Mantel's 1907 case, half a century before the
generalisation.  Extremal example: balanced $K_{\lfloor\nu/2\rfloor,\lceil\nu/2\rceil}$ with $\lfloor\nu^{2}/4\rfloor$
edges.

    {V : Type*} [Fintype V] {G : SimpleGraph V} [DecidableRel G.Adj]

informal_statement:
triangle_of_not_bipartite_of_card_edgeFinset_gt. Forbidding bipartiteness on top of triangle-freeness drops the cap from $\nu^{2}/4$ to
$(\nu-1)^{2}/4 + 1$.  A triangle-free non-bipartite graph contains an odd cycle of
length $\ge 5$, which is an inefficient use of vertices; the densest such graph is
essentially $C_{5}$ blown up.

The \textbf{stability} phenomenon of extremal graph theory: near-extremal graphs all
resemble the extremal one, so departing from it costs edges.

Cleared to $(\nu-1)^{2} + 4 < 4\varepsilon$.

    (h : (Fintype.card V - 1) ^ 2 + 4 < 4 * #G.edgeFinset) :
    ¬ G.CliqueFree 3 := sorry

informal_statement:
Thm 5.4 (Tutte): $G$ has a perfect matching iff $o(G - S) \le |S|$ for all $S$. The obstruction to a perfect matching is a set $S$ whose removal leaves more odd
pieces than $S$ has vertices --- each odd piece must "export" a vertex to be
matched into $S$.
formal_statement:
import Mathlib

open scoped Pointwise

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
theorem tutte_perfect_matching {V : Type*} [Finite V] (G : SimpleGraph V) :
    (∃ M : G.Subgraph, M.IsPerfectMatching) ↔
      ∀ S : Set V, ((⊤ : G.Subgraph).deleteVerts S).coe.oddComponents.ncard ≤ S.ncard := sorry
end SimpleGraph
title: Thm 5.4 (Tutte): $G$ has a perfect matching iff $o(G - S) \le |S|$ for all $S$
statement_informal:
Thm 5.4 (Tutte): $G$ has a perfect matching iff $o(G - S) \le |S|$ for all $S$. The obstruction to a perfect matching is a set $S$ whose removal leaves more odd
pieces than $S$ has vertices --- each odd piece must "export" a vertex to be
matched into $S$.

informal_statement:
Definitions:
- Two $u$--$v$ walks are internally disjoint if they share no internal vertex. Specialised to a family of \emph{two} $u$--$v$ walks.  "$x$ is an internal vertex of
$p$" is \texttt{x $\in$ p.support $\land$ x $\ne$ u $\land$ x $\ne$ v}, so "no $x$ is internal to both" becomes

    $\forall$ x, x $\in$ p.support $\to$ x $\in$ q.support $\to$ x = u $\lor$ x = v.

\textbf{!} Note this does \textbf{not} forbid $p = q$.  For adjacent $u, v$ the single edge
satisfies it with $p = q$, its only vertices being the two endpoints.  Theorem
3.2 as stated therefore cannot yield a cycle, which is why Corollary 3.2.1 is
derived from the edge-disjointness-carrying strengthening
\texttt{exists\_two\_internally\_disjoint\_paths\_of\_two\_connected} rather than from
\texttt{two\_connected\_iff\_two\_internally\_disjoint\_paths} directly.
- A vertex cut: a proper subset $S$ whose deletion leaves $G$ disconnected. $V'$ is a \texttt{Finset V}, and "$G - V'$ is disconnected" is
\texttt{$\lnot$ (G.induce (↑S)$^{c}$).Connected}.  The conjunct \texttt{↑S $\subset$ Set.univ} records that a
vertex cut is a \emph{proper} subset: without it $S = V$ would qualify vacuously,
since Mathlib's \texttt{Connected} is false on the empty induced graph.

A $k$-vertex cut is the pair \texttt{G.IsVertexCut S $\land$ S.card = k}; that is exactly
what \texttt{vertexConnectivity} minimises over.
- Vertex connectivity $\kappa(G)$. The book's case split is on "$G$ has a pair of distinct nonadjacent vertices";
the Lean split is on the equivalent "$G$ has a vertex cut at all", which is the
condition the two branches actually need.  So
\item some cut exists $\Rightarrow$ \texttt{$\kappa$ = sInf \{S.card | G.IsVertexCut S\}};
\item no cut exists (the complete graphs) $\Rightarrow$ $\kappa = \nu - 1$.

\texttt{sInf} on $\mathbb{N}$ is Mathlib's \texttt{Nat.sInf}, with \texttt{sInf $\emptyset$ = 0}; the $if$ guard means
that fallback is never reached here.  Natural subtraction makes $\nu - 1 = 0$
when $V$ is empty, matching "trivial $\Rightarrow$ $\kappa = 0$".

Statement: two_connected_iff_two_internally_disjoint_paths. (Whitney, 1932).

($\Rightarrow$) is discharged by forgetting the extra edge-disjointness conjunct supplied by
the strengthened form.

($\Leftarrow$) unpacks the book's "clearly".  Two steps:
\item $G$ is connected --- the hypothesis hands back a path between any two distinct
  vertices, and \texttt{Reachable.refl} covers $a = b$;
\item $G$ has no cut vertex --- if $w$ were one, $G - w$ would be disconnected, giving
  $a, b$ unreachable in $G - w$.  Both supplied paths $p, q$ must then pass
  through $w$ (else \texttt{reachable\_induce\_of\_support\_subset} would transport them
  into $G - w$).  So $w$ is a common internal vertex of $p$ and $q$, and
  \texttt{InternallyDisjoint} forces $w = a$ or $w = b$ --- contradicting that $a, b$
  live in ${w}^{c}$.
Then \texttt{two\_le\_vertexConnectivity\_of\_no\_cutVertex} converts "no cut vertex" into
$\kappa \ge 2$, which is where $\nu \ge 3$ is consumed.
formal_statement:
import Mathlib

open scoped Classical

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
def InternallyDisjoint {u v : V} (p q : G.Walk u v) : Prop :=
  ∀ x : V, x ∈ p.support → x ∈ q.support → x = u ∨ x = v
end SimpleGraph

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
def IsVertexCut (G : SimpleGraph V) (S : Finset V) : Prop :=
  (↑S : Set V) ⊂ Set.univ ∧ ¬ (G.induce ((↑S : Set V)ᶜ)).Connected
end SimpleGraph

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
noncomputable def vertexConnectivity (G : SimpleGraph V) : ℕ :=
  if ∃ S : Finset V, G.IsVertexCut S then
    sInf {n : ℕ | ∃ S : Finset V, G.IsVertexCut S ∧ S.card = n}
  else
    Fintype.card V - 1
end SimpleGraph

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
theorem two_connected_iff_two_internally_disjoint_paths
    (h : 3 ≤ Fintype.card V) :
    2 ≤ G.vertexConnectivity ↔
      ∀ u v : V, u ≠ v → ∃ p q : G.Walk u v,
        p.IsPath ∧ q.IsPath ∧ G.InternallyDisjoint p q := sorry
end SimpleGraph

\item $G$ has no cut vertex --- if $w$ were one, $G - w$ would be disconnected, giving

Statement: two_connected_vertices_on_common_cycle. Travel out along one path and back along the other; because the two paths meet
only at the endpoints, the round trip repeats no vertex, so it is a cycle.

\textbf{!} The book's "immediately" does \textbf{not} transfer directly.  As noted on
\texttt{InternallyDisjoint}, this file's predicate permits $p = q$, so
\texttt{two\_connected\_iff\_two\_internally\_disjoint\_paths} alone would let both paths be
the same single edge and \texttt{p.append q.reverse} would not be a cycle.  The proof
must therefore go through the strengthened

\texttt{p.edges.Disjoint q.edges} rules that degenerate case out.

informal_statement:
Definitions:
- An edge cut: a set of edges of $G$ whose deletion leaves $G$ disconnected. Rather than carry the book's $[S, \bar{S}]$ presentation, the definition is taken in
its \emph{operative} form --- a set of edges whose removal disconnects $G$:
\texttt{↑F $\subseteq$ G.edgeSet $\land$ $\lnot$ (G.deleteEdges ↑F).Connected}.

The two agree on what is minimised: every $[S, \bar{S}]$ disconnects $G$, and every
disconnecting edge set contains one (take $S$ a component of $G - F$).  Since
\texttt{edgeConnectivity} only ever asks for the \emph{minimum} size, the coarser form is
equivalent for all purposes in this chapter.

Definitions:

independent sets are exactly complementary.

\textbf{!} Duplicated from \texttt{Matchings.lean}, textually identical.  Neither file imports the
other; see \texttt{log/graphtheory-ISSUES.md} \S{}F.
- The covering number $\beta(G)$. The fewest vertices touching every edge.  $\alpha$ is Mathlib's \texttt{indepNum}; only $\beta$
needs defining here.

Statement: two_mul_coveringNumber_le. Stated as $2\beta \le \varepsilon + 1$ to avoid division.

A minimum covering touches every edge, and in a connected graph the edges are
linked tightly enough that each covering vertex can be charged at least two
edges, with one left over for a spanning tree's root.

but part (b) does \textbf{not} assume $\beta$-criticality, only connectivity, and the Lean
signature correctly reflects that.  (The docstring previously implied the
$\beta$-critical hypothesis carried over; it does not.)

violates the bound for $k \ge 2$.

open scoped Finset

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
noncomputable def coveringNumber {V : Type*} (G : SimpleGraph V) : ℕ :=
  sInf {n | ∃ K : Set V, G.IsCovering K ∧ K.ncard = n}
end SimpleGraph

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
theorem two_mul_coveringNumber_le
    {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] {G : SimpleGraph V} [DecidableRel G.Adj]
    (hconn : G.Connected) :
    2 * G.coveringNumber ≤ #G.edgeFinset + 1 := sorry
end SimpleGraph

Statement: vertexConnectivity_eq_minDegree_of_delta_ge. a simple graph with $\delta \ge \nu - 2$ has $\kappa = \delta$.

The hypothesis says every vertex is non-adjacent to at most one other vertex, so
the graph is complete or very nearly so.  Theorem 3.1 already gives $\kappa \le \delta$, so

adjacent outright or share a common surviving neighbour.

allows $\kappa < \delta$.

informal_statement:
welsh_powell. Colour greedily in order of decreasing degree.  When the $i$-th
vertex's turn comes, two things bound the colours forbidden to it: it has $d_{i}$
neighbours, so at most $d_{i}$ colours are blocked; and only $i - 1$ vertices are
coloured so far, so at most $i - 1$ colours exist.  Hence \texttt{min\{d$_{i}$ + 1, i\}} colours
suffice at step $i$, and the worst case over $i$ bounds $\chi$.  This genuinely
improves $\chi \le \Delta + 1$ (corollary 8.1.2): high-degree vertices are handled while few
colours exist, low-degree ones later when the count $i$ no longer binds.
Exercise 8.1.4 derives two further bounds from it.

The sorted degree sequence is presented as an equivalence
\texttt{$\sigma$ : Fin (card V) $\simeq$ V} together with $h\sigma$, which says \texttt{i $\mapsto$ deg ($\sigma$ i)} is antitone ---
i.e. $\sigma$ enumerates the vertices in nonincreasing degree order, so
\texttt{G.degree ($\sigma$ i)} \emph{is} the book's $d_{i}$.  $i + 1$ rather than $i$ because \texttt{Fin} is
0-indexed and the book is 1-indexed.

Worth knowing while filling: \textbf{$h\sigma$ is not needed for the proof}, only for the
statement.  Steps 1--4 bound $\chi$ by that \texttt{sup} for \emph{any} enumeration $\sigma$; what $h\sigma$
buys is that the \texttt{sup} is then the book's \texttt{max$_{i}$ min\{d$_{i}$ + 1, i\}} for the sorted
sequence, which is the small quantity worth having.  So do not go looking for a
place to use $h\sigma$ --- there isn't one.

import Mathlib

open scoped Classical

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
theorem welsh_powell {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
    (σ : Fin (Fintype.card V) ≃ V) (hσ : Antitone fun i => G.degree (σ i)) :
    G.chromaticNumber ≤ (Finset.univ.sup fun i : Fin (Fintype.card V) =>
      min (G.degree (σ i) + 1) (i + 1)) := sorry
end SimpleGraph

Definitions:
- An edge cut: a set of edges of $G$ whose deletion leaves $G$ disconnected. Rather than carry the book's $[S, \bar{S}]$ presentation, the definition is taken in
its \emph{operative} form --- a set of edges whose removal disconnects $G$:

disconnecting edge set contains one (take $S$ a component of $G - F$).  Since

equivalent for all purposes in this chapter.

vertex cut is a \emph{proper} subset: without it $S = V$ would qualify vacuously,
since Mathlib's \texttt{Connected} is false on the empty induced graph.

A $k$-vertex cut is the pair \texttt{G.IsVertexCut S $\land$ S.card = k}; that is exactly
what \texttt{vertexConnectivity} minimises over.
- Edge connectivity $\kappa'(G)$: the minimum size of an edge cut (\texttt{sInf $\emptyset$ = 0}). \texttt{$\kappa$' = sInf \{F.card | G.IsEdgeCut F\}}, with no $if$ guard: the book's special
case "$G$ trivial $\Rightarrow$ $\kappa' = 0$" is already delivered by \texttt{Nat.sInf $\emptyset$ = 0}, since a

used directly in \texttt{edgeConnectivity\_le\_minDegree}.

\item some cut exists $\Rightarrow$ \texttt{$\kappa$ = sInf \{S.card | G.IsVertexCut S\}};

Statement: whitney_inequalities. (Whitney).  The full chain $\kappa \le \kappa' \le \delta$.

The conjunction of the two halves proved just above, packaged as the book states
it.  See \texttt{vertexConnectivity\_le\_edgeConnectivity} for the $\kappa \le \kappa'$ proof and
\texttt{edgeConnectivity\_le\_minDegree} for $\kappa' \le \delta$.
formal_statement:
import Mathlib

open scoped Classical

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
def IsEdgeCut (G : SimpleGraph V) (F : Finset (Sym2 V)) : Prop :=
  (↑F : Set (Sym2 V)) ⊆ G.edgeSet ∧ ¬ (G.deleteEdges (↑F : Set (Sym2 V))).Connected
end SimpleGraph

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
def IsVertexCut (G : SimpleGraph V) (S : Finset V) : Prop :=
  (↑S : Set V) ⊂ Set.univ ∧ ¬ (G.induce ((↑S : Set V)ᶜ)).Connected
end SimpleGraph

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
noncomputable def edgeConnectivity (G : SimpleGraph V) : ℕ :=
  sInf {n : ℕ | ∃ F : Finset (Sym2 V), G.IsEdgeCut F ∧ F.card = n}
end SimpleGraph

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
noncomputable def vertexConnectivity (G : SimpleGraph V) : ℕ :=
  if ∃ S : Finset V, G.IsVertexCut S then
    sInf {n : ℕ | ∃ S : Finset V, G.IsVertexCut S ∧ S.card = n}
  else
    Fintype.card V - 1
end SimpleGraph

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
theorem whitney_inequalities [Nonempty V] :
    G.vertexConnectivity ≤ G.edgeConnectivity ∧ G.edgeConnectivity ≤ G.minDegree := sorry
end SimpleGraph

Definitions:
- The 0/1 adjacency matrix of $D$. Record a $1$ where an arrow runs from $v_{i}$ to $v_{j}$ and $0$ otherwise.
Unlike the undirected case (\S{}1.3) this matrix is \emph{not} symmetric --- its asymmetry
encodes the orientations.  Exercise 10.1.8 shows $A^{k}$ counts directed walks of
length $k$, and \S{}10.7 uses the powers of $A$ to rank tournament players via the
level score vectors $s_{i} = A^{i}J$.

\textbf{!} Restated: \texttt{Digraph} has no arc multiplicities, so entries are
$0$ or $1$ rather than a count.  For strict digraphs --- which every \S{}10.7 statement
is about, tournaments being orientations --- the two agree, so nothing is lost where
it is used.  The value type $\alpha$ is left generic so the same matrix serves the
$\mathbb{N}$-valued counting of exercise 10.1.8 and any later numeric work.
- The bridge \texttt{Digraph $\to$ Quiver}: \texttt{Quiver.\{0\} V} has \texttt{Hom : V $\to$ V $\to$ Prop},\dots. A quiver is a vertex set together with, for each ordered pair, a
\emph{type} of arrows.  Taking that type to be a \texttt{Prop} --- arrow or no arrow --- recovers
exactly a digraph, and Mathlib's \texttt{Quiver.Path} then supplies directed walks for
free, which \texttt{Digraph} (a bare \texttt{Adj} with a lattice API) does not.

\textbf{!} Deliberately \textbf{not} an \texttt{instance}.  The chapter routinely
handles several digraphs on one vertex type at once --- $D$ and its converse $\breve{D}$,
$D$ and a reorientation of one arc (exercise 10.2.1) --- and a global instance would
make \texttt{Quiver.Path} ambiguous between them.  The cost is that every use site must
write \texttt{@Quiver.Path V D.toQuiver u v} explicitly, which is why the statements below
are visually heavy.

Statement: adjMatrix_pow_apply_eq_card_directedWalk. The $(i,j)$ entry of $A$ counts arcs, i.e. walks of length one; matrix
multiplication sums over an intermediate vertex, and every walk of length $k$
decomposes uniquely as a shorter walk plus a final arc.  This is the directed
counterpart of exercise 1.6.2, and it is what makes \S{}10.7's ranking work: the
$i$-th level score vector is $A^{i}J$, counting directed walks of length $i$ out of
each player.  Theorem 10.7 consumes it directly.

\textbf{!} Restated for a $0/1$ matrix, \texttt{Digraph} having no arc
multiplicities; for the strict digraphs of \S{}10.7 this is no loss.  The right-hand
side is \texttt{Nat.card} of a subtype of \texttt{Quiver.Path}, which is finite because the length
is pinned --- but that finiteness may need to be supplied for \texttt{Nat.card} to behave.

import Mathlib

open scoped Classical

namespace Digraph
def adjMatrix {V : Type*} (D : Digraph V) [DecidableRel D.Adj] (α : Type*) [Zero α] [One α] :
    Matrix V V α := Matrix.of fun u v => if D.Adj u v then 1 else 0
end Digraph

namespace Digraph
def toQuiver {V : Type*} (D : Digraph V) : Quiver.{0} V := ⟨D.Adj⟩
end Digraph

theorem adjMatrix_pow_apply_eq_card_directedWalk
    {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (D : Digraph V) [DecidableRel D.Adj]
    (k : ℕ) (u v : V) :
    (D.adjMatrix ℕ ^ k) u v =
      Nat.card {p : @Quiver.Path V D.toQuiver u v // @Quiver.Path.length V D.toQuiver u v p = k} := sorry

informal_statement:
Definitions:
- An edge cut: a set of edges of $G$ whose deletion leaves $G$ disconnected. Rather than carry the book's $[S, \bar{S}]$ presentation, the definition is taken in
its \emph{operative} form --- a set of edges whose removal disconnects $G$:
\texttt{↑F $\subseteq$ G.edgeSet $\land$ $\lnot$ (G.deleteEdges ↑F).Connected}.

The two agree on what is minimised: every $[S, \bar{S}]$ disconnects $G$, and every
disconnecting edge set contains one (take $S$ a component of $G - F$).  Since
\texttt{edgeConnectivity} only ever asks for the \emph{minimum} size, the coarser form is
equivalent for all purposes in this chapter.
- The associated digraph $D(G)$: each edge becomes two opposite arcs. \texttt{G.Adj} is already symmetric,\dots. Make every street two-way.  This embeds undirected graph theory inside
directed graph theory: exercise 10.3.6 shows paths in $G$ correspond exactly to
directed paths in $D(G)$, and $D(G)$ is $k$-arc-connected exactly when $G$ is
$k$-edge-connected.  Exercise 10.3.1 uses the embedding to derive Dirac's theorem
4.3 from Ghouila-Houri's 10.4.

One line: \texttt{G.Adj} is already symmetric and irreflexive, so it
\emph{is} the arc relation of $D(G)$ --- the "two oppositely oriented arcs" are the two
directions of the symmetric relation.  Note $D(G)$ is emphatically \textbf{not} an
orientation of $G$ (\texttt{IsOrientationOf}'s second clause fails at every edge); the
contrast between doubling and orienting is exactly what \S{}10.6 is about.
- B&M's $(S, T)$: arcs with tail in $S$, head in $T$. The arcs crossing from $S$ into $T$, counted with their direction.
Unlike the undirected edge cut $[S, \bar{S}]$, the directed version splits into two
generally \emph{unequal} halves $(S, \bar{S})$ and $(\bar{S}, S)$ --- which is precisely what
$k$-arc-connectivity measures, and what theorem 10.6 has to balance.

A \texttt{Finset (V $\times$ V)} obtained by filtering the product $S \times^{s} T$,
so $|(S, T)|$ is its \texttt{card}.  Used in \texttt{IsKArcConnected} and in Moon's theorem 10.3,
where the book's "$(S, T)$ must be nonempty" becomes a cardinality claim.
- $D$ is $k$-arc-connected: every nonempty proper cut has $\ge k$ outgoing arcs. However you split the vertices in two, at least $k$ arrows point from
the first part to the second.  Exercise 10.3.5 says $1$-arc-connected is the same
as diconnected, and exercise 10.3.6(b) that $D(G)$ is $k$-arc-connected exactly when
$G$ is $k$-edge-connected.  Nash-Williams' theorem --- of which theorem 10.6 is the
easy special case --- says every $2k$-edge-connected graph has a $k$-arc-connected
orientation.

\textbf{!} The book says \textbf{nontrivial} digraph, and this definition
drops that.  On a one-vertex carrier there is no nonempty proper $S$, so the
condition is vacuously true for \emph{every} $k$ --- which is why statements consuming it
must supply \texttt{[Nontrivial V]} themselves.  \texttt{diconnected\_iff\_isKArcConnected\_one}
does; \texttt{associatedDigraph\_isKArcConnected\_iff} does not, and is false in consequence
(see its docstring).
- Edge connectivity $\kappa'(G)$. The least number of edges one must cut to break $G$ apart.  "$G$ is
$k$-edge-connected" is spelled \texttt{k $\le$ edgeConnectivity G} throughout this file --- see
\texttt{robbins\_orientation} ($k = 2$) and \texttt{exists\_kArcConnected\_orientation\_of\_eulerian}.

Mathlib has no edge-connectivity, so this is the repo's notion
restated locally.  \texttt{sInf $\emptyset$ = 0} in $\mathbb{N}$ reproduces the book's trivial-graph
convention automatically --- but it also means a graph with \emph{no} edge cut (a
one-vertex graph) gets $\kappa' = 0$, which is the source of the \texttt{[Nontrivial V]} gap in
\texttt{associatedDigraph\_isKArcConnected\_iff} below.

Statement: associatedDigraph_isKArcConnected_iff. *$D(G)$ is $k$-arc-connected if and only if $G$ is
$k$-edge-connected.*

The associated digraph faithfully preserves connectivity, so the
directed notion generalises the undirected one.  Contrast \S{}10.6, where the question
is which \emph{orientations} --- not the doubling --- preserve it; there the answer is much
more delicate (Robbins, Nash-Williams).

"$G$ is $k$-edge-connected" is spelled \texttt{k $\le$ edgeConnectivity G},
per \S{}3.1.  Step 2 needs that a minimal edge cut is $[S, S^{c}]$ for a component $S$,
which is the same fact the local \texttt{IsEdgeCut} docstring notes when reconciling the
book's shape-based definition with the deletion-based one used here.

\textbf{+} \textbf{Statement repaired --- \texttt{[Nontrivial V]} added.}  The $\leftrightarrow$ was \textbf{false on a
one-vertex carrier}.  Take \texttt{card V = 1}, so $G = \bot$, and $k = 1$.  \emph{Left side:} there
is no nonempty proper \texttt{S : Finset V}, so \texttt{IsKArcConnected 1} holds vacuously.  *Right
side:* $\bot$ on one vertex is \texttt{Connected}, so nothing disconnects it, $G$ has no edge cut
at all, and \texttt{edgeConnectivity G = 0}; the claim $1 \le 0$ fails.

\texttt{[Nontrivial V]} excludes exactly that carrier and is the hypothesis the book's
"nontrivial digraph" convention supplies implicitly (compare
\texttt{diconnected\_iff\_isKArcConnected\_one} above, which already carries it).  \textbf{!} Both Menger
statements in \texttt{Networks.lean} consume this lemma, so their hypotheses must be checked
against the added \texttt{Nontrivial} when they are proved.
formal_statement:
import Mathlib

open scoped Classical

namespace SimpleGraph
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
def IsEdgeCut (G : SimpleGraph V) (F : Finset (Sym2 V)) : Prop :=
  (↑F : Set (Sym2 V)) ⊆ G.edgeSet ∧ ¬ (G.deleteEdges (↑F : Set (Sym2 V))).Connected
end SimpleGraph

namespace Digraph
def arcsBetween {V : Type*} (D : Digraph V) [DecidableRel D.Adj] (S T : Finset V) : Finset (V × V) :=
  (S ×ˢ T).filter fun p => D.Adj p.1 p.2
end Digraph

namespace Digraph
def IsKArcConnected {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (D : Digraph V) [DecidableRel D.Adj]
    (k : ℕ) : Prop :=
  ∀ S : Finset V, S.Nonempty → S ≠ Finset.univ → k ≤ (D.arcsBetween S Sᶜ).card
end Digraph

noncomputable def edgeConnectivity {V : Type*} [Fintype V] (G : SimpleGraph V) : ℕ :=
  sInf {n : ℕ | ∃ F : Finset (Sym2 V), G.IsEdgeCut F ∧ F.card = n}

theorem associatedDigraph_isKArcConnected_iff
    {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [Nontrivial V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V)
    [DecidableRel G.Adj] (k : ℕ) :
    G.associatedDigraph.IsKArcConnected k ↔ k ≤ edgeConnectivity G := sorry
title: associatedDigraph_isKArcConnected_iff
statement_informal:
associatedDigraph_isKArcConnected_iff. *$D(G)$ is $k$-arc-connected if and only if $G$ is
$k$-edge-connected.*

The associated digraph faithfully preserves connectivity, so the
directed notion generalises the undirected one.  Contrast \S{}10.6, where the question
is which \emph{orientations} --- not the doubling --- preserve it; there the answer is much
more delicate (Robbins, Nash-Williams).

"$G$ is $k$-edge-connected" is spelled \texttt{k $\le$ edgeConnectivity G},
per \S{}3.1.  Step 2 needs that a minimal edge cut is $[S, S^{c}]$ for a component $S$,
which is the same fact the local \texttt{IsEdgeCut} docstring notes when reconciling the
book's shape-based definition with the deletion-based one used here.

\textbf{+} \textbf{Statement repaired --- \texttt{[Nontrivial V]} added.}  The $\leftrightarrow$ was \textbf{false on a
one-vertex carrier}.  Take \texttt{card V = 1}, so $G = \bot$, and $k = 1$.  \emph{Left side:} there
is no nonempty proper \texttt{S : Finset V}, so \texttt{IsKArcConnected 1} holds vacuously.  *Right
side:* $\bot$ on one vertex is \texttt{Connected}, so nothing disconnects it, $G$ has no edge cut
at all, and \texttt{edgeConnectivity G = 0}; the claim $1 \le 0$ fails.

\texttt{[Nontrivial V]} excludes exactly that carrier and is the hypothesis the book's
"nontrivial digraph" convention supplies implicitly (compare
\texttt{diconnected\_iff\_isKArcConnected\_one} above, which already carries it).  \textbf{!} Both Menger
statements in \texttt{Networks.lean} consume this lemma, so their hypotheses must be checked
against the added \texttt{Nontrivial} when they are proved.

definitions.title: An edge cut: a set of edges of $G$ whose deletion leaves $G$ disconnected
definitions.informal:
Rather than carry the book's $[S, \bar{S}]$ presentation, the definition is taken in
its \emph{operative} form --- a set of edges whose removal disconnects $G$:
\texttt{↑F $\subseteq$ G.edgeSet $\land$ $\lnot$ (G.deleteEdges ↑F).Connected}.

The two agree on what is minimised: every $[S, \bar{S}]$ disconnects $G$, and every
disconnecting edge set contains one (take $S$ a component of $G - F$).  Since
\texttt{edgeConnectivity} only ever asks for the \emph{minimum} size, the coarser form is
equivalent for all purposes in this chapter.

definitions.title: The associated digraph $D(G)$: each edge becomes two opposite arcs. \texttt{G.Adj} is already symmetric,\dots
definitions.informal:
Make every street two-way.  This embeds undirected graph theory inside
directed graph theory: exercise 10.3.6 shows paths in $G$ correspond exactly to
directed paths in $D(G)$, and $D(G)$ is $k$-arc-connected exactly when $G$ is
$k$-edge-connected.  Exercise 10.3.1 uses the embedding to derive Dirac's theorem
4.3 from Ghouila-Houri's 10.4.

One line: \texttt{G.Adj} is already symmetric and irreflexive, so it
\emph{is} the arc relation of $D(G)$ --- the "two oppositely oriented arcs" are the two
directions of the symmetric relation.  Note $D(G)$ is emphatically \textbf{not} an
orientation of $G$ (\texttt{IsOrientationOf}'s second clause fails at every edge); the
contrast between doubling and orienting is exactly what \S{}10.6 is about.

definitions.title: B&M's $(S, T)$: arcs with tail in $S$, head in $T$
definitions.informal:
The arcs crossing from $S$ into $T$, counted with their direction.
Unlike the undirected edge cut $[S, \bar{S}]$, the directed version splits into two
generally \emph{unequal} halves $(S, \bar{S})$ and $(\bar{S}, S)$ --- which is precisely what
$k$-arc-connectivity measures, and what theorem 10.6 has to balance.

A \texttt{Finset (V $\times$ V)} obtained by filtering the product $S \times^{s} T$,
so $|(S, T)|$ is its \texttt{card}.  Used in \texttt{IsKArcConnected} and in Moon's theorem 10.3,
where the book's "$(S, T)$ must be nonempty" becomes a cardinality claim.

definitions.title: $D$ is $k$-arc-connected: every nonempty proper cut has $\ge k$ outgoing arcs
definitions.informal:
However you split the vertices in two, at least $k$ arrows point from
the first part to the second.  Exercise 10.3.5 says $1$-arc-connected is the same
as diconnected, and exercise 10.3.6(b) that $D(G)$ is $k$-arc-connected exactly when
$G$ is $k$-edge-connected.  Nash-Williams' theorem --- of which theorem 10.6 is the
easy special case --- says every $2k$-edge-connected graph has a $k$-arc-connected
orientation.

\textbf{!} The book says \textbf{nontrivial} digraph, and this definition
drops that.  On a one-vertex carrier there is no nonempty proper $S$, so the
condition is vacuously true for \emph{every} $k$ --- which is why statements consuming it
must supply \texttt{[Nontrivial V]} themselves.  \texttt{diconnected\_iff\_isKArcConnected\_one}
does; \texttt{associatedDigraph\_isKArcConnected\_iff} does not, and is false in consequence
(see its docstring).

definitions.title: Edge connectivity $\kappa'(G)$
definitions.informal:
The least number of edges one must cut to break $G$ apart.  "$G$ is
$k$-edge-connected" is spelled \texttt{k $\le$ edgeConnectivity G} throughout this file --- see
\texttt{robbins\_orientation} ($k = 2$) and \texttt{exists\_kArcConnected\_orientation\_of\_eulerian}.

Mathlib has no edge-connectivity, so this is the repo's notion
restated locally.  \texttt{sInf $\emptyset$ = 0} in $\mathbb{N}$ reproduces the book's trivial-graph
convention automatically --- but it also means a graph with \emph{no} edge cut (a
one-vertex graph) gets $\kappa' = 0$, which is the source of the \texttt{[Nontrivial V]} gap in
\texttt{associatedDigraph\_isKArcConnected\_iff} below.

informal_statement:
Definitions:
- $D$ is an orientation of $G$ --- the chapter's keystone gap. Make every edge one-way, choosing a direction for each.  Orientations
are the chapter's central object: exercise 10.1.1 counts them ($2^\varepsilon$), the remark
after theorem 10.1 builds one whose directed paths are short, exercise 10.1.10 one
that is degree-balanced, and \S{}10.6 asks which graphs admit \emph{diconnected} ones ---
Robbins' theorem 10.5.

Two clauses.  The first, \texttt{D.toSimpleGraphInclusive = G}, says
the underlying graph comes back out as $G$.  The second,
\texttt{$\forall$ u v, $\lnot$(D.Adj u v $\land$ D.Adj v u)}, forbids making an edge two-way --- without it the
associated digraph $D(G)$ would count as an orientation of $G$, which it is not.
Taking $u = v$ in the second clause also forces looplessness, so an orientation is
automatically strict.

Statement: card_orientations. An orientation is a choice, independently for each edge, of one of its
two directions; with $\varepsilon$ edges and two choices each the product rule gives $2^\varepsilon$.
These are \emph{labelled} objects: two orientations differing only by a symmetry of $G$
still count separately.

Step 1 is the whole exercise and the \texttt{Sym2} bookkeeping is the
only fiddly part --- the natural first move is to prove a helper turning
\texttt{IsOrientationOf} into "for each edge, exactly one of the two directions".
formal_statement:
import Mathlib

open scoped Classical

namespace Digraph
def IsOrientationOf {V : Type*} (D : Digraph V) (G : SimpleGraph V) : Prop :=
  D.toSimpleGraphInclusive = G ∧ ∀ u v, ¬(D.Adj u v ∧ D.Adj v u)
end Digraph

theorem card_orientations
    {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj] :
    Nat.card {D : Digraph V // D.IsOrientationOf G} = 2 ^ G.edgeFinset.card := sorry
title: card_orientations
statement_informal:
card_orientations. An orientation is a choice, independently for each edge, of one of its
two directions; with $\varepsilon$ edges and two choices each the product rule gives $2^\varepsilon$.
These are \emph{labelled} objects: two orientations differing only by a symmetry of $G$
still count separately.

Step 1 is the whole exercise and the \texttt{Sym2} bookkeeping is the
only fiddly part --- the natural first move is to prove a helper turning
\texttt{IsOrientationOf} into "for each edge, exactly one of the two directions".

informal_statement:
chvatal_komlos_monotone_directedPath. \emph{ (Chv\'atal and Koml\'os).  }Let $D$ be a digraph with
$\chi > mn$, and let $f$ be a real-valued function on $V$.  Then $D$ has either a
directed path $(u_{0}, \dots, u_m)$ with $f(u_{0}) \le f(u_{1}) \le \dots \le f(u_m)$, or a directed path
$(v_{0}, \dots, v_n)$ with $f(v_{0}) > f(v_{1}) > \dots > f(v_n)$.*

Theorem 10.1 says a high chromatic number forces a long directed path;
this refines it by controlling how $f$ behaves along that path.  A large enough
chromatic number forces a \emph{monotone} directed path --- weakly increasing of length
$m$, or strictly decreasing of length $n$.  Part (b) reads off Erd\H{o}s--Szekeres.

Paths are \texttt{List V} with two \texttt{IsChain}s --- one for adjacency, one
for the $f$-comparison --- plus \texttt{Nodup}, rather than \texttt{Quiver.Path}s, so that the
monotonicity condition can be stated alongside.  Note the asymmetry $\le$ versus $>$
is the book's and is essential: with two weak orders step 3 would fail on an arc
where $f u = f w$.
formal_statement:
import Mathlib

open scoped Classical

theorem chvatal_komlos_monotone_directedPath
    {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (D : Digraph V) [DecidableRel D.Adj]
    (f : V → ℝ) {m n : ℕ}
    (hchi : (m * n : ℕ∞) < D.toSimpleGraphInclusive.chromaticNumber) :
    (∃ l : List V, l.length = m + 1 ∧ l.IsChain D.Adj ∧ l.Nodup ∧ l.IsChain (f · ≤ f ·)) ∨
    (∃ l : List V, l.length = n + 1 ∧ l.IsChain D.Adj ∧ l.Nodup ∧ l.IsChain (f · > f ·)) := sorry
title: chvatal_komlos_monotone_directedPath

informal_statement:
chvatal_lovasz_semikernel. (Chv\'atal and Lov\'asz, 1974).  *A loopless digraph $D$ has an
independent set $S$ such that each vertex of $D$ not in $S$ is reachable from a
vertex in $S$ by a directed path of length at most two.*

Such a set is called a \textbf{semi-kernel}.  The independence requirement
is what makes it non-trivial --- one wants mutually non-adjacent "dominators" from
which everything else is within two steps.  Corollary 10.2 is the tournament case,
where independence forces $|S| = 1$.

The $u = v$ disjunct in the goal covers the reflexive case and is
not in the book, which says "each vertex \emph{not in} $S$"; it is harmless and makes the
statement easier to instantiate.  \texttt{hloop : Irreflexive D.Adj} is B&M's "loopless".
\texttt{IsIndepSet} is taken in \texttt{toSimpleGraphInclusive}, matching "independent set" for the
underlying graph.
formal_statement:
import Mathlib

open scoped Classical

theorem chvatal_lovasz_semikernel
    {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (D : Digraph V) [DecidableRel D.Adj]
    (hloop : Irreflexive D.Adj) :
    ∃ S : Set V, D.toSimpleGraphInclusive.IsIndepSet S ∧
      ∀ v ∉ S, ∃ u ∈ S, u = v ∨ D.Adj u v ∨ ∃ w, D.Adj u w ∧ D.Adj w v := sorry
title: chvatal_lovasz_semikernel
statement_informal:

informal_statement:
Definitions:
- The bridge \texttt{Digraph $\to$ Quiver}: \texttt{Quiver.\{0\} V} has \texttt{Hom : V $\to$ V $\to$ Prop},\dots. A quiver is a vertex set together with, for each ordered pair, a
\emph{type} of arrows.  Taking that type to be a \texttt{Prop} --- arrow or no arrow --- recovers
exactly a digraph, and Mathlib's \texttt{Quiver.Path} then supplies directed walks for
free, which \texttt{Digraph} (a bare \texttt{Adj} with a lattice API) does not.

\textbf{!} Deliberately \textbf{not} an \texttt{instance}.  The chapter routinely
handles several digraphs on one vertex type at once --- $D$ and its converse $\breve{D}$,
$D$ and a reorientation of one arc (exercise 10.2.1) --- and a global instance would
make \texttt{Quiver.Path} ambiguous between them.  The cost is that every use site must
write \texttt{@Quiver.Path V D.toQuiver u v} explicitly, which is why the statements below
are visually heavy.
- A directed cycle: a positive-length closed walk whose vertices (bar the repeated endpoint) are distinct. Follow the arrows all the way round and return to where you started,
never repeating a vertex en route.  Directed cycles are the subject of \S{}10.3: Moon
(theorem 10.3) finds them of every length in a diconnected tournament, and
Ghouila-Houri (theorem 10.4) finds a spanning one under a degree condition.

\texttt{0 < length} excludes \texttt{nil}; \texttt{vertices.tail.Nodup} allows the
repeated basepoint at the two ends while forbidding any other repeat.  Note a
\textbf{loop} \texttt{D.Adj v v} counts as a directed cycle of length $1$ under this
definition, which is what makes the acyclicity hypotheses below (\texttt{hacyc})
automatically exclude loops --- relied on by \texttt{exists\_topological\_ordering}.
- The condensation $\hat{D}$: dicomponents contracted. Shrink each dicomponent to a single point and keep the arcs between
them.  Exercise 10.1.9 shows the condensation is \emph{acyclic} --- a directed cycle among
dicomponents would merge them into one --- so by exercise 10.1.3(b) the dicomponents
can be topologically ordered, which is what \S{}10.7 uses to rank the participants of a
non-diconnected tournament, and what exercise 10.2.1 uses on tournaments.

\textbf{!} The $a \ne b$ clause is a \textbf{recorded correction}, not a
transcription.  Taken literally the book's condition puts an arc from $w_{i}$ to $w_{i}$
whenever $D_{i}$ has any internal arc --- a loop at every non-trivial dicomponent --- which
would make \texttt{condensation\_acyclic} false, since a loop is a directed cycle of length
$1$.  B&M plainly intend $i \ne j$.

The vertex type is \texttt{Quiver.StronglyConnectedComponent}, Mathlib's quotient by mutual
reachability, which is exactly the set of dicomponents.

Statement: condensation_acyclic. A directed cycle among dicomponents would merge them into one, so
contracting always produces an acyclic digraph --- which by exercise 10.1.3(b) can be
topologically ordered.  \S{}10.7 uses exactly this to rank the dicomponents of a
non-diconnected tournament in a dominance-preserving order, and exercise 10.2.1 uses
it on tournaments.

Step 3 is where \texttt{Quiver.StronglyConnectedComponent}'s defining
property is consumed; the useful form is "same component $\leftrightarrow$ mutually reachable",
which should be extracted first.  Note the statement quantifies over all base points
$c$, since \texttt{IsDirectedCycle} is stated for closed paths at a given vertex.
formal_statement:
import Mathlib

open scoped Classical

namespace Digraph
def toQuiver {V : Type*} (D : Digraph V) : Quiver.{0} V := ⟨D.Adj⟩
end Digraph

namespace Digraph
def IsDirectedCycle {V : Type*} (D : Digraph V) {u : V} (p : @Quiver.Path V D.toQuiver u u) : Prop :=
  0 < (@Quiver.Path.length V D.toQuiver u u p) ∧
    (@Quiver.Path.vertices V D.toQuiver u u p).tail.Nodup
end Digraph

theorem condensation_acyclic {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (D : Digraph V) :
    ∀ (c : @Quiver.StronglyConnectedComponent V D.toQuiver)
      (p : @Quiver.Path _ D.condensation.toQuiver c c), ¬ D.condensation.IsDirectedCycle p := sorry
title: condensation_acyclic
statement_informal:
condensation_acyclic. A directed cycle among dicomponents would merge them into one, so
contracting always produces an acyclic digraph --- which by exercise 10.1.3(b) can be
topologically ordered.  \S{}10.7 uses exactly this to rank the dicomponents of a
non-diconnected tournament in a dominance-preserving order, and exercise 10.2.1 uses
it on tournaments.

Step 3 is where \texttt{Quiver.StronglyConnectedComponent}'s defining
property is consumed; the useful form is "same component $\leftrightarrow$ mutually reachable",
which should be extracted first.  Note the statement quantifies over all base points
$c$, since \texttt{IsDirectedCycle} is stated for closed paths at a given vertex.

informal_statement:
Definitions:
- The converse $\breve{D}$: reverse every arc. Turn every arrow around.  It is an involution ($\breve{\breve{D}} = D$), it swaps
indegree with outdegree, and it reverses reachability --- so every theorem about
digraphs comes with a free dual, obtained by applying it to the converse.  Exercise
10.1.5(a) records exactly these three facts and (b) puts them to work.

A one-line \texttt{Digraph.mk} with the arguments of \texttt{Adj} swapped, so
\texttt{converse\_converse} should be \texttt{rfl}-adjacent.  Because \texttt{Reachable} is defined from
\texttt{Adj} and not through a \texttt{Quiver} instance, $D$ and \texttt{D.converse} can appear in the
same statement without ambiguity --- see \texttt{converse\_reachable}.

Statement: converse_converse. Reversing every arrow twice returns each to its original direction, so
the converse is an involution.  That is what makes it a genuine duality: any
statement proved for all digraphs yields its mirror image for free, with in- and
outdegrees and the direction of reachability exchanged --- as parts (ii), (iii) and
(b) then exploit.

The shortest item in the file; a good first fill to shake out the
\texttt{Digraph} extensionality API.
formal_statement:
import Mathlib

open scoped Classical

namespace Digraph
def converse {V : Type*} (D : Digraph V) : Digraph V := ⟨fun u v => D.Adj v u⟩
end Digraph

theorem converse_converse {V : Type*} (D : Digraph V) : D.converse.converse = D := sorry
title: converse_converse
statement_informal:
converse_converse. Reversing every arrow twice returns each to its original direction, so
the converse is an involution.  That is what makes it a genuine duality: any
statement proved for all digraphs yields its mirror image for free, with in- and
outdegrees and the direction of reachability exchanged --- as parts (ii), (iii) and
(b) then exploit.

import Mathlib

open scoped Classical

namespace Digraph
def indegree {V : Type*} [Fintype V] (D : Digraph V) [DecidableRel D.Adj] (v : V) : ℕ :=

namespace Digraph
def outdegree {V : Type*} [Fintype V] (D : Digraph V) [DecidableRel D.Adj] (v : V) : ℕ :=
  (Finset.univ.filter fun w => D.Adj v w).card

theorem converse_indegree {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V]
    (D : Digraph V) [DecidableRel D.Adj] (v : V) :

Definitions:
- $v$ is reachable from $u$. You can get from $u$ to $v$ travelling only along arrows in their
given direction.  Reachability is \emph{not} symmetric --- that asymmetry is the whole
point of directing a graph, and is what makes diconnection a strictly stronger
condition than connection.

\texttt{Quiver.Path}.  The two agree (a path witnesses reachability and conversely), but
\texttt{ReflTransGen} comes with induction principles and is \emph{reflexive}, matching the
book's convention that every vertex reaches itself.  Being defined directly from
\texttt{Adj}, it needs no \texttt{Quiver} instance, so $D$ and \texttt{D.converse} coexist freely ---
which \texttt{converse\_reachable} relies on.

indegree with outdegree, and it reverses reachability --- so every theorem about

is in play, so $D$ and \texttt{D.converse} appear in the same statement without

def Reachable {V : Type*} (D : Digraph V) (u v : V) : Prop := Relation.ReflTransGen D.Adj u v

    D.converse.Reachable u v ↔ D.Reachable v u := sorry

informal_statement:
Definitions:
- The de Bruijn digraph $D_n$: vertices are $(n-1)$-bit strings, arcs are left-shifts. A vertex is a window of $n-1$ bits; following an arc shifts the window
one place, dropping the leading bit and appending a new one.  Each arc therefore
corresponds to an $n$-bit string --- its label --- and a directed Euler tour reads off
every $n$-bit string exactly once, giving a cyclic binary sequence of length $2^{n}$ in
which all $2^{n}$ windows are distinct.

\emph{The application (\S{}10.5).}  A rotating drum's surface is divided into $2^{n}$
insulating or conducting sections, read by $k$ consecutive contacts.  *First note
that $k$ contacts yield a $k$-digit binary number, and there are $2^{k}$ such numbers.
Therefore, if all $2^{n}$ positions are to give different readings, we must have
$2^{k} \ge 2^{n}$, that is, $k \ge n$* --- and the de Bruijn sequence shows $n$ contacts
suffice.  For $n = 4$ the tour of figure 10.10 gives $0000111100101101$.  Due to
Good (1946).

\textbf{!} Missing from Mathlib and the Archive (0 hits).  A vertex is a
function \texttt{Fin (n-1) $\to$ Bool} rather than a list, so the shift condition is indexed:
\texttt{p ⟨i+1, \_⟩ = q i} for every $i$ with $i + 1 < n - 1$, which is the book's
$1 \le i \le n-2$ in 0-indexed form.  The last coordinate of $q$ is unconstrained, giving
the two out-arcs.  $D_n$ has \textbf{loops} (the all-zeros and all-ones vertices) but no
parallel arcs --- so it is not strict, which is fine, as no \S{}10.5 statement needs
strictness.  Arc labels are not modelled: the label is recoverable from the arc, and
\texttt{exists\_deBruijn\_sequence} states the conclusion about the sequence directly.

Statement: deBruijnDigraph_connected. From any binary string one can reach any other by shifting in the
target's bits one at a time; after $n - 1$ shifts the window contains exactly the
target.  Together with the degree balance above, this is the second half of the
Euler-tour criterion of exercise 10.3.2.

The explicit walk of step 1 is the whole content; a slick
argument is unlikely to be shorter than just writing the $n - 1$ intermediate
vertices down as a function of the step index.
formal_statement:
import Mathlib

open scoped Classical

def deBruijnDigraph (n : ℕ) : Digraph (Fin (n - 1) → Bool) :=
  ⟨fun p q => ∀ i : Fin (n - 1), (h : (i : ℕ) + 1 < n - 1) → p ⟨(i : ℕ) + 1, h⟩ = q i⟩

theorem deBruijnDigraph_connected (n : ℕ) (hn : 2 ≤ n) :
    (deBruijnDigraph n).toSimpleGraphInclusive.Connected := sorry
title: deBruijnDigraph_connected
statement_informal:
deBruijnDigraph_connected. From any binary string one can reach any other by shifting in the
target's bits one at a time; after $n - 1$ shifts the window contains exactly the
target.  Together with the degree balance above, this is the second half of the

The explicit walk of step 1 is the whole content; a slick
argument is unlikely to be shorter than just writing the $n - 1$ intermediate
